versions.s: He hath made me a father to Pharaoh. An Egyptian administrative title, not a family claim.

b.t: Every version reads father to Pharaoh, accurately translating the Hebrew, but without noting that the phrase names a known ancient Egyptian court title rather than describing an actual family relationship.

English father names a family role. A modern equivalent to this ancient title might be something like chief advisor, or elder statesman, an honorific for a senior official's wisdom and standing, not a literal parental claim, the way a company might informally call a longtime advisor its godfather without meaning it genealogically.

Egyptian inscriptions independently attest father of the god, it-netjer, as a title held by senior advisors and officials serving a pharaoh, unrelated to blood kinship and instead marking someone as a trusted source of wisdom and counsel, paired here with lord of all his household and ruler over all the land of Egypt, both concrete administrative claims matching the historically attested role of a vizier.

English father, standing alone, suggests literal parentage or, at best, a vague honorific; it does not carry the specific, documented administrative weight the Egyptian title held, so a reader unfamiliar with Egyptian court titulature can miss that Joseph is describing a specific, historically real office rather than a sentimental relationship.

When a biblical figure describes a foreign court position using a kinship word, father, brother, son, check whether the surrounding culture used that vocabulary as an administrative title before reading it as a literal family claim.

Father to Pharaoh is an accurate rendering of the Hebrew, and no version disputes that. What it needs is the extrabiblical Egyptian background confirming this was a real administrative title, which strengthens rather than merely illustrates the account's claim that Joseph held genuine high office.
אָב לְפַרְעֹה av le-Pharaoh · H1 + H6547

src: Egyptian 'father of the god,' it-netjer, as a documented vizierial title
The paired titles lord of his household and ruler of all Egypt: Genesis 45:8

versions.s: To work it and keep it. The same two verbs describe the Levites guarding the tabernacle.

b.t: Every version reads some pair like work and keep, till and keep, or cultivate and guard. None can show that the identical pair recurs elsewhere as a fixed phrase for priestly duty.

**He tends the garden.** **He guards the temple.** English keeps those as two different jobs done by two different kinds of people. This verse uses the same two verbs for Adam that a later book uses for priests on duty.

Abad, to work or serve, and shamar, to keep or guard, appear together describing Adam's task in the garden. The same two verbs appear together describing the Levites' duty toward the tabernacle at Numbers 3:7-8 and 18:5-6, and shamar alone covers guarding it from intruders at Numbers 1:53. The garden is being described in the vocabulary later used for sanctuary service.

English work and keep are ordinary household words. They carry none of the specialized, cultic resonance the same two verbs carry when the same corpus later uses them for tabernacle duty, so the priestly overtone of Adam's job is simply not visible in translation.

A common-sounding word pair can be a technical phrase elsewhere in the same body of literature. Before assuming ordinary vocabulary, check whether the same combination recurs in a specialized context.

There is no dispute about the plain gloss, work and keep. The disagreement is how much weight to put on the Numbers parallel, whether the echo is a deliberate signal that Eden is being described as sanctuary space, or a coincidence of two common verbs appearing together twice.
עָבַד abad · H5647 / שָׁמַר shamar · H8104

src: Same verb pair for the Levites: Numbers 3:7-8; 18:5-6
shamar for guarding the tabernacle from intruders: Numbers 1:53
The cherubim guarding Eden's entrance after the expulsion use related guard vocabulary: Genesis 3:24

versions.s: The elder shall serve the younger. Or: the elder, shall the younger serve. The Hebrew word order does not decide it.

b.t: Every English version reads the elder shall serve the younger, settling the ambiguity one way, the reading that fits how the rest of Jacob and Esau's story actually plays out.

English word order tells you who does what: **the dog bit the man** and **the man bit the dog** are opposites, and the order alone carries the meaning. Biblical Hebrew poetry can drop the marker that would normally clarify this, and this oracle is exactly that kind of sentence: both readings are grammatically live.

Verav ya'avod tsa'ir lacks the object marker et that would normally clarify which noun is doing the serving and which is being served, and Hebrew word order alone does not settle it here, since Job 14:19 shows the same pattern can run either direction, subject-object or object-subject. The medieval commentators Radak and Ibn Kaspi already noted the sentence could mean either the elder shall serve the younger or the elder, the younger shall serve, and the cantillation marks in the Masoretic tradition arguably lean toward the second, less common reading.

English syntax fixes word order to meaning in a way Hebrew poetry does not always require, so a translation must pick one direction, and once picked, an English reader is left with no clue that the original oracle was genuinely, grammatically ambiguous rather than plainly stated.

When a Hebrew clause lacks the object marker et and involves two nouns that could each plausibly be subject or object, do not assume word order alone settles the sentence the way it would in English. Check whether ancient commentators already flagged the same ambiguity.

The elder shall serve the younger fits the narrative's outcome, Esau's household eventually subordinate to Jacob's line, and is the reading every translation adopts. The reverse reading, argued from the missing object marker and supported by some cantillation evidence, would make the oracle a genuinely opaque riddle rather than a plain prediction, which some rabbinic tradition takes to be the point.
וְרַב יַעֲבֹד צָעִיר verav ya'avod tsa'ir · H7227 + H5647 + H6810

src: Radak and Ibn Kaspi's noted ambiguity over the missing object marker
The same subject/object ambiguity pattern at Job 14:19
Masoretic cantillation marks as weighed by later commentators on this verse

versions.s: She called his name Joseph, saying, the LORD shall add to me another son. A second, earlier pun on the same name used a different root, for taking away.

b.t: Every version reads Joseph as a transliterated name, with the explanation the LORD shall add to me another son translated in full, but the earlier, different pun two verses before, God hath taken away my reproach, is not shown to be connected to the name at all.

Imagine a name explained twice in the same conversation, once because it sounds like **gone**, meaning a burden lifted, and again because it sounds like **more**, meaning hope for what is still to come. English Joseph carries neither echo; Hebrew's Yoseph carries both, from two different roots.

At 30:23 Rachel says God hath taken away, asaph, my reproach; at 30:24 she names the child Yoseph, may He add, from yasaph, a different root that merely resembles asaph in sound. The name is explained by the second, add, root explicitly, while the first, taken away, root supplies an additional, unstated echo immediately before it, layering two near-homonymous roots onto one name within two verses.

English Joseph is a single transliterated word; it cannot simultaneously echo two different, only sound-alike Hebrew roots the way the birth narrative's two consecutive statements do, so a reader gets both explanations in English prose with no sense that they are doing double, overlapping wordplay on the boy's one name.

When a name's explanation is preceded immediately by a similar-sounding but etymologically separate statement, check whether the narrative is layering two puns rather than one. Joseph's naming is the clearest case of this doubling in the whole cluster of birth-name puns in these two chapters.

Joseph as the name, and both of Rachel's statements, are not in dispute among translators. What matters is that the layered wordplay, two near-homonymous roots both feeding into one name within two verses, is a Hebrew sound effect no single English name or explanation can reproduce.
יוֹסֵף Yoseph (יָסַף yasaph, add / אָסַף asaph, take away) · H3130 / H3254 / H622

src: The two consecutive statements: Genesis 30:23-24
The broader birth-naming-pun pattern this doubling belongs to: Genesis 29:32-30:24

versions.s: Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed. The Hebrew word order is a mirror around the center.

b.t: Every version reads whoever sheds man's blood, by man his blood shall be shed, correctly following the sense, but English sentence order, subject before verb, cannot reproduce a mirror shape the way Hebrew's more flexible word order can.

English can say **the punishment fits the crime**, but that is commentary, a sentence about the sentence. Hebrew builds the fit directly into word order: sheds, blood, man, man, blood, shed, the same words running forward and then backward around a hinge in the middle.

The Hebrew runs shofekh dam ha'adam, ba'adam damo yishafekh: sheds blood-of-man, by-man his-blood shall-be-shed. The verb for shedding opens the first half and closes the second, the noun for blood and the noun for man swap positions around the center, a structure grammarians call a chiasm, an A-B-C-C'-B'-A' pattern that visually and aurally enacts the very reciprocity, blood for blood, that the sentence is announcing.

English word order is comparatively fixed, subject-verb-object, so it cannot rearrange itself into a mirror shape the way Hebrew's freer word order allows here. A translation can state the principle of equal retribution but cannot make the sentence's shape perform it the way the Hebrew does.

Look for chiastic word order whenever a verse states a principle of exact correspondence, reciprocity, or reversal. Hebrew narrative and law use mirrored word order as a rhetorical device in its own right, not merely as a stylistic accident, and it rarely survives translation intact.

The legal content itself isn't contested; every version agrees on the sense. What is lost is entirely formal: the chiastic shape itself, which is not a matter of word choice but of an arrangement English syntax is not free enough to reproduce.

versions.s: He will be a wild man. The Hebrew literally reads a wild-donkey of a man, animal first.

b.t: Every version reads wild man, wild donkey of a man, or similar, generally preserving the sense but not always flagging the unusual word order that puts the animal image first.

English **a wild man** puts man first and wild as a description. Hebrew here reverses that: pere adam is closer to **a wild-donkey, a human one**, animal noun first, human noun second, the reverse of the ordinary Hebrew word order where the describing word comes after the noun it describes.

Pere, wild donkey, stands before adam, man, reversing the normal Hebrew pattern where a modifying word follows its noun; the expected order would put man first and wild donkey as the descriptor. Instead the wild donkey, an animal proverbial in the ancient Near East for fierce independence, untamed freedom, and life beyond settled territory, is named first, making it the dominant image and man almost an afterthought clarifying which kind of creature is meant.

English word order cannot easily reproduce this reversal without sounding broken; a wild-donkey man puts the animal first the way the Hebrew does but reads as odd English, so translators default to the more natural wild man, losing the emphasis the unusual Hebrew order creates.

When a Hebrew phrase's word order runs backward from what the grammar normally expects, that reversal is itself doing rhetorical work, foregrounding whichever word was moved to the front. Do not read past unusual word order as a translator's stylistic accident.

Wild man keeps a natural English sentence but loses the foregrounded animal image. Wild donkey of a man, closer to the Hebrew word order, keeps the emphasis but reads awkwardly in English, the standard tradeoff between literal word order and natural target-language phrasing.

versions.s: Human, and the ground he was taken from. The pun is the point.

b.t: Versions read man, Adam, mankind, or human beings; adamah is ground or land.
**Human** and **humus** are related in English, and almost nobody knows it. Now imagine the connection being obvious to every reader and used as an argument.
Adam is humanity collectively and also the personal name. Adamah is the ground. Genesis 2:7 forms the one from the other and 3:19 returns him to it, and the wordplay frames the whole account.
English man and ground share nothing, so the pun has to be footnoted every time.
Hebrew narrative argues with sound as often as with statement. When a name is explained in the text, the sound is usually doing the explaining.
Man is the majority rendering; mankind and human beings are increasingly common where the collective is in view.
אָדָם adam · H120

versions.s: Esau, red at birth. Edom, from the red stew he later sells his birthright for. One Hebrew color word, twice.

b.t: Every version reads red or ruddy at his birth and Edom as a bare name later, both correct but disconnected in English, since Edom reads as a proper noun with no visible link back to the earlier description.

Imagine a character introduced as **Ruddy** at birth, who years later is nicknamed **Red** for trading away his inheritance for a bowl of red stew. English could do this too, in theory, but Genesis actually does it, in Hebrew, using the same root both times, a detail lost once red at birth and Edom become two separate, unconnected-sounding words in translation.

Admoni, ruddy or red, describes Esau at birth at 25:25; the same root gives adom, red, describing the stew he demands at 25:30, which the text explicitly says is why he was called Edom, red. The wordplay brackets his introduction and his defining bad decision with the identical color root, marking both moments, and the nation descended from him, with the same word.

English red and ruddy at his birth, and the transliterated name Edom later, share no visible connection for an English reader, so the deliberate bracketing, red at birth, red at his worst decision, red as his descendants' national name, is invisible without knowing the underlying Hebrew root ties all three together.

When a character's name or nickname is explained later in a story, check whether it echoes a word already used to describe him earlier. Genesis regularly uses this device to tie a character's introduction to his defining moment, and the connection is carried entirely by sound.

Nothing here divides translators; red, ruddy, and Edom are all correctly rendered. What matters is that the repeated root connecting Esau's birth description to his stew and his nation's name is a purely Hebrew-sound feature that transliteration and ordinary translation both necessarily sever.
אַדְמוֹנִי admoni / אָדֹם adom / אֱדוֹם Edom · H132 / H122

src: The explicit naming explanation: Genesis 25:30, 'therefore was his name called Edom'
The same naming-pun device used throughout Genesis for Cain, Noah, Peleg, Japheth, Moab, and Jacob

versions.s: Esau, red at birth. Edom, from the red stew he later sells his birthright for. One Hebrew color word, twice.

b.t: Every version reads red or ruddy at his birth and Edom as a bare name later, both correct but disconnected in English, since Edom reads as a proper noun with no visible link back to the earlier description.

Imagine a character introduced as **Ruddy** at birth, who years later is nicknamed **Red** for trading away his inheritance for a bowl of red stew. English could do this too, in theory, but Genesis actually does it, in Hebrew, using the same root both times, a detail lost once red at birth and Edom become two separate, unconnected-sounding words in translation.

Admoni, ruddy or red, describes Esau at birth at 25:25; the same root gives adom, red, describing the stew he demands at 25:30, which the text explicitly says is why he was called Edom, red. The wordplay brackets his introduction and his defining bad decision with the identical color root, marking both moments, and the nation descended from him, with the same word.

English red and ruddy at his birth, and the transliterated name Edom later, share no visible connection for an English reader, so the deliberate bracketing, red at birth, red at his worst decision, red as his descendants' national name, is invisible without knowing the underlying Hebrew root ties all three together.

When a character's name or nickname is explained later in a story, check whether it echoes a word already used to describe him earlier. Genesis regularly uses this device to tie a character's introduction to his defining moment, and the connection is carried entirely by sound.

Nothing here divides translators; red, ruddy, and Edom are all correctly rendered. What matters is that the repeated root connecting Esau's birth description to his stew and his nation's name is a purely Hebrew-sound feature that transliteration and ordinary translation both necessarily sever.
אַדְמוֹנִי admoni / אָדֹם adom / אֱדוֹם Edom · H132 / H122

src: The explicit naming explanation: Genesis 25:30, 'therefore was his name called Edom'

versions.s: The LORD said unto my Lord. Two different Hebrew words, and English uses one.

b.t: Every version distinguishes them by capitalisation: LORD in small capitals for the first, Lord for the second. No version uses two different words, and the convention is explained in a preface most readers skip.

Imagine a sentence where two people are both called **sir**, and your only clue to which is which is how the printer set the type. That is what an English Bible is doing here, and almost nobody has been told the convention.

The first word is the divine name, printed LORD in small capitals wherever it occurs. The second is adoni, my lord, an ordinary term used of human superiors. So the line is the divine name speaking to someone the psalmist calls my lord. Jesus builds an argument on exactly this at Matthew 22:41-46, and it only works if the two are different.
English has one word for both and has solved it with typography rather than vocabulary. That works in print and fails completely when read aloud, which is how most people meet the verse.
Small capitals in an English Old Testament are not emphasis. They mark the divine name. Once you know that, a large number of verses become visible that were not before.
Nothing is disputed in translation. The convention is universal and the failure is that it is never taught, so a verse the New Testament quotes constantly reads as a repetition in English.

versions.s: Lord, master, sir. An ordinary word, and also what is said aloud in place of the divine name.

b.t: Versions print Lord for this word and LORD in small capitals for the divine name.
**Yes, sir.** That is a form of address, not a title. Now imagine using it every time a particular name came up, out of respect, until people forgot the name underneath.
Adon is a master or superior and is used of ordinary men. Adonai, my lord, became the spoken substitute for the divine name, and the Septuagint's kurios follows the practice.
English uses typography to carry a distinction Hebrew carries in vocabulary, and typography is silent when read aloud.
Small capitals mark the divine name. Ordinary capitals mark this word. Learn the convention once and a large number of verses open up.
Lord is the majority rendering; the small-capital convention is universal across English versions.

versions.s: Rejoiced to see my day. The verb is closer to exulted, and the seeing is aorist.

b.t: Versions read rejoiced to see, or was glad that he would see.
**He was thrilled to see it.** **He was thrilled that he would see it.** English marks that with extra words. Greek marks it with the form of the verb.

Agalliaomai is to exult, a stronger verb than ordinary joy. The construction, hina with the aorist subjunctive ide, can mean rejoiced in order to see or rejoiced that he would see, and the following clause, he saw it and was glad, uses a plain aorist.
English has to supply a time relation between the rejoicing and the seeing that the Greek leaves for the reader.
When two verbs sit next to each other and the versions differ about their order in time, look at the form of the second one.
Rejoiced to see is the majority rendering; that he would see appears in some modern versions.
ἀγαλλιάομαι agalliaomai · G21

versions.s: Both love-words, one chapter, the same relationship. Whatever they are doing, they are not ranking it.

b.t: No English version distinguishes them, and almost no study Bible notes that both appear here.

If someone calls the same person **my mate** in one sentence and **my friend** two sentences later, you do not conclude the friendship got upgraded. Same thing here, except a lot of sermons draw exactly that conclusion.

Verse 3 uses phileo, on the sisters' lips. Verse 5 uses agapao, in the narrator's voice, about the same three people. Verse 36 uses phileo again, on the crowd's lips. One relationship, one chapter, both verbs.
English merges the two, so an English reader cannot see the alternation at all, and therefore cannot see that it does not line up with any hierarchy.
Before accepting that two words rank each other, find a passage where both are used of the same thing. If the ranking survives that, it is real. Here it does not.

There is no dispute in the text. The dispute is in the pulpit, and this chapter is the cleanest evidence against the claim that agapao is the higher love and phileo the lesser one. It is the same evidence that John 21 supplies, in a different book of the same Gospel.
φιλέω phileo · G5368 / ἀγαπάω agapao · G25

src: John 11:3 phileis; 11:5 egapa; 11:36 ephilei

versions.s: Two different Greek words for love, and the sermon you have heard about them is probably overselling it.

b.t: No English version distinguishes the two verbs, because English has one word. Study Bibles and pulpits supply the distinction instead.

**He sipped his coffee, then he drank his tea.** Did the writer mean something by sip against drink, or was he just avoiding saying drink twice? Good writers vary words for the sound of it. Before you build anything on a word change, check whether the writer changed other words in the same breath.

Jesus asks twice using agapao and once using phileo. Peter answers all three times with phileo. The standard sermon builds a hierarchy out of this, with agapao as the higher divine love and phileo as mere friendship.
English has one verb where Greek has several, so the variation vanishes. That is a real loss. The question is whether anything was in it.
Before building a doctrine on a word change, check whether the writer varies other words in the same passage. John does, four times over in these three verses, and nobody preaches on those.

John also swaps two words for sheep, two for know, and two for feed and tend in the same exchange. None of those carry theological weight, which makes it hard to argue that one of the five variations is loaded and the other four are style. The honest verdict is that the distinction is probably stylistic, that the Septuagint and Koine use the two verbs largely interchangeably, and that this entry exists to show you what a divergence looks like when it turns out not to matter.
ἀγαπάω agapao · G25 / φιλέω phileo · G5368

versions.s: Husbands, love your wives. The word is agape, and the word you would expect is the one that is missing.

b.t: Every English version reads love, because there is only one word to use. The choice Paul made is invisible in English.

You are writing a wedding card and you have two words available, one for wanting someone and one for standing by them. You pick one. The choice is the message. A reader with both words sees which you left out. A reader with only one word cannot.

The verb is agapate, from agapao. Paul is writing about marriage, the one relationship where a Greek writer had eros available and might be expected to use it, and he does not. He reaches for the word he uses for God's love and then defines it in the same sentence by Christ giving himself up.

English love covers desire and commitment with one word, so the fact that Paul declined one of them cannot be seen. In Greek the absence is loud. In English there is no absence, because there was never a second word to leave out.

When a Greek writer had more than one word available and picked a specific one, the choice is the argument. You cannot see that in English, but you can look for the places where the obvious word would have been a different one.
There is no translation dispute. There is a reading dispute about how much weight to put on the word choice, and the answer depends on whether Paul had a genuine alternative. Here he did.
ἀγαπάω agapao · G25

versions.s: Four Greek words for love, and two of them never appear in the New Testament.

b.t: No English version can show any of this. English has one word, and it is doing the work of four.

English has one word for uncle. Your mother's brother and your father's brother get the same label. Plenty of languages split those, and speakers of those languages find it strange that you do not. Greek splits love the way those languages split uncle. English does not, and the split is invisible to you until someone points at it.

The four-loves scheme is real Greek vocabulary, but it is not a New Testament vocabulary set. It is C. S. Lewis's framework from The Four Loves, published in 1960, built out of classical Greek. Eros does not occur in the New Testament at all. Storge never occurs as a standalone noun or verb; it survives only inside two compounds, astorgos in Romans 1:31 and 2 Timothy 3:3, and philostorgos in Romans 12:10. That leaves philia and agape doing nearly all the work.

English has one noun and one verb for all of it. A language with four words can distinguish the love you did not choose from the love you did, and the love that wants from the love that stays, without ever explaining itself. English has to explain itself every time, or leave it ambiguous.

Learn the four as four verbs, not four nouns. Born into, picked, reaches, stays. Then hold them loosely, because two of them are not in your New Testament and the other two overlap more than the sermons admit.

Nothing to choose, because no translator has the option. The thing worth noticing is what the absences say. A body of literature that never once uses the word for desire, and only ever names family affection by its absence, is not a body of literature indifferent to either. It has simply put its weight somewhere else. The word it reaches for when it commands a husband to love his wife is not eros. It is agape.

versions.s: Hebrew has one word for love, and this is the chapter that proves how wide it is.

b.t: Every version reads loved, because the Hebrew says loved. Some soften it with desired, which is an interpretation rather than a translation.

**I love pizza. I love my wife.** Same English verb, and nobody is confused, because context does everything. Now stop and notice how much work context is doing, and that it can carry the word into places you would rather it did not.

The root is ahav. It is the word for God's covenant love in Deuteronomy 6:5, for the love between David and Jonathan, for the love poetry of the Song, and for this. Hebrew does not have the four-part Greek scheme. It has one root and lets context do the work.

English readers arrive at the Old Testament already holding the Greek categories, because that is what they were taught. Those categories are not in the Hebrew, and applying them produces a sanitized reading of texts that are not sanitized.

Do not carry Greek word distinctions backward into Hebrew. The Old Testament does not run on them. When a Hebrew text uses ahav, the shade is supplied entirely by what is happening in the passage, and sometimes what is happening is horrifying.
Nothing to choose. The discomfort is the point of the entry. A single word that covers Deuteronomy 6 and 2 Samuel 13 tells you something about Hebrew that no amount of Greek vocabulary will.
אָהַב ahav · H157

src: Same root at Deuteronomy 6:5; 1 Samuel 18:1; Song of Songs throughout; 2 Samuel 13:1, 15
The narrative itself supplies the reversal in verse 15, which is the strongest internal comment on the word's range

versions.s: Age. The noun behind the adjective English renders eternal.

b.t: Versions read age, world, or forever depending on the phrase. One noun behind all three.
**The Victorian age.** **Ages ago.** English uses the word both for a bounded era and for a vague long time, and you sort them instantly.
Aion is an age or era, and the New Testament regularly contrasts this age with the age to come. Rendered world in older English, as in the end of the world, which meant the end of the age.
English has age but uses world and forever in the fixed biblical phrases, so the temporal structure of this-age and the-age-to-come becomes invisible.
When one noun is rendered by three unrelated English words across one book, list them. The list is usually more instructive than the lexicon entry.
Age is the majority rendering in modern versions; the King James reads world in most of these places.

src: this age and the age to come: Matthew 12:32; Ephesians 1:21
aion rendered world in the KJV: Matthew 24:3

versions.s: Everlasting life. The Greek adjective is built on the word for age, not the word for endless.

b.t: King James reads everlasting. Most modern versions read eternal. Neither carries the age sense, and no major version attempts it.

**Medieval architecture.** That does not mean architecture that lasts a long time. It means architecture belonging to a particular age. Now imagine your only word for that idea had drifted to mean unending, and you had been reading it that way your whole life.

Aionios is the adjective from aion, an age or era, and one influential scholarly reading treats its primary force as belonging to the age to come rather than lasting without end, with endlessness following as a consequence of which age you belong to rather than the word's own content. That reading is contested, not settled: standard lexicons such as BDAG also list a distinct sense, without beginning or end, and note that Greek had a separate word for strict endlessness, aidios, which New Testament writers mostly did not reach for. Which sense is primary in a given verse is part of a live debate tied to larger arguments about universalism, annihilationism, and eternal punishment.
English eternal and everlasting are both about duration. There is no English adjective meaning of the coming age, so the temporal reading is the only one on offer.
Adjectives built on nouns usually carry the noun with them. Find the noun before you accept the adjective.

Nothing textual is at stake, but the semantic question underneath is genuinely live, not settled: whether aionios here primarily means belonging to the age to come or primarily means without end is disputed among lexicographers and theologians. English eternal and everlasting both commit to the duration sense regardless of which side is right, so no English version marks that a real dispute exists underneath the word.
αἰώνιος aionios · G166

src: aion as age: Matthew 12:32, neither in this world nor in the world to come; Ephesians 1:21
aionios of things explicitly bounded: Romans 16:25, kept secret since the world began
John 17:3 defines the life by relationship rather than by duration
BDAG's separate 'without beginning or end' sense for aionios, and aidios as Greek's dedicated word for strict endlessness

versions.s: Every branch that beareth not fruit he taketh away. The verb also means lifts up.

b.t: Nearly every version reads takes away or cuts off. A minority of commentators and study notes argue for lifts up. No major version prints it.
**He picked up the coat.** **He picked up the litter.** Same verb, and one means raising something and the other means removing it. Only the object and the situation tell you which.

Airo means to lift, to raise, to carry, and also to take away or remove. It is the verb used for taking up a bed at John 5:8 and for taking away sin at John 1:29. Vinedressers did lift trailing branches off the ground so they could fruit, which is the practical case for the other reading.
No English verb means lift-and-therefore-carry-off. Pick up comes close, and reads too casual for the register.
When a verb covers both raising and removing, the choice is usually made by what the interpreter already thinks the passage is about. That is worth noticing in yourself before you settle it.

Takes away has the weight of usage, the parallel with the burning in verse 6, and nearly every translation. Lifts up has the horticulture and a kinder reading of the chapter. The lexicon permits both and the context leans toward the first.

versions.s: Full of grace and truth. That is a Hebrew pair, and it comes from Exodus 34.

b.t: All English versions read grace and truth. None can show that the phrase is a quotation of a formula.

**Come good and early.** That is not two instructions. Good and early is one idea said with two words, and nobody hears it as a list. English does this and then forgets it does. Hebrew does it constantly.

Charis kai aletheia is widely taken as the Greek rendering of hesed we-emet, steadfast love and faithfulness, the pair God speaks over himself in Exodus 34:6 when Moses asks to see his glory. John has just said we beheld his glory. The allusion is to a specific scene.
English grace and truth reads as two abstract nouns joined by and. In Hebrew the pair is a fixed formula with a single referent, covenant loyalty, and the second word steadies the first.

When two abstract nouns are joined in the New Testament and both are common Septuagint words, check whether they are a Hebrew word-pair rather than two separate ideas. Hebrew often says one thing with two words.
Nothing in the translation is contested. What is contested is how firmly to press the Exodus 34 allusion, and the glory language in the same verse is the strongest argument for pressing it.
χάρις charis · G5485 / ἀλήθεια aletheia · G225

src: Exodus 34:6, rav hesed we-emet, in the Septuagint polyeleos kai alethinos
John 1:17 names Moses in the next verse, which supports the allusion

versions.s: True worshippers. The adjective means real as against counterfeit, not sincere.

b.t: Every version reads true worshippers.
**A true friend.** You mean a real one, not a sincere one. English keeps the sense and uses it less often than it used to.

Alethinos is genuine, real, the thing itself rather than a representation. It is the word behind the true light, the true bread and the true vine in this Gospel, where in each case something is being contrasted with a lesser version.
English true covers both genuine and sincere, and the second sense now dominates, so a claim about authenticity reads as a claim about attitude.
When John calls something true, he is usually contrasting it with a copy. List the other occurrences and the pattern becomes obvious.
True is universal; genuine or real appear in footnotes.

src: the true light: John 1:9

versions.s: Virgin or young woman. One Hebrew word, seven occurrences, and an argument that has run for two thousand years.

b.t: Most English versions read virgin. The RSV read young woman and set off a decade of controversy. The NET reads young woman with a long note.

**She is a maiden.** In 1611 that told you her age and her household position and let you draw your own conclusion about the rest. Now the word barely exists and the conclusion has to be stated. Some words carry an implication instead of a fact, and English usually wants the fact.

The word is almah. It appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible: Genesis 24:43, Exodus 2:8, Psalm 68:25, Proverbs 30:19, Song of Songs 1:3 and 6:8, and here. Hebrew has a second word, bethulah, which appears about fifty times and is the term that most directly means virgin. Isaiah knew that word and uses it four times elsewhere in his book.

English makes you declare a sexual status. Almah declares an age and a social position, unmarried and of childbearing years, from which a first century reader would ordinarily infer virginity without the word having to say it. There is no English word that carries the inference without stating the fact.

When translations split on a single noun, check how many times the word appears in the whole Bible. Seven is a small enough sample that every occurrence is part of the argument, and small samples are exactly where lexicons get stretched.

The case for young woman is that bethulah was available and was not used. The case for virgin is that wherever the context of almah is clear enough to judge, Genesis 24:43 and Exodus 2:8 and Song 6:8, the woman is in fact unmarried, and that the Septuagint translators, working two centuries before Christ with no stake in the question, chose parthenos. Both arguments are real. Neither is a knockout.
עַלְמָה almah · H5959

src: J. A. Motyer, The Prophecy of Isaiah, on almah never being used of a married woman
Septuagint Isaiah 7:14, parthenos
Matthew 1:23 quotes the Greek, not the Hebrew
All seven occurrences: Gen 24:43; Exod 2:8; Ps 68:25; Prov 30:19; Song 1:3, 6:8; Isa 7:14

versions.s: He believed in the LORD. The verb is the root behind amen.

b.t: All versions read believed. None can show the root, and none shows the verb form.

**He trusted the bridge.** **He believed the story.** English believe drifts toward agreeing with a claim. The older sense is closer to leaning your weight on something, and you can still hear it in **the ice held**.

He'emin is the hiphil of aman, a root meaning to be firm, reliable, to support. The noun from it is emunah, faithfulness, and the word you say at the end of a prayer is the same root. The verb is closer to he found God reliable and rested on Him than to he accepted a proposition.
English believe has moved toward mental assent. There is no English verb meaning to treat as load-bearing, so the root sense has to be explained rather than translated.
When a verse is the foundation of a doctrine, look up the root of its main verb. Doctrinal vocabulary drifts faster than ordinary vocabulary, because it gets used more.
No dispute in the rendering. The dispute, where there is one, is about how much the root sense should shape the doctrine built on the verse.
אָמַן aman · H539

src: Same root as emunah, faithfulness: Habakkuk 2:4
Same root as amen: Deuteronomy 27:15-26
Romans 4:3 and Galatians 3:6 quote the Septuagint of this verse

versions.s: Cain talked with Abel his brother. The Hebrew text never says what he said; other ancient witnesses supply Let us go into the field.

b.t: Most modern versions insert Let us go out to the field or similar, following the Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint, Vulgate and Syriac. The King James and other translations that follow the Masoretic Text as it stands print only talked, with no quoted words.

**She told him, and he left.** Told him what? A sentence that introduces speech and never quotes it reads as broken in English the same way it does in Hebrew. Most Bibles quietly patch the gap; the King James, following the Hebrew as it stands, does not.

The Hebrew verb for said normally introduces a direct quotation, and here none follows, a real grammatical gap. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the only Hebrew witness among the group, along with the Septuagint, Vulgate and Syriac, all supply nechlecha hasadeh, let us go into the field, closing the gap in slightly different wording across the four.

English cannot leave a said with no quotation and read as ordinary narrative; a translator has to either supply words or leave a sentence English readers will find abrupt. The choice between them is a real textual decision quietly made for most readers by whichever committee translated their Bible.

When a Hebrew sentence has a grammatical gap that multiple independent ancient versions fill the same way, that convergence is real evidence, even though the Masoretic Hebrew itself may still be defended as original. Check whether a smoothed-over English reading is hiding a textual decision.

Supplying let us go into the field, as most modern versions do, produces a smoother, more natural narrative and has broad ancient support outside the Masoretic tradition. Leaving the gap, as the King James does, keeps the harder, better-attested Hebrew text and lets the abruptness stand as Cain's own evasive silence.
וַיֹּאמֶר vayomer (אמר amar, to say) · H559

src: Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint, Vulgate and Peshitta all supply the missing line, in varying wording
Masoretic Text as printed in BHS lacks any quoted speech after vayomer
Standard text-critical discussions of Genesis 4:8 (e.g. in the Anchor Bible and Word Biblical Commentary)

versions.s: And defiled her. The verb anah is used elsewhere explicitly for rape, and elsewhere more broadly for affliction.

b.t: Most versions read violated, humbled, or defiled, all reasonable attempts at a verb whose full weight, forced sexual violation, some English words soften more than others.

English has separate words, **afflicted** and **raped**, that name very different things. Hebrew anah, in this intensive form, spans both, used in some places for general oppression and, in others, including two other biblical assault narratives, explicitly for sexual violation. Context, not the word alone, tells you which is meant here.

Innah, the piel of anah, is used explicitly for rape at Deuteronomy 22:24, 29 and for Amnon's assault on Tamar at 2 Samuel 13:12, 14, establishing a clear pattern of usage for sexual violation elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible. The same root can also mean afflict, oppress, or humble in non-sexual contexts, which has occasionally allowed softer readings here, but the verb's use in the two other explicit assault narratives strongly supports reading it the same way in Dinah's case.

English translators must choose a specific word, violated, defiled, humbled, raped, that commits to a level of explicitness the single Hebrew verb does not by itself require, since anah's precise force depends on comparing its use across several passages rather than on the word in isolation.

When a Hebrew verb has both a broad, non-sexual sense and a narrower, explicitly sexual one attested elsewhere, check its use in comparable narratives before assuming a translation has softened or sharpened the original beyond what the evidence supports.

Defiled or humbled, the older, softer English glosses, can obscure the verb's explicit force in comparable assault narratives. Violated or raped more directly conveys what the parallel uses of the same verb at Deuteronomy 22 and 2 Samuel 13 indicate the word is doing here as well.
וַיְעַנֶּהָ vaye'aneha (עָנָה anah, piel) · H6031

src: The same verb explicitly for rape: Deuteronomy 22:24, 29; 2 Samuel 13:12, 14
Broader, non-sexual senses of anah elsewhere: Exodus 1:11-12; Genesis 15:13

versions.s: He will shew you things to come. The verb is announce, and the phrase need not mean prediction.

b.t: Versions read things to come, what is yet to come, or things that are coming.
**What's coming** can mean next week or it can mean the thing already on its way down the track.

Ta erchomena is a participle, the coming things. Anangello is to announce or report rather than to predict. Together they may point at the events immediately ahead rather than at the future in general.
English things to come defaults to prophecy, so a phrase about imminent events reads as a promise of foresight.
Participles used as nouns are usually about what is happening rather than about a fixed category. The coming things is a description, not a genre.
What is yet to come is what most modern versions print.

versions.s: Resurrection. The noun means a standing up again, and it is a bodily word.

b.t: Every version reads resurrection or rising.
**He got back on his feet.** English uses standing for recovery all the time. The Greek noun is that, made literal.
Ana, up or again, plus histemi, to stand. The word is concrete, which is part of why the Athenians at Acts 17 reacted to it as they did: it was not a metaphor for survival.
English borrowed a Latin word, resurrectio, so the English term is opaque where the Greek was transparent.
Words borrowed from Latin into English usually lose the picture the Greek had. Taking the Greek compound apart restores it.
Resurrection is universal in English versions.

versions.s: The meek shall inherit the earth. Anav ranges from humble in spirit to poor and afflicted in circumstance.

b.t: Most English versions read meek or humble, emphasizing character. Some scholars and a minority of translations lean toward poor or oppressed, emphasizing social and economic reversal, closer to the concerns voiced throughout the rest of Psalm 37 about the wicked prospering at others' expense.

English meek names a personality trait, gentle, unassuming. Hebrew anav can mean that, but just as often names an economic and social condition, the poor, the oppressed, people ground down by circumstance rather than people who have simply cultivated humility. The verse could be promising a virtue's reward or the poor's vindication, or both at once.

Anav describes both a virtue, humility or gentleness, and a social condition, poverty or affliction, throughout the Hebrew Bible, including of Moses at Numbers 12:3. The Septuagint's Greek praeis, gentle, behind Matthew 5:5's meek, leans toward the virtue sense, but the wider context of Psalm 37, contrasting the wicked's temporary prosperity with the eventual vindication of those they oppress, fits the social-economic sense just as naturally, perhaps more so.

English meek carries almost entirely personality-trait connotations today, gentle, unassertive, so a modern reader easily misses that the same Hebrew word could equally, or primarily, be naming the economically and socially oppressed, whose inheritance of the land is a reversal of fortune, not merely a reward for good temperament.

If a Hebrew word spans both a character trait and a social-economic condition, check the surrounding context for which sense is doing the heavier lifting, rather than defaulting to whichever sense your own culture's translation tradition has favored.

Meek or humble, following the Septuagint's praeis and most English tradition, reads the promise as a reward for personal virtue. Poor or oppressed, following anav's equally attested social sense and Psalm 37's larger theme of reversal for the oppressed, reads the same promise as vindication for those ground down by the wicked the psalm spends most of its length condemning.
עָנָו anav · H6035

src: anav of Moses: Numbers 12:3
Septuagint praeis behind Matthew 5:5's quotation
The social-economic sense of anav elsewhere: Isaiah 61:1; Amos 2:7

versions.s: Born again, or born from above. The Greek word means both and Nicodemus hears only one.

b.t: King James, NIV and NASB read again. The NRSV and NET read from above and footnote again. The margin of almost every version carries the other.

**Can you run that by me again?** **The order came down from on high.** Two different ideas, and imagine one word covering both. Now watch someone answer the wrong one and build a whole confused reply on it.

Anothen means from above and also again, a second time. John uses it in the from above sense at 3:31 and 19:11. Jesus almost certainly means from above. Nicodemus takes it as again and asks about re-entering a womb, which is why the next three verses are about correcting him.
English has no word carrying both a direction and a repetition. Whichever one a translator picks, the misunderstanding in verse 4 stops making sense.
When a character in a narrative misunderstands a saying, check the word they tripped on. A deliberate double meaning is often the reason the scene exists.

Again fits Nicodemus's reply and four hundred years of English usage. From above fits John's own use of the word elsewhere and fits the born of the Spirit line that follows. Most commentators take from above as the meaning and again as the misunderstanding the passage is built on.

versions.s: Grace for grace. The preposition normally means instead of, which makes the phrase hard rather than warm.

b.t: Versions read grace upon grace, or one blessing after another, or grace in place of grace. The spread is unusually wide.

**I traded one car for another** against **I stacked one book on another.** For and on point in opposite directions. One replaces, one piles up. The Greek word here is normally the trading one, and almost every English Bible prints the stacking one.

Anti ordinarily means instead of or in place of, as in a substitution. It is the preposition behind antichrist and anti-type. Reading charin anti charitos as grace piled on grace requires anti to mean something closer to upon or succeeding, which is a much rarer use.

English has no preposition that means one thing replacing another of the same kind in a continuous series. In place of sounds like a swap and upon sounds like a stack, and the Greek sits between them.

When a preposition is doing unexpected work, look up what it ordinarily means before accepting a rendering that feels comfortable. Comfortable renderings of prepositions are where a lot of quiet interpretation hides.

Grace upon grace reads as abundance and is the majority modern choice. Grace in place of grace reads as the new covenant replacing the old, which is exactly what verse 17 goes on to describe with Moses and Christ. The context supports the harder reading more than the translations do.

entries.where: apeitheo is tagged 14 times, across 5 books: romans 5 · 1peter 4 · acts 2 · hebrews 2 · john 1.

versions.s: He that believeth not. The Greek verb in the second half is disobey, not disbelieve.

b.t: The King James reads believeth not. The ESV and NASB read does not obey. The NIV reads rejects.
**He did not agree.** **He did not comply.** Two different failures, and only one of them is about the mind.
The first clause uses pisteuo, believe. The second uses apeitheo, to refuse to be persuaded, to disobey. The contrast is between trusting and refusing, not between two states of opinion.
English believe has no natural opposite that means refuse to comply, so versions either print does not believe and lose the switch or print does not obey and surprise the reader.
When a verse sets up a contrast, check whether both halves use the same root. If they do not, the switch is the argument.
Most modern English versions print does not obey; the King James reads believeth not.

versions.s: Apostle. The noun simply means one who is sent, with authority to act for the sender.

b.t: Every version reads apostle, and messenger in the handful of places where the sense is plainly ordinary.
**He is our man in Berlin.** An envoy speaks with the authority of whoever sent him. That is the whole idea, and it is a job description rather than a rank.

Apostolos is from apostello, to send out. A sent one carries the authority of the sender, which is what makes the word more than messenger. It is applied to the Twelve, to Paul, to Barnabas, to Epaphroditus and to Andronicus and Junia.
English apostle has become a proper title and cannot be used of an ordinary envoy, so the range is invisible.
When an English word has become a title, look up every occurrence of the original. Titles narrow faster than any other kind of vocabulary.
Apostle is the majority rendering; messenger appears at Philippians 2:25 and 2 Corinthians 8:23 in most versions.
ἀπόστολος apostolos · G652

versions.s: Put out of the synagogue. A compound word that appears nowhere before John.

b.t: Versions read put out of the synagogue, or excommunicated.
A word that appears nowhere earlier can mean the writer coined it, or that the thing it names was new, or simply that nothing else survives. Those are three different conclusions from one fact.

Aposunagogos occurs three times, all in John, and nowhere else in Greek literature before him. Whether it reflects a formal first-century policy or an informal local exclusion is argued at length, and the dating of the Gospel is often attached to the answer.
No single English word covers it, so every version uses a phrase, and the fact that the Greek is one coined word disappears.
When a word occurs only in one author, the absence of other witnesses is a fact about what survives as much as about what existed.
Put out of the synagogue is the majority rendering.
ἀποσυνάγωγος aposunagogos · G656

src: All three occurrences: John 9:22; 12:42; 16:2

versions.s: His hand took hold on Esau's heel, and his name was called Jacob. The same root also means deceiver, supplanter.

b.t: Every version reads Jacob as a bare transliterated name at his birth, with the heel-grabbing detail explained but the second, darker meaning left for a reader to discover only later, if ever, since English Jacob carries neither sense on its own.

Imagine naming a baby **Grabby** for literally grabbing his twin's foot at birth, and years later, after he cheats that same brother twice, everyone realizes **Grabby** also meant **cheater** the whole time. That double meaning is built into Jacob's name from his very first verse.

Ya'akov is built on akev, heel, describing the literal detail of his birth, but the same root akav also carries the sense to deceive, to overreach, or to supplant, a meaning Esau explicitly invokes at 27:36 after Jacob has taken both his birthright and his blessing: is he not rightly named Jacob? for he hath supplanted me these two times. The name functions as both a birth detail and a character prophecy from its first appearance.

English Jacob is a bare proper name carrying neither the physical heel-grabbing sense nor the deceiving-supplanter sense that make the name a small, ongoing joke, and later an accusation, throughout the rest of his story.

When a name given for a physical circumstance at birth turns out to share a root with a character trait that defines the rest of that person's story, treat the double meaning as intentional from the first mention, not as a coincidence noticed only when the second sense surfaces later.

Jacob as the transliterated name is not in question. What matters is that both senses of the root, the literal heel-grabbing and the figurative supplanting, are doing real work across the narrative that only the shared Hebrew root, not the English name, can carry.
יַעֲקֹב Ya'akov (עָקֵב akev, heel / עָקַב akav, deceive) · H3290 / H6117

src: Esau's explicit wordplay accusation: Genesis 27:36

versions.s: Mine own familiar friend hath lifted up his heel against me. Akev, heel, the same root as Jacob's name, applied by Jesus to Judas's betrayal.

b.t: Every version reads lifted up his heel against me or a similar phrase, correctly, and John 13:18's Gospel citation of this verse for Judas is well known, but neither translation shows an English reader that heel here is the same word running through Jacob's whole story.

English lifted up his heel reads as an odd, archaic idiom for betrayal, with no built-in connection to anything else in the Bible. In Hebrew, the heel-word carries a long history: it is Jacob's own name, tied since Genesis to grasping, supplanting, and betrayal, and this psalm's use of it for betrayal by a trusted friend is precisely the verse Jesus applies to Judas.

Akev, heel, is the same root behind Ya'akov, Jacob, first explained at Genesis 25:26 as grasping his brother's heel at birth, and reinterpreted by Esau at Genesis 27:36 as supplanted, deceived, a betrayal sense the root carries elsewhere too. Jesus quotes this exact verse, he that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me, at John 13:18, applying it directly to Judas's betrayal at a shared meal, drawing on the same heel-vocabulary that has carried treachery and supplanting since Jacob's own birth.

English lifted up his heel is an isolated, archaic-sounding idiom for betrayal with no visible connection to anything else in the Bible; the Hebrew reader, by contrast, hears the same root that has already carried deception and supplanting since Genesis, so Jesus's quotation of this verse for Judas draws on a much older web of association an English reader cannot access.

If a quotation applies an Old Testament verse to a specific act of betrayal, check whether the underlying Hebrew vocabulary already carries that association elsewhere in the Bible. The heel-root's long history with deception, running from Jacob through this psalm to Judas, is exactly this kind of accumulated resonance.

Lifted up his heel is the uncontested sense here; no rendering is in dispute. What's worth tracing is this verse's vocabulary back through the same root's long biblical history with deception and betrayal, a thread running from Jacob's birth through this psalm to Jesus's own application of the verse to Judas.

versions.s: Extol him that rideth upon the heavens. A title, rider of the clouds, borrowed directly from Baal's own standing epithet.

b.t: Every version reads rideth upon the heavens or rides through the deserts, both reasonable translations of an ambiguous Hebrew word, but neither flags that the underlying phrase closely matches a specific, attested divine title from the surrounding culture.

Imagine a hymn calling your God by the exact title a rival religion uses for its own storm-god, on purpose, to claim that title belongs to the true God instead. That is what this verse very likely does, taking rider of the clouds straight from Canaanite mythology and redirecting it.

Rokev ba'aravot, rider on the clouds or plains, closely parallels rkb 'rpt, rider of the clouds, a fixed epithet for Baal repeated throughout Ugaritic mythological texts. Applying the identical image directly to the LORD is very likely a deliberate theological claim, that Israel's God, not Baal, is the true rider of the storm clouds, joining Psalm 29's storm-theophany language and Psalm 48's likely claim on Mount Zaphon as a third instance of this same polemical pattern in the Psalter.

English readers meeting rideth upon the heavens hear generic, majestic imagery with no signal that the phrase is likely quoting, and redirecting, a specific rival deity's own standing title, a claim that only registers once the Ugaritic parallel is known.

When the Psalter applies storm or sky imagery to the LORD using phrasing that closely parallels an attested Canaanite divine epithet, read it as part of a consistent, deliberate pattern of theological reclamation running through multiple psalms, not as an isolated poetic coincidence.

Reading the phrase as generic praise imagery misses the likely polemical point. Reading it as a direct appropriation of Baal's own title, alongside Psalm 29 and Psalm 48's similar moves, casts this verse as part of a sustained pattern across the Psalter, actively contesting Canaanite religious claims rather than merely borrowing poetic flourish.

versions.s: As the hart panteth after the water brooks. Arag, a rare verb for an audible cry of longing, not quiet heavy breathing.

b.t: Every version reads panteth, an accurate but physically narrower English verb than the Hebrew's onomatopoeic, sound-based image of a distressed animal's cry.

English pants describes a physical action, hard breathing, mostly silent. Hebrew arag pictures something noisier and more desperate, closer to a lost animal crying out, bleating for its mother or its herd, unable to find its way. The soul is not merely tired and breathing hard; it is crying aloud in desperation.

Arag occurs only here, twice in this psalm, and once more at Joel 1:20, always describing the desperate, audible longing of an animal, close to a bleating or braying cry rather than simple physical panting. The image is not a deer breathing hard after running; it is a deer crying out, its very life depending on finding water, a cry the psalmist applies directly to his own soul's desperation for God.

English panteth suggests only physical exertion, quiet and mostly involuntary; it misses the vocal, almost anguished cry the rare Hebrew verb actually pictures, an animal crying out because it knows it will perish without what it seeks.

When a translated verb for physical action sounds ordinary in English, check whether the Hebrew original is describing something more vocal or desperate. A rare, nearly onomatopoeic verb like arag often carries far more emotional weight than its common English gloss suggests.

Panteth is the traditional, poetic English rendering and captures physical desperation well. Cries out, or a more vivid rendering closer to bleats, better conveys arag's audible, almost anguished sense, an animal, or a soul, crying aloud rather than merely breathing hard.

versions.s: The mountains of Ararat. A region, plural mountains, not a single named peak.

b.t: Every version reads the mountains of Ararat, plural, correctly matching the Hebrew. Popular usage, hymns, and most modern maps nonetheless speak of Mount Ararat, a single volcanic peak in eastern Turkey, as though that were what the verse specifies.

**The ark landed in the Rockies** names a mountain range. **The ark landed on Pikes Peak** names one mountain. Genesis says the first kind of thing, and centuries of popular tradition, and most maps and paintings, quietly upgraded it to the second.

Ararat corresponds to Urartu, a real historical kingdom attested in Assyrian records, centered on the highlands around Lake Van in what is now eastern Turkey, Armenia, and northwestern Iran, roughly the ninth through sixth centuries BC. The Hebrew names a mountainous region, not a single summit; the specific volcanic peak now called Mount Ararat received that name only later, as a traditional identification laid onto the biblical region rather than a claim the text itself makes.

English the mountains of Ararat is grammatically plain, but centuries of art, hymnody, and geography teaching have collapsed the region into a single named mountain, an identification English readers absorb from culture rather than from the actual wording of the verse, which never narrows the landing site that far.

Check whether a familiar geographic identification is actually in the text or was supplied later by tradition. A named region in Hebrew narrative is not automatically a named peak, however confidently later maps draw it that way.

Every version renders the wording the same way, mountains, plural; that much is settled. The dispute, where there is one, is entirely about a post-biblical identification, whether the traditional Mount Ararat is the right guess for where in the ancient region of Urartu the ark actually came to rest, a question the Hebrew text does not itself try to answer.

versions.s: They pierced my hands and my feet, or like a lion. One letter, and it is the wrong length in some copies.

b.t: Almost every Christian English version reads pierced. Jewish publications read like a lion. The NIV footnotes both. The King James reads pierced without a note.

Imagine two letters in your alphabet that differ only by how far the stroke comes down. A tired copyist in poor light makes one slightly short, and four hundred years later two communities are arguing about what the sentence says. Nobody had to be dishonest for that to happen.

The Masoretic Text reads ka'ari, like a lion, which leaves the line with no verb. The Septuagint, the Peshitta, and Jerome's earlier Gallican Psalter (the version behind the standard Vulgate text) all read a verb meaning dug or pierced. A fragment from Nahal Hever, 5/6HevPs, dated to roughly the middle of the first century, has the word ending in a vav rather than a yod, which makes it a third-person plural verb.
The difference is a vav against a yod, two letters distinguished mainly by length. This is not a translation problem at all. It is a copying problem, and English can only report the outcome.

When two communities read the same verse in opposite directions, find out whether the disagreement is about meaning or about letters. Here it is letters, which makes it checkable rather than merely arguable.

The case for pierced: three ancient versions, the Nahal Hever fragment, the minority Masoretic notes, and the fact that the Masoretic reading leaves the clause without a verb. The case against: Nahal Hever is not Qumran and is later than the Qumran material, the fragment is faded and has been read both ways, the Targum supports the lion reading, and Aquila, Symmachus, and Jerome's later translation direct from the Hebrew (his Psalterium iuxta Hebraeos, a different edition from the Gallican Psalter cited above) all render the hands and feet as bound rather than pierced. Anyone who tells you this is closed has not read the other side.
כָּאֲרוּ / כָּאֲרִי ka'aru / ka'ari · H3738 / H738

Septuagint oruxan, they dug; Peshitta and Vulgate agree
Masoretic ka'ari, like a lion, with ka'aru in a minority of manuscripts and in the Masoretic notes
Kristin Swenson argues for the lion reading and disputes the legibility of the fragment

versions.s: Naked, and not ashamed. Then: the serpent was more crafty. Two words that are near-twins in Hebrew.

b.t: Every version reads naked at 2:25 and crafty, subtil, or shrewd at 3:1, two ordinary, unrelated-sounding English words. None can show that the Hebrew words are built from nearly the same consonants.

Imagine a story ending one scene with **the couple was bare** and opening the next with **the snake was rare**. You would hear the echo instantly. Hebrew does exactly that with naked and crafty, and English naked and crafty do not rhyme at all.

Arummim, naked, at 2:25 and arum, crafty, at 3:1 share three of their root letters and are near-homonyms in Hebrew, even though most lexicons trace them to distinct roots. The narrator sets the pair back to back on purpose: the humans are arummim and unashamed, and the next creature introduced is arum, using almost the same sound to introduce the opposite of innocence.

English naked and crafty share no sound at all, so a reader moving from 2:25 to 3:1 gets no auditory cue that the story is doing wordplay across the chapter break. The literary hinge the Hebrew builds the scene transition on disappears entirely.

Chapter and verse divisions are medieval additions, not part of the original text. Read straight across a chapter break before assuming the scene has fully changed; sometimes the Hebrew is still finishing a sound, if not a sentence.

No real translation dispute; naked and crafty are both correct. What is worth flagging is that the pun connecting them is a genuine literary feature invisible in every English Bible, not a stretch imposed after the fact.

versions.s: He was put in a coffin in Egypt. The Hebrew word, aron, is the same word later used for the Ark of the Covenant.

b.t: Every version reads coffin, correctly, since English has no reason to use the same word it will later use for the Ark of the Covenant, severing a connection the Hebrew text itself preserves by repeating the identical noun.

English keeps coffin and ark as entirely separate words, one for the dead, one for the sacred. Hebrew aron names both a burial box and the gold-covered chest holding the covenant tablets, the very same noun doing both jobs, so Genesis closes with a word it will not fully cash in until Exodus and beyond.

Aron names Joseph's coffin here, the very first occurrence of the word anywhere in the Bible, and the same word later names the Ark of the Covenant carrying the tablets of the law through the wilderness. Jewish tradition already noticed the parallel: two arons traveled with Israel through the wilderness, one holding the bones of the dead Joseph, the other holding the covenant of the living God, Joseph's own bones eventually carried out of Egypt at the Exodus and buried in the promised land.

English coffin and ark share no sound or spelling at all, so the deliberate closing image, Genesis ending on the same word its sequel will use for its most sacred object, is entirely invisible without knowing the underlying Hebrew noun is identical in both cases.

Pay attention to a book's very last word as carefully as its first. Genesis opens with bereshit, a word already carrying interpretive weight, and closes with aron, a word that will not detonate its full significance until much later in the story, a deliberate structural echo across the whole Torah.

Coffin is the correct sense here, and no version renders it otherwise. What matters is the word's later, much weightier reuse for the Ark of the Covenant, a connection built entirely into the Hebrew vocabulary, invisible the moment English gives the two objects two different names.

versions.s: Let us make. A plural announcement followed immediately by a singular act.

b.t: Every version reads let us make. The disagreement is entirely about who us refers to, and no translation can help.

**Let's build a shed.** **I built a shed.** The first sentence includes other people. The second says who swung the hammer. Both can be true of the same shed, and nobody thinks the second contradicts the first.

Na'aseh is a cohortative, the Hebrew form for let me or let us. Verse 27 then uses a singular verb three times. Whatever the plural is doing, it is not distributing the act of creating, because the next verse assigns that to one actor.
English let us is the same whether it includes an audience or is a royal flourish. Hebrew has a specific form, and the argument is about what that form is doing here.
When a verse is famous for one grammatical feature, find out what the next verse does with the same subject. Adjacent verses settle more arguments than lexicons do.

A plural of majesty has trouble with this verb form. A Trinitarian reading may be true and still does not describe what a first hearer understood. Address to a divine council explains the plural and leaves the singular in verse 27 intact. All three leave something unexplained, and this one leaves the least.

entries.title: astorgos
entries.where: astorgos is tagged 2 times, across 2 books: 2timothy 1 · romans 1.

versions.s: The only way storge appears in the New Testament is as a thing people have lost.

b.t: Modern versions read heartless, or unloving. All of them are rendering one negated word.

**Unfeeling** only exists because feeling does. You can learn a lot about what a group valued by which words they only ever use with un in front. Sometimes a language names a thing solely by pointing at its absence.

Astorgos is storge with an alpha privative in front of it, the Greek equivalent of the English un-. It occurs twice, both times inside a list diagnosing a society. Paul is not saying these people are unfriendly. He is saying the affection that ordinarily holds families together is gone.
English heartless and unloving are general. The Greek is specific: it names the failure of one particular kind of love, the kind nobody chooses and everybody is supposed to have by default.
A word can be present in a text only as a negative, and that is still evidence. When a translation gives you a broad word like heartless, check whether the Greek was negating something narrower.

Without natural affection, the King James rendering, is closer to the Greek and sounds archaic. Heartless is readable and loses the family reference. Both are defensible and the older one is more precise.
ἄστοργος astorgos · G794

src: Both occurrences: Romans 1:31; 2 Timothy 3:3
The alpha privative construction, as in agnostos, apistos, adikos

versions.s: One fold, and one shepherd. The Greek uses two different nouns and the King James uses one.

b.t: The King James reads one fold. Every modern version reads one flock.
**One pen** and **one herd** are not the same claim. One is about the enclosure. The other is about the animals.

The first noun in the verse is aule, a fold or enclosure. The second is poimne, a flock. The Greek says other sheep not of this aule, and they shall become one poimne, one shepherd. The King James printed fold for both, following the Vulgate's ovile.
English has both words. The error is not in the language but in the 1611 rendering, which follows the Latin rather than the Greek.
Where the King James follows the Vulgate against the Greek, a real correction is available and the modern versions have made it.
One flock is what modern versions overwhelmingly print, and outside the King James tradition the correction is universal.
αὐλή aule · G833 / ποίμνη poimne · G4167

src: aule at John 10:1, 16a
poimne at John 10:16b
Vulgate ovile for both; the King James follows it

versions.s: Iniquity. The act, the guilt, and the consequence, in one noun.

b.t: Versions read iniquity, guilt, or punishment according to context.
**He'll pay for that.** English fuses the offence and the consequence in an idiom. Hebrew fuses them in a noun.
Avon is from a root meaning bent or twisted. It covers the crooked act, the guilt incurred, and the punishment that follows, and Hebrew does not mark which is meant.
English separates deed, guilt and penalty into different words, so a sentence that means all three reads as ambiguous rather than as compressed.
When a translation footnote offers punishment as an alternative to guilt, the word is probably covering both and the sentence may not be choosing.
Iniquity is the majority rendering; guilt and punishment appear where context forces them.

versions.s: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. Or: unto the hills, where does my help come from?

b.t: Older versions read the line as a statement, help comes from the hills, treating the hills favorably. Most modern versions instead punctuate it as a question, where does my help come from, deliberately setting up verse 2's answer, my help cometh from the LORD, as a correction or clarification.

English needs a question mark to signal a question; Hebrew, written originally without any punctuation at all, relies on word order and interrogative particles that can be genuinely ambiguous. Read one way, the hills themselves are the source of help; read the other way, the hills are only where the question is asked, and the real answer follows in the next verse: the LORD.

Me'ayin, from where, functions grammatically as an interrogative in Hebrew, supporting the question reading, though older translation tradition read the sentence as a simple declarative statement instead. Read as a question, the psalm sets up a deliberate contrast: looking toward the hills, which in the ancient Near East were often associated with pagan high places and local shrines, only to answer that true help comes not from the hills themselves but from the LORD who made them.

English readers of the older, statement-based translation hear the hills themselves credited as a source of help; readers of the modern question-based translation instead hear the psalm posing a question it deliberately answers in the very next line, a considerably different rhetorical structure with real theological stakes about where help actually originates.

When Hebrew poetry lacks the punctuation cues English relies on, check whether an interrogative particle like me'ayin is present and whether reading the line as a question versus a statement changes the passage's theological logic. The difference is not merely stylistic.

Reading the opening line as a statement credits the hills themselves as a source of help, an older but now less favored translation tradition. Reading it as a question, now the dominant modern approach, sets up a pointed contrast with verse 2's answer, redirecting help away from the hills and toward the LORD who made them.
מֵאַיִן יָבֹא עֶזְרִי me'ayin yavo ezri (from where does my help come) · H370

versions.s: Keep me as the apple of the eye. Literally, the little man, or the daughter of the eye: the pupil.

b.t: Every version reads apple of the eye, correctly preserving the sense, precious and closely guarded, but the actual images behind the Hebrew words, a tiny reflected person, a daughter, are entirely absent from apple, which has no connection to eyes in ordinary English at all.

Look closely into someone's eye and you will see a tiny reflection of yourself in the dark center. Hebrew names that reflection ishon, a little man, and calls the pupil itself bat ayin, daughter of the eye. English apple has nothing to do with either image; it entered the phrase only because Old English speakers happened to also call the pupil an apple, for its round shape.

Ishon, commonly translated pupil here, more literally means little man, describing the miniature reflected image visible in someone's eye when you look closely into it; bat ayin, daughter of the eye, is a separate Hebrew idiom for the same part of the eye. English apple entered this specific phrase from Old English, itself a separate, unrelated tradition of calling the pupil an apple for its round shape, coincidentally landing near enough in sense to survive translation even though it shares no image with the Hebrew at all.

English apple of the eye is now a fixed idiom meaning precious and beloved, entirely detached from any eye-related image for most speakers; it happens to preserve roughly the right sentiment while completely replacing the Hebrew's actual pictures, a tiny reflected person, a daughter, with a fruit that has nothing to do with either.

A translated idiom that still works can hide the fact that its underlying image has been entirely swapped out. Check what the original words are actually picturing, not just whether the resulting English phrase still makes emotional sense.

No translation dispute over the sentiment, precious and closely guarded. The entry exists because apple of the eye survives as a working English idiom purely by coincidence of separate traditions, not because it translates the Hebrew's actual images of a little reflected man or a daughter of the eye.
