versions.s: The Canaanite was then in the land. The word then implies the writer already knows a time when the Canaanite was not.

b.t: Every version reads was then in the land, correctly translating az, then, but the English reader does not necessarily catch that the word implies a later vantage point the way careful readers of the Hebrew, ancient and modern alike, have.

If a modern account said **the mill was then still standing on Main Street**, you would assume the writer already knew it later burned down. The word then does that work quietly, and Genesis uses it exactly the same way about the Canaanites.

Az, then, at this point, most naturally implies a contrast with the narrator's own time, when the Canaanite was no longer in the land, a condition that only obtained centuries after the events described, once Israel had taken the territory. The twelfth-century Jewish commentator Ibn Ezra was already flagging this phrase, along with several others, as evidence that at least some material in the Torah could not have been written by Moses in its final form, a genuinely old observation rather than a modern critical invention.

English then carries the same implication English readers would recognize in any other narrative, but Bible readers often do not pause to apply ordinary reading habits to a text they assume was written entirely at the time of the events it describes.

Read a small time-marking word like then the same way you would read it in any other narrative: as a signal about the writer's vantage point relative to the events, not only about the events themselves. Doing so here raises a genuine, old, and unresolved authorship question rather than settling one.

Reading then as an ordinary editorial aside, whether by Moses or a later editorial hand within an otherwise Mosaic Torah, treats the note as a minor updating gloss. Reading it as evidence of substantially later authorship is a larger claim the single word alone cannot carry by itself, though it has carried real interpretive weight since well before modern critical scholarship existed.

versions.s: Therefore is the name of it called Babel, because the LORD did there confound. A pun that mocks the city's own name for itself.

b.t: Every version reads Babel and confounded or confused, correctly translating both, but with no way to show that the connection between them is a pun rather than an actual derivation, since Babel is simply carried over as a name in English.

Imagine a city calling itself **Gateway**, and a rival nation nicknaming it **Gatecrash**, close enough in sound to land the joke, and different enough in meaning to be an insult. That is exactly the move Genesis makes with Babel and the Hebrew word for confuse.

In Akkadian, the city's own language, Babel is bab-ilu, gate of god, the name Babylon proudly gave itself as the meeting place of heaven and earth. Genesis instead connects the name to the unrelated Hebrew root balal, to confuse or mix up, close enough in sound to register as deliberate wordplay, not a genuine etymology. The Hebrew narrator takes Babylon's own grand self-description and replaces it with mockery, using the empire's most famous city as the counter-example to the naming device used positively for Peleg and Noah earlier in the same block of chapters.

English Babel is simply a transliterated proper name carrying no built-in meaning either way, so an English reader cannot hear either the Akkadian gate of god the city claimed for itself or the Hebrew confusion the narrator substitutes for it.

When Genesis renames a place or a person with a pun rather than an etymology, ask what the original, often foreign, name was claiming, and read the Hebrew pun as a deliberate answer to that claim rather than a neutral linguistic note.

Confounded is the settled sense of balal in every version. The polemical edge, that this pun specifically answers and undercuts Babylon's own proud self-naming, is a matter of reading Genesis against its ancient Near Eastern background, not a textual question translation alone can resolve.

versions.s: Kiss the Son. Or: kiss purely, do homage in purity. The word bar is Aramaic for son, but also Hebrew for grain, clean, or pure.

b.t: The King James reads kiss the Son, capitalizing it as a messianic title. Some Jewish translations and a number of scholarly treatments read kiss purely, or do homage in purity, treating bar as the Hebrew word for pure or clean rather than as an Aramaic loanword.

Imagine a poem written in English that suddenly drops in a French word for exactly one line, close enough in spelling to an ordinary English word that readers argue for centuries about which one was meant. That is the situation with bar here: an Aramaic loanword for son, or a Hebrew word for purity, spelled almost the same way.

Bar, in Aramaic, is the ordinary word for son, used throughout Aramaic portions of Daniel and Ezra; the same consonants in Hebrew mean grain, or, adjectivally, pure or clean. The rest of the psalm, including verse 7's begotten language, uses the ordinary Hebrew ben for son, making bar's sudden appearance here either a deliberate, striking Aramaism, possibly chosen for its impact on Gentile kings who would have understood Aramaic, or simply the ordinary Hebrew word for purity, unrelated to sonship at all.

English Son capitalizes and commits to the Aramaic-loanword reading; English purity commits to the alternative Hebrew reading entirely. A translator must choose one, permanently closing off the other possibility that the bare Hebrew consonants themselves leave genuinely open.

When a single word could belong to two different languages sharing a script, check whether the surrounding text is otherwise consistent in its language choices. An isolated switch, as bar would be here, is unusual enough to weigh both directions seriously rather than defaulting to whichever reading a translation tradition has already settled on.

Kiss the Son fits the psalm's messianic trajectory and its influential place in later messianic reading, but requires accepting an isolated Aramaic loanword in an otherwise Hebrew composition. Kiss purely or do homage in purity keeps the whole psalm in consistent Hebrew vocabulary but loses the direct filial title some later interpreters, and much later devotional tradition, have built upon this verse.
נַשְּׁקוּ־בַר nashequ bar (בַּר bar, Aramaic 'son' / Hebrew 'pure') · H1247 / H1249

src: bar as the ordinary Aramaic word for son: Daniel 3:25; Ezra 5:1-2
The rest of Psalm 2 using Hebrew ben for son, e.g. verse 7
Jewish tradition and the Targum both favor the 'purity' reading, while the Septuagint and the Christian tradition that follows it favor 'son'

versions.s: Created. A verb with only one possible subject in the whole Hebrew Bible.

b.t: Every version reads created. No dispute about the rendering, and a long dispute about what the verb implies.

Imagine an English verb that only ever takes one subject. Nobody else in the language is allowed to do it. You would learn a lot about what the writers thought of that subject just from the grammar, before anyone made an argument.

Bara occurs around fifty times and God is the subject every single time. Humans never bara anything. The word says nothing on its own about whether material already existed; that argument runs through other verses and through later theology, not through this verb.
English create is used of anyone. A novelist creates a character, a chef creates a dish. The exclusivity is invisible in translation because English has no reserved verb.
Before deciding what a word means, check who is allowed to do it. Subject restriction is one of the strongest signals a language gives about a word's weight.
Nothing is disputed in translation. What is disputed is whether bara implies creation from nothing, and the honest answer is that the verb alone does not settle it.
בָּרָא bara · H1254

src: bara with God as subject throughout: Genesis 1:21, 27; 2:3; Isaiah 40:26; 45:7
Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One, argues bara concerns function rather than material (the dissent)
No occurrence of bara with a human subject exists in the Hebrew Bible

versions.s: Create in me a clean heart. The verb is the one only God is ever allowed to do.

b.t: All versions read create. The reservation of the verb cannot be shown and is not footnoted anywhere.
If a language had one verb reserved for a single person, and a petitioner used it about himself, you would notice. In English the same request reads as a polite way of saying please change me.

Bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1, used around fifty times and never with a human subject. David is not asking for improvement. He is asking for the creation verb to be used on him, which is a request for something that does not yet exist rather than repair of something damaged. Lev here is the seat of thought and will, the same word as the Shema.
English create is used of anyone and anything. There is no way to signal that a verb is restricted, so the echo of the first sentence of the Bible simply does not survive.
When a psalm uses an unusual verb, check where else that verb appears. Hebrew poets quote Genesis constantly and almost never announce it.
Nothing to choose. Create is correct and carries none of the weight.

versions.s: In thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. Passive, or reflexive: blessed through you, or blessing themselves by your name.

b.t: Every English version reads a passive sense, shall be blessed, following the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Targums, and this is the reading Paul follows in Galatians 3:8, applying it to the gospel reaching the nations through Christ.

English **he was blessed** is passive, something done to him. English **he blessed himself** is reflexive, something he does using himself as the reference point, the way people still say **as rich as Rockefeller** without Rockefeller doing anything for them personally. Hebrew's one verb form here could be doing either job.

The niphal stem of barakh here can carry a passive sense, will be blessed, or, as niphal sometimes does, a reflexive-reciprocal sense, will bless themselves or one another. When the same promise recurs at Genesis 22:18 and 26:4, it switches to the hitpael stem, which leans more clearly reflexive, nations invoking Abraham's name as a byword for blessing, you have done well, like Abraham, rather than nations passively receiving blessing through him.

English must choose one grammatical voice, passive or reflexive, and commit to it in translation, while Hebrew's niphal here sits genuinely between the two senses in a way no single English verb form preserves, so a reader cannot see that the promise's later restatements shift toward the more clearly reflexive stem.

When a Hebrew verb stem is capable of more than one voice, check whether the same promise or phrase recurs elsewhere in a different stem. A later restatement in a less ambiguous form, as with the hitpael at 22:18 and 26:4, is real evidence for how an earlier ambiguous form might have been heard.

The passive reading, blessed through Abraham as an active channel, is the traditional and Pauline reading and fits the covenant's forward momentum toward a Messiah. The reflexive reading, nations blessing themselves by invoking Abraham's name, fits the hitpael restatements later in Genesis and does not require Abraham to be an active agent of anyone else's blessing, only a byword for it.

versions.s: The iron entered into his soul. The Hebrew more literally reads his soul came into iron, a difficult phrase ancient translators handled differently.

b.t: Most versions read some form of describing Joseph's affliction in prison, his feet hurt with fetters, his neck or person constrained by iron, with varying degrees of literalness about the famous his soul entered iron phrase.

English the iron entered into his soul is now a familiar idiom for deep inner anguish, but it is also a slightly unusual translation choice: the Hebrew word order more literally has his soul entering iron, not the other way around, a small but real difference ancient translators noticed and handled in at least three different ways.

The Hebrew reads nephesh, soul, life, or person, as entering into iron, backward from the more intuitive image of iron entering a person. The Syriac keeps this direction, his soul went into iron; the Aramaic Targum reverses it, the chain of iron went into his soul; the widely beloved English phrase, the iron entered into his soul, popularized through the Book of Common Prayer, follows the Targum's reversed direction rather than the more literal Hebrew word order.

English readers who know the phrase the iron entered into his soul as a beautiful, familiar idiom for suffering may not realize the phrase's exact grammatical direction was already being debated and reversed by ancient translators, since the literal Hebrew has the person entering the iron, not the iron entering the person.

When a beloved, idiomatic English Bible phrase sounds too poetically perfect to be a plain translation, check its actual grammatical direction against the Hebrew. Some of the most famous English biblical phrases, like this one, already represent an ancient interpretive choice rather than a purely literal rendering.

His soul entered into iron, closer to the literal Hebrew word order, pictures Joseph's whole self being absorbed into confinement. The iron entered into his soul, the beloved reversed idiom following the Targum, pictures suffering piercing inward instead, the version that became proverbial in English despite reversing the Hebrew's own direction.

src: Syriac Peshitta keeping the Hebrew's direction, 'his soul went into iron'
Aramaic Targum reversing it, 'the chain of iron went into his soul'

versions.s: One flesh. A kinship word, not only a body word.

b.t: Every version reads one flesh, and the physical union is certainly included. What is harder to see in English is that basar for kinship is ordinary Hebrew usage on its own, not a special sense invented for this verse.

**He's my flesh and blood.** English keeps this sense alive for family, but only as a fixed idiom, sitting beside the ordinary meaning of flesh as tissue. Hebrew basar carries the kinship sense as one of its normal, everyday meanings, not as a leftover expression.

Basar, flesh, is used of blood relatives at Genesis 29:14, Judges 9:2, and 2 Samuel 5:1, where 'your bone and your flesh' means your relative, with no reference to sex or the body. One flesh at 2:24 draws on that same kinship vocabulary: the man and woman become each other's next of kin, a new family unit, with the physical union as the sign of that bond rather than its entire content.

English flesh has narrowed mostly to the physical body, with flesh and blood surviving only as a fixed idiom for family. Hebrew basar keeps both senses live at once, so a single English reading tends to collapse the verse into the physical union alone.
When a body-part or body-substance word appears in a covenant or family context, check whether the same word carries a kinship sense elsewhere before assuming only the physical meaning is in view.

One flesh is not in dispute as a translation. The question is emphasis: whether the phrase is chiefly about sexual union, chiefly about kinship status, or, as the parallel usage suggests, both at once by design.

versions.s: Flesh, body, meat, and by extension kinship and human frailty.

b.t: Versions read flesh, body, meat, or people according to context.
**My own flesh and blood.** English does the kinship sense already and nobody hears anatomy in it.
Basar is meat, the body, and all living creatures collectively, as in all flesh. The kinship sense at Genesis 2:24 and 29:14 is ordinary. Weakness rather than sinfulness is the moral edge it carries.
English flesh keeps the physical and the kinship senses, so most of the range survives; what does not survive is the collective sense of all living things.
A New Testament word with a Hebrew word standing behind it deserves a look at that Hebrew range before you credit the Greek writer with inventing the usage.
Flesh is the majority rendering.

versions.s: Kingdom. Closer to kingship or reign than to a territory.

b.t: Every version reads kingdom. A minority of study notes offer reign or rule.
**During the reign of Elizabeth.** **Across the kingdom.** English has both a rule word and a place word. Greek leans on the first.
Basileia can be a realm, but its primary force is the exercise of kingship. The Aramaic and Hebrew behind the Gospel phrase point the same way.
English kingdom is overwhelmingly territorial, so a phrase about God's reign arriving reads as a phrase about a place being established.
When an abstract noun in English sounds like a location, check whether the original was an activity. Rule words and place words drift into each other in every language.
Kingdom is the majority rendering by a wide margin and no major version has replaced it.

versions.s: Keep me as the apple of the eye. Literally, the little man, or the daughter of the eye: the pupil.

b.t: Every version reads apple of the eye, correctly preserving the sense, precious and closely guarded, but the actual images behind the Hebrew words, a tiny reflected person, a daughter, are entirely absent from apple, which has no connection to eyes in ordinary English at all.

Look closely into someone's eye and you will see a tiny reflection of yourself in the dark center. Hebrew names that reflection ishon, a little man, and calls the pupil itself bat ayin, daughter of the eye. English apple has nothing to do with either image; it entered the phrase only because Old English speakers happened to also call the pupil an apple, for its round shape.

Ishon, commonly translated pupil here, more literally means little man, describing the miniature reflected image visible in someone's eye when you look closely into it; bat ayin, daughter of the eye, is a separate Hebrew idiom for the same part of the eye. English apple entered this specific phrase from Old English, itself a separate, unrelated tradition of calling the pupil an apple for its round shape, coincidentally landing near enough in sense to survive translation even though it shares no image with the Hebrew at all.

English apple of the eye is now a fixed idiom meaning precious and beloved, entirely detached from any eye-related image for most speakers; it happens to preserve roughly the right sentiment while completely replacing the Hebrew's actual pictures, a tiny reflected person, a daughter, with a fruit that has nothing to do with either.

A translated idiom that still works can hide the fact that its underlying image has been entirely swapped out. Check what the original words are actually picturing, not just whether the resulting English phrase still makes emotional sense.

No translation dispute over the sentiment, precious and closely guarded. The entry exists because apple of the eye survives as a working English idiom purely by coincidence of separate traditions, not because it translates the Hebrew's actual images of a little reflected man or a daughter of the eye.

entries.lemmaLine: beer sheba  ·  בְּאֵר שֶׁבַע  ·  Strong’s H884

versions.s: Beersheba, well of the oath, or well of seven. One root, sheva, carries both meanings.

b.t: Every version reads Beersheba as a transliterated place name, or occasionally glosses it well of the oath, capturing one half of the pun but not the other, since English seven and swear share no etymology at all.

Imagine a place named **Sevenswear**, where the same syllable meant both the number of witnesses paid and the promise itself. English would need two separate words, seven and swear, sharing no sound. Hebrew's sheva does both jobs with one root.

Be'er sheva combines be'er, well, with sheva, a root meaning both seven, the number of ewe lambs Abraham gives Abimelech as witness to the treaty, and the verb shava, to swear an oath, the very act the two men perform at that well. The name commemorates both the seven animals and the oath in a single word, a deliberate double meaning built into the place's Hebrew name.

English seven and swear are entirely unrelated words with no shared sound, so a place name built on their shared Hebrew root cannot be translated into English without either picking one sense and losing the other, or transliterating the name and losing both.

When a place name is explained in the surrounding narrative, as Beersheba is here, check whether the explanation is drawing on more than one sense of the underlying root. Hebrew etiological place names frequently carry a double meaning that a single English gloss cannot hold at once.

Beersheba as a transliterated name draws no disagreement. Well of the oath and well of seven are both correct halves of a single Hebrew pun; English simply cannot say both at once the way the one Hebrew root does.
בְּאֵר שֶׁבַע Be'er Sheva (שֶׁבַע sheva, seven / שָׁבַע shava, swear) · H884

src: The seven ewe lambs as witness: Genesis 21:28-30
The oath itself: Genesis 21:31
The same double meaning noted again when Isaac's servants dig a well there: Genesis 26:33

versions.s: The sons of God saw the daughters of men. The oldest reading takes sons of God as divine beings, not a human family line.

b.t: Most modern versions read sons of God without further comment, leaving the identification to footnotes or study notes. The King James likewise reads sons of God, unglossed.

English son of can mean a literal child or a member of a category, **son of the soil**, **sons of thunder**. Hebrew bene elohim works the same way, and here the category in view, sons of the divine realm, is a real option English son of does not rule out but does not spell out either.

Bene elohim and the singular ben elohim identify members of the divine council elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, at Job 1:6, 2:1, 38:7, and Psalm 89:6, all contexts where no one reads the phrase as human beings. The earliest interpreters, including the Septuagint tradition, 1 Enoch, and Jubilees, took Genesis 6:2 the same way, as heavenly beings intermarrying with humans. The alternative, that sons of God means the righteous line of Seth marrying Cain's corrupted daughters, is a later reading associated with Julius Africanus and Augustine, developed in reaction against the angelic view rather than growing from Hebrew usage of the phrase itself.

English sons of God carries no built-in link to a divine council, an idea unfamiliar to most modern readers, so the phrase reads as loosely poetic rather than as a technical term with a fixed range of reference elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible.

Before deciding what a phrase means in one passage, survey every other place the same phrase occurs in the same corpus. Bene elohim is not ambiguous where it appears elsewhere; the ambiguity here is imported by later theological discomfort with what those other passages already say.

The divine-council reading is both the oldest attested interpretation and the one that matches every other biblical use of the phrase. The Sethite reading, sons of God as godly men, has no other biblical use of the phrase to support it and arose specifically to avoid the angelic implications, which makes it weaker as a reading of the Hebrew even though it became dominant in later Western Christianity.
בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים bene ha'elohim · H1121 + H430

src: Bene elohim / bene ha'elohim as divine-council beings: Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7; Psalm 89:6
1 Enoch and Jubilees read Genesis 6:2 as fallen divine beings; so does the Septuagint tradition and Josephus
The Sethite view associated with Julius Africanus and developed by Augustine, City of God 15.23

versions.s: The steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus. A rare word, ben-meshek, that nobody fully agrees on.

b.t: Most versions read steward of my house or heir of my house, smoothing the phrase into a clear English office. A few older or more literal renderings preserve more of the Hebrew's actual strangeness.

Imagine a legal document naming an heir with a title so unusual that lawyers today still argue whether it means owner, manager, or errand-runner. That is roughly the situation with ben-meshek here, a phrase modern translations gloss confidently while quietly disagreeing about what it actually names.

Ben-meshek is unusual enough that proposals range from son of acquisition, meaning the one who will inherit, to a verb related to running about in service, to reading meshek as a proper name, Masek, making Eliezer the son of a servant woman by that name rather than a household title at all. Many scholars additionally note that ben-meshek was likely chosen partly for its assonance with the following word, Dammesek, Damascus, a wordplay layered on top of an already rare and difficult phrase.

English steward reads as a clear, ordinary job title; the Hebrew phrase behind it is contested enough that no single English word can represent the genuine uncertainty scholars still have about what ben-meshek names.

When a translation reads smoothly and confidently, check whether the underlying Hebrew is actually that clear. A fluent English rendering can paper over real uncertainty that specialists are still debating.

Steward or heir of my house gives English readers a working sense of the passage without pretending to settle a genuinely contested phrase. No consensus exists on ben-meshek's precise force, and every translation is making a judgment call the Hebrew itself does not fully support.
בֶּן־מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי ben-meshek beythi · H1121 + H4943

src: The proposed assonance with Dammesek, Damascus: noted in Jewish Bible Quarterly and standard commentaries
Alternative readings, heir/owner vs. a servant's proper name Masek: surveyed in major Genesis commentaries

versions.s: Ascribe unto the LORD, O ye mighty. Literally, sons of the elim, gods, the divine council again.

b.t: Most versions read O ye mighty, sons of the mighty, or heavenly beings, a range reflecting real disagreement about how directly to render bene elim's divine-council background into English.

English mighty ones reads as a vague compliment, powerful people or important figures. Bene elim is the same technical phrase already met describing heavenly beings surrounding God's throne, an audience of gods, not an audience of impressive humans, being summoned to worship.

Bene elim, sons of the elim, gods, occurs only here and at Psalm 89:6, and closely parallels the Canaanite divine-council phrase sons of El attested in Ugaritic mythological texts, where it names the assembly of lesser gods surrounding the high god El. The psalm opens by summoning this same heavenly assembly, not human worshippers, to acknowledge the LORD's glory, the same divine-council imagery already met at Genesis 6:2 and Psalm 82:1.

English mighty ones or you heavenly beings both lose the specific technical weight bene elim carries as a recognized ancient Near Eastern divine-council term, so a reader cannot easily connect this opening line to the same council imagery running through Genesis 6, Psalm 82, and Psalm 89.

Track bene elohim, bene elim, and edat el, each a variant of the same divine-council phrase, across their several occurrences rather than treating each one as an isolated poetic flourish. The psalms and Genesis are drawing on one shared, coherent picture of a heavenly assembly.

Mighty ones or heavenly beings both work as general English glosses. Sons of the gods, or sons of the elim, kept closer to the Hebrew, more directly connects this opening summons to the same council-of-gods imagery already established at Genesis 6:2, Psalm 82:1, and Psalm 89:6.
בְּנֵי אֵלִים bene elim · H1121 + H410

src: The same phrase at Psalm 89:6
The Canaanite parallel, 'sons of El,' in Ugaritic divine-council texts
Psalm 82:1's edat el, council of El, as the closely related phrase

entries.def: Ben-Oni, the original name of Benjamin

versions.s: She called his name Ben-oni: but his father called him Benjamin. Son of my sorrow, overridden by son of the right hand.

b.t: Every version reads both names as given, Ben-oni and Benjamin, correctly, but without necessarily flagging how unusual it is, within the pattern established by every other Genesis naming scene, for a name to be immediately replaced rather than simply accepted.

Imagine a mother naming a baby **Sorrow** with her final breath, and the father immediately renaming him **Fortune** instead. Every other naming in Genesis stands as given; this is the one clear case where a name chosen at birth gets overturned within the same verse.

Ben-oni, built from oni, sorrow or trouble, is Rachel's last act, naming her son for the grief of her own death in childbirth. Jacob renames him Binyamin, son of the right hand, either honoring the boy's position as youngest, born in the south relative to the other sons, or invoking the right hand's ancient association with strength, honor, and good fortune. Every other name given in Genesis' many birth-naming scenes stands unchallenged; this is the sole instance where a second party immediately overrides the first name given.

English keeps both names as bare transliterations, so the fact that this is a genuine override, not simply two names offered for consideration, and the only one of its kind among Genesis's many birth-naming scenes, is invisible without knowing what oni and yamin actually mean.

When a Hebrew narrative gives two different names for the same person in immediate succession, check whether one is replacing the other rather than merely supplementing it. This is the only such override among Genesis's many birth namings, which makes it worth noticing rather than reading past as ordinary variation.

Both names are translated accurately by every version. What matters here is the override itself: a grieving mother's last word overturned by the surviving father, a meaningful structural break from the pattern set by every other naming scene in the book, a detail bare transliteration cannot flag on its own.

versions.s: The LORD made a covenant with Abram. Literally, cut a covenant, and the chapter just showed you the cutting.

b.t: Every version reads made a covenant, using English's own dead metaphor for finalizing an agreement, correctly conveying the sense but losing any connection to actual cutting.

English **cut a deal** is a dead metaphor; nobody pictures an actual knife. Hebrew **cut a covenant** started out exactly that literal, and Genesis 15 is the one chapter where you get to watch the literal cutting happen right before the idiom is used.

Karat berit, cut a covenant, is the standing Hebrew idiom for covenant-making throughout the Old Testament, and this chapter preserves the ritual behind the dead metaphor: animals are cut in half, and a smoking firepot and flaming torch, representing God, pass between the pieces, a self-maledictory oath in which walking between severed halves meant may I become like these animals if I break this covenant.

English cut a deal is used and heard purely figuratively, with no live memory of an actual cutting ceremony behind it. Hebrew karat berit sits closer to its literal origin, and this chapter is the rare place in the Bible where the idiom's backstory is narrated rather than merely assumed.

When you meet a fossilized idiom, cut a deal, cut a covenant, ask whether the Bible anywhere narrates the literal action the dead metaphor came from. Genesis 15 is exactly that kind of narration, and it is easy to read straight past it if you already think of covenant-making as an abstract legal event.

Translators aren't actually divided here; made a covenant is the only workable English rendering. This note is meant to reconnect the abstract English phrase to the concrete ritual Genesis 15 actually describes just before the idiom is used.
כָּרַת בְּרִית karat berit · H3772 + H1285

src: The ritual of cutting animals and passing between the pieces: Genesis 15:9-17
karat berit as the standard covenant-making idiom throughout the Hebrew Bible: e.g. Genesis 21:27, 32; 26:28; 31:44

versions.s: Covenant. A binding arrangement, and in Hebrew you cut one rather than make one.

b.t: Every version reads covenant. Some render treaty or agreement in political contexts.
**They struck a deal.** English keeps a physical verb in the idiom for making an agreement, and nobody is striking anything.

Berit is a binding arrangement with obligations, sanctions and often a ceremony. Hebrew says to cut a covenant, which refers to the animals divided at Genesis 15. The ancient Near Eastern treaty form sits behind Deuteronomy's structure.
English covenant survives only as a legal or religious word, so the physical ceremony behind the idiom is invisible.
When the original uses an unexpected verb with a noun, the verb is usually a fossil of a practice.
Covenant is universal in English versions; treaty appears in political contexts.
בְּרִית berit · H1285

src: karat berit, to cut a covenant: Genesis 15:18; Jeremiah 34:18
The divided animals at Genesis 15:9-17

versions.s: She called his name Ben-oni: but his father called him Benjamin. Son of my sorrow, overridden by son of the right hand.

b.t: Every version reads both names as given, Ben-oni and Benjamin, correctly, but without necessarily flagging how unusual it is, within the pattern established by every other Genesis naming scene, for a name to be immediately replaced rather than simply accepted.

Imagine a mother naming a baby **Sorrow** with her final breath, and the father immediately renaming him **Fortune** instead. Every other naming in Genesis stands as given; this is the one clear case where a name chosen at birth gets overturned within the same verse.

Ben-oni, built from oni, sorrow or trouble, is Rachel's last act, naming her son for the grief of her own death in childbirth. Jacob renames him Binyamin, son of the right hand, either honoring the boy's position as youngest, born in the south relative to the other sons, or invoking the right hand's ancient association with strength, honor, and good fortune. Every other name given in Genesis' many birth-naming scenes stands unchallenged; this is the sole instance where a second party immediately overrides the first name given.

English keeps both names as bare transliterations, so the fact that this is a genuine override, not simply two names offered for consideration, and the only one of its kind among Genesis's many birth-naming scenes, is invisible without knowing what oni and yamin actually mean.

When a Hebrew narrative gives two different names for the same person in immediate succession, check whether one is replacing the other rather than merely supplementing it. This is the only such override among Genesis's many birth namings, which makes it worth noticing rather than reading past as ordinary variation.

Both names are translated accurately by every version. What matters here is the override itself: a grieving mother's last word overturned by the surviving father, a meaningful structural break from the pattern set by every other naming scene in the book, a detail bare transliteration cannot flag on its own.
בֶּן־אוֹנִי Ben-oni (אוֹן on, sorrow) / בִּנְיָמִין Binyamin (יָמִין yamin, right hand) · H1126 / H1144

src: oni as sorrow or trouble: standard Hebrew lexicons
yamin's association with strength and honor: Psalm 118:15-16; Exodus 15:6

versions.s: The iron entered into his soul. The Hebrew more literally reads his soul came into iron, a difficult phrase ancient translators handled differently.

b.t: Most versions read some form of describing Joseph's affliction in prison, his feet hurt with fetters, his neck or person constrained by iron, with varying degrees of literalness about the famous his soul entered iron phrase.

English the iron entered into his soul is now a familiar idiom for deep inner anguish, but it is also a slightly unusual translation choice: the Hebrew word order more literally has his soul entering iron, not the other way around, a small but real difference ancient translators noticed and handled in at least three different ways.

The Hebrew reads nephesh, soul, life, or person, as entering into iron, backward from the more intuitive image of iron entering a person. The Syriac keeps this direction, his soul went into iron; the Aramaic Targum reverses it, the chain of iron went into his soul; the widely beloved English phrase, the iron entered into his soul, popularized through the Book of Common Prayer, follows the Targum's reversed direction rather than the more literal Hebrew word order.

English readers who know the phrase the iron entered into his soul as a beautiful, familiar idiom for suffering may not realize the phrase's exact grammatical direction was already being debated and reversed by ancient translators, since the literal Hebrew has the person entering the iron, not the iron entering the person.

When a beloved, idiomatic English Bible phrase sounds too poetically perfect to be a plain translation, check its actual grammatical direction against the Hebrew. Some of the most famous English biblical phrases, like this one, already represent an ancient interpretive choice rather than a purely literal rendering.

His soul entered into iron, closer to the literal Hebrew word order, pictures Joseph's whole self being absorbed into confinement. The iron entered into his soul, the beloved reversed idiom following the Targum, pictures suffering piercing inward instead, the version that became proverbial in English despite reversing the Hebrew's own direction.
בַּרְזֶל בָּאָה נַפְשׁוֹ barzel ba'ah naphsho (his soul came into iron) · H1270 + H935 + H5315

src: Syriac Peshitta keeping the Hebrew's direction, 'his soul went into iron'
Aramaic Targum reversing it, 'the chain of iron went into his soul'

versions.s: Feed my lambs, tend my sheep. Four words vary, not two.

b.t: No version distinguishes any of the pairs, because English has one word for each.
A writer who swaps four pairs of words in three sentences is avoiding repetition. A writer who swaps one is making a point.
Three pairs beyond the love verbs: bosko and poimaino for feed and tend, arnia and probata for lambs and sheep, oida and ginosko for know. All four variations run through the same exchange.
English has one word for each pair, so all four variations vanish and only the first is ever preached.
Before building on one word change, count the others in the same passage. Four is a style. One is an argument.
Feed and take care of are the majority renderings; no version marks any of the pairs.
βόσκω bosko · G1006 / ποιμαίνω poimaino · G4165

versions.s: I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God. Histopheph, a verb used only here, meaning to sit at the threshold.

b.t: Every version reads doorkeeper, stand at the threshold, or a similar phrase, generally capturing the sense of humble proximity, though the King James's doorkeeper implies an active job the rare verb does not specifically require.

English doorkeeper names a job, someone who controls who comes and goes. The rarer Hebrew verb behind it more literally pictures simply sitting on the threshold itself, not necessarily working there, just being allowed to occupy that lowest, humblest spot at the edge of the sanctuary rather than dwelling comfortably inside wickedness.

Histopheph, from a root connected to saph, threshold, occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, making its precise nuance a matter of informed inference rather than confirmed usage. Its likely sense is simply to sit or linger at the threshold, a posture of humble access rather than active employment as a gatekeeper, fittingly written in a psalm attributed to the sons of Korah, whose own hereditary role was guarding the tabernacle's entrances.

English doorkeeper suggests active employment, a job with responsibilities; the rarer Hebrew verb's likely sense, simply sitting at the threshold, pictures something more passive and humble, being allowed to remain at the edge rather than performing a role, a real difference in what the psalmist is actually preferring.

When a hapax legomenon is translated with a confident-sounding English job title, check whether the Hebrew root actually specifies an occupation or simply a posture or location. Doorkeeper implies more active duty than sit at the threshold does.

Doorkeeper is the traditional, vivid English rendering, fitting the Korahite family's actual temple role. Sit at the threshold, closer to the verb's probable root sense, emphasizes humble proximity over active employment, a subtly different, more passive picture of what the psalmist says he would prefer.

versions.s: Selah. A notation appearing seventy-one times in the Psalms whose exact meaning nobody today can confirm.

b.t: Every version simply transliterates Selah rather than translating it, since there is no settled English equivalent, a rare case where a whole word is left untouched precisely because its meaning cannot be pinned down.

Imagine a symbol printed seventy times across a hymnal that every choir director interprets slightly differently, some reading it as a rest, some as a key change, some as a cue to raise their voices, because nobody alive actually knows what the symbol's original composer meant by it. That is Selah's situation today.

Selah occurs seventy-one times in the Psalms and three more in Habakkuk, almost always in poems marked for a choirmaster or musical performance, strongly suggesting some kind of musical or liturgical function: a pause, a musical interlude, a signal to raise the volume or change key, a cue for the singers or a physical gesture like prostration. No single explanation commands scholarly consensus, and the word's precise etymology remains debated.

English readers meet Selah as an untranslated word sitting inconspicuously at the end of a verse, easy to skip entirely, with no built-in signal of how significant, or how genuinely mysterious, that one word actually is to specialists who have studied it for centuries without settling its meaning.

A transliterated word that recurs dozens of times across a book, rather than being translated even loosely, is often a strong signal of real uncertainty, not merely a technical term everyone already understands. Selah is one of the clearest examples of this pattern anywhere in the Bible.

No English translation is offered by any major version, appropriately, given the genuine uncertainty. Whether Selah functioned as a pause, an instrumental interlude, a dynamic marking, or a congregational cue remains an open question that seventy-one occurrences have not resolved.

versions.s: Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD. Or: then it became common, in a profaning sense, to call on that name.

b.t: Nearly every English version reads began, a positive account of the first public worship of God. This is the majority reading and the one nearly all translations print.

English **began** and English **profaned** share no letters and no sound; nobody would confuse them. The Hebrew word behind began shares its root with the word for profane, and which one this verse means is a live question, not a translator's typo.

Huchal is a hophal form that most naturally derives from chalal I, to begin, giving began to call. But chalal is also the root behind chalal III, to profane or defile, and at least one ancient Jewish reading, reflected in Rashi's comment, takes the verse in the profaning sense: it became common, in a degraded way, to invoke the LORD's name, fitting the chapter's downward arc from Cain through Lamech.

English has entirely separate words for began and profaned, so a translation must commit to one root or the other. Hebrew's two roots converge in this one conjugated form, huchal, so the ambiguity that troubles Hebrew readers is invisible the moment an English verb is chosen.

A Hebrew word that could derive from more than one root with unrelated meanings needs its immediate context checked, and the larger unit it sits in, not just the dictionary entry with the highest frequency. A chapter's overall trajectory, here Cain's line sliding toward Lamech's violence, can be genuine evidence for which root fits.

Began to call is the reading nearly every translation prints, treating the verse as a bright note of true worship starting early in human history. The profaning reading, held by Rashi and a minority of modern scholars, fits the chapter's decline from Cain to Lamech but requires choosing the rarer sense of a shared root against the grain of most translation tradition.

versions.s: Joy. Built on the same root as grace, which is not an accident.

b.t: Every version reads joy.
**Grateful** and **gratitude** and **gratis** all share a root in English, and you feel the connection without being taught it. Greek does the same with joy and gift.
Chara, joy, and charis, grace or gift, come from the same root, along with charisma and eucharisto, to give thanks. Joy in the New Testament is regularly the response to a gift rather than a mood.
English joy and grace have no shared root, so the family is invisible and has to be explained rather than heard.
Word families in the original language often do argumentative work. When two English words feel unrelated, check whether the originals were cousins.
Joy is universal.
χαρά chara · G5479

src: charis, chara, charisma and eucharisteo from one root

versions.s: Full of grace and truth. That is a Hebrew pair, and it comes from Exodus 34.

b.t: All English versions read grace and truth. None can show that the phrase is a quotation of a formula.

**Come good and early.** That is not two instructions. Good and early is one idea said with two words, and nobody hears it as a list. English does this and then forgets it does. Hebrew does it constantly.

Charis kai aletheia is widely taken as the Greek rendering of hesed we-emet, steadfast love and faithfulness, the pair God speaks over himself in Exodus 34:6 when Moses asks to see his glory. John has just said we beheld his glory. The allusion is to a specific scene.
English grace and truth reads as two abstract nouns joined by and. In Hebrew the pair is a fixed formula with a single referent, covenant loyalty, and the second word steadies the first.

When two abstract nouns are joined in the New Testament and both are common Septuagint words, check whether they are a Hebrew word-pair rather than two separate ideas. Hebrew often says one thing with two words.
Nothing in the translation is contested. What is contested is how firmly to press the Exodus 34 allusion, and the glory language in the same verse is the strongest argument for pressing it.
χάρις charis · G5485 / ἀλήθεια aletheia · G225

src: Exodus 34:6, rav hesed we-emet, in the Septuagint polyeleos kai alethinos
John 1:17 names Moses in the next verse, which supports the allusion

versions.s: He counted it to him for righteousness. The verb belongs in a ledger.

b.t: The King James reads counted. Modern versions read credited, reckoned or counted. Romans 4 uses the Greek equivalent eleven times in one chapter.

**Put it on my account.** That is a statement about a ledger, not about the truth of anything. Whether the entry reflects what is in your pocket is a separate question from whether the entry was made.

Chashav means to think, to plan, and also to reckon or impute in the bookkeeping sense. The Septuagint renders it logizomai, which is likewise an accounting verb, and that is the word Paul repeats through Romans 4. Two languages, the same commercial metaphor, deliberately kept.
English credited carries the accounting sense well. Reckoned has drifted toward supposed. Counted sits between them and is what the King James chose.
When the Septuagint picks a Greek word in the same semantic field as the Hebrew, that is a translator two thousand years ago telling you what he heard. Those choices are evidence.
No real dispute about the verb. What the accounting metaphor implies theologically is a separate and much older argument, and the verb does not settle it.
חָשַׁב chashav · H2803

src: chashav in the reckoning sense: Leviticus 7:18; 17:4; 2 Samuel 19:19
Septuagint logizomai here; the same verb eleven times in Romans 4
Psalm 32:2 uses chashav the same way and Paul quotes it at Romans 4:8

versions.s: Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. The same verb, chashav, reckon, used of Abraham's faith at 15:6.

b.t: Every version reads meant or intended, both reasonable general translations that lose the more technical, ledger-like flavor chashav carries, and its earlier, weightier use at 15:6.

English think and mean are ordinary, general verbs. Hebrew chashav is closer to an accountant's word, to reckon or calculate a value, and the same word used of God crediting Abraham's faith as righteousness earlier in Genesis is used twice in this one sentence, once for the brothers' malicious calculation, once for God's redemptive one.

Chashavtem alai ra'ah, chashvah l'tovah, you reckoned against me evil, He reckoned it for good, repeats the same root twice with opposite objects in one verse, the very verb rendered counted at Genesis 15:6, where the LORD counted Abraham's faith as righteousness. The whole Joseph narrative, and in a sense the whole patriarchal history Genesis has been tracking, closes on the same accounting vocabulary it used to describe the foundational moment of Abraham's faith.

English think and mean are colorless, general-purpose verbs; they do not preserve the specific, weighted accounting sense that ties Joseph's closing statement back to Abraham's reckoned faith fourteen chapters and several generations earlier in the same book.

When a book's final major statement repeats a rare or theologically loaded verb from earlier in the same book, read the recurrence as a deliberate bookend, not a coincidence of common vocabulary. Chashav's return here closes a loop opened at 15:6.

Meant or intended captures the sentence's plain sense, and every version agrees on that much. What matters is the specific word choice, chashav, which ties Joseph's closing theological statement about providence directly back to Abraham's reckoned faith, a connection no English synonym preserves.
חָשַׁב chashav · H2803

src: The same verb at Genesis 15:6, God reckoning Abraham's faith as righteousness
chashav's accounting/ledger sense: standard Hebrew lexicons

versions.s: Sin, and also the offering that deals with it. One word for both.

b.t: Versions read sin, sin offering, or purification offering according to context.
Imagine one word meaning both **the debt** and **the payment**. You would never have to explain the relationship between them.
Chatta't is the commonest Hebrew word for sin and is also the technical term for the offering prescribed in Leviticus. The verb behind it carries the sense of missing or failing.
Every time, English has to choose between sin and sin offering, and the choice hides that they are one word.
When one word names both a problem and its remedy, the language has built the solution into the vocabulary.
Sin and sin offering are both majority renderings in their own contexts; purification offering is a minority modern rendering.
חַטָּאת chatta't · H2403

src: chatta't as offering: Leviticus 4:3, 8, 20
chatta't as sin: Genesis 4:7; Psalm 51:2

versions.s: He called her Eve, because she was the mother of all living. The name means life.

b.t: Every English version keeps the King James's transliteration Eve, which carries no meaning to an English ear at all. The meaning survives only in the explanation the verse itself gives, never in the name.

Imagine naming a child **Hope** the same afternoon a doctor gives you bad news. The name itself is the argument: things are not only what they look like today. Adam names his wife Life immediately after hearing they will die.

Chavah, the Hebrew name behind Eve, is built on the same root as chayah, to live, and chay, living or alive, the same root supplying the explanation the verse itself gives, mother of all living. The name is chosen and explained in the same breath, directly after the curses of chapter 3, as if the verse insists on naming the source of ongoing life at the exact moment mortality is announced.

English Eve is a transliterated sound with no built-in meaning, so an English reader needs the verse's own explanation to know the name means anything at all. In Hebrew the name and its sense are nearly the same word, doing in one breath what English needs a whole clause to do.

Biblical names are rarely just labels; check whether a name is built on a live root before assuming it is only an identifier. Where the text supplies its own explanation for a name, as it does here, that is the author flagging a wordplay you would otherwise miss.

No translation dispute; Eve is the standard transliteration and every version explains the meaning in the clause that follows. This is here only because transliteration, unlike translation, necessarily strips the sense out of a name that was doing real work in Hebrew.
חַוָּה Chavah · H2332 (חָיָה chayah, to live · H2421)

src: Chavah built on the root chayah/chay, to live: standard in BDB and HALOT
The Genesis 3:20 explanation itself, 'mother of all living,' ties the name directly to the root
Septuagint renders the name Zoe, Life, translating the sense rather than transliterating the sound

versions.s: Man became a living soul. The same phrase is used of the animals.

b.t: The King James reads a living soul here and a living creature at Genesis 1:24 for the same two words. Modern versions read living being or living creature in both places, which is the correction.

**She is a living creature.** That is a statement about being alive, not about having an invisible part. Now imagine your translation used a more spiritual-sounding word in one place and a plainer one somewhere else, for the same original phrase.

Nephesh chayyah. The phrase appears at Genesis 1:20, 21, 24 and 30 of sea creatures, birds and land animals. Nephesh is closer to a life, a self, an appetite, even a throat, than to an immaterial soul. The verse says the man became alive, not that he received a soul the animals lack.
English soul carries centuries of Greek and Christian anthropology that Hebrew nephesh does not. There is no neutral English word, and creature sounds dismissive where soul sounds elevated.

When one Hebrew phrase is rendered two different ways in the same book, look up the other occurrences. Translators sometimes signal a theology by their choice of English word, and the King James does it here.
No Hebrew dispute. Modern versions have standardised on living being, and the King James rendering is the one that produced the popular reading.

src: The identical phrase at Genesis 1:20, 21, 24, 30
nephesh as throat or appetite: Isaiah 5:14; Proverbs 23:2

versions.s: Life. Plural in form, singular in meaning.

b.t: Every version reads life.
**Goods.** **Wits.** English has plural nouns for single ideas and nobody argues about them.
Chayim is plural in form and means life. Hebrew uses plural forms for several abstractions and for some single objects, which is why a plural form on its own proves very little.
A few English nouns follow the same pattern, so nothing is lost here. What matters is the precedent it sets for reading other plurals.
Before drawing a conclusion from a plural form in Hebrew, check whether the word is simply plural by nature. Many are.
Life is universal.
חַיִּים chayim · H2416

src: chayim at Genesis 2:7; Deuteronomy 30:19; Proverbs 3:2
Other plural abstractions: zequnim, old age; betulim, virginity
Compare elohim, plural in form

versions.s: He called her Eve, because she was the mother of all living. The name means life.

b.t: Every English version keeps the King James's transliteration Eve, which carries no meaning to an English ear at all. The meaning survives only in the explanation the verse itself gives, never in the name.

Imagine naming a child **Hope** the same afternoon a doctor gives you bad news. The name itself is the argument: things are not only what they look like today. Adam names his wife Life immediately after hearing they will die.

Chavah, the Hebrew name behind Eve, is built on the same root as chayah, to live, and chay, living or alive, the same root supplying the explanation the verse itself gives, mother of all living. The name is chosen and explained in the same breath, directly after the curses of chapter 3, as if the verse insists on naming the source of ongoing life at the exact moment mortality is announced.

English Eve is a transliterated sound with no built-in meaning, so an English reader needs the verse's own explanation to know the name means anything at all. In Hebrew the name and its sense are nearly the same word, doing in one breath what English needs a whole clause to do.

Biblical names are rarely just labels; check whether a name is built on a live root before assuming it is only an identifier. Where the text supplies its own explanation for a name, as it does here, that is the author flagging a wordplay you would otherwise miss.

No translation dispute; Eve is the standard transliteration and every version explains the meaning in the clause that follows. This is here only because transliteration, unlike translation, necessarily strips the sense out of a name that was doing real work in Hebrew.
חַוָּה Chavah · H2332 (חָיָה chayah, to live · H2421)

src: Chavah built on the root chayah/chay, to live: standard in BDB and HALOT
The Genesis 3:20 explanation itself, 'mother of all living,' ties the name directly to the root
Septuagint renders the name Zoe, Life, translating the sense rather than transliterating the sound

versions.s: Goodness and mercy shall follow me. Mercy is chesed, and mercy is the weakest word for it.

b.t: The King James reads mercy. Modern versions read steadfast love, unfailing love, faithful love, loyal love or covenant loyalty. No two agree, which tells you the word has no English equivalent.
**She stood by him.** That is not kindness, and it is not duty either. It is both at once, and English needs a phrase because it has no noun for it. Some languages have the noun.

Chesed is loyalty inside a committed relationship: what you owe and also what you freely give, with no line between them. It is the word in Exodus 34:6 where God describes himself, and the Greek behind John's grace and truth. Mercy suggests leniency toward someone in trouble, which is only a corner of it.
English split obligation from affection. Duty is cold, love is warm, and chesed is both in one noun, so every English rendering has to pick a side or use two words.
When you see five different English renderings of one word across five Bibles, stop looking for the right one. The spread is the information.

Mercy is memorable and narrow. Steadfast love is accurate and clumsy. Covenant loyalty is precise and reads like a legal term. The line is quoted at funerals, which is why nobody has been willing to change it.
חֶסֶד chesed · H2617

src: Exodus 34:6, rav chesed we-emet, in the self-description of God
Hosea 6:6, I desired chesed and not sacrifice, quoted at Matthew 9:13
Septuagint eleos; compare charis kai aletheia at John 1:14

versions.s: Wisdom. It includes skill with your hands.

b.t: Versions read wisdom, skill, or ability according to context.
**He is good with his hands.** English keeps skill and intelligence in separate compartments. Hebrew does not.

Chokmah covers practical skill, craft, shrewdness and moral discernment. Bezalel is filled with chokmah for metalwork and weaving at Exodus 31. The same noun runs through Proverbs for skill in living.
English wisdom is abstract and intellectual, so the craft sense has to be rendered by a different word and the connection breaks.
When a word is rendered skill in one book and wisdom in another, the two are one idea and your categories are the problem.
Wisdom is the majority rendering; skill appears in the tabernacle passages.

versions.s: Free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave. Chophshi ordinarily means released or liberated, an odd, bitter word choice for death.

b.t: The King James reads free among the dead, following chophshi's ordinary sense. Some modern versions read forsaken, abandoned, or cast off, reading the word's application to death as inherently bitter rather than literally about freedom.

English free among the dead sounds almost like a comfort, freedom from earthly troubles. The Hebrew word's ordinary sense, released or liberated, applied to the dead, has struck many readers as bitterly ironic rather than comforting, and scholars disagree sharply about what specific, grim idea the psalmist actually means by it.

Chophshi ordinarily describes a freed slave or someone released from obligation, a positive term everywhere else it occurs. Applied to the dead here, proposals range from freed from God's obligations and no longer able to serve or praise Him, to stripped, like a corpse looted on a battlefield, to a reading connecting the word to a term for a leper's isolated house, marking the psalmist, or the dead generally, as ritually cut off. No single proposal has won full scholarly consensus.

English free carries entirely positive connotations; if the Hebrew word is being used ironically or in some specialized, grim sense scholars still debate, the plain English rendering can accidentally make the verse sound comforting when it may be doing the opposite, describing utter abandonment.

When an ordinarily positive word is applied to a grim or negative subject, resist smoothing the translation into straightforward positive English. The friction between the word's normal sense and its dark context is very likely the point, not an accident to resolve.

Free among the dead keeps chophshi's ordinary sense and lets the reader feel the strangeness of applying freedom-language to death. Forsaken, abandoned, or stripped resolve the friction into more straightforwardly negative English, at the cost of losing the word's genuinely ironic, unsettling original ambiguity.
חָפְשִׁי chophshi (freed, released) · H2670

src: chophshi's ordinary sense, a freed slave: Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12
Multiple unresolved scholarly proposals for its sense here: stripped, abandoned, ritually cut off

versions.s: Without me ye can do nothing. The preposition is closer to apart from.

b.t: The King James reads without me. Modern versions read apart from me.
**Without a coat.** **Apart from the tree.** The first is missing something. The second is detached from it.
Choris means separated from, apart from. In a passage about branches being cut off, the spatial sense is doing the work, and without flattens it to lacking.
English without covers both absence and separation and defaults to absence.
In a passage built on one image, prepositions usually belong to the image. Read them spatially first.
Apart from me is how most modern versions read it; without me is the King James.

src: choris at Hebrews 4:15; 9:22

versions.s: Time as duration. The other half of the pair, and the one English defaults to.

b.t: Every version reads time.
**Chronic.** **Chronology.** English borrowed this root for exactly the duration sense and left the other one behind.
Chronos is extent of time, the ticking kind. Acts 1:7 uses both nouns in one sentence, times and seasons, which is the clearest place to see the pair.
English has no second noun, so the pairing at Acts 1:7 reads as an idiom rather than as two distinct ideas.
Learn the pair, not the word. Half of what a Greek word means is which other word it was chosen over.
Time is universal.
χρόνος chronos · G5550

src: chronos and kairos together at Acts 1:7 and 1 Thessalonians 5:1
English chronic, chronology, chronicle from this root

versions.s: Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me. A statement about the depth of David's guilt, later read as a doctrine of universal inherited sin.

b.t: Every version reads shapen or brought forth in iniquity, correctly, and in sin did my mother conceive me, tracing sinfulness back to conception, though the theological weight placed on that tracing varies enormously between traditions.

Saying **I've been like this my whole life** can be an ordinary way of confessing how deep-rooted your own fault is, without making a claim about every other person who has ever been born. Whether David's statement here works the same way, or is meant to describe something true of all humanity, is exactly what later theology had to decide.

Chollalti, shapen or brought forth, uses a verb for the pains and process of birth, tracing David's sinfulness rhetorically back to the very beginning of his existence, a hyperbolic intensification of his guilt in a psalm of extreme penitence rather than, on its own, a formal doctrinal statement about the inherited sinfulness of every human being. Augustine's later use of this verse as a foundational proof-text for original sin reads a universal, systematic claim into language that in its immediate context is emphasizing the depth and totality of one particular man's guilt.

English shapen in iniquity and conceived in sin, read through centuries of the doctrine of original sin, now carry theological freight for many readers that the Hebrew poetry's own immediate purpose, David's personal, hyperbolic confession of total guilt, may not itself have been making as a systematic claim about human nature in general.

When a devotional or poetic statement becomes a doctrinal proof-text centuries later, check what work the language was doing in its own immediate context before assuming the later doctrine is simply reading the text straight. Intensifying personal confession and systematic theological claim are not automatically the same thing.

Reading the verse as a personal, hyperbolic confession keeps it inside David's own psalm of extreme penitence, emphasizing the totality of his guilt rather than making a claim about anyone else. Reading it as a foundational statement about universal inherited sinfulness, the reading Augustine established and much later theology followed, extends the verse considerably beyond what its immediate poetic context by itself requires.
חוֹלַלְתִּי chollalti (חוּל chul/chil, writhe in birth) · H2342

versions.s: A ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven. A word used only here, likely naming a staircase like a ziggurat's.

b.t: Every version reads ladder or stairway, a reasonable guess for a word with no second biblical occurrence to confirm its precise shape.

English **ladder** pictures two rails and rungs. The Hebrew word, attested nowhere else in the Bible, is more plausibly related to a ramped, stepped staircase, the kind built into Mesopotamian temple towers, the very structure humanity tried and failed to build up to heaven at Babel, now let down from heaven instead.

Sullam appears only at Genesis 28:12 in the entire Hebrew Bible, likely built on the root salal, to cast up or pile up, related to mesillah, a raised highway. A widely noted proposed cognate is Akkadian simmiltu, the ramped staircase structure of a ziggurat, itself the same kind of monument behind the Babel tower whose top was meant to reach unto heaven at Genesis 11:4. If the connection holds, Jacob's vision reverses Babel: rather than humans building upward to breach heaven by their own effort, God opens a connection downward, unprompted and freely given.

English ladder is a specific, ordinary household object; it carries none of the monumental, ziggurat-scale associations the Akkadian cognate and the word's single, unparalleled biblical occurrence may be pointing toward, and it obscures any deliberate echo of the Babel tower's own reach unto heaven language.

When a rare or unique word appears in a scene that echoes an earlier story's themes, check whether a proposed cognate strengthens or complicates that echo. Sullam's likely connection to the ziggurat vocabulary of Genesis 11 is exactly this kind of case, turning a single translated word into a pointed reversal of an earlier episode.

Ladder is the traditional, serviceable English rendering for a word attested only once. Stairway or ramp, closer to the proposed Akkadian cognate, better supports reading the scene as a deliberate structural echo of, and reversal of, the Babel tower's own failed reach toward heaven.
סֻלָּם sullam · H5551

versions.s: Word, thing, matter, event. Speech and the thing spoken are one noun.

b.t: Versions read word, thing, matter, or event according to context.
**That's the thing.** **He gave his word.** English uses thing and word in ways that almost touch, and then keeps them apart.

Davar covers an utterance and also a matter or affair. The Ten Commandments are the ten devarim, the ten words. A word of the LORD is not merely speech about an event; the categories are not separated.
English split speech from substance, so the Hebrew idea has to be argued rather than heard.
When a language uses one word for a statement and for the state of affairs it describes, that is a claim about how speech works and it is built into the vocabulary.
Word is the majority rendering; thing and matter appear where word would be nonsense.
דָּבָר davar · H1697

src: the ten devarim: Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13
davar as matter: Genesis 21:11; 1 Samuel 10:16

versions.s: Jesus wept. A different verb from the weeping of everyone else in the scene.

b.t: Every version reads Jesus wept.
**She was wailing.** **He shed tears.** Two different sounds, and English has words for both.

Dakruo, to shed tears, occurs only here in the New Testament. The mourners at verse 33 klaio, which is loud lamentation. The contrast between the professional wailing and the quiet tears is in the vocabulary.
English wept covers both, so the contrast is invisible and the verse reads as the same activity as everyone else's.
When a narrative uses two different verbs for what looks like the same action, the difference is usually the description.
Wept is universal.
δακρύω dakruo · G1145

src: Only occurrence of dakruo in the New Testament
klaio at John 11:31, 33; 20:11
The professional mourners at John 11:19, 31

versions.s: Thy brother's blood crieth. The Hebrew word is plural, bloods, and English cannot say that.

b.t: Every version reads blood, singular, because bloods is not usable English. The Septuagint and Vulgate also read the singular, so the flattening is not only a modern-English problem.

English blood does not pluralize the way apple does; **bloods** is not a normal English word at all. Hebrew can pluralize dam, blood, to intensify or generalize it, and does so here, and every English version has to silently drop the plural to produce a normal sentence.

Damim, the plural of dam, blood, appears here instead of the ordinary singular. The plural of this word elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible regularly marks bloodguilt, violence, or blood shed by violence, rather than blood in the ordinary biological sense, so the grammar itself is already doing some of the accusing before the sentence's meaning is even considered.

English blood is a mass noun with no plural that carries meaning the way Hebrew damim does; bloods simply is not English. A translator has no live option but to render the plural as a singular, which quietly erases a grammatical signal Hebrew readers would have registered automatically.

Some Hebrew nouns carry meaning in their plural form that has no equivalent plural in English. When a translation looks like a straightforward singular noun, check whether the Hebrew behind it might be plural, and if the plural itself might be idiomatic.

Translators never had a real choice here; blood is the only workable English rendering. The interesting question, whether the plural points to bloodguilt generally, multiple wounds, or Abel's unborn descendants, as one old Jewish tradition suggested, cannot be settled by grammar alone and is not something any English translation can flag either way.
דָּמִים damim (דָּם dam) · H1818

src: Damim in the sense of bloodguilt or violent bloodshed elsewhere: Exodus 22:2; 2 Samuel 16:8
Rabbinic tradition (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, echoed by Rashi) reading the plural as the blood of Abel's descendants
Standard lexicons (BDB, HALOT) distinguish dam, blood, from the idiomatic plural damim

versions.s: Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed. The Hebrew word order is a mirror around the center.

b.t: Every version reads whoever sheds man's blood, by man his blood shall be shed, correctly following the sense, but English sentence order, subject before verb, cannot reproduce a mirror shape the way Hebrew's more flexible word order can.

English can say **the punishment fits the crime**, but that is commentary, a sentence about the sentence. Hebrew builds the fit directly into word order: sheds, blood, man, man, blood, shed, the same words running forward and then backward around a hinge in the middle.

The Hebrew runs shofekh dam ha'adam, ba'adam damo yishafekh: sheds blood-of-man, by-man his-blood shall-be-shed. The verb for shedding opens the first half and closes the second, the noun for blood and the noun for man swap positions around the center, a structure grammarians call a chiasm, an A-B-C-C'-B'-A' pattern that visually and aurally enacts the very reciprocity, blood for blood, that the sentence is announcing.

English word order is comparatively fixed, subject-verb-object, so it cannot rearrange itself into a mirror shape the way Hebrew's freer word order allows here. A translation can state the principle of equal retribution but cannot make the sentence's shape perform it the way the Hebrew does.

Look for chiastic word order whenever a verse states a principle of exact correspondence, reciprocity, or reversal. Hebrew narrative and law use mirrored word order as a rhetorical device in its own right, not merely as a stylistic accident, and it rarely survives translation intact.

The legal content itself isn't contested; every version agrees on the sense. What is lost is entirely formal: the chiastic shape itself, which is not a matter of word choice but of an arrangement English syntax is not free enough to reproduce.
שֹׁפֵךְ דַּם הָאָדָם shofekh dam ha'adam (chiastic word order) · H8210 + H1818 + H120

src: The chiastic ABCC'B'A' structure of the Hebrew clause: standard treatments of Hebrew poetic and legal syntax
Genesis 1:26-27's image of God as the stated ground for the principle

versions.s: In our image, after our likeness. Two nouns, and probably one idea.

b.t: Every version reads image and likeness. Some older theological systems treat them as separate endowments, one lost at the fall and one retained.

**Safe and sound.** **Null and void.** English pairs words that mean nearly the same thing all the time, and nobody hunts for the difference between null and void. Hebrew does the same, and readers hunt anyway.

Tselem is a physical representation, including a carved idol. Demut is a resemblance. In Genesis 5:3 the two are swapped around with the prepositions reversed, which is what makes a technical distinction hard to sustain. Read together they say one thing: humanity is God's representative image on the ground, the way a king's statue in a province represented the king.
English can print both nouns but cannot signal that the pair is a single idea, so readers naturally assume two.
When two near-synonyms appear together, check whether the writer ever swaps or reverses them. If he does, the distinction you are looking for is probably not there.
There is no translation dispute. There is a long tradition of distinguishing the two, and the internal evidence at Genesis 5:3 is the argument against it.
צֶלֶם tselem · H6754 / דְּמוּת demut · H1823

src: Genesis 5:3 reverses the prepositions and the order
tselem of an idol: 2 Kings 11:18; Amos 5:26
The royal-statue background is standard in ANE treatments; Walton, Ancient Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament

versions.s: One of you is a devil. The Greek noun is slanderer, and it has no article here.

b.t: The King James reads a devil. Modern versions read a devil or a slanderer, and some read the devil.
**He is the accountant.** **He is an accountant.** One picks out a person, the other describes a kind. Greek marks that with the article and here there is none.
Diabolos means slanderer or accuser, and with the article it becomes the standard title for the accuser. Here it is anarthrous, which is why most versions print a devil rather than the devil.
English devil is only ever a title, so using it descriptively reads as an identification the Greek does not make.
The same article rule that governs John 1:1 governs ordinary nouns everywhere else. Once you have it, it is reusable.
A devil is the majority rendering; a slanderer appears in more literal versions.

versions.s: Servant. The word behind deacon, and it is not a lesser word than the one for slave.

b.t: Versions read servant, minister or deacon depending on the verse and sometimes on the person.
**She serves on the board.** **She serves the tables.** Same verb, opposite social weight, and only the context tells you.
Diakonos is one who serves, including at table. It becomes a church office in the Pastorals. The same word is used of Phoebe at Romans 16:1, of Paul, and of Christ at Romans 15:8.
English has three words where Greek has one, and choosing between them is an interpretive act rather than a translation one.
When a single word is rendered three ways in one Bible, check whether the renderings track the context or track the person being described.
Servant is the majority rendering; deacon appears where an office is clearly in view.

versions.s: Deuteronomy lists three. Jesus lists four. The extra one tells you how the first century read the original.

b.t: No version can flag this, because both passages are translated accurately and the discrepancy only appears when you lay them side by side.
Someone quotes a family saying back to you and slips in an extra word. They are not correcting it. They are telling you what it always meant, in case you had stopped hearing it.

Deuteronomy 6:5 has heart, soul and strength. Mark has heart, soul, mind and strength. The added word is dianoia, mind or understanding. The Greek kardia had narrowed toward the emotional by the first century in a way Hebrew levav never had, so a Greek-speaking audience hearing kardia alone would have missed the thinking half of the original.

Neither translation is wrong. The gap opens because Hebrew put thought in the heart and Greek was already moving it out, so the same command needed four words in Greek to say what three said in Hebrew.

A mismatch between a New Testament quotation and its Old Testament source is data, not an error. Sometimes the writer is using the Septuagint. Sometimes, as here, he's spelling out a word his audience would have taken too narrowly.
There is no translation choice being made. The evidence only shows up when you lay two accurate translations side by side, which is a skill worth more than any single word study.
καρδία kardia · G2588 / διάνοια dianoia · G1271

src: Deuteronomy 6:5 in Hebrew: levav, nephesh, meod
Mark 12:30 and the parallel at Luke 10:27, which lists the same four terms in a different order; Matthew 22:37 keeps only three (heart, soul, mind) and drops strength
Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, on leb as the seat of intellect and will
