versions.s: To justify. A courtroom verb meaning to declare in the right, not to make good.

b.t: Every version reads justify or declare righteous. No major version departs.
**Justify your answer.** **The court found in his favour.** The second is the sense. The first is what English drifted into.
Dikaioo is built on the same root as dikaiosune and belongs in legal vocabulary: to pronounce someone in the right. It is a statement about standing, not a description of character improvement.
English justify moved toward offering an excuse, which is nearly the opposite of a verdict handed down by someone else.
Verbs ending in this Greek shape are usually declarative rather than causative. The verdict language is in the grammar, not just in the theology built on it.
Justify is the settled majority rendering. Declare righteous appears where a translator wants the verdict sense to be unmissable.
δικαιόω dikaioo · G1344

versions.s: Righteousness. English splits this into righteousness and justice; Greek and Hebrew do not.

b.t: Nearly every English version reads righteousness in Paul and justice in some Old Testament contexts, from one Greek and one Hebrew word.
**That was not right.** **That was not just.** English keeps two words and lets you pick which complaint you are making. Imagine one word and no choice.
Dikaiosune translates Hebrew tsedaqah, which is rightness inside a relationship, including doing right by people who have no claim on you. The legal and the moral senses are one idea.
English divided the word centuries ago along a line Greek never drew, and the two halves now feel like different subjects.
When one original word is rendered by two English words in different books, read a passage substituting the other one. It is the fastest way to hear what was lost.
Righteousness is the majority rendering in the New Testament and justice in the Prophets, from the same underlying vocabulary.
δικαιοσύνη dikaiosune · G1343

versions.s: My spirit shall not always strive with man. A verb used only this once, and nobody is fully certain what it says God's spirit will stop doing.

b.t: Most versions read strive or contend, following one proposed derivation. A minority tradition reads abide or remain, following a different proposed derivation, giving a noticeably different picture of what is ending.

Imagine a verb that shows up exactly once in every book you own. You would have exactly one sentence to reconstruct its meaning from, and reasonable readers could disagree. That is the situation with the verb translated strive here.

Yadon shows up nowhere else in the Hebrew Old Testament outside this one verse. One proposal derives it from din, to judge or contend, giving strive or contend, God arguing with or opposing humanity's corruption. A second proposal derives it from a root meaning to remain or abide, giving my spirit will not remain in man forever, a statement about withdrawal of presence rather than a legal contest. Both derivations require reasoning from other roots rather than from other occurrences of this exact form.

English strive and English abide describe different relationships, contest versus presence, and a translator must choose one before an English reader ever sees the sentence. With only one occurrence to work from, Hebrew itself does not settle which picture is correct, and English cannot show that uncertainty within the text.

A word attested exactly once anywhere in a corpus is being reconstructed from etymology and context, not read off a body of established usage. Hold single-occurrence definitions more loosely than a lexicon's confident gloss might suggest.

Strive or contend fits a chapter about escalating human violence and portrays God as long-suffering rather than instantly punitive. Abide or remain fits a chapter about the Spirit's presence being withdrawn from corrupted humanity, closer to an exhaustion of patience than an argument. Both readings are defended by serious grammarians working from the same single data point.
יָדוֹן yadon (roots proposed: דין din, judge, or דּוּן dun, remain) · H1777

src: Only occurrence: Genesis 6:3
din, to judge/contend, as one proposed root: standard lexicons
An alternative root related to abiding/remaining, argued by other grammarians, given the word's singular attestation

versions.s: The truth shall make you free. And the next sentence is about slavery, not about employment.

b.t: The King James reads servant of sin. Modern versions read slave of sin, which keeps the pair intact.
**He's free now.** Free from what? The sentence only means something once you know what was holding him.

Eleutheroo, to set free, and doulos, slave, are the two poles of the argument from verse 32 to verse 36. In Greek the reply in verse 33, we were never in bondage, uses the same root, so the whole exchange is one vocabulary.
English servant implies wages and the option of leaving, which removes the force of the contrast with freedom.
When a paragraph turns on a contrast, check that both halves are rendered from the same word family. Breaking the family breaks the argument.
Modern versions overwhelmingly read slave here; the King James reads servant.
ἐλευθερόω eleutheroo · G1659 / δοῦλος doulos · G1401

src: The word family across John 8:32-36
Romans 6:16-22 runs the same pair
doulos as ownership rather than employment

versions.s: Slave. English versions mostly print servant, and the two are not the same relationship.

b.t: The King James, NIV and ESV mostly read servant. The CSB and NET read slave. The HCSB shifted toward slave and drew argument for it.
**He works for her.** **He belongs to her household.** One is employment and one is belonging, and English only really has the first.
Doulos is a slave, owned property, and Greek had separate words for a hired worker. The word is used of Paul, of Christ at Philippians 2:7, and of believers generally.
English servant implies wages and the option of leaving. Slave carries the American chattel system with it, which is a different institution from the ancient one and is why translators hesitate.
When translators avoid the plain rendering of a word, ask what they were protecting the reader from. Sometimes the protection costs more than it saves.
Servant is the majority rendering in English versions. Slave is the more literal one and is gaining ground in recent translations.
δοῦλος doulos · G1401

src: doulos of Paul: Romans 1:1; Philippians 1:1; Titus 1:1
doulos of Christ: Philippians 2:7
misthios, a hired worker, is the contrasting word: Luke 15:17

versions.s: Glory. In ordinary Greek it meant opinion or reputation; the Septuagint loaded it with Hebrew weight.

b.t: Every version reads glory. No version departs.
**Orthodox.** **Doxology.** The same root gives a word about correct opinion and a word about praise. That is how far the noun travelled.

Classical doxa is opinion, and from there reputation and honour. The Septuagint used it for Hebrew kavod, which is weight and substance, and the New Testament inherits the Hebrew sense rather than the Greek one.
English glory came in from Latin gloria, about renown and splendour, so English is reproducing the Greek word's old sense rather than its biblical one.
When a Greek word means one thing in Plato and another in Paul, the Septuagint is almost always what happened in between.
Glory is universal in English versions.

src: doxa for kavod throughout the Septuagint

versions.s: The first day. Literally, one day, a cardinal number, while every later day uses an ordinal.

b.t: Most versions read the first day, smoothing yom echad into the ordinal pattern the rest of the week uses, treating the grammatical oddity as insignificant.

English happily uses **day one** and **the first day** interchangeably. Hebrew does not default that way: yom echad is built like counting **day: one** the way you might count reps, while yom sheni, the second day, and every day after it, uses a true ordinal, like second, third, fourth. Only day one breaks the ordinal pattern.

Yom echad, day one, uses the cardinal number one rather than the ordinal rishon, first, which Hebrew does have and uses elsewhere. Every subsequent day in the creation week switches to a true ordinal. One classical explanation, offered by the medieval commentator Ramban, is that first only makes sense once a second exists to compare it to, so before any other day existed, only one, a simple count, was possible; other proposed explanations range from stylistic variation to marking this day as categorically different from the rest.

English first day is a normal, expected ordinal with no oddity to notice, so nothing in translation signals that the underlying Hebrew grammar actually breaks its own pattern on exactly this one day, a small irregularity commentators have found worth explaining for centuries.

When Hebrew breaks its own established grammatical pattern, as the cardinal yom echad does against the following days' ordinals, treat the break as a detail worth investigating rather than noise a fluent translation can safely smooth away.

The first day, the standard English rendering, treats the Hebrew oddity as insignificant variation. Reading yom echad more literally as day one, following Ramban's logic that no second day yet existed to make first meaningful, keeps the grammatical irregularity in view as a deliberate feature rather than papering over it.
יוֹם אֶחָד yom echad · H3117 + H259

src: Ramban's commentary on Genesis 1:5
The switch to ordinals starting with yom sheni, the second day, at Genesis 1:8

versions.s: One flesh. A kinship word, not only a body word.

b.t: Every version reads one flesh, and the physical union is certainly included. What is harder to see in English is that basar for kinship is ordinary Hebrew usage on its own, not a special sense invented for this verse.

**He's my flesh and blood.** English keeps this sense alive for family, but only as a fixed idiom, sitting beside the ordinary meaning of flesh as tissue. Hebrew basar carries the kinship sense as one of its normal, everyday meanings, not as a leftover expression.

Basar, flesh, is used of blood relatives at Genesis 29:14, Judges 9:2, and 2 Samuel 5:1, where 'your bone and your flesh' means your relative, with no reference to sex or the body. One flesh at 2:24 draws on that same kinship vocabulary: the man and woman become each other's next of kin, a new family unit, with the physical union as the sign of that bond rather than its entire content.

English flesh has narrowed mostly to the physical body, with flesh and blood surviving only as a fixed idiom for family. Hebrew basar keeps both senses live at once, so a single English reading tends to collapse the verse into the physical union alone.
When a body-part or body-substance word appears in a covenant or family context, check whether the same word carries a kinship sense elsewhere before assuming only the physical meaning is in view.

One flesh is not in dispute as a translation. The question is emphasis: whether the phrase is chiefly about sexual union, chiefly about kinship status, or, as the parallel usage suggests, both at once by design.
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד basar echad · H1320 + H259

src: Kinship sense of basar: Genesis 29:14; Judges 9:2; 2 Samuel 5:1, 'your bone and your flesh'

entries.title: ed
entries.where: ed is tagged 2 times, across 2 books: genesis 1 · job 1.

versions.s: A mist went up. A word used only here and once in Job, and nobody is certain what it names.

b.t: Most English versions read mist or streams. The Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate both read spring or fountain, not mist, showing the fog reading is not the oldest one on record.

Imagine a word that survives in only two sentences of an entire library. Every dictionary entry for it is built from those two sentences alone. Now picture two ancient translations disagreeing about which of two very different pictures, fog or flood, the word was even pointing at.

Ed occurs at Genesis 2:6 and Job 36:27, and nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. The traditional mist reading leans on the Job passage; an alternative connects the word to Akkadian edu, a flood or high water, which would make the verse describe subterranean water welling up to irrigate the ground rather than fog settling on it.

English mist and spring point to two different weather pictures, and a word attested twice cannot arbitrate between them. Whichever English word a translator picks quietly closes a question the Hebrew itself leaves open.

A word this rare is a live question, not a settled fact, however confident a single English gloss makes it look. Check how many times a word occurs before resting an argument on its dictionary definition.

Mist keeps the older picture of dew or fog settling. Spring or stream follows the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and the proposed Akkadian cognate, and fits a garden being irrigated by water rising from below rather than settling from above. Both are defensible; neither is provable from two data points.
אֵד ed · H108

src: Only two occurrences: Genesis 2:6; Job 36:27
Septuagint reads pege, spring or fountain, at Genesis 2:6; the Vulgate reads fons, fountain
Proposed cognate: Akkadian edu, flood or high water

versions.s: Before Abraham was, I am. The verb is wrong on purpose.

b.t: Nearly every version reads I am. A handful render I have been, which repairs the grammar and removes the reason anyone reached for a stone.
**Before the war started, I am here.** Your ear rejects that, and rightly. A speaker who says it in front of you is not making a grammar mistake. They are doing something with the mistake.

Ego eimi is present tense against a past clause, which is ungrammatical in Greek as it is in English. The same two words render the divine name in the Septuagint at Exodus 3:14, and they run through this Gospel as a formula. The crowd's reaction in verse 59 is the commentary.
English can print the clash, but English readers absorb it as odd phrasing rather than as a claim, because English has no formula attached to those two words.
When a sentence is grammatically broken in the original and the crowd reacts violently, the breakage is the message. Translations that repair the grammar delete the evidence.
I have been is smoother and loses the formula. I am is rough and keeps it. The stones in verse 59 are the argument for keeping it.

versions.s: Was, and came to be. Two verbs one verse apart, and the whole prologue turns on the difference.

b.t: English uses was for the first and were made for the second, which hides that both are ordinary verbs of being and becoming.

**The house was there. The shed came to be there.** Both sentences put something in a yard. The first one does not tell you the house ever started. The second one tells you the shed had a beginning. English can say this if it works at it. Greek says it with two different verbs and never has to explain.

Verse 1 uses en, the imperfect of eimi, to be. Verse 3 uses egeneto, the aorist of ginomai, to become or come into existence. John keeps them apart with complete discipline through the whole prologue: everything created gets ginomai, and the Word gets eimi. Verse 14 is the hinge, where the Word finally takes egeneto, became flesh.
English was covers both existing and starting to exist. Greek has separate verbs, so the distinction is built into the vocabulary rather than argued in a footnote.
Watch which verb a writer uses for existence. If a Greek text alternates between eimi and ginomai in the same passage, the alternation is almost never accidental.

No translator disputes the parsing. The difficulty is that no English rendering can keep the two verbs visibly distinct without paraphrasing, so every version loses the pattern and study Bibles have to point at it in a note.
εἰμί eimi · G1510 / γίνομαι ginomai · G1096

src: The pattern across John 1:1-14: en at verses 1, 2, 4, 9, 10, 15; egeneto at 3, 6, 10, 12, 14, 17
Standard commentaries treat the alternation as deliberate: Carson, The Gospel According to John (PNTC), at 1:1-3

versions.s: Peace. In Greek it is mainly the absence of war; in the Bible it carries Hebrew shalom.

b.t: Every version reads peace.
**Peace and quiet.** English peace is mostly about things stopping. Now imagine a word that is mostly about things being complete.

Classical eirene is the absence of conflict. The Septuagint uses it for shalom, which is wholeness, completeness, everything in its proper state. The New Testament greeting formula inherits the Hebrew sense.
English peace inherited the Greek narrowness rather than the Hebrew fullness, so a blessing of shalom reads as a wish for calm.
Greeting formulas are the most conservative part of a language. When a New Testament letter opens with one, it is usually carrying an older idea intact.
Peace is universal in English versions.

versions.s: Church. A civic word for a called-out assembly, with no religious content of its own.

b.t: Every version reads church. A few render assembly or congregation in Old Testament quotations.
**The assembly voted.** That is a description of people gathered, not of a building they gathered in. English still has the plain word and reserves a different one for religion.

Ekklesia was the citizen assembly of a Greek city, summoned to decide public business. The Septuagint uses it for the assembly of Israel. It appears in Acts 19 of an ordinary and rather disorderly civic crowd.
English church comes from a different Greek word entirely, kuriakon, belonging to the Lord, and has meant a building for most of its life in English.
When the English word and the Greek word have different etymologies, the English word is telling you about English history rather than about the text.
Church is universal in English versions and no major translation has departed from it.
ἐκκλησία ekklesia · G1577

src: ekklesia of a civic crowd: Acts 19:32, 39, 41
ekklesia for the assembly of Israel in the Septuagint: Deuteronomy 31:30

versions.s: Melchizedek, priest of the most high God. A title shared with Canaanite religion, which Abraham treats as naming his own God.

b.t: Every version reads most high God without comment, since El Elyon reads in English as a straightforward divine title with no built-in signal that it was also, independently, a title used of a chief Canaanite deity.

Imagine meeting a priest from another country who blesses you in the name of **the Almighty**, a title your own religion also uses. Do you correct him, or recognize the same God under a shared word? Genesis has Abraham do the second, and the choice carries weight.

El and Elyon both function as attested divine titles in the wider Canaanite religious world, El as the head of the pantheon and Elyon as a title meaning highest or most high. Melchizedek, a Canaanite king-priest of Salem, blesses Abram by El Elyon, and two verses later Abram swears an oath by the LORD, El Elyon, explicitly equating his own God's name with Melchizedek's title, treating them as the same God under different peoples' vocabulary rather than correcting or rejecting the foreign priest's language.

English most high God reads as a generic superlative description; it carries no signal that the underlying Hebrew phrase was also a known title in the surrounding Canaanite religious vocabulary, so the theological move Genesis is making, claiming a foreign priest's God-language as legitimately naming Israel's own God, is invisible without that background.

When a biblical text uses a title also attested in a neighboring culture's religious vocabulary, ask whether the text is borrowing, rejecting, or reclaiming that vocabulary. Genesis 14 reclaims it: Abraham does not treat Melchizedek as a pagan to be corrected but as a genuine priest of the same God under a shared ancient Near Eastern title.

Most high God is the uncontested sense of El Elyon in every version. The larger question, how much weight the shared Canaanite background carries for how this scene functions theologically, is a matter of ancient Near Eastern religious history layered on top of an otherwise straightforward translation.
אֵל עֶלְיוֹן El Elyon · H410 + H5945

src: El and Elyon as attested Canaanite divine titles: Ugaritic religious texts
Abraham's explicit equation of El Elyon with the LORD (YHWH) at Genesis 14:22
Melchizedek referenced again at Psalm 110:4 and Hebrews 5-7

versions.s: I am the Almighty God. El Shaddai, a title whose root meaning is genuinely uncertain.

b.t: Every version reads Almighty God, a strong, confident English translation supplying a settled sense the Hebrew word's own etymology does not actually have.

Almighty is confident, clear English. Shaddai's own root is not confident or clear at all; serious scholars have proposed it comes from words for a mountain, for a breast, and for violent overpowering, three pictures of God's power that would each shape the sentence differently if any one were certain.

Shaddai's derivation is disputed among three live proposals: from Akkadian shadu, mountain, giving God of the mountain, ancient imagery of strength and permanence; from Hebrew shad, breast, giving a nourishing, sustaining God, an image some scholars connect to Jacob's later blessing at Genesis 49:25, blessings of the breasts and of the womb; or from the root shadad, to overpower or destroy, giving a God of overwhelming might. A later Jewish tradition reads it instead as a compound, sha, who, plus dai, is sufficient, giving the all-sufficient one, but this is a homiletical reading of the sound rather than a linguistic derivation.

English Almighty commits to one general sense, overwhelming power, that happens to fit the shadad proposal reasonably well but flattens the genuinely live possibility that the name instead pictures God as a mountain or as a nurturing, breast-like source of sustenance, pictures Almighty does not evoke at all.

When a divine name's etymology is genuinely disputed among proposals that shape entirely different pictures of God, translating it with one confident English word settles a question scholarship has not settled. Hold the translation more loosely than its confident sound suggests.

Almighty is the traditional and functional English rendering, generically capturing power without committing to any one etymology. Each specific proposal, mountain, breast, or overpowering, produces a genuinely different mental picture of what this particular covenant scene is emphasizing about God's character.
אֵל שַׁדַּי El Shaddai · H410 + H7706

The shadad, overpower/destroy, proposal: standard Hebrew lexicons note this as a live option

versions.s: Ascribe unto the LORD, O ye mighty. Literally, sons of the elim, gods, the divine council again.

b.t: Most versions read O ye mighty, sons of the mighty, or heavenly beings, a range reflecting real disagreement about how directly to render bene elim's divine-council background into English.

English mighty ones reads as a vague compliment, powerful people or important figures. Bene elim is the same technical phrase already met describing heavenly beings surrounding God's throne, an audience of gods, not an audience of impressive humans, being summoned to worship.

Bene elim, sons of the elim, gods, occurs only here and at Psalm 89:6, and closely parallels the Canaanite divine-council phrase sons of El attested in Ugaritic mythological texts, where it names the assembly of lesser gods surrounding the high god El. The psalm opens by summoning this same heavenly assembly, not human worshippers, to acknowledge the LORD's glory, the same divine-council imagery already met at Genesis 6:2 and Psalm 82:1.

English mighty ones or you heavenly beings both lose the specific technical weight bene elim carries as a recognized ancient Near Eastern divine-council term, so a reader cannot easily connect this opening line to the same council imagery running through Genesis 6, Psalm 82, and Psalm 89.

Track bene elohim, bene elim, and edat el, each a variant of the same divine-council phrase, across their several occurrences rather than treating each one as an isolated poetic flourish. The psalms and Genesis are drawing on one shared, coherent picture of a heavenly assembly.

Mighty ones or heavenly beings both work as general English glosses. Sons of the gods, or sons of the elim, kept closer to the Hebrew, more directly connects this opening summons to the same council-of-gods imagery already established at Genesis 6:2, Psalm 82:1, and Psalm 89:6.

versions.s: God. The shortest word for deity, and also the name of the high god of Canaan.

b.t: Every version reads God, or transliterates in compound names like El Shaddai and El Elyon.
**Lord** is an English common noun and also a title someone holds. The same word doing both jobs is normal and only becomes confusing when you are reading about a rival.

El is the general Semitic word for a god and the personal name of the head of the Canaanite pantheon at Ugarit. Genesis uses compound titles, God Most High and God Almighty, which is both ordinary Hebrew and a claim about who that figure actually is.
English has no word that is simultaneously the common noun and a rival's proper name.
A Hebrew word for God inside a compound title needs the compound looked up, not just the word alone. The compounds are where the argument is.
God is the majority rendering; the compounds are usually transliterated.

versions.s: Reprove the world of sin. One verb, three objects, and no agreed rendering.

b.t: The King James reads reprove. Modern versions read convict, prove the world to be in the wrong, or convince.
**He showed them up.** **He talked them round.** Two different operations, and English keeps them apart.

Elencho covers exposing a fault, convicting in a legal sense, and convincing someone of the truth. All three senses are attested and the verse gives no decisive context, which is why the versions scatter.
English has separate words for each sense and no word that covers all three, so the translator must choose.
When four versions give four different verbs, the Greek word covers all four and none of them is wrong.
Convict is the modern reading; reprove is the King James; prove the world to be in the wrong is the NIV's expansion.

versions.s: Mercy. In the Septuagint it is the word chosen for Hebrew chesed, which is much larger.

b.t: Every version reads mercy. Some render compassion or lovingkindness where the Old Testament background is being quoted.
**He showed mercy.** You picture someone being let off. Now picture a word that also covers standing by someone for thirty years, and you can see the join not fitting.

Eleos translates chesed hundreds of times in the Septuagint. So when a New Testament writer quotes Hosea 6:6, I desired mercy and not sacrifice, the word underneath is covenant loyalty rather than leniency.
English split obligation from kindness. Greek eleos on its own is nearer pity, and it is carrying a Hebrew load it was not built for.

When a Greek word sits under a quotation from the Old Testament, find the Hebrew word it is standing in for. Septuagint vocabulary is the bridge between the two Testaments and almost nothing else explains it.
Mercy is the majority rendering and has been since Tyndale. Nothing else has ever been in serious contention.

versions.s: The truth shall make you free. And the next sentence is about slavery, not about employment.

b.t: The King James reads servant of sin. Modern versions read slave of sin, which keeps the pair intact.
**He's free now.** Free from what? The sentence only means something once you know what was holding him.

Eleutheroo, to set free, and doulos, slave, are the two poles of the argument from verse 32 to verse 36. In Greek the reply in verse 33, we were never in bondage, uses the same root, so the whole exchange is one vocabulary.
English servant implies wages and the option of leaving, which removes the force of the contrast with freedom.
When a paragraph turns on a contrast, check that both halves are rendered from the same word family. Breaking the family breaks the argument.
Modern versions overwhelmingly read slave here; the King James reads servant.

versions.s: The sons of God saw the daughters of men. The oldest reading takes sons of God as divine beings, not a human family line.

b.t: Most modern versions read sons of God without further comment, leaving the identification to footnotes or study notes. The King James likewise reads sons of God, unglossed.

English son of can mean a literal child or a member of a category, **son of the soil**, **sons of thunder**. Hebrew bene elohim works the same way, and here the category in view, sons of the divine realm, is a real option English son of does not rule out but does not spell out either.

Bene elohim and the singular ben elohim identify members of the divine council elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, at Job 1:6, 2:1, 38:7, and Psalm 89:6, all contexts where no one reads the phrase as human beings. The earliest interpreters, including the Septuagint tradition, 1 Enoch, and Jubilees, took Genesis 6:2 the same way, as heavenly beings intermarrying with humans. The alternative, that sons of God means the righteous line of Seth marrying Cain's corrupted daughters, is a later reading associated with Julius Africanus and Augustine, developed in reaction against the angelic view rather than growing from Hebrew usage of the phrase itself.

English sons of God carries no built-in link to a divine council, an idea unfamiliar to most modern readers, so the phrase reads as loosely poetic rather than as a technical term with a fixed range of reference elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible.

Before deciding what a phrase means in one passage, survey every other place the same phrase occurs in the same corpus. Bene elohim is not ambiguous where it appears elsewhere; the ambiguity here is imported by later theological discomfort with what those other passages already say.

The divine-council reading is both the oldest attested interpretation and the one that matches every other biblical use of the phrase. The Sethite reading, sons of God as godly men, has no other biblical use of the phrase to support it and arose specifically to avoid the angelic implications, which makes it weaker as a reading of the Hebrew even though it became dominant in later Western Christianity.
בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים bene ha'elohim · H1121 + H430

src: Bene elohim / bene ha'elohim as divine-council beings: Job 1:6; 2:1; 38:7; Psalm 89:6

The Sethite view associated with Julius Africanus and developed by Augustine, City of God 15.23

versions.s: A mighty prince among us. Literally, a prince of God, using elohim as a superlative.

b.t: Every version reads mighty prince or great chieftain, correctly conveying the superlative sense without the literal words prince of God ever appearing in translation.

English intensifies with words like **super** or **mega**, or with an adverb, **incredibly great**. Hebrew has another option: attach the word for God to a noun to mean very or utterly. Elohim here is not claiming Abraham is divine; it is doing the job English mega does.

Nesi elohim, literally prince of God, uses elohim the way Hebrew occasionally uses divine vocabulary to intensify an ordinary noun or adjective to its greatest possible degree, a pattern also seen in phrases like an exceedingly great city, literally a city great to God, at Jonah 3:3. The construction is a superlative device, not a theological claim about Abraham's status.

English has no equivalent habit of using God's name as a grammatical intensifier, so a literal translation, prince of God, would mislead an English reader into hearing a theological claim the Hebrew idiom was never making.

When elohim or a divine name appears attached to an ordinary noun in a way that does not fit a normal statement about deity, check whether Hebrew is using it as a superlative intensifier rather than making a religious claim. The construction is rare but attested and easy to over-read.

Translators are not divided here; mighty prince correctly captures the sense and rightly avoids the misleading literal rendering. Worth noting is a genuine grammatical curiosity: Hebrew can reach for God's own name simply to say very, in a way English idiom has no parallel for.
נְשִׂיא אֱלֹהִים nesi elohim · H5387 + H430

src: The same superlative pattern at Jonah 3:3, 'an exceedingly great city,' literally 'great to God'
D. Winton Thomas, 'A Consideration of Some Unusual Ways of Expressing the Superlative in Hebrew,' Vetus Testamentum 3 (1953), on this construction as a Hebrew superlative device

versions.s: A little lower than the angels. The Hebrew says elohim.

b.t: The King James and NIV read the angels. The ESV and NASB read the heavenly beings or God, with footnotes. The NET reads the heavenly beings. The split runs straight down the middle of the modern versions.

Suppose a sentence said someone was ranked just below **the management**, and a later translation rendered it just below **the supervisors**. Narrower, tidier, and it quietly decides a question the original left open.

The Hebrew is elohim, the same word used of God, of the divine council, and of a dead prophet at 1 Samuel 28:13. The Septuagint rendered it angelous, angels, and Hebrews 2:7 quotes that Greek. So the New Testament is not translating the Hebrew here; it is quoting a translation.
A rank is something English is forced to pick. Elohim marks which realm a being belongs to rather than where it stands in a hierarchy, and no English noun does that.

When the New Testament quotes an Old Testament verse and the wording does not match your Old Testament, check the Septuagint before assuming anyone made a mistake. Very often the quotation is accurate to a different text.

God fits the Hebrew word and makes a strong claim about human status. Angels fits the Septuagint, the letter to the Hebrews, and a long tradition. Heavenly beings splits the difference and is the most common modern compromise. All three are defensible and the Hebrew alone does not settle it.
אֱלֹהִים elohim · H430

versions.s: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever. The king addressed directly as elohim, quoted of the Son at Hebrews 1:8.

b.t: Most versions read thy throne, O God, following the vocative reading and the Septuagint's own rendering, which Hebrews 1:8 quotes directly. A minority reading takes it as God is your throne, avoiding a direct divine address to the human king.

English can say **your throne, God**, addressing someone as God directly, or **God is your throne**, making God the foundation rather than the one addressed. The Hebrew grammar here genuinely supports reading it the first way, and whether a human king is really being called God, even in an exalted, honorific sense, is exactly what makes the verse so debated.

Elohim occurs four times in this psalm, at verses 2, 6, and twice in 7, with the surrounding occurrences clearly referring to God; the vocative reading, thy throne, O God, treats verse 6 as continuing that pattern, an extraordinarily exalted address to the Davidic king as God's own representative, perhaps even more than merely representative. The Septuagint reads it the same vocative way, and Hebrews 1:8 quotes that Greek text directly, applying the address to the Son as part of its argument for his superiority over the angels.

English must choose a subject and an address; thy throne, O God directly calls the addressee God, while God is your throne makes God a foundation rather than a title, two genuinely different claims that the Hebrew grammar, ambiguous enough to be argued for centuries, does not force in only one direction.

When a psalm's grammar allows a human figure to be addressed with divine vocabulary, take the ambiguity seriously rather than resolving it by assuming discomfort with the direct reading. Ancient Israelite royal ideology could apply exalted, even startling language to its kings as God's representatives.

Thy throne, O God follows the Septuagint, matches the surrounding elohim occurrences in the same psalm, and is the reading Hebrews 1:8 explicitly builds on. God is your throne avoids directly calling a human king God but requires reading the Hebrew syntax somewhat less naturally against its immediate context.

versions.s: Hope. Confident expectation, not wishing.

b.t: Every version reads hope.
**I hope it doesn't rain.** **The train is due at six.** The first is a wish. The second is an expectation. English uses the same word for the first and a different construction for the second.

Elpis is expectation, and in the New Testament it is expectation grounded in a promise. Classical Greek could use it neutrally of expecting something bad, which shows the word itself is about expectation rather than optimism.
English hope has drifted almost entirely toward the uncertain wish, so a word about confidence reads as a word about doubt.
When a word reads as weaker in English than the argument around it requires, the English word has probably weakened.
Hope is universal in English versions.

versions.s: Melchizedek, priest of the most high God. A title shared with Canaanite religion, which Abraham treats as naming his own God.

b.t: Every version reads most high God without comment, since El Elyon reads in English as a straightforward divine title with no built-in signal that it was also, independently, a title used of a chief Canaanite deity.

Imagine meeting a priest from another country who blesses you in the name of **the Almighty**, a title your own religion also uses. Do you correct him, or recognize the same God under a shared word? Genesis has Abraham do the second, and the choice carries weight.

El and Elyon both function as attested divine titles in the wider Canaanite religious world, El as the head of the pantheon and Elyon as a title meaning highest or most high. Melchizedek, a Canaanite king-priest of Salem, blesses Abram by El Elyon, and two verses later Abram swears an oath by the LORD, El Elyon, explicitly equating his own God's name with Melchizedek's title, treating them as the same God under different peoples' vocabulary rather than correcting or rejecting the foreign priest's language.

English most high God reads as a generic superlative description; it carries no signal that the underlying Hebrew phrase was also a known title in the surrounding Canaanite religious vocabulary, so the theological move Genesis is making, claiming a foreign priest's God-language as legitimately naming Israel's own God, is invisible without that background.

When a biblical text uses a title also attested in a neighboring culture's religious vocabulary, ask whether the text is borrowing, rejecting, or reclaiming that vocabulary. Genesis 14 reclaims it: Abraham does not treat Melchizedek as a pagan to be corrected but as a genuine priest of the same God under a shared ancient Near Eastern title.

Most high God is the uncontested sense of El Elyon in every version. The larger question, how much weight the shared Canaanite background carries for how this scene functions theologically, is a matter of ancient Near Eastern religious history layered on top of an otherwise straightforward translation.

entries.def: to have indignation on, i.e. (transitively) to blame, (intransitively) to sigh with chagrin, (specially) to sternly enjoin
entries.where: embrimaomai is tagged 5 times, across 3 books: john 2 · mark 2 · matthew 1.

versions.s: He groaned in the spirit. The verb is an anger word, not a grief word.

b.t: The King James reads groaned in the spirit. Modern versions read deeply moved, or greatly disturbed, and some footnote angry.
**He was moved.** **He bristled.** Two very different reactions, and English has both words available.

Embrimaomai is used of a horse snorting and of giving a stern charge. At Mark 1:43 and Matthew 9:30 it carries sternness. Here and at verse 38 it is paired with troubled himself, and translators who print deeply moved are smoothing a word that ordinarily carries indignation.
No English verb for anger also carries the sense of being inwardly shaken, so every rendering picks one and drops the other.
When a version's footnote offers angry as an alternative to moved, the word ordinarily means the first and the text has been softened.
Deeply moved is the modern reading; the King James reads groaned; angry appears in footnotes.
ἐμβριμάομαι embrimaomai · G1690

src: embrimaomai at Matthew 9:30; Mark 1:43; 14:5
Both occurrences here: John 11:33, 38
The pairing with etaraxen heauton, troubled himself

versions.s: Manasseh, for God hath made me forget; Ephraim, for God hath caused me to be fruitful. Two more names built from the naming sentence itself.

b.t: Every version reads Manasseh and Ephraim as bare transliterated names, with Joseph's explanatory statements translated separately and accurately, but without connecting either name back to its own root the way the Hebrew explicitly does.

By now the pattern should look familiar: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and now Manasseh and Ephraim, thirteen names in a row each built as a pun on the parent's own explanatory sentence. English transliteration keeps none of the wordplay, in Canaan or, as here, in Egypt.

Menashsheh echoes nashah, to forget, from Joseph's own words, God hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house. Ephraim echoes parah, to be fruitful, from for God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. Both names complete the pattern established across every one of Jacob's own sons' births, now applied one generation later, to children born not in Canaan but in Egypt, under Joseph's Egyptian name and Egyptian wife.

English Manasseh and Ephraim are bare proper nouns; the sentences explaining them read as separate commentary rather than as the linguistic source the names were extracted from, so the pattern completing itself one generation later, in a foreign land, is invisible without the Hebrew roots.

Continue tracking the birth-naming-pun device established across Genesis 29-30 all the way through the Joseph narrative. The device does not stop with Jacob's own sons; it continues into the next generation, even after the family relocates to Egypt.

Neither name nor its accompanying explanation is in dispute in any version. This entry rounds out the pattern already established for the rest of the twelve tribes' names, showing it persists one generation further, into Joseph's own Egyptian-born sons.
מְנַשֶּׁה Menashsheh (נָשָׁה nashah, forget) / אֶפְרַיִם Ephraim (פָּרָה parah, fruitful) · H4519 / H5382 / H669 / H6509

src: The same naming-pun pattern across all twelve tribal names: Genesis 29:32-30:24; 35:18

versions.s: Daily bread. The word translated daily occurs twice in all of Greek literature, both times here.

b.t: Every English version reads daily. Footnotes offer bread for tomorrow, or bread necessary for existence. The Latin tradition split, with Jerome rendering the same word supersubstantialem in Matthew and quotidianum in Luke.

Someone hands you a sentence: **The flimsock was open.** There is no other sentence in English with flimsock in it. You can guess from the shape of the word, you can guess from the context, and that is all you will ever have. That is what a word appearing once looks like.

Epiousios is a dis legomenon, a word occurring exactly twice: Matthew 6:11 and the Lukan parallel at 11:3. A single claimed occurrence outside the New Testament, on a papyrus, is regarded as highly doubtful. There is a strong argument against daily that most readers never meet: every other New Testament passage rendered daily contains the word hemera, day, and this one does not.

A word with no comparative evidence cannot be translated by comparison. Translators are reduced to breaking it into parts, epi plus a form of einai or of ienai, and the two paths give different answers.

A word occurring once is a hapax legomenon; twice is a dis legomenon. Either way there are no outside witnesses to check a meaning against. When your Bible's footnote offers two unrelated meanings for one word, that is usually what has happened.

BDAG lists four live possibilities: necessary for existence, for the current day, for the following day, and for the future. The first takes the word from einai, to be. The last two take it from ienai, to come, which would make it bread for tomorrow asked for today and turn the petition into a request for the provision of the age to come. Daily is the traditional rendering and most scholars now reject it, partly on the hemera argument above.
ἐπιούσιος epiousios · G1967

src: Origen, On Prayer 27.7, already reports that the word was not in use among the Greeks and appears to have been coined
The Vulgate reads supersubstantialem at Matthew 6:11 and quotidianum at Luke 11:3, the same word rendered two ways by one translator; the older Vetus Latina read quotidianum in both

versions.s: Coming into the world. Nothing in the Greek tells you whether that describes the light or the man.

b.t: Modern versions almost all attach it to the light: the true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.

**I saw the man with the telescope.** Who had the telescope, you or the man? Nothing in those seven words decides it. English does this constantly and you usually work it out from context. When the context does not settle it, a translator has to.

The participle erchomenon can attach to the light or to every man. Greek word order is flexible enough that position does not settle it, and the participle's form fits either. This is attachment ambiguity, the same phenomenon as an English sentence where you cannot tell which noun a trailing phrase modifies.
English forces the phrase to sit next to one noun or the other. Word order in English is what carries grammatical relationship, so the moment you write the sentence in English you have decided.

When a modern version rearranges a King James sentence rather than changing its words, look for a participle or a modifying phrase that could attach in more than one place. The rearrangement is the decision.

Attaching it to the man produces the King James reading, every man that comes into the world, which is a Jewish idiom for everyone born. Attaching it to the light produces a statement about the incarnation and fits the next verse, he was in the world. The second has the better contextual case and the first has the older tradition.

versions.s: The heaven and the earth. Not two items. One idea named by its opposite ends.

b.t: All versions read the heavens and the earth. None flags the construction, and none needs to, because English has the same figure.

**They searched high and low.** Nobody thinks two altitudes were searched. **She read it cover to cover.** Naming the two ends is how English says everything in between, and you have never once stopped to notice.

This is a merism: two opposite terms standing for the whole. Hebrew uses it constantly. The phrase does not mean sky plus ground. It means the entire ordered cosmos, and Hebrew had no single word for that.
English does have this figure, which is why nothing is lost. The problem is that English readers treat biblical phrases as technical and stop hearing the figure they use themselves every day.
A pair of opposites joined by and is usually one idea, not two. Test it by asking whether the writer meant to exclude the middle. If not, you have a merism.
Nothing to choose. This entry is here because readers argue about what heaven means as though it were a separate item being inventoried, rather than half of a single figure of speech.
שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ shamayim wa-arets · H8064 + H776

src: Merism elsewhere: Psalm 139:2, sitting down and rising up; Deuteronomy 6:7, when thou liest down and when thou risest up
Genesis 2:4 repeats the phrase as a summary of the whole account

versions.s: Land, earth, country. Which one it means is usually the whole question.

b.t: Versions read earth, land, country, or ground according to context.
**He returned to his country.** **The whole world watched.** English keeps land and earth apart. Hebrew does not.

Erets is the ground, a territory, a nation's land, and the whole earth. Genesis 1:1 is usually read as the whole earth; the promises to Abraham are the land; and in the Prophets the choice between them changes the scope of a promise.
English has separate words for a plot, a country and the planet, so translators must decide a scope Hebrew leaves open.
When a translation footnote offers land as an alternative to earth, the scope of the verse is in play, not just the wording.
Earth and land are both majority renderings in their own contexts.
אֶרֶץ erets · H776

entries.title: ereunao
entries.where: ereunao is tagged 6 times, across 5 books: john 2 · 1corinthians 1 · 1peter 1 · revelation 1 · romans 1.

versions.s: Search the scriptures. The Greek form is both a command and a statement.

b.t: The King James reads search the scriptures as a command. Most modern versions read you search the scriptures as a statement.
**You're reading.** **Read!** In English those look different. Imagine one form that could be either, and only the sentence around it deciding.

Eraunate is identical in form as a present indicative and a present imperative. Read as indicative, the sentence is you search the scriptures because you think you have life in them, and they testify of me, and you will not come to me. That reading fits the rebuke that follows.
English has different forms for a command and a statement, so the printing settles it and the reader never sees the choice.
Some Greek forms are identical across mood. When a version prints a command and another prints a statement, this is usually why.
The statement reading, you search the scriptures, is what most modern versions print; the King James reads it as a command instead.
ἐραυνάω eraunao · G2045

src: The identical indicative and imperative forms in the present active second plural
The argument of John 5:39-47 as a rebuke

versions.s: Blessed is the man. The Hebrew is a plural exclamation, not a description.

b.t: All versions read blessed or happy. None renders it as an exclamation, because English has no comfortable way to shout a noun.

**Lucky him!** is not the same sentence as **He is lucky.** The first is something you shout. The second is something you assess. English can do both and the difference is in the punctuation more than the words.

Ashrei is a plural noun in the construct, closer to O the happinesses of the man who. It is not the same word as barak, which is the verb for blessing someone. The psalm opens with a cry, not a definition, and the Septuagint's makarios carries that into the Beatitudes.
English blessed is a participle and behaves like an adjective. There is no English noun you can put at the front of a sentence to mean how fortunate is the one who.

When a verse opens with a single word that feels like a verdict, check whether the original is a noun. Hebrew exclamations often arrive as nouns and English converts them to adjectives without asking.

Every version agrees on blessed; nothing here is a rendering dispute. What needs correcting is the mental picture: readers routinely take blessed as a state conferred rather than a condition observed, and the grammar points the other way.
אַשְׁרֵי ashrei · H835

versions.s: I have gotten a man from the LORD. Or: a man, the LORD. The little word between them decides which.

b.t: Every English version reads from the LORD, with the LORD's help, or a similar rendering that treats et as the preposition with. None reads the more literal, and far stranger, a man, namely the LORD.

**I baked a cake, the winner.** Read that as an appositive and you just said the cake is the winner. Read the comma as separating two items and you said something else. Hebrew's et normally marks exactly the appositive-style reading, and that is the problem here.

Et is overwhelmingly the marker introducing a definite direct object, not a preposition meaning with. Read that way, qaniti ish et YHWH would mean I have gotten a man, the LORD, an equation most readers find unthinkable in Eve's mouth. Grammarians have proposed et functioning here as with the help of, but no clearly parallel case elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible confirms that use, which is why the question stays open rather than settled by grammar alone.

English with and English the marker of a direct object are different words doing different jobs, so a translator has to choose one before the sentence reaches an English reader. The ambiguity that makes Hebrew scholars argue about this verse cannot survive into English at all; the English sentence necessarily picks a side.

When a small grammatical word carries the whole weight of a verse's meaning, check whether its unusual reading here is attested anywhere else in the same corpus. An unparalleled use should be held more loosely than a common one, however theologically attractive it looks.

With the LORD's help is the reading every version prints, and it fits ordinary Hebrew usage of et poorly but fits the context comfortably. A man, the LORD, keeps the ordinary grammar but produces a claim nothing else in the passage supports. Both options have a real cost.
אֶת et (with קָנִיתִי qaniti, I have gotten) · H853 / H7069

src: Et as the standard direct-object marker: any standard Hebrew grammar (e.g. GKC, Joüon-Muraoka)
Dillmann's commentary on Genesis, noting no clearly parallel instrumental use of et elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible
Targum Onkelos and most premodern Jewish and Christian readings take the 'with the LORD's help' sense

versions.s: He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken. Quoted at John 19:36, itself echoing the Passover lamb's own unbroken bones.

b.t: Every version reads not one of them is broken here and a bone of him shall not be broken at John 19:36, both accurate translations, but with no built-in cross-reference showing the deliberate three-way echo running from Exodus through this psalm to the Gospel.

English readers meeting John 19:36's claim, a bone of him shall not be broken, may not immediately connect it backward to this psalm, or further back still to the instructions for the Passover lamb, three texts chained together by one repeated detail most translations do not flag as connected.

The promise that the righteous sufferer's bones will be kept unbroken here is picked up explicitly at John 19:36, applied to the soldiers' decision not to break Jesus's legs, itself already echoing Exodus 12:46's regulation that none of the Passover lamb's bones be broken. John's Gospel draws all three together, casting Jesus's death in the vocabulary both of this psalm's righteous sufferer and of the Passover lamb whose blood marked Israel's houses for deliverance.

English readers of John 19:36 alone may recognize the quotation as scriptural without necessarily tracing it back through this specific psalm to the even older Passover regulation, a three-text chain that requires deliberately cross-referencing rather than reading any one passage in isolation.

When the New Testament explicitly quotes an Old Testament verse using fulfilled language, check whether that Old Testament verse is itself already echoing something still earlier in the Hebrew Bible. Fulfillment quotations are sometimes the last link in a chain, not the first.

The wording of both passages translates without dispute. What's easy to miss is the full three-part chain, Passover lamb, righteous sufferer, crucified Jesus, that a reader encountering only one of the three texts at a time would likely never notice.
עֹצְמוֹתָיו etzmotav (bones) · H6106

src: John 19:36's explicit quotation
Exodus 12:46's Passover lamb regulation, 'neither shall ye break a bone thereof'

versions.s: Gospel. In ordinary Greek it was the announcement of a royal victory or an emperor's accession.

b.t: Every version reads gospel or good news. Both are majority renderings depending on the version.
**Breaking news.** A phrase that belongs to broadcasting, not to religion. Now imagine a religious movement adopting it as its central term.
Euangelion is a good announcement, used in the Roman world for news of a military victory or the birth or accession of an emperor. The Priene inscription uses it of Augustus.
English gospel is now exclusively religious and carries none of the public, political register the Greek had.
A New Testament word that also turns up in Roman imperial inscriptions is not a coincidence; the overlap is the point. The vocabulary was borrowed, and borrowing is a claim.
Gospel and good news are both standard; good news is increasingly the majority in newer versions.
εὐαγγέλιον euangelion · G2098

src: The Priene calendar inscription applying euangelion to Augustus
Isaiah 52:7 and 61:1 in the Septuagint use the verb form
Mark 1:1 opens with the noun

versions.s: Power to become the sons of God. The word is closer to right or authority than to power.

b.t: Modern versions read right, or authority. Power has dropped out because English power now means capacity, and the Greek is about entitlement.
**I gave him the power to sign the cheque.** In 1611 that meant permission. Today most people hear ability. The sentence never changed. The word slid underneath it.
Exousia is delegated authority, the right to do something because someone with standing has granted it. Greek has a separate word for raw capability, dunamis. John chose the authority word.
English power slid toward capacity and strength. In 1611 it still covered granted authority, which is why the King James reading was accurate then and misleads now.

When the King James and a modern version differ by one abstract noun, check whether the English word moved. Power, conversation, prevent, suffer, let and comfort have all shifted since 1611, and the Greek behind them has not.
There is no Greek dispute. This is an English shift, and the modern renderings are correcting for it rather than correcting the King James translators.
ἐξουσία exousia · G1849

src: Exousia against dunamis: Luke 4:36 uses both in one sentence

versions.s: She sat in an open place. The Hebrew could be a place name, Enaim, or literally the opening of the eyes.

b.t: The King James reads in an open place, treating the phrase as a description. Other versions, ancient and modern, read it as the place name Enaim, following Joshua 15:34's mention of a town by that name in the same region.

English **open place** reads as a simple description of visibility. The underlying Hebrear could instead be naming an actual town, or could be building a scene where a woman positions herself to be seen at exactly the place named eyes, a difference between plain geography and deliberate staging.

Petach eynayim, most literally opening of the eyes, or the entrance to Eynayim, sits at a genuine crossroads of interpretation: eynayim, eyes, is also plausibly the name of a real town (Joshua 15:34 names Eynayim in the same district), so the phrase could simply mean at the entrance to Eynayim, a geographic marker, or it could be functioning idiomatically, describing a conspicuous, visible spot where Tamar deliberately positions herself to be noticed, playing on the literal sense of eyes even if the place also had that name.

English open place picks the idiomatic, staging-focused reading and loses any sense that a real place name might be doing double duty; a straightforward place-name translation, Enaim, loses the wordplay on eyes and visibility that a scene built around deception and seeing so pointedly seems to want.

When a place name in Hebrew is also a meaningful common word, consider that the narrator may be using it for both functions at once, real geography and pointed wordplay, rather than choosing between them.

Reading it as a real place name, Enaim, keeps the scene concretely located. Reading it idiomatically, the opening of the eyes, or a visible crossroads, keeps the wordplay alive in a story centrally about who sees and who is deceived. Both readings may be simultaneously true, which no single English rendering can hold at once.

versions.s: Help meet. Two English words that were never one word, and a Hebrew phrase that says something else again.

b.t: Modern versions read a helper suitable for him, or a helper corresponding to him, or a helper as his complement.

**That is a meet reward.** Meet used to mean fitting. It died, and people who still heard it in the phrase started running the two words together into helpmeet, then helpmate. A word that never existed got invented by ears rather than pens.

The Hebrew is ezer kenegdo. Ezer is a helper, and the word is used most often in the Hebrew Bible of God himself helping Israel, which is not the sense of assistant. Kenegdo is built on neged, meaning in front of or opposite, so the phrase is a helper corresponding to him, one who stands facing him.

Two separate problems stack here. English lost the word meet, meaning fitting, so help meet was misheard as helpmeet and then as helpmate, a word that never existed in the text. And English helper carries a junior connotation that the Hebrew ezer does not.

When a King James phrase has become a single familiar word, check whether it was ever one word. English drift produces some of the most confident misreadings in the Bible, and they are invisible to a reader who only has the English.

There is no real translation dispute here. There is an English-language accident, and then a genuine question about the force of ezer, which every modern version handles slightly differently while none of them says assistant.

versions.s: The Angel which redeemed me from all evil. The first use of go'el, redeemer, in the Bible, applied to an angel.

b.t: Every version reads redeemed or delivered, correctly conveying rescue, but without necessarily flagging that go'el is a specific legal-kinship term, not a general word for saving someone.

English redeemer sounds like a purely spiritual title. In Hebrew law, go'el names something concrete and legal: the nearest relative obligated to buy back a family member's lost land, freedom, or life, the way a modern next of kin might be legally bound to step in. Jacob is applying that specific, legal family role to the angel who has watched over him.

Go'el names the kinsman-redeemer throughout the Hebrew Bible, the nearest relative legally obligated to redeem land, avenge blood, or rescue a family member from servitude, most fully developed later in Ruth and in Levitical law. This is the word's first appearance in the Bible, and Jacob applies it not to God under His ordinary names but to the angel who has accompanied him, treating that figure as functioning in the specific legal role of nearest kinsman-protector.

English redeemed carries broad, largely religious connotations by now; it does not automatically evoke the specific legal picture of a family member obligated by kinship law to rescue you, so the precision of Jacob's word choice, applying a technical family-law term to an angel, is easy to miss.

When a word's first biblical occurrence is doing specific legal or social work later developed at length elsewhere, as go'el is here, read that first occurrence in light of its fuller later development rather than assuming it is simply a poetic synonym for saved or helped.

Redeemed is the agreed sense in every version. The larger question, whether this angel is a created being functioning in a kinsman-redeemer role or something more, is a live theological debate the word's first, loaded appearance here helps generate rather than settle.
הַמַּלְאָךְ הַגֹּאֵל hamal'ach hago'el (גָּאַל ga'al, redeem) · H1350

versions.s: Kinsman-redeemer. A legal role English has no word for at all.

b.t: Versions read kinsman, redeemer, kinsman-redeemer, or guardian-redeemer.
**Next of kin.** English has a phrase for who the relative is and no word at all for what that relative is obliged to do.

The goel is the nearest male relative, obliged to buy back sold family land, redeem a relative sold into slavery, avenge a killing, and marry a widow to raise an heir. It is a legal office, not a sentiment.
English has no equivalent institution, so every rendering is either a paraphrase or an invented compound.
Where a word names an institution your culture does not have, no translation will work. Learn the institution.
Kinsman-redeemer and redeemer are the majority renderings; guardian-redeemer is the NIV's.

versions.s: The Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha. Another gloss, in the other direction.

b.t: Every version keeps both names.
Writing **the Underground, or as Americans say the subway** tells a reader where you think they live.

Lithostrotos is Greek for a stone pavement. Gabbatha is Aramaic, probably meaning a ridge or height, and it is not a translation of the Greek but a different name for the same place. John calls it Hebrew, which in this period regularly means Aramaic.
Nothing is lost. The reversal of order and the fact that the two names are not equivalents are the details worth noticing.
When a writer gives two names for one place, check whether the second translates the first or merely renames it. Often it renames.
Both names are printed in every version; Aramaic appears in modern footnotes where the text says Hebrew.

entries.def: Galed, a memorial cairn East of the Jordan

versions.s: Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha; Jacob called it Galeed. Two languages, same meaning, spoken by two members of the same extended family.

b.t: Every version keeps both names as transliterations, Jegar-sahadutha and Galeed, usually with a footnote that both mean heap of witness, but without necessarily flagging that the first is Aramaic and the second Hebrew, two related but distinct languages, not two dialects of one.

Imagine two cousins from different countries naming the same landmark, each in their own language, and the story records both names side by side without translating either into a third, shared language. Genesis does exactly that here, in the middle of an otherwise all-Hebrew book.

Yegar sahaduta, Aramaic for heap of witness, is generally recognized as the first identifiable stretch of Aramaic in the Bible, distinct from the Hebrew that surrounds it on every side. Jacob's own name for the same heap, Gal-ed, Hebrew for the identical meaning, sits right beside it in the very same verse, making the linguistic difference between Laban the Aramean and Jacob the Hebrew-speaker explicit in their own recorded words rather than merely inferred from their genealogy.

English translation renders both names into transliterated proper nouns and glosses both meanings in English, so the fact that the underlying words are in two genuinely different Semitic languages, not two versions of the same language, disappears entirely once both are handled the same way in translation.

When two characters name the same thing differently in the same verse, check whether the difference is dialectal, linguistic, or simply stylistic before assuming it is incidental. This verse is doing real sociolinguistic work, marking Laban and Jacob as speakers of two related but separate languages.

Neither name's meaning, heap of witness, is disputed among translators. What matters is that Laban's version is Aramaic and Jacob's is Hebrew, two different languages rather than two names in one, a linguistic detail no English rendering of either name preserves.
יְגַר שָׂהֲדוּתָא Yegar Sahaduta (Aramaic) / גַּלְעֵד Gal-ed (Hebrew) · H3026 / H1567

src: Standard recognition of this verse as the earliest identifiable Aramaic passage in the Hebrew Bible: comparative Semitic linguistics and standard Genesis commentaries
Laban explicitly identified elsewhere as an Aramean: Genesis 25:20; 31:20, 24

versions.s: Abraham gave up the ghost. One Hebrew verb, meaning expired or breathed his last; ghost has since become a word for a spirit-apparition.

b.t: Modern versions read breathed his last or simply died, avoiding the archaic phrase and its modern connotations entirely.

In 1611, **ghost** still carried its older sense of breath or spirit, as in Holy Ghost. Today **ghost** mainly means a translucent apparition haunting a house. The Hebrew verb never changed meaning; the English word built around it picked up a new, spookier sense over four centuries.

Gava is a single verb meaning to expire, to breathe one's last, used of ordinary death throughout the Hebrew Bible with no supernatural or spectral connotation whatsoever. The King James rendering, gave up the ghost, reflects ghost's older English sense of breath or spirit leaving the body, not a claim about apparitions.

English ghost has narrowed and shifted from a general word for breath or spirit toward its now-dominant sense of a spectral apparition, so a phrase accurate in 1611 now unintentionally suggests something supernatural that neither the Hebrew verb nor the original English phrase ever meant.

Add gave up the ghost to the short list of King James phrases, alongside tempt and repented, where the English words themselves drifted after 1611 while the underlying Hebrew or Greek stayed exactly where it always was.

Breathed his last or simply died uses current English accurately without the accidental supernatural suggestion. Gave up the ghost was accurate English in 1611 and has only become misleading because ghost itself changed meaning, not because the Hebrew was ever in question.
גָּוַע gava (to expire) · H1478

src: gava used of ordinary death with no supernatural connotation: e.g. Genesis 6:17; 7:21; 49:33

versions.s: Was, and came to be. Two verbs one verse apart, and the whole prologue turns on the difference.

b.t: English uses was for the first and were made for the second, which hides that both are ordinary verbs of being and becoming.

**The house was there. The shed came to be there.** Both sentences put something in a yard. The first one does not tell you the house ever started. The second one tells you the shed had a beginning. English can say this if it works at it. Greek says it with two different verbs and never has to explain.

Verse 1 uses en, the imperfect of eimi, to be. Verse 3 uses egeneto, the aorist of ginomai, to become or come into existence. John keeps them apart with complete discipline through the whole prologue: everything created gets ginomai, and the Word gets eimi. Verse 14 is the hinge, where the Word finally takes egeneto, became flesh.
English was covers both existing and starting to exist. Greek has separate verbs, so the distinction is built into the vocabulary rather than argued in a footnote.
Watch which verb a writer uses for existence. If a Greek text alternates between eimi and ginomai in the same passage, the alternation is almost never accidental.

No translator disputes the parsing. The difficulty is that no English rendering can keep the two verbs visibly distinct without paraphrasing, so every version loses the pattern and study Bibles have to point at it in a note.

versions.s: This is life eternal, that they might know thee. Knowing here is relational, not informational.

b.t: Every version reads know.
**I know him.** **I know about him.** English has the distinction and uses about to mark it. Hebrew and Greek lean on context instead.

Ginosko translates Hebrew yada, which covers experiential acquaintance, including intimacy. The verse defines the life not by duration but by relationship, which is the strongest internal argument for reading aionios as quality rather than length.
English know covers both senses, so nothing is lost in the word. What is lost is the Hebrew background that makes the relational sense the default.
When a verse defines a term, the definition outranks every lexicon. John 17:3 defines eternal life inside the text.
Know is universal.

entries.title: golem
entries.def: a wrapped (and unformed mass, i.e. as the embryo)

versions.s: Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect. Golmi, an unformed, still-shapeless mass, the word later Judaism borrowed to name the golem.

b.t: The King James reads my substance, yet being unperfect, while modern versions typically read my unformed substance or my unformed body, both attempts at the same rare, vivid word for shapeless, still-forming matter.

English substance is a broad, generic word for material or stuff. The Hebrew golmi is far more specific and vivid: something rolled up, folded, or wadded together, still without shape, like an embryo or a formless lump of clay, an image later Jewish folklore turned into a proper name, the golem, an artificial being shaped from clay before receiving breath or speech.

Golem, from the root galam, to wrap or fold up, is a hapax legomenon with no other biblical occurrence, making its precise sense harder to fix from context alone, though cognate evidence and later usage both point toward an unformed, rolled-together mass, fitting the verse's larger picture of God observing and recording a body before it has taken shape in the womb. Later Rabbinic and medieval Jewish tradition took this same rare word and used it to name an artificially animated being formed from clay, the golem of folklore, borrowing directly from this psalm's picture of unformed material awaiting its final shape.

English substance gives no hint that the underlying Hebrew word is rare enough to appear only this once in the entire Bible, or that it is the very word later Jewish folklore would adopt to name an animated clay figure, a etymological thread entirely invisible in translation.

A Hebrew word that occurs only once in the entire Bible has no other biblical context to check it against, so its precise sense often has to be reconstructed from its root and from how later tradition used the same word.

My substance, yet being unperfect, and my unformed substance both attempt to render a word with no other biblical occurrence to compare it against. What is worth surfacing is the word's vivid, concrete root sense, a rolled-up, shapeless mass, and its unexpected afterlife as the name for the golem of later Jewish legend.

versions.s: Golgotha, that is to say, a place of a skull. And John says it the other way round.

b.t: Every version keeps both.
Two glosses in one chapter, in opposite orders, is a pattern rather than a habit.

Golgotha is Aramaic gulgolta, skull. John glosses it kraniou topos, place of a skull. Latin calvaria gives the English Calvary, which enters through the Vulgate and appears in the King James only at Luke 23:33.
Nothing is lost. Calvary being a Latin word rather than a biblical name is the part most readers have never been told.
When an English Bible has a familiar name that appears only once, check whether it came in through Latin.
Golgotha with the gloss is universal; Calvary appears only in the King James at Luke 23:33.

entries.title: gopher
entries.def: a kind of tree or wood (as used for building), apparently the cypress

versions.s: Gopher wood. A word used exactly once, and no one knows for certain what tree it names.

b.t: Every version reads gopher wood, transliterating rather than translating, because there is no second occurrence anywhere to translate from. Some modern notes suggest cypress or another conifer as a guess, never as a certainty.

Every English Bible just says **gopher wood**, which sounds specific but is really a translator's shrug: this word occurs nowhere else, so rather than guess at a species, translators simply carried the Hebrew sound into English wholesale.

Gopher occurs only at Genesis 6:14, a true hapax legomenon with no other biblical or extrabiblical Hebrew attestation to compare it against. Every proposal for its botanical identity, cypress being the most common modern guess, is inferred from context, from shipbuilding plausibility, or from similar-sounding words in related languages, not from a second usage that would confirm it.

English gopher wood looks like a specific, confident botanical term, the way oak or cedar would be, but it is a transliteration standing in for total uncertainty. An English reader cannot tell the difference between a well-attested wood name and a total guess dressed in the same grammatical clothing.

A transliterated word in an English Bible is often a flag, not a translation: it usually means no one has been confident enough to translate it. Treat every untranslated Hebrew term you meet in English as an invitation to ask why it was left that way.

No real choice was available to translators; there is nothing to choose between since the word has no second occurrence to weigh against another. Every specific identification, cypress or otherwise, is an educated guess dressed as a footnote, not a finding.

versions.s: In his law doth he meditate day and night. The verb, hagah, means mutter or growl, not silent reflection.

b.t: Every version reads meditate, a reasonable English word but one that has drifted toward silence and stillness in modern usage, away from the vocal, physical picture the Hebrew verb actually paints.

English meditate suggests sitting quietly with your eyes closed, thinking. Hagah pictures something noisier: lips moving, words repeated under your breath, closer to how you might quietly recite a phone number to remember it, or the low, steady growl of an animal that will not let go of what it has caught.

Hagah is used elsewhere of a lion growling low over its kill at Isaiah 31:4 and of a dove's mournful cooing at Isaiah 38:14, an onomatopoeic word for a low, continuous vocal sound. Applied to studying the law day and night, it pictures someone murmuring the text aloud, repeating it under their breath, physically working it over with their mouth, not sitting in silent contemplation.

English meditate has shifted toward quiet, internal mental stillness, especially through modern popular usage, so a reader pictures something close to the opposite of what hagah actually describes: an active, murmuring, half-vocal engagement with the words themselves.

When a spiritual practice-word in the Bible sounds like a modern wellness term, meditate, contemplate, check whether the underlying Hebrew or Greek word describes something more physical, vocal, or active than the modern English term now suggests.

Meditate keeps the traditional, respected English rendering but invites a picture closer to modern mindfulness than the Hebrew supports. Mutter or murmur is more accurate to hagah's sound-based sense but strips away the devotional dignity English readers expect the verse to carry.

versions.s: Holy. The idea is set apart for a purpose, not morally spotless.

b.t: Versions read holy, and saints for the plural noun. Some read God's people or holy ones.
**The good china.** It is not better china morally. It is the china you do not use on a Tuesday, because it has been set aside for something.
Hagios and Hebrew qadosh both carry separation for a purpose as the core idea. Moral purity follows from whose purpose it is rather than being the word's own content.
English holy and saint both imply attained goodness, which reverses the direction: the word is about designation, and the conduct is the response.
When a word describes a status, check whether English has turned it into an achievement. Status words become merit words very easily.
Holy is the majority rendering and saints is the majority for the plural, though God's holy people is gaining ground.
