versions.s: Not of blood. The Greek says bloods, plural, and the plural is a Hebrew way of speaking.

b.t: No English version renders the plural, because bloods is not English.

**He comes from money.** English lets you say that about a family line. It does not let you say **he comes from bloods**, even though several other languages do exactly that. When a language makes a word plural where yours never would, the writer is probably thinking in another language.

The Greek is ex haimaton, a plural of haima. Greek does not ordinarily pluralize blood. Hebrew and Aramaic do, most clearly for bloodshed and blood-guilt; some interpreters extend the same idiom to descent and bloodline as the sense at work here, though that extension leans more on how this verse itself is read than on independent Hebrew examples of damim meaning lineage. Either way, this is Semitic idiom coming through a Greek sentence.
English blood has no meaningful plural. Bloods reads as an error, so every translator silently singularizes it, and the trace of the underlying idiom disappears.

When a Greek noun is plural where English would never pluralize it, suspect a Hebrew or Aramaic idiom underneath. The New Testament is Greek written largely by people who thought in a Semitic language.

The core observation is not in question: Greek does not ordinarily pluralize blood, and this plural is a trace of Semitic idiom. How far that idiom extends to a sense of lineage is a separate, more interpretive question. Either way, the loss is unavoidable and worth knowing about, because it is one of the small pieces of evidence that the writer's first language is showing.

versions.s: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him. The refrain breaks, and the verb for walked is unusual.

b.t: Every version reads walked with God and God took him, correctly, but the contrast with the surrounding refrain, and he died, and he died, and he died, is a formatting effect a printed English Bible does not reproduce the way a continuous Hebrew reading does.

Imagine a list where every entry ends **and then he died**, except one, which instead says **and then he was gone**. The break itself is the announcement, before you even read what filled the gap. Hebrew builds that exact surprise into this one verse.

Vayithhalech, walked, is a hitpael, a reflexive or intensive stem, used of Enoch here and later of Noah at 6:9, rare enough as a description of a human relationship with God that its two uses in Genesis are usually read together. Where the chapter's refrain would put vayamot, and he died, this entry instead has einenu, he was not, and God took him, laqach, the same verb used of Elijah's departure centuries later.

English walked with God reads as an ordinary idiom for a godly life; it does not carry the reflexive intensity of the Hebrew stem, nor does it signal, without a reader already knowing the pattern, that this is the one entry in ten where the expected refrain is deliberately withheld.

In a formulaic passage, the exception is where the meaning concentrates. Before treating a broken pattern as incidental, ask what the formula was doing everywhere else and read the break as the chapter's real point.

Translators aren't divided on the plain sense here. What is lost is structural: seeing this entry against the refrain it breaks, and noticing that the same rare verb form recurs for Noah two chapters later, both of which require reading the Hebrew continuously rather than verse by isolated verse.
וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ vayithhalech (הָלַךְ halach, hitpael) · H1980

versions.s: Get thee out. Literally go, for yourself, or go, to yourself: a pronoun added where none was grammatically needed.

b.t: Most versions read get thee out, go forth, or simply go, all reasonable renderings that lose the grammatical oddity, an unneeded reflexive pronoun, that Hebrew readers immediately notice.

**Go.** That is a complete command. **Go, for yourself.** That is the same command with something added that changes nothing about the instruction and everything about its weight, making the journey personal rather than merely logistical. Hebrew does exactly that here.

Lech lecha pairs the plain imperative lech, go, with lecha, to or for yourself, a dative pronoun that is not required to complete the sentence's grammar. Its presence signals personal investment or benefit, go for your own sake, into your own becoming, rather than a bare travel instruction, and the same construction recurs at Genesis 22:2 when Abraham is told to go to Moriah, framing his story with two commands that are more than they need to be.

English go is already grammatically complete, so an English translator either drops the redundant pronoun entirely, matching ordinary usage, or must add an interpretive phrase like for your own sake to signal what the Hebrew conveys by the pronoun's mere unnecessary presence.

Watch for grammatically superfluous words in a Hebrew imperative; a pronoun that is not required to complete the sentence is often doing emphatic or reflexive work that a bare English imperative cannot carry without extra vocabulary.

Get thee out and go forth both lose the pronoun's redundancy but keep the sense of departure. No translation captures the personal-stakes nuance of lecha without either paraphrasing or adding a phrase the Hebrew itself achieves with one small, technically unnecessary word.
לֶךְ־לְךָ lech lecha (הָלַךְ halach, to go) · H1980

versions.s: Sin. The word carries an image of a shot that misses.

b.t: Every version reads sin. No dispute exists about the rendering.
**He missed.** That tells you the arrow went somewhere else. It does not tell you why, or whether he was aiming.

The root sense involves failing to hit, and Greek used it of an archer and of a traveller losing a road. Whether that image was live for New Testament writers is a separate question from whether it is the word's origin, and mostly it was not.
English sin is a purely moral and religious word with no physical picture in it at all.
An origin is not a definition. Missing the mark is where the word came from, not what Paul means by it, and preaching the etymology as the meaning is the commonest word-study error there is.
Every English version reads sin, and no translator has proposed an alternative.
ἁμαρτία hamartia · G266

versions.s: A flaming sword which turned every way. The verb form says the sword turns itself.

b.t: Every version reads some form of turning, flashing, or whirling. None can mark, without an added phrase, that the Hebrew verb form itself specifies the sword is the one doing the turning, to itself, continuously.

English can say **self-turning** or **a sword that kept turning on its own**, but it takes extra words to say it. Hebrew builds the same reflexive idea, something happening to itself, directly into one verb form, no extra word needed.

Hammithhapeket is a hitpael participle from haphak, to turn or overturn; the hitpael stem regularly marks reflexive or reciprocal action, something happening to or by the subject itself. The sword is not turned by an unnamed hand; the grammar makes it the agent of its own continuous turning, guarding the way to the tree of life on its own.

English marks reflexive action with a separate word, self- or itself, or with a whole clause. Hebrew can fold that same sense into the verb's own form, so a single participle does work that English needs extra vocabulary to do, and translations regularly drop the reflexive nuance rather than add the extra words.

The hitpael stem is one of the places Hebrew grammar itself carries meaning with no one-word English equivalent. When you meet it, ask what would need to be added in English to say the same thing, and notice that the Hebrew needed nothing added.

No real translation dispute over turned every way as a general sense. The finer point, that the grammar specifies self-turning rather than being turned by something else, is a detail every version states, if at all, with an added phrase rather than showing where it lives in the single Hebrew word.
מִתְהַפֶּכֶת mithhapeket (הָפַךְ haphak) · H2015

versions.s: Touch me not. The Greek is stop doing what you are already doing.

b.t: The King James reads touch me not. Modern versions read do not cling to me, do not hold on to me, or stop clinging to me. The correction is now near-universal.

**Do not shout.** **Stop shouting.** The first is a rule for the future. The second says you are shouting right now and should quit. English uses different words. Greek uses different tenses of one verb.

Haptou is a present imperative with a negative. In Greek that construction ordinarily means stop an action in progress rather than forbid one not yet begun. Mary is already holding him. The command is to let go, not to keep away.
English negative commands have no aspect. Do not touch me is the same shape whether the touching has started or not, so a translator must add words like stop or cling to carry it.
A negated present imperative in Greek usually means stop. A negated aorist subjunctive usually means do not start. That single distinction fixes a surprising number of hard verses.
There is no real dispute left. The King James rendering reflects a grammatical understanding that has since been refined, and every modern version has moved.
ἅπτομαι haptomai · G680

versions.s: The mountains of Ararat. A region, plural mountains, not a single named peak.

b.t: Every version reads the mountains of Ararat, plural, correctly matching the Hebrew. Popular usage, hymns, and most modern maps nonetheless speak of Mount Ararat, a single volcanic peak in eastern Turkey, as though that were what the verse specifies.

**The ark landed in the Rockies** names a mountain range. **The ark landed on Pikes Peak** names one mountain. Genesis says the first kind of thing, and centuries of popular tradition, and most maps and paintings, quietly upgraded it to the second.

Ararat corresponds to Urartu, a real historical kingdom attested in Assyrian records, centered on the highlands around Lake Van in what is now eastern Turkey, Armenia, and northwestern Iran, roughly the ninth through sixth centuries BC. The Hebrew names a mountainous region, not a single summit; the specific volcanic peak now called Mount Ararat received that name only later, as a traditional identification laid onto the biblical region rather than a claim the text itself makes.

English the mountains of Ararat is grammatically plain, but centuries of art, hymnody, and geography teaching have collapsed the region into a single named mountain, an identification English readers absorb from culture rather than from the actual wording of the verse, which never narrows the landing site that far.

Check whether a familiar geographic identification is actually in the text or was supplied later by tradition. A named region in Hebrew narrative is not automatically a named peak, however confidently later maps draw it that way.

Every version renders the wording the same way, mountains, plural; that much is settled. The dispute, where there is one, is entirely about a post-biblical identification, whether the traditional Mount Ararat is the right guess for where in the ancient region of Urartu the ark actually came to rest, a question the Hebrew text does not itself try to answer.

versions.s: I have slain a man. Or: I would slay a man. The same Hebrew perfect tense supports both.

b.t: Most versions read a completed action, I have killed a man, which is the natural sense of the Hebrew perfect tense read straightforwardly and is how nearly every translation renders it.

English can say **I killed him**, reporting a fact, or **I would kill him**, threatening a future act, and the two verbs look completely different. Hebrew's perfect tense can sometimes carry either sense from context alone, and this poem is exactly the case where scholars cannot agree which one it is doing.

Haragti, I have killed, is a Hebrew perfect, ordinarily a completed action, and that is how almost every translation reads it: Lamech has already killed someone and is boasting that his vengeance will exceed Cain's sevenfold protection. Some scholars instead read the perfect as a so-called conditional or hypothetical use, common in poetry, so that Lamech is warning any future attacker rather than confessing a past murder: I would kill a man who wounded me, and take vengeance seventy-sevenfold.

English tense marks completed and hypothetical action with entirely different verb forms, so a translator must resolve an ambiguity Hebrew poetry can leave open. Whichever choice is made, the English reader receives a confident portrait, either a murderer boasting or a threat issued in advance, that the Hebrew itself does not force.

Hebrew's verbal system marks aspect, not strictly tense, and poetry in particular can use the same form for a completed act, a general truth, or a hypothetical one. Where the difference matters to how a character is being portrayed, check whether the verse is prose or poetry, since poetic usage is looser.

A completed killing reads Lamech as escalating violence into confessed murder, matching the chapter's downward trajectory from Cain. A hypothetical threat reads the poem as a boast about invincibility rather than a confession, closer to a war-song bravado than a murder record. Both readings are argued by serious commentators and the Hebrew perfect alone does not decide between them.
הָרַגְתִּי haragti (הָרַג harag, to kill) · H2026

versions.s: I AM, or I WILL BE. The Hebrew is one form and it carries both.

b.t: Nearly every English Bible reads I AM. The NET, NRSV and JPS all footnote I WILL BE. The RSV put I AM WHO I AM in the text and I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE in the margin.

**I am here.** **I will be here.** English makes you pick a time before you can finish the sentence. Now imagine a verb form that is both, that means something like **I am-and-go-on-being here**, and that a speaker could use without ever choosing. Hebrew has that form. English does not, so a translator has to choose for you.

Ehyeh is the first person singular imperfective of hayah, to be. Hebrew verbs do not mark time the way English verbs do. They mark whether an action is viewed as complete or incomplete. The imperfective covers what is going on now and what is not yet finished, which in English has to become either a present tense or a future tense. The form itself refuses to choose.
There's no English verb form that is present and future at once. A translator has to pick a tense, and picking one deletes the other. The Hebrew reader was never asked to pick.

When a Hebrew verb sits in a promise or a self-description and your translations split present against future, you are looking at the imperfective. The split is not a disagreement about the words. It is two attempts to carry one form that English cannot hold.

I AM makes the name a statement about God's being, which is how the Greek of the Septuagint took it and how most of Christian theology has read it. I WILL BE makes it a promise attached to the next sentence, where God says he will be with Moses. Both are in the grammar. The chapter itself pushes toward the promise, since the same verb form appears in verse 12 as I will be with you.

src: G. H. Parke-Taylor, Yahweh: The Divine Name in the Bible, 51, on ehyeh as both I am and I will be

versions.s: Vapour, breath. The word Ecclesiastes repeats and English calls vanity.

b.t: The King James reads vanity. Modern versions read meaningless, futile, fleeting, or vapour.
**Breath on a cold morning.** Real, visible, and gone. That is a picture, not an insult.
Hevel is a breath or vapour. Ecclesiastes uses it around thirty-eight times as the frame of the whole book. It is also the name Abel, which is unlikely to be accidental.
English vanity meant emptiness in 1611 and now means conceit, and meaningless is a philosophical verdict the Hebrew image does not deliver.
When a book repeats one word as its thesis, the rendering of that word decides how the whole book reads. This is the clearest case of it in the Bible.
Meaningless is the NIV's choice and the common modern one; vanity is the King James; fleeting and vapour are gaining ground.

versions.s: Except the Father draw him. The verb is used of hauling a net and drawing a sword.

b.t: Every version reads draw or drag.
**He drew the curtain.** **They dragged him out.** One English family, and the force in it depends entirely on what is being moved.
Helkuo is used of hauling a net at John 21:6 and 21:11, of drawing a sword at John 18:10, and of dragging people before magistrates at Acts 16:19. John 12:32 uses the same verb of drawing all people.
English draw covers the whole range too, from a gentle pull to a haul, so the range survives and the force is still decided by context rather than by the word.
Listing every occurrence of a verb is more useful than any lexicon gloss, especially where a doctrine rests on how forceful it is.
Draw is the majority rendering; drag appears where the context is clearly violent.
ἑλκύω helkuo · G1670

src: Hauling a net: John 21:6, 11
Drawing a sword: John 18:10
Dragging to court: Acts 16:19; 21:30; James 2:6
Drawing all people: John 12:32

versions.s: I will draw all men unto me. The same verb as the drawing in chapter six.

b.t: Versions read draw all people, or draw everyone. All men in the King James; all people in most modern versions.
**He pulled them in.** Said of a fisherman and of a preacher, and the force differs entirely with the object.

Helkuo again, as at 6:44. Here the subject is Christ lifted up and the object is all. Whether all means all without exception or all without distinction is the argument, and the verb does not settle it.
English draw carries the same range, so the question is preserved rather than created.
Read every occurrence of a verb across a book before deciding how strong it is. One verse is not a sample.
Draw all people is what most modern versions print; all men is the King James.
ἑλκύω helkuo · G1670

versions.s: Destroy this temple. Greek has two words for temple and this is the inner one.

b.t: Every version reads temple for both Greek words.
**The house** and **the grounds**. If someone says tear down the house, nobody thinks he means the estate. One word for both and the sentence gets much harder.

Naos is the sanctuary proper, the inner building. Hieron is the whole temple precinct including the courts. Verse 14 has Jesus in the hieron; verse 19 has him saying destroy this naos. John then tells you in verse 21 that he meant his body.
English has one word, so the shift from precinct to sanctuary inside five verses cannot be seen.
Where Greek has two words for one English word, watch for a passage that uses both. The switch is usually doing the work.
Temple is universal for both. Some study Bibles note the distinction; no translation marks it.
ναός naos · G3485 / ἱερόν hieron · G2411

src: hieron at John 2:14; naos at 2:19-21
The accusation at Mark 14:58 uses naos
Paul uses naos of believers: 1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19

versions.s: Way. A road, and the first name the movement had for itself.

b.t: Every version reads way, and the Way with a capital where the movement is meant.
**He is in the trade.** **She is in the Church.** Groups name themselves with ordinary nouns all the time, and the ordinariness is why the name sticks.
Hodos is a road or a journey, and by extension a manner of life. Acts calls the movement the Way six times, against two uses of Christian in the whole book (11:26; 26:28).
English way is so general that a capital letter is the only signal, and the metaphor of a road being walked disappears.
Capitalisation in an English New Testament marks a translator's judgment that a common noun is being used as a name.
Way is universal; the capitalised Way in Acts is standard across versions.
ὁδός hodos · G3598

src: hodos as a road: Matthew 7:13-14
Christian first at Acts 11:26

versions.s: Mine hour is not yet come. A word John uses as a countdown to one event.

b.t: Every version reads hour or time.
**His hour had come.** English uses hour for a decisive moment too, and never means sixty minutes when it does.
Hora is an hour, but John uses it as a technical marker. It is not yet come at 2:4, 7:30 and 8:20; it has come at 12:23, 13:1 and 17:1. The pattern is a structural device across the book.
English hour carries the decisive sense, so little is lost in the word. What is lost is that these are the same word used deliberately across twenty chapters.
When a common word recurs in the same phrasing across a book, track every occurrence before interpreting any one of them.
Hour is the majority rendering and no version departs.
ὥρα hora · G5610

src: Not yet: John 2:4; 7:30; 8:20

versions.s: For God so loved the world. So means in this way, not so very much.

b.t: Every English version reads so. The CSB footnotes in this way. The NET renders it this is the way God loved the world, which is the only major version to force the issue.

**He so loved the work that he stayed late.** Modern ears hear how much. **Hold the brush so.** That is the older sense, meaning in this manner. English kept the word and quietly dropped one of its two jobs.

Houtos is an adverb of manner, not degree. It points forward to the clause that follows: God loved the world in this way, namely that he gave. The verse is not measuring the size of God's love. It is naming the shape of it.
English so does carry both senses, which is why the rendering survives untouched. But usage has shifted so far toward degree that almost no reader hears manner.
The most dangerous English words are the ones that still technically carry the original range but have drifted in everyday use. Nothing looks wrong, so nobody checks.
There is no dispute in the Greek. The dispute is whether a translator should override four centuries of familiarity to rescue an adverb, and only the NET has been willing to.
οὕτως houtos · G3779

versions.s: He shall bruise thy head. The Hebrew pronoun is unambiguously masculine, singular, he.

b.t: Nearly every English version reads he or it, correctly following the Hebrew masculine singular pronoun. Some older Catholic translations made from the Latin Vulgate read she, following a Latin manuscript tradition that used the feminine ipsa instead of the masculine ipse.

A single letter can flip a pronoun from **he** to **she** in translation, the way a typo can turn **him** into **her** in English. That is what happened to the Latin Bible used across Europe for over a thousand years, in the one verse that names the serpent's ultimate defeat.

Zera, seed or offspring, is grammatically singular and collective, and the pronoun attached to it, hu, is third person masculine singular: he, not she, will crush the serpent's head. Jerome's own Hebrew-based commentary on Genesis confirms the masculine reading; the feminine ipsa that later appeared in some Vulgate copies is now widely regarded as a scribal error introduced after Jerome, not his own translation choice. The modern official Catholic Latin text, the Nova Vulgata, corrected the erroneous ipsa to ipsum, neuter, simply restoring ordinary Latin grammatical agreement with the neuter noun semen, seed; it does not print a masculine ipse, since Latin gender concord here tracks the Latin noun, not a claim about the Hebrew pronoun.

English he and she map cleanly onto Hebrew masculine and feminine pronouns, so there is no translation gap here. The gap was a transmission error inside the Latin manuscript tradition, which English versions, working from Hebrew, never inherited.

A doctrine built on a single translation's pronoun is only as strong as that translation's manuscript history. Where two major textual traditions disagree, trace the disagreement back to its source before assuming either one preserves the original by default.

He or it follows the Hebrew directly and is essentially undisputed among Hebraists across confessional lines, including current Catholic scholarship. She survives mainly in older devotional use built on the Vulgate's feminine variant, which the Catholic Church's own modern Latin text no longer prints.
הוּא hu (with זֶרַע zera) · H1931 / H2233

src: Jerome, Quaestiones Hebraicae in Genesim, reading the masculine pronoun against the Old Latin
Nova Vulgata (1979, the Catholic Church's official Latin text) reads ipsum, neuter agreeing with semen, correcting the earlier feminine ipsa

versions.s: Verily I say unto you. The you is plural, and Jesus has been talking to one man.

b.t: No modern version can show it. English lost the distinction when ye and thou dropped out, which the King James still had and no longer communicates.

**Are you coming?** One person, or everybody in the room? English cannot tell you. Southerners fixed it with y'all because the language lost something it used to have. It used to be you for a crowd and thou for one person, and the King James still has both.

Nathanael is the one being addressed, and the pronoun turns plural at this verse. The promise widens from one man to everyone standing there and, arguably, to the reader. The King James actually marks it with ye, which modern English cannot.

English merged the plural you and the singular thou into one word. Every other major European language kept the distinction and English gave it up, which means every New Testament you is ambiguous in English and unambiguous in Greek.
Whenever a New Testament promise or command feels personal, check whether the you is plural. A very large share of them are, and they are addressed to a congregation rather than to an individual.
No dispute exists. English simply cannot do it without writing you all, which no version will print.
ὑμῖν hymin · G5213, plural

src: The switch from singular to plural across John 1:50-51

versions.s: Endurance. The word is built on staying under a weight, not on waiting quietly.

b.t: The King James reads patience. Modern versions mostly read endurance or perseverance.
**He stood up under it.** That is a posture, not a mood. English has the idea and uses a phrase rather than a noun.
Hupomone is hupo, under, plus meno, to remain. It is active, not passive, and is usually paired with suffering or pressure rather than with delay.
English patience drifted toward temperament. Endurance is closer and sounds athletic rather than moral.
Compound words tell you their own meaning if you take them apart, as long as you check the result against how the word is actually used.
Endurance and perseverance are the majority renderings in modern versions; patience is the King James rendering.

versions.s: She shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. A pun that sounds like a derivation.

b.t: Every version keeps the wordplay by translating ish as man and ishah as woman, since English happens to have a matching pair. The English pair is a real derivation; the Hebrew pair, read this way, is not.

English **woman** really is built from **man**; it comes from Old English wifman. An English reader has no reason to doubt Adam's line is doing the same thing. It is doing something else: making a pun, not reporting where the word came from.

Ish and ishah sound almost identical, and Genesis 2:23 plays on that resemblance. But the words are generally traced to different roots, ish to a root meaning strength, ishah to a separate root associated with frailty or humanity in general, so the verse is a paronomasia, a sound-based pun dressed up as a derivation, not an actual etymology.

English woman genuinely does derive from man, so an English reader assumes the Hebrew must work the same way and has no signal that it does not. The pun survives in translation only because English happens to have its own unrelated derivation that looks like a match.

A wordplay that sounds like an etymology is not evidence of one. Ancient authors used sound-based puns constantly and did not intend them as historical linguistics, even where, as here, the pun is doing real literary work.

No translation avoids the pun; man and woman is the correct rendering and the resemblance is deliberate in the Hebrew. The only correction needed is not to the translation but to what the wordplay is taken to prove about where the Hebrew words themselves come from.

entries.title: ishon
entries.def: the little man of the eye; the pupil or ball; hence, the middle (of night)
entries.where: ishon is tagged 5 times, across 3 books: proverbs 3 · deuteronomy 1 · psalms 1.

versions.s: Keep me as the apple of the eye. Literally, the little man, or the daughter of the eye: the pupil.

b.t: Every version reads apple of the eye, correctly preserving the sense, precious and closely guarded, but the actual images behind the Hebrew words, a tiny reflected person, a daughter, are entirely absent from apple, which has no connection to eyes in ordinary English at all.

Look closely into someone's eye and you will see a tiny reflection of yourself in the dark center. Hebrew names that reflection ishon, a little man, and calls the pupil itself bat ayin, daughter of the eye. English apple has nothing to do with either image; it entered the phrase only because Old English speakers happened to also call the pupil an apple, for its round shape.

Ishon, commonly translated pupil here, more literally means little man, describing the miniature reflected image visible in someone's eye when you look closely into it; bat ayin, daughter of the eye, is a separate Hebrew idiom for the same part of the eye. English apple entered this specific phrase from Old English, itself a separate, unrelated tradition of calling the pupil an apple for its round shape, coincidentally landing near enough in sense to survive translation even though it shares no image with the Hebrew at all.

English apple of the eye is now a fixed idiom meaning precious and beloved, entirely detached from any eye-related image for most speakers; it happens to preserve roughly the right sentiment while completely replacing the Hebrew's actual pictures, a tiny reflected person, a daughter, with a fruit that has nothing to do with either.

A translated idiom that still works can hide the fact that its underlying image has been entirely swapped out. Check what the original words are actually picturing, not just whether the resulting English phrase still makes emotional sense.

No translation dispute over the sentiment, precious and closely guarded. The entry exists because apple of the eye survives as a working English idiom purely by coincidence of separate traditions, not because it translates the Hebrew's actual images of a little reflected man or a daughter of the eye.

entries.title: itstsabon
entries.where: itstsabon is tagged 3 times, across one book: genesis 3.

versions.s: Sorrow in childbearing, toil in the field. One Hebrew word, two English words.

b.t: The King James reads sorrow in verse 16 and sorrow in verse 17, keeping the link. Several modern versions read pain for the woman and toil or painful labour for the man, breaking it.
If a story gave two characters the same punishment word and your translation rendered it **sorrow** for one and **toil** for the other, you would read two different sentences. The writer wrote one.

Itsabon occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible: twice here, at verses 16 and 17, and once at Genesis 5:29. The word is about painful labour in the sense of hard work, not specifically physical pain. Both sentences are about work becoming hard.
No one English word covers both the pain of childbirth and the grind of farming. Any rendering has to pick a shade, and the parallel dissolves.
When two verses in the same passage sound like different subjects, check whether they share a word. Passages are often built on repetition that translation smooths away.

Pain reads naturally for childbirth and badly for agriculture. Toil reads naturally for agriculture and coldly for childbirth. The King James kept one word for both and is more faithful to the structure than most modern versions here.

versions.s: Subdue it, and have dominion. Forceful, even military and royal vocabulary, standing beside Genesis 2's gentler verbs for the same job.

b.t: Every version reads subdue and have dominion, correctly conveying real force, though without necessarily flagging how sharply that force contrasts with the gentler abad and shamar, work and keep, used for the same basic human task at Genesis 2:15.

English subdue and have dominion already sound fairly strong, but the underlying Hebrew is stronger still: kabash is the verb for military conquest, putting a defeated enemy under your foot; radah is royal rule language, a king governing subjects. Two chapters later, the same task is described with work and keep, priestly, custodial language entirely different in tone.

Kabash elsewhere describes military subjugation, putting a conquered population under your feet; radah names the kind of rule a king exercises over subjects. Applied to humanity's relationship with the earth and its creatures, both verbs are considerably more forceful than the abad, serve, and shamar, guard, used of Adam's task in the garden at 2:15, creating a real tension between two pictures of the same human vocation, conquest and custodianship, that the text does not explicitly resolve.

English subdue and dominion already register as fairly strong, but readers moving between chapters 1 and 2 in translation do not necessarily notice that the vocabulary shifts from military and royal force to priestly service and guarding, a genuine change in tone between two accounts of humanity's purpose that disappears once both are smoothed into ordinary English.

When two passages describe what looks like the same task using visibly different registers of vocabulary, forceful versus gentle, royal versus priestly, read the contrast as a real feature of the text's fuller picture rather than assuming the two must simply restate one identical idea.

Reading kabash and radah at full force keeps humanity's mandate as active, even aggressive, shaping of a wild and unfinished world. Reading Genesis 2:15's abad and shamar as the fuller, correcting picture treats dominion as answerable to a prior, gentler custodial calling. The text offers both pictures without explicitly ranking one over the other.

versions.s: The heavens declare the glory of God. The Hebrew noun means weight before it means brightness.

b.t: Every version reads glory. None can carry the root, and the English word has drifted toward radiance and applause.

**His word carries weight.** **That was a weighty decision.** English already uses heaviness for importance, and nobody thinks about scales. Now imagine that were your only word for importance, and it never lost the physical sense.

Kavod is from a root meaning heavy. The same root gives the verb in honour thy father, which is closer to treat as weighty than to feel warmly toward. Kavod is substance, the reason something registers, and in the Septuagint it becomes doxa, which then carries the Hebrew sense into the New Testament.
English glory came in through Latin gloria, which was about renown and splendour. The heaviness never made the trip, so the English word and the Hebrew word overlap without matching.
Abstract theological nouns almost always come from concrete roots. Find the concrete sense and the abstract one stops floating.
Nothing is disputed. No English word means weight and importance and radiance at once, so glory is the least bad option and has been for a thousand years.

versions.s: Blessed is he whose sin is covered. Kasah, cover, a near relative of kaphar, the atonement verb.

b.t: Every version reads covered, correctly, but without necessarily connecting the image to the broader covering-vocabulary, kaphar, atonement, kapporet, the mercy seat, that structures Israel's entire sacrificial system.

English forgiven describes a legal or relational state, a debt cancelled. Hebrew covered pictures something more concrete: sin as a thing hidden from view, the way pitch covered the ark's seams against the flood. The two Hebrew cover-words, kasah and kaphar, are separate roots but sit in the same conceptual family running through Israel's sacrificial vocabulary.

Kesui, covered, here comes from kasah, a distinct root from kaphar, to cover or atone, the verb already met describing Noah pitching the ark at Genesis 6:14 and standing behind kippurim, atonement, and kapporet, the mercy seat. The two roots are not identical, but they occupy the same semantic neighborhood, covering as the central image for how sin is dealt with, whether by a flood-proof coat of pitch or by sacrificial atonement.

English forgiven and covered read as roughly synonymous religious vocabulary; the specific, concrete image of covering, and its resonance with the unrelated-but-neighboring root kaphar running through the sacrificial system, is invisible without tracking the Hebrew vocabulary of covering across these related but distinct words.

When a psalm uses covering language for sin or forgiveness, listen for an echo of the sacrificial system's own covering vocabulary, kaphar, kapporet, even where the specific root used, as here, is a different, related word rather than the identical one.

Covered is the uncontested sense of kasah here. What's worth seeing is how this verse's covering image sits inside the larger family of Hebrew covering-vocabulary for sin and atonement, connecting an ordinary psalm of confession to the sacrificial system's central metaphor.
כְּסוּי kesui (כָּסָה kasah, cover; cf. כָּפַר kaphar, atone) · H3680 / H3722

versions.s: A new commandment. The word for new means fresh in kind, not recent in time.

b.t: Every version reads new commandment.
**A new car.** **A new lease of life.** One means recently made. The other means a fresh kind of the same thing. English uses one word for both.

Kainos is new in kind, fresh, of a different quality. Neos is new in time, recent. The commandment to love is not chronologically new, since Leviticus 19:18 has it, and kainos is the adjective that lets it be both old and new, which is exactly the point 1 John 2:7-8 makes.
English new covers both, so the paradox in 1 John reads as a contradiction rather than as a play on two available adjectives.
A New Testament writer who seems to contradict himself about whether something is new is usually just switching adjectives; check which one he used.
New commandment is universal.
καινός kainos · G2537

versions.s: Time. The right moment, as against time on a clock.

b.t: Every version reads time, season, or occasion.
**Timing is everything.** **What time is it?** English uses one word for both and you never confuse them, because the sentence around it does the work.
Kairos is an opportune or decisive moment. Chronos is duration, clock and calendar time. Mark 1:15 is about a moment having arrived, not about a date.
English has one noun and supplies the distinction with adjectives, so a word that means the decisive moment reads as a neutral word for time.
Where a language has two words and yours has one, the choice between them is information you will never see in translation.
Time is the majority rendering; season and appointed time appear where the decisive sense is unmistakable.

versions.s: To call. The verb behind church, calling, and the word for those called out.

b.t: Versions read call, calling, or vocation.
**He found his calling.** English uses the word for vocation and hears nothing else in it. The older sense is closer to being summoned by someone.
Kaleo is to call or summon. Klesis is the calling. Ekklesia, the assembly, is built on the same root with a prefix meaning out. The family holds together in Greek and scatters in English.
English took vocation from Latin and calling from Anglo-Saxon, so the family that produced church is invisible.
Follow the root across a writer's vocabulary. Greek families argue by themselves; English translations break them apart.
Call and calling are the majority renderings; vocation appears in the King James at Ephesians 4:1.

versions.s: The good shepherd. The adjective is not the ordinary word for good.

b.t: Every version reads good shepherd.
**A good man.** **A good knife.** English uses one word and you know which is meant. Greek has two and the speaker has to choose.

Kalos is beautiful, fine, excellent, fit. Agathos is morally good. The shepherd is kalos, the model shepherd, the one who does the job as it should be done, and the definition given in the same verse is that he lays down his life.
English good covers both and nothing is lost in accuracy, but the choice John made is invisible.
Where a language has two adjectives for one English word, the one not chosen tells you as much as the one chosen.
Good shepherd is universal; model shepherd and true shepherd appear in commentaries.

versions.s: Pitch it within and without with pitch. The noun for pitch and the verb for cover share the root behind atonement.

b.t: Every version reads pitch or tar for the verse's substance and its verb, correctly and unremarkably. No version can show that the same consonants return later as the ordinary Hebrew word for atonement.

English **tar** and English **atone** share no sound, no spelling, nothing. A reader moving from Noah's ark to the Day of Atonement chapters later would never connect them. In Hebrew, the two ideas are built from the same three letters.

Kopher, pitch, and the verb kaphar, to cover, here describing waterproofing, come from the same root as kippurim, atonement, the word behind Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, and kapporet, the mercy seat covering the ark of the covenant later in the Torah. The ark of Noah is, in the vocabulary of the sentence describing it, covered the same way sin is later covered.

English has entirely separate words for a waterproofing tar and a ritual atonement, so the shared Hebrew root, and the theological resonance some readers hear in it, one covering that saves from judgment prefiguring another, cannot survive translation into two unrelated English vocabularies.

When a mundane, technical instruction, here waterproofing a boat, uses a root that recurs in a book's central ritual vocabulary, that repetition is worth flagging even if the immediate context is entirely practical. Hebrew narrative frequently plants vocabulary early that ritual law develops later.

Pitch and cover are the plainly correct sense here, and no version disputes it; the verse is giving construction instructions, not making an atonement statement. The connection to kippurim is an observation about shared vocabulary across the Torah, not a claim that Genesis 6 is itself describing a ritual.

versions.s: Blessed is he whose sin is covered. Kasah, cover, a near relative of kaphar, the atonement verb.

b.t: Every version reads covered, correctly, but without necessarily connecting the image to the broader covering-vocabulary, kaphar, atonement, kapporet, the mercy seat, that structures Israel's entire sacrificial system.

English forgiven describes a legal or relational state, a debt cancelled. Hebrew covered pictures something more concrete: sin as a thing hidden from view, the way pitch covered the ark's seams against the flood. The two Hebrew cover-words, kasah and kaphar, are separate roots but sit in the same conceptual family running through Israel's sacrificial vocabulary.

Kesui, covered, here comes from kasah, a distinct root from kaphar, to cover or atone, the verb already met describing Noah pitching the ark at Genesis 6:14 and standing behind kippurim, atonement, and kapporet, the mercy seat. The two roots are not identical, but they occupy the same semantic neighborhood, covering as the central image for how sin is dealt with, whether by a flood-proof coat of pitch or by sacrificial atonement.

English forgiven and covered read as roughly synonymous religious vocabulary; the specific, concrete image of covering, and its resonance with the unrelated-but-neighboring root kaphar running through the sacrificial system, is invisible without tracking the Hebrew vocabulary of covering across these related but distinct words.

When a psalm uses covering language for sin or forgiveness, listen for an echo of the sacrificial system's own covering vocabulary, kaphar, kapporet, even where the specific root used, as here, is a different, related word rather than the identical one.

Covered is the uncontested sense of kasah here. What's worth seeing is how this verse's covering image sits inside the larger family of Hebrew covering-vocabulary for sin and atonement, connecting an ordinary psalm of confession to the sacrificial system's central metaphor.

versions.s: They pierced my hands and my feet, or like a lion. One letter, and it is the wrong length in some copies.

b.t: Almost every Christian English version reads pierced. Jewish publications read like a lion. The NIV footnotes both. The King James reads pierced without a note.

Imagine two letters in your alphabet that differ only by how far the stroke comes down. A tired copyist in poor light makes one slightly short, and four hundred years later two communities are arguing about what the sentence says. Nobody had to be dishonest for that to happen.

The Masoretic Text reads ka'ari, like a lion, which leaves the line with no verb. The Septuagint, the Peshitta, and Jerome's earlier Gallican Psalter (the version behind the standard Vulgate text) all read a verb meaning dug or pierced. A fragment from Nahal Hever, 5/6HevPs, dated to roughly the middle of the first century, has the word ending in a vav rather than a yod, which makes it a third-person plural verb.
The difference is a vav against a yod, two letters distinguished mainly by length. This is not a translation problem at all. It is a copying problem, and English can only report the outcome.

When two communities read the same verse in opposite directions, find out whether the disagreement is about meaning or about letters. Here it is letters, which makes it checkable rather than merely arguable.

The case for pierced: three ancient versions, the Nahal Hever fragment, the minority Masoretic notes, and the fact that the Masoretic reading leaves the clause without a verb. The case against: Nahal Hever is not Qumran and is later than the Qumran material, the fragment is faded and has been read both ways, the Targum supports the lion reading, and Aquila, Symmachus, and Jerome's later translation direct from the Hebrew (his Psalterium iuxta Hebraeos, a different edition from the Gallican Psalter cited above) all render the hands and feet as bound rather than pierced. Anyone who tells you this is closed has not read the other side.
כָּאֲרוּ / כָּאֲרִי ka'aru / ka'ari · H3738 / H738

versions.s: The LORD made a covenant with Abram. Literally, cut a covenant, and the chapter just showed you the cutting.

b.t: Every version reads made a covenant, using English's own dead metaphor for finalizing an agreement, correctly conveying the sense but losing any connection to actual cutting.

English **cut a deal** is a dead metaphor; nobody pictures an actual knife. Hebrew **cut a covenant** started out exactly that literal, and Genesis 15 is the one chapter where you get to watch the literal cutting happen right before the idiom is used.

Karat berit, cut a covenant, is the standing Hebrew idiom for covenant-making throughout the Old Testament, and this chapter preserves the ritual behind the dead metaphor: animals are cut in half, and a smoking firepot and flaming torch, representing God, pass between the pieces, a self-maledictory oath in which walking between severed halves meant may I become like these animals if I break this covenant.

English cut a deal is used and heard purely figuratively, with no live memory of an actual cutting ceremony behind it. Hebrew karat berit sits closer to its literal origin, and this chapter is the rare place in the Bible where the idiom's backstory is narrated rather than merely assumed.

When you meet a fossilized idiom, cut a deal, cut a covenant, ask whether the Bible anywhere narrates the literal action the dead metaphor came from. Genesis 15 is exactly that kind of narration, and it is easy to read straight past it if you already think of covenant-making as an abstract legal event.

Translators aren't actually divided here; made a covenant is the only workable English rendering. This note is meant to reconnect the abstract English phrase to the concrete ritual Genesis 15 actually describes just before the idiom is used.

b.t: No version can flag this, because both passages are translated accurately and the discrepancy only appears when you lay them side by side.
Someone quotes a family saying back to you and slips in an extra word. They are not correcting it. They are telling you what it always meant, in case you had stopped hearing it.

Deuteronomy 6:5 has heart, soul and strength. Mark has heart, soul, mind and strength. The added word is dianoia, mind or understanding. The Greek kardia had narrowed toward the emotional by the first century in a way Hebrew levav never had, so a Greek-speaking audience hearing kardia alone would have missed the thinking half of the original.

Neither translation is wrong. The gap opens because Hebrew put thought in the heart and Greek was already moving it out, so the same command needed four words in Greek to say what three said in Hebrew.

A mismatch between a New Testament quotation and its Old Testament source is data, not an error. Sometimes the writer is using the Septuagint. Sometimes, as here, he's spelling out a word his audience would have taken too narrowly.
There is no translation choice being made. The evidence only shows up when you lay two accurate translations side by side, which is a skill worth more than any single word study.
καρδία kardia · G2588 / διάνοια dianoia · G1271

src: Deuteronomy 6:5 in Hebrew: levav, nephesh, meod
Mark 12:30 and the parallel at Luke 10:27, which lists the same four terms in a different order; Matthew 22:37 keeps only three (heart, soul, mind) and drops strength

versions.s: The darkness did not comprehend it, or did not overcome it. The verb means both and John probably wanted both.

b.t: Modern versions split. Some read overcome, some read understand, and most footnote the other.

**I could not grasp the rope.** **I could not grasp the idea.** One English verb, two completely different failures, and only the rest of the sentence tells you which. Now imagine a sentence where the rest does not tell you. That is this verse.
Katalambano means to seize, to take hold of. Applied to the mind it becomes grasp, understand. Applied to a hand or an army it becomes seize, overpower. Both are ordinary uses of the same verb.
No single English verb means both grasp-with-the-mind and grab-by-force. Comprehend and overcome are two different English words, and a translator has to pick one.

Some Greek verbs cover a physical action and a mental one with the same word, because the mental sense is a metaphor the language never stopped noticing. When your versions split between a physical and a mental rendering, this is usually why.

Comprehended, the older reading, fits the theme of recognition that runs through the prologue and into verses 10 and 11. Overcome fits the light-darkness conflict and reads more naturally in a sentence about darkness. John writes with deliberate double meanings elsewhere in this Gospel, at 3:3 and 3:8 and 19:30, which is the argument for not choosing.
καταλαμβάνω katalambano · G2638

src: The physical sense: Mark 9:18; John 8:3-4; 1 Thessalonians 5:4
The mental sense: Acts 4:13; Ephesians 3:18

versions.s: No room at the inn. The word is not the word for inn, and Luke uses the right one two chapters later.

b.t: Most versions still read inn. The CSB and NET read guest room, and the NIV now reads guest room with a note.

**There was no room at the hotel.** **There was no room in the spare bedroom.** One word swap, and you have changed who was there, who turned them away, and whether anyone was unkind. Nouns carry scenery.

The word is kataluma, a place to unloose or lodge, used of the upper guest room where Jesus eats the Passover in Luke 22:11. When Luke means a commercial inn, in the parable of the Good Samaritan, he uses a different word, pandocheion.

English inn drags in an innkeeper, a no-vacancy sign and a family turned away in the cold, none of which is in the Greek. The picture is closer to a village house whose guest space was full, with the family moved in among the animals under the same roof.
When a translation gives you a scene, check whether the scene is in the words. The innkeeper of every nativity play does not appear in any Gospel. He is an inference from one English noun.

Inn has four hundred years of tradition and the Latin diversorium behind it. Guest room has Luke's own usage two chapters later, and the absence of the word he uses elsewhere for an inn. The lexical argument is fairly one-sided.
κατάλυμα kataluma · G2646

src: Kenneth E. Bailey, Jesus Through Middle Eastern Eyes, ch. 1
Luke 22:11 and Mark 14:14 use kataluma of the upper room; Luke 10:34 uses pandocheion of an inn
Published: jayms.com/the-birth-of-jesus-kataluma

versions.s: The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up. The verb is consume, and the tense was changed in the quotation.

b.t: Every version reads consume or eat up.
Quote a song lyric back at someone but shift it from **it broke me** to **it will break me**, and you have said something the original did not.

Katesthio is to eat up, devour, consume. The Septuagint of Psalm 69:9 has the aorist, it consumed me. John has the future, it will consume me, which turns a description of past devotion into a prediction.
English can carry the tense, but a reader has to look up the psalm to see that the tense was changed.
Line up a New Testament quotation against its Old Testament source instead of assuming they match. The differences are almost always deliberate and almost never flagged.
Consume is the majority rendering and no version notes the tense change in the text.
κατεσθίω katesthio · G2719

src: Psalm 69:9, quoted here
Septuagint aorist against John's future
Psalm 69 quoted elsewhere: John 15:25; Romans 15:3

versions.s: John stops the narrative twice to translate a word for you, which tells you who he thought was reading.

b.t: Versions keep the glosses because they are in the text. Some smooth them into parentheses.

**He grabbed the bonnet, which is what the British call the hood.** You just learned two things. What a bonnet is, and that the writer assumes you are American. Writers who stop to translate are telling you who they expect to be reading.

Messias and Kephas are Aramaic words carried into a Greek sentence, and John immediately supplies the Greek equivalent. He does the same thing at 1:38 with Rabbi, at 9:7 with Siloam, and at 20:16 with Rabboni.
There's no translation loss here. The point is what the habit reveals: the writer is working from an Aramaic-speaking setting and writing for readers who are not in it.

When a biblical writer translates a word inside his own sentence, he is telling you about his audience. Those glosses are some of the most direct evidence in the New Testament about who a book was written for.
There is nothing to choose. The entry is here because it is the clearest example in John of the seam between the language of the events and the language of the book.
Μεσσίας Messias · G3323 / Κηφᾶς Kephas · G2786

src: John's other glosses: 1:38 Rabbi; 9:7 Siloam; 19:13 Gabbatha; 19:17 Golgotha; 20:16 Rabboni
Mark does the same at 5:41 and 15:34, which makes it a habit of the tradition rather than of one writer

versions.s: A coat of many colours. Modern scholarship increasingly favors a long-sleeved robe, not a rainbow garment.

b.t: The King James reads coat of many colours, following the Septuagint and Vulgate's variegated. Modern versions increasingly read a long robe with sleeves or an ornamented robe, following medieval and modern Hebraists who connect passim to pas, the palm of the hand or sole of the foot, suggesting a garment reaching to the hands and feet rather than one displaying colors.

Picture a phrase translators have guessed at for two thousand years without ever finding a second example to confirm the guess. That is ketonet passim. The colorful coat is a famous, beloved image; it may also simply be wrong.

Passim occurs in this exact phrase only twice in the Hebrew Bible, here and at 2 Samuel 13:18-19 describing the royal garment worn by unmarried princesses, including Tamar, before her own assault. Neither occurrence confirms colors; the connection to pas, palm or sole, suggests a garment with long sleeves and a long hem, marking its wearer as someone who does not do manual labor, a mark of privileged status rather than a rainbow of dyed cloth.

English many colours is vivid, specific, and has anchored centuries of art and storytelling, but the Hebrew phrase behind it is genuinely uncertain, and the strongest linguistic evidence, its only other biblical occurrence describing royal children's clothing, points toward a long, sleeved, privileged garment rather than a colorful one.

A translation tradition this old and this beloved can still rest on a guess. Before trusting a famous image, check whether the Hebrew phrase behind it has a confirmed meaning or only an inherited one, especially when the word recurs elsewhere in a context that points a different direction.

Coat of many colours preserves the image nearly every reader already carries and is not disprovable outright. A long robe with sleeves better fits the word's only other biblical occurrence and its likely connection to pas, and shifts the story's point from bright dye to Joseph being marked as exempt from a laborer's life, a distinction his brothers, who did that labor, would have resented just as sharply.
כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים ketonet passim · H3801 + H6446

src: The only other occurrence, describing royal children's clothing: 2 Samuel 13:18-19
Proposed connection to pas, palm/sole, suggesting long sleeves and hem: Rabbi David Kimhi and modern lexicons
Septuagint poikilos, variegated, behind the Vulgate and King James rendering

versions.s: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever. The king addressed directly as elohim, quoted of the Son at Hebrews 1:8.

b.t: Most versions read thy throne, O God, following the vocative reading and the Septuagint's own rendering, which Hebrews 1:8 quotes directly. A minority reading takes it as God is your throne, avoiding a direct divine address to the human king.

English can say **your throne, God**, addressing someone as God directly, or **God is your throne**, making God the foundation rather than the one addressed. The Hebrew grammar here genuinely supports reading it the first way, and whether a human king is really being called God, even in an exalted, honorific sense, is exactly what makes the verse so debated.

Elohim occurs four times in this psalm, at verses 2, 6, and twice in 7, with the surrounding occurrences clearly referring to God; the vocative reading, thy throne, O God, treats verse 6 as continuing that pattern, an extraordinarily exalted address to the Davidic king as God's own representative, perhaps even more than merely representative. The Septuagint reads it the same vocative way, and Hebrews 1:8 quotes that Greek text directly, applying the address to the Son as part of its argument for his superiority over the angels.

English must choose a subject and an address; thy throne, O God directly calls the addressee God, while God is your throne makes God a foundation rather than a title, two genuinely different claims that the Hebrew grammar, ambiguous enough to be argued for centuries, does not force in only one direction.

When a psalm's grammar allows a human figure to be addressed with divine vocabulary, take the ambiguity seriously rather than resolving it by assuming discomfort with the direct reading. Ancient Israelite royal ideology could apply exalted, even startling language to its kings as God's representatives.

Thy throne, O God follows the Septuagint, matches the surrounding elohim occurrences in the same psalm, and is the reading Hebrews 1:8 explicitly builds on. God is your throne avoids directly calling a human king God but requires reading the Hebrew syntax somewhat less naturally against its immediate context.

versions.s: Priest. A functionary of the sanctuary, and the word used of foreign priests too.

b.t: Every version reads priest.
**Doctor.** It tells you what someone does, not who they work for.

Kohen is used of Aaron's line, of Melchizedek at Genesis 14:18, of Jethro priest of Midian, and of Egyptian priests. The office is defined by function: sacrifice, instruction, and mediating between people and the sanctuary.
English priest is now heavily denominational, so a neutral functional term reads as a claim about church order.
Job-description nouns usually apply across religions in the ancient world. The word tells you the function, not the allegiance.
Priest is universal.

versions.s: Fellowship. A word for shared ownership and partnership, including in money.

b.t: Versions read fellowship, sharing, participation or contribution.
**We went in on it together.** That is a partnership with a stake, not a coffee morning. English has the idea and uses a phrase.
Koinonia is from koinos, common. It covers partnership in a business, sharing in something, and is used by Paul for a financial collection at Romans 15:26.
English fellowship lost its commercial and property senses and kept only the social one.
When a version renders one word as fellowship in one verse and contribution in another, both are in the word and English has lost the overlap.
Fellowship is the majority rendering; sharing and participation are increasingly common in newer versions.

versions.s: Esau said, I have enough. Jacob said, I have all things. Two different Hebrew words, rav and kol, for two different postures toward wealth.

b.t: Most versions read Esau saying I have enough and Jacob saying I have enough or I have all, sometimes flattening both brothers' statements to the same English phrase and losing the distinction the Hebrew text itself draws between them.

English **I have plenty** and **I have everything** sound similar but are not identical claims. Hebrew marks this same distinction precisely: Esau's rav, much or sufficient, is a claim of comfortable abundance; Jacob's kol, all, is a stronger, almost complete claim, and the two brothers each choose their own word.

Esau's yesh li rav, I have much, uses the ordinary word for abundance or sufficiency, a comfortable, unremarkable claim. Jacob's yesh li kol, I have all, or everything, reaches further, a stronger and more complete claim of provision, spoken by the brother who has spent the chapter making amends and securing goodwill. The difference in word choice, not merely tone, marks a real contrast in how each brother frames his own situation at this reunion.

English translations that render both statements identically, I have enough, erase a distinction the Hebrew vocabulary itself preserves between comfortable sufficiency, rav, and total fullness, kol, a difference some readers connect to Jacob's changed character after Peniel.

When two characters make parallel statements using different vocabulary for what looks like the same idea, check whether the words are actually synonyms or whether one is deliberately stronger than the other. A flattened translation can erase a contrast the original author built on purpose.

Rendering both as I have enough treats the exchange as merely polite and symmetrical. Preserving the distinction, Esau's enough versus Jacob's everything, or all, reads Jacob's word choice as reflecting the transformed outlook of a man who has just wrestled with God and lived.

versions.s: Pitch it within and without with pitch. The noun for pitch and the verb for cover share the root behind atonement.

b.t: Every version reads pitch or tar for the verse's substance and its verb, correctly and unremarkably. No version can show that the same consonants return later as the ordinary Hebrew word for atonement.

English **tar** and English **atone** share no sound, no spelling, nothing. A reader moving from Noah's ark to the Day of Atonement chapters later would never connect them. In Hebrew, the two ideas are built from the same three letters.

Kopher, pitch, and the verb kaphar, to cover, here describing waterproofing, come from the same root as kippurim, atonement, the word behind Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, and kapporet, the mercy seat covering the ark of the covenant later in the Torah. The ark of Noah is, in the vocabulary of the sentence describing it, covered the same way sin is later covered.

English has entirely separate words for a waterproofing tar and a ritual atonement, so the shared Hebrew root, and the theological resonance some readers hear in it, one covering that saves from judgment prefiguring another, cannot survive translation into two unrelated English vocabularies.

When a mundane, technical instruction, here waterproofing a boat, uses a root that recurs in a book's central ritual vocabulary, that repetition is worth flagging even if the immediate context is entirely practical. Hebrew narrative frequently plants vocabulary early that ritual law develops later.

Pitch and cover are the plainly correct sense here, and no version disputes it; the verse is giving construction instructions, not making an atonement statement. The connection to kippurim is an observation about shared vocabulary across the Torah, not a claim that Genesis 6 is itself describing a ritual.

versions.s: World. The root idea is order and arrangement, which is why it also gives cosmetics.

b.t: Every version reads world. No version distinguishes the senses.
**Cosmos.** **Cosmetics.** Same root. One is the ordered universe and the other is putting a face in order. The idea underneath is arrangement.

Kosmos is an ordered arrangement, then the ordered universe, then the inhabited world, then the human system organised against God. John uses the last two senses close together and expects the reader to track it.
English world covers the planet and the social system, so the range survives, but the deliberate switching does not.
When a writer uses one word in two opposed senses inside a paragraph, that is a rhetorical move, not sloppiness.
World is universal in English versions.

versions.s: Condemned already. The Greek word is judged, and the noun in the next verse is the judgment.

b.t: The King James reads condemned and condemnation. Most modern versions read judged and judgment.
**Judge** and **judgment** are obviously related in English. **Condemn** and **judgment** are not, and the connection breaks the moment you print the first one.
Krino is to judge, to decide, to separate. Krisis is the act or result. Verses 17 to 19 use the word family four times, and the paragraph is built on the repetition.
English condemn presumes the outcome; judge does not. Choosing condemn decides the verse before the reader gets there.
Word families argue by themselves in Greek. When an English version breaks a family into unrelated words, the argument stops being visible.
Judged and judgment are the majority modern renderings; the King James reads condemned and condemnation.

versions.s: Lord. Also sir, and also the Septuagint's replacement for the divine name.

b.t: Every version reads Lord, with lowercase lord or sir where a human is addressed.
**Yes, sir.** **He is lord of the manor.** **The Lord.** English has the same word doing three jobs and separates them with a capital letter.

Kurios covers a polite sir, a master or owner, and in the Septuagint it stands in for YHWH wherever the name occurs. So a quotation like Joel 2:32 arriving in Romans 10:13 carries the divine name inside an ordinary Greek noun.
English uses capitalisation to mark the difference, a device Greek manuscripts do not have and speech cannot carry.
If a quotation hinges on the word Lord, look up whether the underlying Hebrew had the divine name there. That's usually the whole argument.
Lord is the universal rendering; sir appears where a stranger is addressed, as at John 4:11.

versions.s: Thou hast received gifts for men. Ephesians 4:8 quotes it as gave gifts to men, matching the Aramaic Targum's own reading, not the Hebrew or Greek Old Testament.

b.t: Old Testament translations of the Psalm read received gifts, following the Hebrew and Septuagint. Ephesians 4:8 reads gave gifts, matching neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament but matching the Aramaic Targum's rendering of the same verse.

English received and gave describe opposite transactions, one direction of gift-giving versus the other. The Hebrew and the Septuagint's Greek both read received; Paul's letter reads gave. Rather than a simple error, this exact reversal already exists in the Aramaic Targum, a translation tradition Paul may well have known and be deliberately following.

The Hebrew and the Septuagint's Greek both read the victor receiving tribute-gifts from conquered peoples after ascending in triumph. The Aramaic Targum on this psalm instead reads gave gifts to the sons of men, and Ephesians 4:8 follows that same direction, either drawing directly on the Targum tradition or on a similar interpretive current, applying the psalm to Christ distributing spiritual gifts to the church after his ascension rather than receiving tribute as a conquering king.

English readers of Ephesians 4:8 encountering a New Testament quotation reversed from their Old Testament translation may assume an error or a loose paraphrase, when in fact an entire, attested Jewish translation tradition, the Targum, already reads the verse the same reversed way Paul does.

A New Testament quotation that appears to reverse or significantly alter its Old Testament source is worth checking against the Aramaic Targum tradition before you call it careless or wrong. Targums frequently interpret rather than merely translate, and New Testament writers sometimes follow that interpretive tradition directly.

Received gifts, following the Hebrew and Septuagint, reads the psalm as describing a conquering king collecting tribute. Gave gifts, following the Targum and Ephesians 4:8, reads the same ascension imagery as a generous king distributing gifts to his people, the reading Paul needs for his argument about spiritual gifts given to the church.
לָקַחְתָּ מַתָּנוֹת lakachta matanot (received gifts) · H3947 + H4979

src: The Aramaic Targum on Psalm 68:19 reading 'gave gifts to the sons of men'
Ephesians 4:8's direct quotation matching the Targum's direction, not the Hebrew or LXX
Septuagint elabes, received, matching the Hebrew

versions.s: Love God with all your heart. In Hebrew that is an instruction about thinking, not feeling.

b.t: Every English version reads heart, because there is no better word. The problem is not the translation. It is what English readers hear.

**I know it in my gut.** You do not mean your stomach. Every language parks thinking and feeling in body parts, and no two languages park them in the same place. English put thinking in the head and feeling in the heart. Hebrew put thinking in the heart and did not ask your permission.

Levav is the seat of thought, will and decision in Hebrew anthropology. When the Hebrew Bible wants the seat of emotion it more often reaches for the bowels or the kidneys. The verse is not asking for a feeling. It is asking for the direction of your mind.

Every language maps interior life onto body parts, and no two languages map it the same way. Heart is the right English word for levav and it carries four hundred years of English sentiment that the Hebrew never had.

Body-part words are almost never safe to read straight across. When a verse tells you to do something with an organ, find out what that organ was thought to do in that culture before you decide what is being asked of you.
No translator has a better option. This is a case where the English is correct and the reader still ends up somewhere the Hebrew was not going, which is why the entry exists.
לֵבָב levav · H3824

src: Hans Walter Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, on leb/levav as the seat of intellect and will
Mark 12:30 adds dianoia, mind, when quoting this verse in Greek, which suggests the first century already read it that way

versions.s: White already to harvest. The colour word points at ripeness, and the verb is a command to look.

b.t: The King James reads white already to harvest. Modern versions read ripe for harvest or white for harvest.
**Golden.** English picked a different colour for the same idea. Colour words for ripeness are cultural and rarely transfer.
Leukos is white or bright. Applied to grain it indicates ripeness, since barley and wheat pale as they dry. Theasasthe is an aorist imperative, a command to look now.
English harvest imagery runs on gold rather than white, so the literal colour reads as odd and most versions substitute ripe.
Colour terms rarely map between languages. When a colour seems wrong, ask what the colour was being used to indicate.
Most modern versions print ripe for harvest; white, the more literal option, is the King James choice.
λευκός leukos · G3022

versions.s: Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces. The multi-headed sea-dragon of the same chaos-combat imagery already met in Genesis.

b.t: Every version reads leviathan, correctly, but without connecting it to the same combat-with-chaos imagery already surfacing at Genesis 1:2's tehom, Genesis 1:21's taninim, and now here, named directly as a multi-headed creature being crushed in battle.

English sea monster sounds like generic mythology, a fantasy creature. In the wider ancient Near East, defeating a multi-headed sea dragon was the specific, well-known story of how a storm-god established order over chaos at the world's beginning, and this psalm applies that same combat imagery directly to the LORD's own creative victory.

Leviathan here, with its plural heads explicitly broken, matches the Canaanite mythological pattern of the storm-god defeating a multi-headed sea serpent, called Lotan in Ugaritic texts, cognate to Hebrew Leviathan. The psalm applies this widely attested ancient combat myth directly to the LORD, casting creation itself as a decisive victory over chaos, the same underlying imagery already met calmly defused at Genesis 1:21's taninim and now presented here in full battle terms.

English leviathan reads as an obscure creature name with no built-in mythological context; the specific, attested ancient Near Eastern combat-with-chaos pattern it draws on, and the way this psalm intensifies that imagery into open battle language compared to Genesis 1's calmer listing, is invisible without the comparative background.

Track chaos-monster vocabulary, tehom, tannin, leviathan, rahab, across its several occurrences and note how differently each context handles it, calmly defused as in Genesis 1, or in full mythological combat as here. The same underlying imagery can be deployed very differently depending on a passage's purpose.

Leviathan as the name is not in question. What matters here is connecting this verse's battle imagery to the same ancient Near Eastern combat-myth pattern already met in a calmer form at Genesis 1:21, showing how differently biblical texts can handle the identical inherited imagery.
לִוְיָתָן Leviathan (רָאשֵׁי livyatan rashei, heads of) · H3882

src: Ugaritic Lotan, the multi-headed sea serpent defeated by Baal, cognate to Leviathan
The calmer, defused use of the same imagery at Genesis 1:21
The same combat imagery again at Isaiah 27:1; Job 41

versions.s: It is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves. Or: and his we are. One preserved letter apart, and Jewish scribal tradition marks both readings.

b.t: Some modern versions follow the marginal note, reading and his we are, others follow the written text, and not we ourselves; the Septuagint and the King James both follow the written text, while the Aramaic Targum and Jerome's separate translation follow the marginal reading.

Imagine a manuscript where the copied text says one thing, but a note in the margin says the correct reading is something else, and later editions have to choose which one to print as the main text. That is exactly the situation here: the Masoretes wrote lo, not, but flagged in the margin that lo, to him, might be intended instead.

The written consonantal text, the ketiv, reads lo with an alef, not, giving he made us, and not we ourselves. A Masoretic marginal note, the qere, suggests lo with a vav instead, to him, giving and his we are, we belong to him. The two readings differ by a single consonant and produce genuinely different theological emphases, human dependence on God for existence itself, or human belonging to God as covenant possession.

English translations must print one reading or the other as the main text, so a reader of any single version cannot tell that the Hebrew textual tradition itself preserves both options side by side, neither one silently erased in favor of the other.

When a Masoretic marginal note, qere, differs from the written consonantal text, ketiv, do not assume the marginal note simply corrects an error. Both readings were deliberately preserved together, and translators genuinely disagree on which to follow as the primary text.

And not we ourselves, following the written consonants and the Septuagint, emphasizes total dependence on God as creator. And his we are, following the marginal note and the Targum, emphasizes covenant belonging. The Masoretic tradition itself declines to resolve which was originally intended, preserving both.
וְלֹא אֲנַחְנוּ / וְלוֹ אֲנַחְנוּ velo anachnu (ketiv, not) / velo anachnu (qere, to him) · H3808 / לוֹ (le + 3ms suffix, no independent Strong's number)
