versions.s: Why call a person a Word? The Greek noun covers far more than a unit of speech, and two different backgrounds are competing for it.

b.t: Every English version reads Word, capitalised. A handful of older attempts tried Reason or Discourse and none of them stuck.

**You have my word.** **Word got around.** **He is a man of his word.** Not one of those is about a unit of speech. English already stretches this noun a long way past its dictionary entry, and you have never once been confused by it. Greek stretched it further, in directions English never went.

Logos covers a spoken word, a statement, an account in the bookkeeping sense, a reasoned argument, and the rational principle ordering the universe. Greek philosophy, especially Stoic, had been using the last of those for centuries. Jewish writers in Greek had their own use: Philo of Alexandria made logos a mediating figure between God and the world, and the Aramaic targums habitually replace the name of God with memra, the word, in exactly the places where God acts.

English word means a unit of speech and very little else. There is no English noun that simultaneously means an utterance, a rational order, and a mediating agent, so a translator prints Word and adds a capital letter to warn you that more is going on.

When a translation capitalises a common noun, that is a translator making an interpretive decision in punctuation. Greek manuscripts were written without any case distinction at all. Ask what the capital is doing before you accept it.

The Greek-philosophy background makes John's opening a bid for a pagan audience, using their word for the ordering principle of reality and then telling them it became a man. The Jewish background makes it a comment on Genesis 1, where God speaks and things exist, and on the targums where the Word of the LORD does what the LORD does. The two are not exclusive and most commentators now take both, with the Genesis echo carrying more weight because John's first three words are the opening of Genesis.
λόγος logos · G3056

versions.s: I had fainted, unless I had believed. The Hebrew leaves the unless-clause without its other half.

b.t: Most versions supply the missing clause in some form, I had fainted, or I would have despaired, to make the sentence read smoothly in English, since English style expects a conditional clause to be completed.

English can do this too: **if you hadn't come when you did...** and just stop there, trusting the listener to feel what would have happened rather than saying it. Hebrew does exactly that here, an unfinished sentence used on purpose, not a translation gap.

Lule, unless, opens the clause and then the sentence simply stops, aposiopesis, a deliberate breaking-off used elsewhere in both Hebrew and Greek rhetoric for emotional effect, the speaker unable or unwilling to name the catastrophe that would otherwise have followed. The word lule itself is among a small set of words the Masoretes marked with unusual pointing, flagging it as textually noteworthy even within the Hebrew tradition's own transmission.

English readers meeting a smoothed-out I had fainted unless I had believed do not experience the sentence as broken at all, so the rhetorical effect of the original, a speaker who cannot finish naming his own despair, is supplied by the translator rather than felt as the text's own deliberate collapse.

When a Hebrew conditional clause seems to be missing its other half, do not assume a copying error before considering aposiopesis, a deliberate broken-off sentence used for genuine emotional weight. Some of Scripture's most intense moments are marked by grammar failing on purpose.

Filling in the missing clause, as every English translation does, produces smooth, readable English at the cost of the original's raw, unfinished quality. Leaving the sentence broken, unless I had believed..., closer to the Hebrew's actual shape, better preserves the emotional collapse the verse is enacting rather than merely describing.
לוּלֵא lule (unless) · H3884

src: lule as one of the words the Masoretes marked with unusual pointing

versions.s: He spake unto them by an interpreter. The same root, melitz, later names a mediator or advocate in Job.

b.t: Every version reads interpreter here, correctly, with no reason for an English reader to connect the word to anything beyond ordinary translation between Hebrew and Egyptian speakers.

English keeps **interpreter** and **advocate** as unrelated professions, one translates languages, the other argues a case. Hebrew melitz can name either role, an intermediary standing between two parties who cannot otherwise communicate, whether the gap is language or guilt.

Melitz names the professional interpreter mediating between Joseph, speaking Egyptian, and his brothers, speaking Hebrew, unaware Joseph understands them. The same root reappears at Job 33:23, where a heavenly melitz, one of a thousand, pleads a sufferer's case and finds a ransom for him, a figurative use scholars regularly read as intercessor or advocate, and again at Isaiah 43:27, of a divinely commissioned spokesman.

Hebrew melitz spans both a language-translator and a legal-or-spiritual advocate; no single English word does, so the incidental detail in Joseph's story and the loaded theological image in Job read as completely unconnected once each gets its own natural English word.

A word doing mundane, logistical work in one passage can be the same root doing theological heavy lifting elsewhere. Track a root's range across the whole Hebrew Bible before assuming its use in a narrative aside is unrelated to its use in a more weighted passage.

Interpreter is the right sense here, and no version renders it otherwise. Worth flagging is the shared root with Job's mediator figure, a connection of vocabulary, not necessarily of theological intent, that Genesis 42:23 on its own gives no indication of anticipating.
מֵלִיץ melitz (לוּץ luts) · H3887

src: The mediator/advocate sense: Job 33:23; 16:20
A divinely commissioned spokesman: Isaiah 43:27

versions.s: As far as the east is from the west. A deliberately chosen pair of directions with no meeting point, unlike north and south.

b.t: Every version reads east and west, accurately translating the specific pair of directions the Hebrew names, though without necessarily prompting a reader to notice why this particular pair, rather than north and south, was chosen.

Travel far enough north and you reach a point where north stops meaning anything, the pole; the same happens going south. Travel east, though, and you are still traveling east forever; there is no eastern pole where the direction runs out. The psalm's choice of east and west, not north and south, pictures a separation with literally no endpoint.

Mizrach, east, and ma'arav, west, name directions that never converge anywhere on the earth's surface, unlike north and south, which meet at the poles. The poetic choice is precise: describing the removal of sin as far as the east is from the west pictures a genuinely infinite, ever-increasing distance, not simply a very large but ultimately bounded one, the way north and south, converging at fixed points, would have implied.

English readers hear east and west as simply one reasonable pair of opposite directions among several, north and south being equally obvious alternatives, with no built-in signal that the poet specifically avoided the pair that has actual meeting points on a globe.

When Hebrew poetry chooses one pair of opposites over an equally available alternative, ask whether the specific pair chosen carries a meaning the alternative would not. Here, the choice of east/west over north/south is doing real conceptual work: describing infinite rather than merely large distance.

East and west as the rendering is not in dispute. What is worth making explicit is the deliberate reasoning behind the choice, a pairing of directions with no geometric meeting point, that most readers absorb as simply poetic without registering as a precise, considered image.
מִזְרָח וּמַעֲרָב mizrach u-ma'arav · H4217 + H4628

src: North and south converging at the poles, a basic geographic fact underlying the poetic choice
Standard commentary observation on this verse's specific choice of directions

versions.s: The flood of waters. The word mabbul names only this flood, never an ordinary one.

b.t: Every version reads flood, using the ordinary English word for rising water. English has no separate vocabulary item reserved the way mabbul is, so this distinction cannot show up in translation at all.

English flood covers a river overflowing its banks, a flash flood, a monsoon. Hebrew has ordinary words for those too. This story uses a different word altogether, one that only ever means this specific, singular catastrophe, the way English capitalizes the Flood when it means this one and no other.

Mabbul appears repeatedly through the flood narrative, Genesis 6-9, and then only once more in the entire Hebrew Bible, at Psalm 29:10, in a poetic line that itself looks back to this event. It is not the Hebrew Bible's general word for a flood or an inundation; those exist separately. A proposed Akkadian cognate exists but is itself rare and specialized rather than the ordinary Akkadian word for flooding, suggesting both languages may have reserved a special term for a catastrophe of this scale.

English flood is a common noun covering any rising water, from a local storm to a global catastrophe, so it cannot mark the same distinction Hebrew draws by using an entirely separate, otherwise unused word only for this one event.

When a narrative's key noun turns up nowhere else in ordinary usage, check whether the language is marking the event as categorically unique rather than simply describing it. A dedicated vocabulary item is itself a claim about how the event should be remembered.

Flood is the only English word on offer, so no version disputes it. The point worth carrying is that Hebrew itself treats this flood as belonging to its own linguistic category, a distinction English flattens the moment the word reaches translation.
מַבּוּל mabbul · H3999

src: Only other occurrence: Psalm 29:10

versions.s: As at Meribah, and as in the day of Massah. Both place names and, simultaneously, the ordinary words for strife and testing.

b.t: Every version reads Meribah and Massah as bare transliterated place names, correctly identifying the location from Exodus 17, but without conveying that both names are, simultaneously, the ordinary Hebrew words for the very behavior being condemned.

Imagine a warning that says **don't act like you did at Grudge City**, where Grudge City is both a real, mappable town and, transparently, a description of what happened there. Meribah, strife, and Massah, testing, work exactly that way, and English place names like Meribah carry none of that built-in description.

Meribah, from the root riv, to strive or contend, and Massah, from nasah, to test, both name the specific location at Exodus 17:7 where Israel quarreled with Moses and tested the LORD over water, and both function as plain common nouns describing exactly that behavior. The Septuagint and Targum translations sometimes render them as common nouns, strife and testing, rather than transliterated place names, making the double function explicit in a way the Hebrew leaves the reader to notice on their own.

English Meribah and Massah are bare geographic labels with no built-in meaning, so the warning's rhetorical force, do not repeat the very thing this place is named for, is completely inaccessible unless a reader is told what the two names actually mean.

When a warning or exhortation invokes a place name from Israel's history, check whether the name itself is also a common noun describing the event that happened there. Hebrew place names frequently double as built-in commentary the way Meribah and Massah do here.

Meribah and Massah, transliterated as bare place names, is the standard and necessary translation, since English has no way to render a word as both proper noun and common noun simultaneously. What matters is recovering the double meaning that the bare transliteration necessarily discards.
מְרִיבָה Meribah (רִיב riv, strive) / מַסָּה Massah (נָסָה nasah, test) · H4809 / H4532

src: The original naming: Exodus 17:7
Hebrews 3:7-19 and 4:3-7 quoting this psalm at length

versions.s: Longsuffering. Literally long-tempered, the opposite of short-tempered.

b.t: The King James reads longsuffering. Modern versions read patience or forbearance.
**He has a short fuse.** English builds the idea out of a metaphor. Greek builds it out of a compound, and they mean the same thing in reverse.
Makros, long, plus thumos, temper or passion. Where hupomone bears up under circumstances, makrothumia holds off with people. The two often appear in the same list.
English patience covers both and so the pairing in Colossians 1:11 reads as repetition.
When two words appear side by side in a list, they are not synonyms. Lists are built out of distinctions.
Patience dominates modern versions; longsuffering is the King James rendering.

versions.s: The angel of the LORD found Hagar. She then says the LORD spoke to her, and names him accordingly.

b.t: Every version reads angel of the LORD throughout, correctly, but the shift in verse 13, where Hagar's own words treat the speaker as God directly, is easy to read past without noticing the identification the Hebrew is making.

Imagine a story where a messenger delivers a message, and the recipient afterward says **I spoke with the president**, not **with the president's messenger**. English would read that as either a mistake or a deliberate blurring. Hebrew does this here without comment, and the text seems entirely comfortable with it.

Malach YHWH, the angel, or messenger, of the LORD, speaks to Hagar in the first person as God, promising to multiply her seed, language elsewhere reserved for God's own covenant promises. Hagar then names Him El Roi, the God who sees, and the text states plainly that she saw God and lived, treating messenger and message-giver as interchangeable in a way that has driven a long theological debate: whether this figure is simply God appearing in a form Hagar could address, a distinct angelic being who speaks with delegated divine authority, or, in later Christian reading, a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son.

English angel reads as clearly distinct from God, a messenger sent by someone else; it carries none of the fluidity the Hebrew text displays here, where the messenger's identity and the sender's identity blur without the narrative treating that blur as strange.

When a figure called the angel of the LORD speaks in the first person as God and is addressed as God by the human who meets him, do not resolve the identification too quickly in either direction. The Hebrew text itself holds messenger and sender together without fully separating them.

Translators agree without exception that angel of the LORD is the correct rendering throughout. The theological question, whether this is God Himself in a form Hagar could face, a distinct heavenly being acting with full divine authority, or specifically the pre-incarnate Son, cannot be settled by the Hebrew grammar alone and has divided readers since the church fathers.

versions.s: Messenger. The same word is used of human envoys and of heavenly ones.

b.t: Versions read angel or messenger depending on whether the sender is God or a person.
**Messenger.** That is a job, not a species. English decided at some point that one kind of messenger needed its own word.
Mal'ak is one sent with a message. Jacob sends mal'akim to Esau and they are men. The word describes a function, and the being performing it has to be identified from context.
English angel is a borrowing of the Greek angelos, which was itself the Septuagint's rendering of this word, so English kept the transliteration for one sense and a native word for the other.
Where English has two words from one original, the split is usually the translator's theology showing, and it is worth checking each occurrence.
Angel is the majority rendering in divine contexts, messenger in human ones.

versions.s: These are the kings that reigned in Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel. The comparison assumes Israel already has kings.

b.t: Every version reads the comparison plainly, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel, without flagging that the sentence's own logic requires a writer living after Israel's monarchy already began.

If a document said **this was before the internet existed**, you would know the writer already lived with the internet. This verse works the same way: comparing Edom's kings to a time before Israel had any assumes the writer already knew Israel's monarchy, which began generations after Moses supposedly wrote this book.

The comparison functions the same way as the 'Canaanite was then in the land' note at Genesis 12:6, another small aside that only makes sense from a vantage point later than the events being narrated. Israel's first king, Saul, is described starting at 1 Samuel 9-10, so this verse's framing requires a writer, or at minimum an editorial note, from Saul's reign or later, a genuinely old observation among both traditional and critical commentators, not a modern critical invention.

English readers moving quickly through a genealogical list often skip past a comparative clause like this without registering that it is making a claim about the writer's own vantage point, the same kind of ordinary reading habit that, applied carefully, raises a real question about when this material was composed or edited.

Treat a comparative aside, before X had ever happened, the same way in Scripture as you would in any other historical document: as a marker of the writer's own later vantage point, not merely as background information about the events themselves.

Reading the verse as a later editorial note within an otherwise earlier Mosaic Torah treats it as a minor updating gloss. Reading it as evidence of substantially later composition or editing is the same larger claim raised at Genesis 12:6, and this verse adds independent, textually explicit support for it rather than settling the question on its own.

versions.s: The LORD reigneth. Malakh could mean has become king, marking a specific moment, or reigns, describing an ongoing state.

b.t: Most versions read the LORD reigneth or the LORD is king, favoring the ongoing-state sense, though many scholarly treatments of this and the other enthronement psalms, 47, 96-99, favor has become king, treating them as ritually commemorating a specific moment of divine coronation.

English reigns describes an ongoing condition, no particular starting point implied. English has become king marks a specific event, a coronation. The single Hebrew verb malakh, in this unusual position after its subject, has been read both ways by serious scholars, and the choice changes whether this psalm is commemorating an event or simply declaring a permanent truth.

Malakh, in the unusual construction of a finite verb following its subject YHWH, fronting the subject ahead of the verb rather than Hebrew's more expected verb-first word order, has been read by many scholars as ingressive, marking entry into a new state, the LORD has just become king, fitting a proposed annual enthronement festival reenacting God's kingship. Others read it as simply durative, the LORD reigns, an ongoing, already-established truth restated rather than newly announced.

A specific verb tense and aspect, has become or reigns, is a choice English is forced to make, committing the translation to one reading of an event that Hebrew's own grammar leaves genuinely more open. It's a real interpretive decision every English translation makes without flagging it as one.

When a psalm's central verb sits in an unusual grammatical position, check whether that position is a recognized marker of ingressive aspect, entering a new state, rather than assuming an ordinary durative sense by default. Word order in Hebrew poetry can carry real grammatical weight.

The LORD reigns, the durative reading, fits a straightforward declaration of God's permanent kingship. The LORD has become king, the ingressive reading, fits a proposed liturgical reenactment of a specific coronation moment, tying this psalm to a cluster of similar enthronement psalms that may have functioned together in a now-lost festival setting.

entries.where: malki-tsedeq is tagged 4 times, across 2 books: genesis 2 · psalms 2.

versions.s: Melchizedek, king of Salem. His name means king of righteousness; Salem means peace.

b.t: Every version reads Melchizedek and Salem as bare proper names, transliterated, since neither carries any built-in meaning once rendered into English letters.

Imagine a story where a stranger named **Justice** arrives from the city of **Peace**, and later readers treat both names as meaningful rather than coincidental. That is exactly the case Hebrews later makes about Melchizedek, and it only works if you know what his name and city mean in the original language.

Melchizedek is built from melech, king, and tsedek, righteousness, giving king of righteousness, while Salem, shalem, shares its root with shalom, peace, giving king of peace, or king of Salem read doubly. Hebrews 7:2 explicitly draws out both meanings, treating the king-priest's very name and title as prefiguring the righteousness and peace later associated with the Messiah, an argument that depends entirely on the reader knowing what the Hebrew names mean.

English transliterates both Melchizedek and Salem as bare proper nouns, so a reader meeting Hebrews 7's argument about righteousness and peace can't tell where those concepts come from unless someone explains that the names themselves are doing the work.

When a name is significant enough that a later biblical writer stops to explain its meaning, as Hebrews does here, treat that explanation as confirmation that Hebrew names throughout Scripture are regularly meant to be heard, not simply used as labels.

Melchizedek and Salem draw no real disagreement among translators as proper names; there is no live alternative rendering. What matters here is that the meaning behind both names, preserved and explained in Hebrews 7:2, stays otherwise completely inaccessible to a reader working only from the English text of Genesis.
מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק Malki-tsedek / שָׁלֵם Shalem · H4442 / H8004

src: Hebrews 7:2 explicitly translates both names, king of righteousness and king of peace
Psalm 76:2 uses Salem as a poetic name for Jerusalem

versions.s: The greater light and the lesser light. Not shemesh, sun, and yareach, moon, the same words as the sun-god and moon-god.

b.t: Every version reads the greater light and the lesser light, correctly, but nothing in the English signals that Hebrew had two perfectly ordinary, available words, shemesh and yareach, for sun and moon that the verse conspicuously does not use.

Imagine a creation account that carefully avoids saying **the sun** and **the moon** by name, calling them only **the big glowing thing** and **the smaller glowing thing**, specifically because those proper names doubled as the names of rival gods everyone around you worshipped. That is exactly what this verse does.

Shemesh, sun, was also the name of Shamash, the Mesopotamian sun-god; yareach, moon, shares its root with Yarikh, the Canaanite moon-god. Genesis 1 calls them simply hama'or hagadol and hama'or hakaton, the greater light and the lesser light, functional, almost deliberately unglamorous descriptions, stripping them of any name that could double as a divine title and reducing them to created objects doing a job, marking appointed times, rather than deities to be worshipped.

English greater light and lesser light already sound intentionally plain, but without knowing that Hebrew had perfectly good, ordinary proper names available and pointedly did not use them, an English reader cannot see that this is a deliberate polemic against the sun and moon worship of Israel's neighbors, not merely a poetic or repetitive style choice.

When a text conspicuously avoids an obvious, available word, ask what that word would have implied if used. Genesis 1's avoidance of shemesh and yareach here is a calculated theological move, not an accident of vocabulary or a coincidence of style.

No translation dispute over greater light and lesser light as accurate renderings. What is worth flagging is that the deliberate avoidance of the ordinary, available words for sun and moon, precisely because those words were also divine names, is a polemical statement entirely dependent on knowing what words were not used.
הַמָּאוֹר הַגָּדֹל / הַקָּטֹן hama'or hagadol / hakaton (cf. שֶׁמֶשׁ shemesh, יָרֵחַ yareach) · H3974 / H8121 / H3394

src: Shemesh as the Mesopotamian sun-god Shamash, attested throughout Akkadian literature

versions.s: Witness. The English word martyr is the same Greek word, after what happened to the witnesses.

b.t: Every version reads witness. Martyr appears only where the context is death, as at Revelation 17:6.
**He gave evidence.** Nothing in that says anything about dying. Now imagine enough witnesses being killed that the word for witness starts to mean the killing.
Martus is a witness in the plain legal sense. The specialised meaning of one who dies for the testimony develops in the second century, and English borrowed the later sense as a separate word.
English now has two words from one Greek word, which is unusual and means the pair looks like a coincidence rather than a history.
When English has two words from one original, the second one usually records something that happened.
Witness is the majority rendering throughout the New Testament.
μάρτυς martus · G3144

src: martus in the legal sense: Matthew 18:16; Acts 1:8

versions.s: Sin lieth at the door. Its desire is to thee, and thou shalt rule over it. The same crouching-word, and the same two words as 3:16.

b.t: Every English version reads lieth, croucheth, or is crouching, all correctly neutral. Almost none of the popular translations use anything that suggests an ambush or a personified threat, though one modern academic version, the New English Bible, does render it demon.

**The dog is lying by the door.** Harmless. Now imagine the word for lying also names a predator waiting in ambush at a doorway in a neighboring language and culture. Lieth sounds passive in English; the word behind it does not.

Rovets is a participle of the common verb for an animal lying down, but this personified use of sin as the subject crouching at a door closely resembles the Akkadian rabisu, a demon that lurks at thresholds to attack. Whether the Hebrew word is a deliberate echo of that image or simply the ordinary verb applied metaphorically is debated, but the doorway setting matches the Akkadian pattern closely. The same verse then reuses teshuqah, desire, and the verb mashal, rule over, the identical pairing used of the woman and the man at Genesis 3:16, this time offered to Cain as a warning rather than a sentence.

English lieth or crouches names a posture; it carries none of the threshold-demon association some scholars hear behind the Hebrew word, and English has no way to signal that the sentence structure repeats 3:16's marriage language word for word, since a reader would need to notice both verses share teshuqah and mashal in Hebrew to catch it at all.

A common word placed in an unusual setting, here an animal-word applied to sin at a doorway, can carry connotations from the culture's wider vocabulary that a plain gloss will not show. And when a rare phrase repeats verbatim a few verses apart, as teshuqah plus mashal does here, treat the second occurrence as commentary on the first.

Lieth or crouches is the safe, literal rendering every version uses. Whether to import the Akkadian demon imagery is a judgment call resting on comparative Semitic philology rather than the Hebrew word by itself, which is exactly why mainstream translations have stayed with the neutral gloss.

versions.s: Anointed one. In the Old Testament it usually means the reigning king.

b.t: Versions read anointed, and Messiah where the technical sense is in view.
**The chosen one.** Sounds like a title. Now use it of your line manager, accurately, and watch it become a description again.

Mashiach means smeared with oil, which is how kings and priests were installed. David calls Saul the LORD's mashiach. Cyrus is called it at Isaiah 45:1. The specialised sense of a coming deliverer develops later.
English Messiah is a transliteration reserved for one figure, so the ordinary usage is invisible.
When English has both a translated and a transliterated form of one word, the transliteration usually marks where a tradition has specialised the meaning.
Anointed is the majority rendering in the Old Testament; Messiah appears where the later sense is being invoked.

versions.s: Sing praises with understanding. Maskil, a term of uncertain meaning, also a mysterious label heading thirteen other psalms.

b.t: Here, most versions read with understanding or wisely, treating maskil as an ordinary adverbial phrase. In the thirteen psalm titles where it appears alone, Psalms 32, 42, 44, 45, 52, 53, 54, 55, 74, 78, 88, 89, and 142, most versions simply transliterate it as Maskil, a proper label rather than a translated word.

Imagine a musical score marked **con espressione** in a language you do not fully speak: you know it means something like play this thoughtfully, but the precise technical instruction is lost. Maskil sits in exactly that gap, translated here as an ordinary phrase but elsewhere standing alone as an unexplained genre label.

Maskil comes from sakal, to be wise, prudent, or to have insight, the same root behind the wisdom vocabulary used throughout Proverbs. As a standalone heading over thirteen psalms, its precise genre meaning, contemplative poem, skillful composition, or didactic instruction-psalm, is genuinely debated, since the label itself is never defined and the psalms it heads do not share an obvious common form.

English readers meeting maskil translated as with understanding in running text, as here, have no way to connect it to the same word standing untranslated as a technical heading over a baker's dozen of other psalms, a term functioning much like Selah: recognized as significant, but not confidently defined.

When a Hebrew root shows up both inside a verse's ordinary vocabulary and as an untranslated technical heading elsewhere in the same book, connect the two rather than treating them as unrelated. The heading use is often the more mysterious, and the ordinary use can be a clue to what the label might mean.

With understanding or wisely works well as ordinary English inside this verse. As a genre heading elsewhere, Maskil is usually left untranslated, honestly reflecting that no one is fully certain what technical instruction or genre classification the word was originally meant to convey.

versions.s: Thou hast received gifts for men. Ephesians 4:8 quotes it as gave gifts to men, matching the Aramaic Targum's own reading, not the Hebrew or Greek Old Testament.

b.t: Old Testament translations of the Psalm read received gifts, following the Hebrew and Septuagint. Ephesians 4:8 reads gave gifts, matching neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament but matching the Aramaic Targum's rendering of the same verse.

English received and gave describe opposite transactions, one direction of gift-giving versus the other. The Hebrew and the Septuagint's Greek both read received; Paul's letter reads gave. Rather than a simple error, this exact reversal already exists in the Aramaic Targum, a translation tradition Paul may well have known and be deliberately following.

The Hebrew and the Septuagint's Greek both read the victor receiving tribute-gifts from conquered peoples after ascending in triumph. The Aramaic Targum on this psalm instead reads gave gifts to the sons of men, and Ephesians 4:8 follows that same direction, either drawing directly on the Targum tradition or on a similar interpretive current, applying the psalm to Christ distributing spiritual gifts to the church after his ascension rather than receiving tribute as a conquering king.

English readers of Ephesians 4:8 encountering a New Testament quotation reversed from their Old Testament translation may assume an error or a loose paraphrase, when in fact an entire, attested Jewish translation tradition, the Targum, already reads the verse the same reversed way Paul does.

A New Testament quotation that appears to reverse or significantly alter its Old Testament source is worth checking against the Aramaic Targum tradition before you call it careless or wrong. Targums frequently interpret rather than merely translate, and New Testament writers sometimes follow that interpretive tradition directly.

Received gifts, following the Hebrew and Septuagint, reads the psalm as describing a conquering king collecting tribute. Gave gifts, following the Targum and Ephesians 4:8, reads the same ascension imagery as a generous king distributing gifts to his people, the reading Paul needs for his argument about spiritual gifts given to the church.
לָקַחְתָּ מַתָּנוֹת lakachta matanot (received gifts) · H3947 + H4979

src: The Aramaic Targum on Psalm 68:19 reading 'gave gifts to the sons of men'
Ephesians 4:8's direct quotation matching the Targum's direction, not the Hebrew or LXX
Septuagint elabes, received, matching the Hebrew

versions.s: Death. Also personified, and paired with Sheol in the poetry.

b.t: Every version reads death.
**Death came for him.** English personifies it too, in poetry and in idiom, without believing anything in particular.
Mavet is the event and also a power that swallows. It is paired with Sheol in poetic parallel, and at Ugarit Mot is the name of a deity, which is background rather than proof.
English personifies the same way, so the poetry translates well.
A personified abstraction in Hebrew poetry is not automatically a claim about a being. Check the genre before the theology.
Death is universal.
מָוֶת mavet · H4194

src: mavet with Sheol: Psalm 18:5; Hosea 13:14
Personified: Jeremiah 9:21; Job 18:13
Mot in the Ugaritic texts as background

versions.s: King. The ordinary word, and the one behind Moloch and Melchizedek.

b.t: Every version reads king.
**Kingdom, kingly, kingship.** English builds a family from one root too, and you read the family without thinking.

Melek is a king. Malkut is kingship. The root appears in Melchizedek, king of righteousness, in Malchus, and in Molech, whose name is the consonants of melek with the vowels of bosheth, shame, a deliberate scribal insult.
English king is a fine equivalent; what is lost is the visibility of the root inside proper names.
Proper names in Hebrew are usually built from ordinary words. Learning twenty common nouns makes hundreds of names readable.
King is universal.

versions.s: Manasseh, for God hath made me forget; Ephraim, for God hath caused me to be fruitful. Two more names built from the naming sentence itself.

b.t: Every version reads Manasseh and Ephraim as bare transliterated names, with Joseph's explanatory statements translated separately and accurately, but without connecting either name back to its own root the way the Hebrew explicitly does.

By now the pattern should look familiar: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and now Manasseh and Ephraim, thirteen names in a row each built as a pun on the parent's own explanatory sentence. English transliteration keeps none of the wordplay, in Canaan or, as here, in Egypt.

Menashsheh echoes nashah, to forget, from Joseph's own words, God hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house. Ephraim echoes parah, to be fruitful, from for God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. Both names complete the pattern established across every one of Jacob's own sons' births, now applied one generation later, to children born not in Canaan but in Egypt, under Joseph's Egyptian name and Egyptian wife.

English Manasseh and Ephraim are bare proper nouns; the sentences explaining them read as separate commentary rather than as the linguistic source the names were extracted from, so the pattern completing itself one generation later, in a foreign land, is invisible without the Hebrew roots.

Continue tracking the birth-naming-pun device established across Genesis 29-30 all the way through the Joseph narrative. The device does not stop with Jacob's own sons; it continues into the next generation, even after the family relocates to Egypt.

Neither name nor its accompanying explanation is in dispute in any version. This entry rounds out the pattern already established for the rest of the twelve tribes' names, showing it persists one generation further, into Joseph's own Egyptian-born sons.
מְנַשֶּׁה Menashsheh (נָשָׁה nashah, forget) / אֶפְרַיִם Ephraim (פָּרָה parah, fruitful) · H4519 / H5382 / H669 / H6509

versions.s: As at Meribah, and as in the day of Massah. Both place names and, simultaneously, the ordinary words for strife and testing.

b.t: Every version reads Meribah and Massah as bare transliterated place names, correctly identifying the location from Exodus 17, but without conveying that both names are, simultaneously, the ordinary Hebrew words for the very behavior being condemned.

Imagine a warning that says **don't act like you did at Grudge City**, where Grudge City is both a real, mappable town and, transparently, a description of what happened there. Meribah, strife, and Massah, testing, work exactly that way, and English place names like Meribah carry none of that built-in description.

Meribah, from the root riv, to strive or contend, and Massah, from nasah, to test, both name the specific location at Exodus 17:7 where Israel quarreled with Moses and tested the LORD over water, and both function as plain common nouns describing exactly that behavior. The Septuagint and Targum translations sometimes render them as common nouns, strife and testing, rather than transliterated place names, making the double function explicit in a way the Hebrew leaves the reader to notice on their own.

English Meribah and Massah are bare geographic labels with no built-in meaning, so the warning's rhetorical force, do not repeat the very thing this place is named for, is completely inaccessible unless a reader is told what the two names actually mean.

When a warning or exhortation invokes a place name from Israel's history, check whether the name itself is also a common noun describing the event that happened there. Hebrew place names frequently double as built-in commentary the way Meribah and Massah do here.

Meribah and Massah, transliterated as bare place names, is the standard and necessary translation, since English has no way to render a word as both proper noun and common noun simultaneously. What matters is recovering the double meaning that the bare transliteration necessarily discards.
מְרִיבָה Meribah (רִיב riv, strive) / מַסָּה Massah (נָסָה nasah, test) · H4809 / H4532

versions.s: The steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus. A rare word, ben-meshek, that nobody fully agrees on.

b.t: Most versions read steward of my house or heir of my house, smoothing the phrase into a clear English office. A few older or more literal renderings preserve more of the Hebrew's actual strangeness.

Imagine a legal document naming an heir with a title so unusual that lawyers today still argue whether it means owner, manager, or errand-runner. That is roughly the situation with ben-meshek here, a phrase modern translations gloss confidently while quietly disagreeing about what it actually names.

Ben-meshek is unusual enough that proposals range from son of acquisition, meaning the one who will inherit, to a verb related to running about in service, to reading meshek as a proper name, Masek, making Eliezer the son of a servant woman by that name rather than a household title at all. Many scholars additionally note that ben-meshek was likely chosen partly for its assonance with the following word, Dammesek, Damascus, a wordplay layered on top of an already rare and difficult phrase.

English steward reads as a clear, ordinary job title; the Hebrew phrase behind it is contested enough that no single English word can represent the genuine uncertainty scholars still have about what ben-meshek names.

When a translation reads smoothly and confidently, check whether the underlying Hebrew is actually that clear. A fluent English rendering can paper over real uncertainty that specialists are still debating.

Steward or heir of my house gives English readers a working sense of the passage without pretending to settle a genuinely contested phrase. No consensus exists on ben-meshek's precise force, and every translation is making a judgment call the Hebrew itself does not fully support.
בֶּן־מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי ben-meshek beythi · H1121 + H4943

versions.s: John stops the narrative twice to translate a word for you, which tells you who he thought was reading.

b.t: Versions keep the glosses because they are in the text. Some smooth them into parentheses.

**He grabbed the bonnet, which is what the British call the hood.** You just learned two things. What a bonnet is, and that the writer assumes you are American. Writers who stop to translate are telling you who they expect to be reading.

Messias and Kephas are Aramaic words carried into a Greek sentence, and John immediately supplies the Greek equivalent. He does the same thing at 1:38 with Rabbi, at 9:7 with Siloam, and at 20:16 with Rabboni.
There's no translation loss here. The point is what the habit reveals: the writer is working from an Aramaic-speaking setting and writing for readers who are not in it.

When a biblical writer translates a word inside his own sentence, he is telling you about his audience. Those glosses are some of the most direct evidence in the New Testament about who a book was written for.
There is nothing to choose. The entry is here because it is the clearest example in John of the seam between the language of the events and the language of the book.
Μεσσίας Messias · G3323 / Κηφᾶς Kephas · G2786

src: John's other glosses: 1:38 Rabbi; 9:7 Siloam; 19:13 Gabbatha; 19:17 Golgotha; 20:16 Rabboni
Mark does the same at 5:41 and 15:34, which makes it a habit of the tradition rather than of one writer

versions.s: Repentance. The Greek noun is about a change of mind, and the Latin behind the English is about penance.

b.t: Every version reads repent or repentance. Some footnote change of mind.
**I changed my mind about him.** That is not an apology and it is not a punishment. It is a reversal of judgment, and everything else follows from it.

Metanoia is meta, after or beyond, plus nous, mind. The Vulgate rendered the verb as do penance, which shaped a thousand years of Western practice before Erasmus and the Reformers argued for the mind sense.
English repent carries sorrow and contrition. The Greek noun carries reversal, and sorrow may follow without being the content.
When a doctrinal word has a long Latin history, find out what the Latin did to it. A surprising number of English theological terms come through Jerome rather than from Greek directly.
Repent is the majority rendering in every English version. The argument is about what it means, not about how to print it.
μετάνοια metanoia · G3341

src: Vulgate paenitentiam agite at Matthew 3:2
Erasmus argued for resipiscite, come to your senses
2 Corinthians 7:10 distinguishes grief from the metanoia it produces

versions.s: Lest they should be defiled. A purity concern stated without explanation.

b.t: Every version reads that they might not be defiled.
A writer who explains one custom and not another is telling you which one he expected you to know.

Miaino, to defile. Entering a Gentile dwelling rendered a Jew ritually unclean, which would have barred participation in the Passover. John glosses Aramaic words for his readers and does not gloss this, which is itself information about what he assumed.
The words themselves lose nothing. It's the background no translation supplies.
Track what a writer explains and what he does not. The unexplained things tell you about his readers.
That they might not be defiled is the majority rendering.

versions.s: Ishmeelites and Midianites both appear as Joseph's captors within the same short passage.

b.t: Every version reads both names as the text presents them, Ishmeelites at 37:25, 27-28, Midianites at 37:28 and 36, without adding a note explaining the apparent switch, since the Hebrew itself offers none.

Imagine a news account naming one group of kidnappers in one paragraph and a different group two paragraphs later, with no explanation for the switch. English narrative convention would flag that as an error needing a fix; ancient Hebrew narrative sometimes preserves exactly this kind of switch without smoothing it over.

Genesis 37:28 has Midianite traders pull Joseph from the pit and sell him to Ishmeelites; 37:36 then has Midianites selling Joseph to Potiphar in Egypt; 39:1 calls the sellers Ishmeelites again. Documentary source criticism reads this as two originally separate accounts, one calling the traders Ishmeelites, one Midianites, combined by an editor; a common harmonizing reading treats Ishmaelite and Midianite as overlapping or nested tribal names for the same caravan, since Midian was itself descended from Abraham alongside Ishmael and the terms could function as broader and narrower labels for related desert traders.

English translations render each name exactly where it occurs, so the switch is visible to a careful reader, but a fluent, fast reading in any language tends to average the two names into one group without noticing that the text itself never resolves which name is correct or explains the alternation.

When a short narrative unit alternates between two different group names for what appears to be the same characters, do not assume the Hebrew is simply careless. Consider both that ancient tribal names could genuinely overlap and that Hebrew narrative sometimes visibly preserves more than one telling of the same event.

Reading Ishmeelite and Midianite as functionally interchangeable or nested labels for one caravan preserves a single, coherent narrative. Reading the alternation as evidence of two combined underlying accounts is the position associated with source-critical scholarship and does not require resolving which name was original.
יִשְׁמְעֵאלִים Yishme'elim / מִדְיָנִים Midyanim · H3459 / H4084

versions.s: Justice, judgment, the right ordering of things, and also a legal decision.

b.t: Versions read justice, judgment, or ordinance.
**He has good judgment.** **The judgment went against him.** English keeps both the faculty and the verdict in one word.
Mishpat is from the verb to judge, and covers a legal ruling, the practice of justice, and the settled order that results. Paired with tsedaqah it is one of the standard prophetic demands.
English judgment leans toward condemnation, so a demand to do mishpat reads as a demand to condemn rather than to put right.
When two words appear as a fixed pair in the Prophets, study them together. They function as one demand.
Justice dominates modern versions; the King James often reads judgment.

versions.s: The LORD watch between me and thee. Not a blessing of closeness; a warning born of mutual distrust.

b.t: Every version reads the LORD watch between me and thee accurately as a translation, but the modern popular use of Mizpah as a warm parting blessing reflects a meaning that developed long after, and separately from, what the verse is actually doing in context.

Imagine a phrase that started as **I'll be watching you**, said warily between two people who just agreed to stay apart, later printed on friendship jewelry as though it meant **I'll be thinking of you fondly**. That is roughly what happened to Mizpah between Genesis and greeting cards.

Mizpah, watchtower, names the place where Laban, still wary of Jacob and speaking immediately after accusing him of theft, proposes that God monitor the two of them precisely because neither trusts the other once they are out of each other's sight. The statement functions as a mutual non-aggression boundary marker between two suspicious parties, not as an affectionate wish for closeness, which is nonetheless how the phrase circulates today on rings, cards, and mottoes.

English readers meeting the LORD watch between me and thee outside its narrative context, as it usually circulates today, have no access to the tense, distrustful scene it comes from, so the phrase's popular meaning has drifted to nearly the opposite of what it originally expressed.

Before adopting a Bible verse as a sentiment, check the scene it comes from. Mizpah is one of the clearest cases where a phrase's popular use has drifted entirely away from, and even reversed, its original narrative meaning.

The wording itself is not contested. This note is here to correct a popular misreading built on the phrase divorced from its context, watchful suspicion between estranged in-laws, not a warm invocation of friendship across distance.

versions.s: As far as the east is from the west. A deliberately chosen pair of directions with no meeting point, unlike north and south.

b.t: Every version reads east and west, accurately translating the specific pair of directions the Hebrew names, though without necessarily prompting a reader to notice why this particular pair, rather than north and south, was chosen.

Travel far enough north and you reach a point where north stops meaning anything, the pole; the same happens going south. Travel east, though, and you are still traveling east forever; there is no eastern pole where the direction runs out. The psalm's choice of east and west, not north and south, pictures a separation with literally no endpoint.

Mizrach, east, and ma'arav, west, name directions that never converge anywhere on the earth's surface, unlike north and south, which meet at the poles. The poetic choice is precise: describing the removal of sin as far as the east is from the west pictures a genuinely infinite, ever-increasing distance, not simply a very large but ultimately bounded one, the way north and south, converging at fixed points, would have implied.

English readers hear east and west as simply one reasonable pair of opposite directions among several, north and south being equally obvious alternatives, with no built-in signal that the poet specifically avoided the pair that has actual meeting points on a globe.

When Hebrew poetry chooses one pair of opposites over an equally available alternative, ask whether the specific pair chosen carries a meaning the alternative would not. Here, the choice of east/west over north/south is doing real conceptual work: describing infinite rather than merely large distance.

East and west as the rendering is not in dispute. What is worth making explicit is the deliberate reasoning behind the choice, a pairing of directions with no geometric meeting point, that most readers absorb as simply poetic without registering as a precise, considered image.
מִזְרָח וּמַעֲרָב mizrach u-ma'arav · H4217 + H4628

versions.s: She called his name Moab. The name echoes me'av, from a father, memorializing how he was conceived.

b.t: Every version reads Moab as a bare proper name, transliterated, with no built-in meaning visible to an English reader at all.

Imagine a family naming a child born under scandalous circumstances something that sounds, to everyone who ever hears it, like a quiet confession of exactly what happened. That is what Moab does in Hebrew, a permanent, audible reminder built into a nation's own name.

Moab, mo'av, closely resembles me'av, from a father, a near-pun rather than a formally marked possessive construction, unlike his half-brother's name, Ben-ammi, son of my people, given to the second daughter's son in the very next verse, which does mark the relationship explicitly. Both names function as the daughters' own memorial of the incestuous circumstances of their sons' births, embedded permanently in the names of the nations, Moab and Ammon, that descend from them.

English Moab is simply a place-name and a people-name with no internal meaning an English reader can access, so the built-in, self-incriminating pun Genesis records is invisible unless a reader is told what the Hebrew consonants echo.

When Genesis names a nation's ancestor at a morally loaded moment in the narrative, check whether the name itself is doing commentary. The naming device Genesis has already used for Cain, Noah, Peleg, and Japheth continues here, aimed at explaining two neighboring nations' origins rather than a single Israelite ancestor.

Moab as a transliterated proper name is not contested. The pun is a matter of Hebrew sound that no English rendering of the name itself can carry, unlike Ben-ammi the following verse, whose meaning, son of my people, is stated as an explicit possessive rather than merely echoed.

versions.s: Let them be for signs, and for seasons. Moedim, the same word later naming Israel's appointed feasts.

b.t: Every version reads seasons, a reasonable general translation, but one that does not carry forward the word's more specific, later technical use for Israel's fixed festival dates.

English seasons suggests spring, summer, fall, winter, a general climate cycle. The Hebrew word instead points toward scheduled appointments, the same word later used for Israel's specific festival calendar, closer to marking out a calendar of appointments than describing weather patterns.

Moedim, appointed times, is the same word Leviticus 23 uses repeatedly for the LORD's own appointed feasts, Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, and the rest. Its use here at creation's fourth day quietly establishes that the sun and moon's created purpose already included marking out the very calendar those later appointed festivals would run on, tying Israel's worship calendar back to the created order itself.

English seasons names a general climate pattern; it does not carry forward the specific, technical sense of scheduled, appointed occasions that moedim has throughout the rest of the Torah, so the link between creation's fourth day and Israel's later festival calendar disappears once the word becomes a generic English noun.

When a word appears early in a book and recurs later as a technical or ritual term, read the early occurrence in light of the later one. Moedim at creation is not incidental vocabulary; it is the same word the Torah will use for its most structured religious calendar.

Seasons is not wrong, but it undersells the specific, later technical sense of moedim as scheduled sacred appointments. Appointed times keeps the link to Leviticus 23's festival calendar visible, a connection worth knowing even though seasons remains a defensible general translation.

entries.title: mone
entries.def: a staying, i.e. residence (the act or the place)

versions.s: In my Father's house are many mansions. The noun means a place to stay.

b.t: The King James reads mansions. Modern versions read rooms, dwelling places, or abiding places.
**Lodgings.** **Quarters.** Neither says anything about grandeur. Mansion did not either, in 1611.

Mone is from meno, to remain, and means a place of staying. The related verb runs through chapter 15 as abide. The Latin mansiones, from which the King James mansions comes, meant stopping places on a road.
English mansion has grown from a dwelling into a large house, so the verse now promises architecture rather than a place with the Father.
When a King James word describes something grand, check whether it was grand in 1611. Several of these words have inflated rather than narrowed.
Rooms and dwelling places are what most modern versions print; mansions is the King James.
μονή mone · G3438

src: mone at John 14:2 and 14:23 only
meno, to abide, throughout John 15
Vulgate mansiones, stopping places

entries.title: monogenes
entries.where: monogenes is tagged 9 times, across 4 books: john 4 · luke 3 · 1john 1 · hebrews 1.

versions.s: The only begotten Son, or the only begotten God. The manuscripts do not agree and the difference is enormous.

b.t: Modern versions read the only God, or God the one and only, or the one and only Son who is himself God. Each is a different decision about the same clause.

Two different problems wearing the same coat. First: two old copies of a letter say different words, so which did your grandmother write? That is a manuscript question. Second: what did she mean by the word she used? That is a dictionary question. Usually you only have one of these at a time. Here you have both, in the same clause.

Two things are happening at once. First a textual split: the earliest papyri and the great uncials read monogenes theos, while the majority of later manuscripts read monogenes huios. Second a lexical question: monogenes is traditionally rendered only begotten, from a supposed link to gennao, to beget, but the second half of the compound is more likely genos, kind or class, giving one of a kind.
English has to resolve both questions before it can print the sentence. There is no way to write a clause that is undecided between Son and God, or between begotten and unique.

When versions differ on a noun this weighty, check whether the split is textual or lexical before assuming an agenda. Here it is both at once, which is rare, and each question has a separate body of evidence.

Son has the weight of tradition, the majority of manuscripts, and the fact that John calls Jesus the Son constantly. God has the earliest manuscripts and is the harder reading, which usually counts in its favour, and it closes the prologue where it opened, with the Word being God. Only begotten is the older lexical reading and one of a kind has the better etymology.
μονογενής monogenes · G3439

src: monogenes theos in P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus; monogenes huios in the later majority
monogenes of Isaac at Hebrews 11:17, who was not Abraham's only son, which bears on the lexical question
Septuagint usage of monogenes for yachid, only or precious

versions.s: Thou shalt surely die. Literally dying, you shall die: the verb said twice.

b.t: Every version adds an adverb, surely or certainly, to carry the emphasis. None can double the verb the way the Hebrew does, because repeating die die in English reads as a mistake, not as emphasis.

English intensifies a verb by adding a word: **you will surely die**, **you will certainly die**. Hebrew has another option: say the verb itself twice, once as a bare noun-form and once conjugated. Dying, you shall die is what the sentence actually does.

Mot tamut pairs the infinitive absolute mot, dying, with the finite verb tamut, you will die, from the same root muth. This infinitive-absolute-plus-finite-verb pattern is a standard Biblical Hebrew device for intensifying a verb, common in legal and covenantal pronouncements, especially death sentences. The same verse already uses the same device positively: akol tokel, freely eat, literally eating you shall eat.

English cannot repeat a bare verb form next to its conjugated self and have it read as intensification rather than a typo. The only available tool is an adverb, which reports that emphasis exists without reproducing the grammatical shape that creates it.

When two words from the same Hebrew root sit next to each other, one uninflected, look for the infinitive absolute construction. It is the language's built-in italics, and English always has to translate it as a separate word rather than a repeated one.

No dispute over the sense; every version agrees the warning is emphatic. What is worth noting is the grammatical device itself: an infinitive doubling a finite verb is a genuine feature of Hebrew with no formal English equivalent, not a stylistic flourish a translator chose.
מוֹת תָּמוּת mot tamut (מוּת muth) · H4191

src: The same construction in a death sentence: Exodus 21:12, 15-17
The positive form in the same verse: 'akol tokel', freely eat, Genesis 2:16

versions.s: And he died. The same two words end almost every entry in the genealogy, on purpose.

b.t: Every version reads and he died at the end of each entry, correctly. No version can show a reader that this is the identical two-word Hebrew phrase, vayamot, closing verse after verse, because English narrative prose naturally varies its wording anyway.

Picture a list where every single line ends with the identical short sentence, on purpose, so the repetition itself becomes the message. English style guides tell writers to vary their sentences. Hebrew narrative sometimes wants the opposite, and this chapter is the clearest example of it in Genesis.

Vayamot, and he died, closes the entries for Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Methuselah, and Lamech, eight refrains in one chapter. The formula is not filler; it is the generational answer to Genesis 3's sentence of death, tolling once per name, following directly after chapter 3's mot tamut warning finally coming due.

English narrative avoids exact repetition as a matter of style, so even a translation that renders and he died correctly every time reads as normal, varied prose rather than as a refrain. The liturgical, tolling effect of the same two words returning eight times is a feature of the Hebrew's deliberate sameness, which English convention works against by instinct.

When a formula repeats with only names and numbers changing around it, read the repetition as the message, not as a scribe's failure of imagination. Genealogies in Hebrew narrative are rarely neutral bookkeeping; the refrain here is doing theological work chapter 2's warning promised.

Every version renders and he died the same correct way, every time; that was never in question. What the English can't preserve, once the repetition is smoothed into ordinary narrative prose, is that the refrain itself is the chapter's real argument.
וַיָּמֹת vayamot (מוּת muth, to die) · H4191

src: The refrain closes Genesis 5:5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 27, 31: eight of the chapter's ten entries

versions.s: Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD. Hoshia na, the Hebrew behind Hosanna, is a plea for rescue, not originally a shout of praise.

b.t: Every version of Psalm 118:25 reads save now or save, I pray, correctly preserving the plea. The transliterated Hosanna, carried untranslated into the Gospels at Jesus's triumphal entry, has since taken on an almost entirely different function as an exclamation of praise rather than a request.

English Hosanna today functions almost entirely as an exclamation of praise, sung joyfully with no sense of urgency or need. Its Hebrew source, hoshia na, save now, please, is a direct, urgent request, closer to help! or save us, please! than to hooray, a request that only gradually softened into a celebratory shout over the centuries.

Hoshia na combines the imperative save with na, a particle of entreaty, please, we beg you, forming a direct, urgent petition for rescue in its original psalm context, thanking God for past deliverance while pleading for continued help. By the time the crowds shout Hosanna at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem, the word may already be functioning more as an acclamation than a literal plea, and it has continued drifting toward pure celebratory praise in most religious usage ever since.

English speakers using or hearing Hosanna today, especially in Christian worship, generally experience it as a shout of triumphant praise with no sense of urgent request, the opposite of hoshia na's original, plain meaning as a plea for God to save, now, please.

When a Hebrew or Aramaic word survives in English purely as a transliterated exclamation, check its original grammatical function, imperative, plea, statement, before assuming its current devotional use matches what the word was actually doing in its source context.

Hosanna as a shout of praise reflects how the word has functioned in worship for most of Christian history. Save now, please save, recovering the word's original urgent, petitionary sense, changes the emotional register of the triumphal entry scene considerably: a crowd crying out for rescue, not simply cheering.
הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא hoshia na (Hosanna) · H3467 + H4994

src: Original petitionary use: Psalm 118:25 itself
Transliterated into the Gospel accounts: Matthew 21:9; Mark 11:9-10; John 12:13

versions.s: Over Edom will I cast out my shoe. A legal gesture claiming ownership, the same custom used to finalize a transaction at Ruth 4:7.

b.t: Every version reads cast out my shoe or throw my sandal, accurately translating the gesture but without necessarily explaining that it names a specific, recognized ancient legal custom rather than a colorful metaphor invented for this poem alone.

Imagine a culture where signing a deed involved physically removing your shoe and handing it to the other party, a small ritual gesture that meant something specific and binding. Casting a shoe over a territory in this psalm performs the same kind of formal claim, not a random insult but a recognized legal act.

Casting or removing a shoe functioned as a formal gesture of transferring or claiming property rights, most explicitly explained at Ruth 4:7-8, where a shoe is removed to finalize a land transaction between kinsmen. Applying the same gesture to Edom in this military psalm claims the territory the way a shoe-casting would finalize any other property claim, a specific legal idiom repurposed for national conquest.

English cast out my shoe reads as an odd, perhaps contemptuous gesture with no built-in explanation, so a reader has no way to connect it to the specific, documented legal custom Ruth 4:7 explains in detail, a connection that turns a strange image into a recognizable formal claim.

When an unusual physical gesture appears in poetry, check whether a narrative passage elsewhere explains the same gesture in a legal or social context. Ruth 4:7's explicit explanation of shoe-removal is exactly the kind of key that unlocks this psalm's otherwise puzzling image.

Cast out my shoe is not seriously disputed as the literal rendering. What the translation leaves out is the legal background, explained directly at Ruth 4:7, that turns what looks like an arbitrary insult into a specific, formal claim of ownership over Edom.
אַשְׁלִיךְ נַעֲלִי ashlich na'ali (cast my shoe) · H7993 / H5275

src: The shoe-removal legal custom explained directly: Ruth 4:7-8
The same custom for renouncing a levirate obligation: Deuteronomy 25:9

versions.s: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. Nabal names moral corruption, not stupidity.

b.t: Every version reads fool, a reasonable general term, though English fool more readily suggests low intelligence than the specifically moral corruption nabal carries in Hebrew.

English fool can mean someone unintelligent or someone acting rashly, but rarely names deliberate moral corruption on its own. Hebrew nabal leans hard toward the second sense: not someone who reasoned badly, but someone whose whole conduct, not merely their opinions, is godless and reckless.

Nabal describes moral disgrace and godless behavior throughout the Hebrew Bible, most vividly embodied in the character actually named Nabal at 1 Samuel 25, whose wife explicitly says his name means what he is, folly is with him. The verse is not describing careful philosophical atheism; it is describing someone whose denial of God flows from, and licenses, a corrupted way of living, closer to godless or morally reckless than to unintelligent.

English fool primarily suggests poor judgment or low intelligence to a modern reader; it does not automatically carry the moral, almost ethical-character weight nabal has throughout the Hebrew Bible, so the verse can be misread as a comment on intellectual sophistication rather than on moral corruption.

A Hebrew word for foolishness in a moral or theological context is worth sorting by family: does it belong with nabal, moral corruption, or with a word for simple lack of understanding? The two are not the same category in Hebrew the way English fool tends to flatten them.

Fool is the traditional and workable English rendering. Godless or morally corrupt more precisely conveys nabal's actual charge, that the denial in view is a matter of character and conduct, not primarily of intellectual argument.

versions.s: His wife looked back from behind him. The verb is a deliberate, longing gaze, not a startled glance.

b.t: Every version reads looked back, an accurate but broad English verb that does not distinguish a reflex from a deliberate gaze the way the underlying Hebrew word does.

English **she looked back** covers everything from a half-second reflex glance to a long, wistful stare. Hebrew nabat leans hard toward the second: an intent, lingering look, closer to gazing after something you want than to a quick backward check.

Nabat means to look intently, to regard with attention, sometimes with implied longing or favor, distinct from more neutral seeing-verbs elsewhere in the same episode, including the different verb the text uses when the two visiting men look down toward Sodom at 18:16, and again when Abraham himself looks toward Sodom the next morning at 19:28. The choice of nabat for Lot's wife signals a fixed, desiring look back at the life and city she was leaving, not a startled reflex any fleeing person might have had.

English looked back is neutral about intent; it fits both an accidental glance and a deliberate lingering gaze equally well, so the verse's implicit moral distinction, that this was chosen longing rather than reflex, requires knowing which Hebrew verb is actually being used.

When a narrative's moral weight depends on whether an action was deliberate or reflexive, check the specific verb Hebrew chose rather than assuming a general seeing-verb was neutral. Hebrew has multiple words for looking, and the choice among them often carries the judgment English has to state separately, if at all.

Looked back as the basic sense is not in dispute among translators. The nuance, that nabat specifically implies a lingering, desiring look rather than a glance, is a matter of vocabulary precision that most English translations do not have the means to flag without an added phrase.

versions.s: He is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee. The word's first use in the Bible names an intercessor, not a predictor.

b.t: Every version reads prophet, correctly, but the word's modern popular sense, foreteller of events, is not what this first, founding occurrence of the word is actually describing Abraham doing.

Modern English **prophet** usually means someone who predicts the future. The very first time the Bible uses the word for a person, at this verse, the job described is prayer on someone else's behalf, not prediction, a baseline sense English usage has since narrowed away from.

Navi, prophet, appears here for the first time applied to a human being anywhere in the Hebrew Bible, and the role attached to it is intercessory prayer that will restore Abimelech's household, not prediction of a future event. The root behind navi is connected to proclaiming or speaking forth, someone who carries and delivers a message from God, of which intercession is one function among several the word will carry through the rest of the Hebrew Bible.

English prophet arrives already loaded with connotations of foretelling and prediction from centuries of usage; a reader meets that connotation before ever noticing that the Bible's own first, defining use of the word describes someone praying for others, not predicting anything at all.

When a key theological term first appears in the Bible, read that occurrence as a baseline for the word's range before importing the sense the word carries by its last or most familiar biblical occurrence, let alone its modern popular meaning.

Prophet as the rendering of navi is settled; translators are not divided here. What is easy to miss is that its first appearance defines the office more by intercession than by prediction, a nuance the English word prophet, loaded with its own later history, does not supply on its own.

versions.s: Prophet. One who speaks for someone else, which is a job rather than a gift of prediction.

b.t: Every version reads prophet.

Navi is one who speaks for another. Exodus 7:1 makes Aaron the navi of Moses, which defines the term inside the text: Moses is as God and Aaron is his mouth. Prediction is a possible content, not the definition.
English prophecy has narrowed almost entirely to foretelling, so forthtelling has to be explained.
When the Bible defines a term inside the narrative, that definition outranks any lexicon. Exodus 7:1 is the definition of this one.

versions.s: God did tempt Abraham. The Hebrew verb means tested or proved, not enticed toward evil.

b.t: Modern versions read tested or put to the test, correcting for the English word's drift. The King James, accurate in its own century, now misleads a reader who only knows tempt in its current sense.

In 1611, **tempt** meant to test or try, the way a metallurgist tempts steel by testing its strength. Today **tempt** means to lure someone toward doing something wrong. The Hebrew word never changed; the English word did, and the King James sentence now says something it did not originally mean.

Nissah means to test, try, or prove, used of testing loyalty, resolve, or genuineness, never of enticing someone toward wrongdoing, a sense that belongs to an entirely different Hebrew vocabulary. The same root gives nes, a banner or a standard used to rally and prove an army, and later gives the word for miracle, both senses built on the idea of putting something on display to be examined or proven, not on luring someone toward failure.

English tempt has narrowed and shifted meaning since the King James was translated; the translators chose an accurate word for their own time, and English drift, not translation error, is what makes the sentence sound wrong to a modern ear.

Before assuming an old translation made a theological error, check whether the English word itself has drifted since. Repented, tempt, and charity are three of the clearest cases in the King James where the Hebrew or Greek never moved, but the English gloss did.

Tested or put to the test uses current English accurately. Tempt, correct in 1611, is misleading today only because English tempt itself changed meaning, not because nissah changed or was mistranslated originally.

versions.s: He called his name Noah, saying, this shall comfort us. Comfort is nacham; the name Noah is built on the different word nuach, rest.

b.t: Every version reads Noah and comfort without comment, since English has no built-in way to notice that the name and its stated reason come from two different Hebrew roots that merely sound alike.

Imagine naming a baby **Grace** and explaining, **because she will bring us gratitude**. Close, related ideas, but not the same word, and a sharp-eared listener would notice the explanation doesn't quite land on the name. Genesis 5:29 does exactly that in Hebrew.

Noach, the name, is generally traced to the root nuach, to rest or settle. Lamech's explanation uses yenachamenu, from nacham, to comfort or console, a related-sounding but distinct root, the same one behind chapter 6's statement that God was grieved, nacham, that He had made man. The name-explanation is a paronomasia, a sound-play, not a strict derivation, the same kind of move Genesis 2:23 makes with ish and ishah.

English comfort and rest share no sound at all, so an English reader has no way to hear that Lamech's explanation is a near-miss pun rather than a precise etymology. The Hebrew wordplay, closely related consonants doing double duty, is simply gone once translated.

When a biblical name's stated explanation does not use the exact same root as the name, check whether the text is punning on sound rather than reporting derivation. Hebrew narrators do this regularly, and it is not an error to be corrected but a literary device to be noticed.

Both comfort and Noah are rendered correctly in every version; neither word is contested. The point is that the verse's own logic, why this name, works by resemblance rather than by strict etymology, which is exactly the kind of connection English translation cannot preserve.
נֹחַ Noach (נוּחַ nuach, rest) / נִחַם nacham, comfort · H5146, H5162

versions.s: It repented the LORD. A verb that means comfort, grieve, relent and change course, all at once.

b.t: Modern versions read regretted, was sorry, or was grieved. Repented has dropped out because English repentance now means turning from sin, which is not what the verb says.

**He was sorry.** Sorry about what happened, or sorry enough to undo it? English splits those into regret and relent. One Hebrew word covers both, and the sentence has to tell you which, and sometimes it does not.

Nacham covers a range that English splits across several words: to be moved to pity, to console oneself, to grieve, and to change a stated course of action. It is used of God relenting from announced judgment and also of human comfort after a death.
No English verb covers grief and reversal in the same breath. Translators have to pick the shade the context supports, and the shade they pick becomes the theology the reader inherits.

When a modern version has quietly replaced a King James word, the usual reason is that the English word moved, not that the Hebrew is in doubt. Check the old word's older meaning before assuming a translation agenda.

Regretted reads the verb as emotion. Relented reads it as a change of course. The verse supplies both in its two halves, and the second half, it grieved him at his heart, is what makes the emotional reading hard to strip out.
נָחַם nacham · H5162

src: The same verb at 1 Samuel 15:11 and 15:29, in the same chapter, in apparently opposite directions

versions.s: Destroy this temple. Greek has two words for temple and this is the inner one.

b.t: Every version reads temple for both Greek words.
**The house** and **the grounds**. If someone says tear down the house, nobody thinks he means the estate. One word for both and the sentence gets much harder.

Naos is the sanctuary proper, the inner building. Hieron is the whole temple precinct including the courts. Verse 14 has Jesus in the hieron; verse 19 has him saying destroy this naos. John then tells you in verse 21 that he meant his body.
English has one word, so the shift from precinct to sanctuary inside five verses cannot be seen.
Where Greek has two words for one English word, watch for a passage that uses both. The switch is usually doing the work.
Temple is universal for both. Some study Bibles note the distinction; no translation marks it.
ναός naos · G3485 / ἱερόν hieron · G2411

src: hieron at John 2:14; naos at 2:19-21
The accusation at Mark 14:58 uses naos
Paul uses naos of believers: 1 Corinthians 3:16; 6:19
