versions.s: Pharaoh shall lift up thine head. For the butler, restored to office. For the baker, the same phrase, with one word added, means beheaded.

b.t: Every version reads lift up thine head for the butler and either the same phrase or lift up thy head from off thee for the baker, correctly conveying restoration and execution respectively, though not every translation preserves how close the two phrasings actually sit to each other in Hebrew.

Imagine telling two coworkers on the same day, **you're getting a promotion** and **you're getting let go**, using the exact same sentence structure for both, except one has a single extra word that flips the entire meaning. That is precisely what Joseph's Hebrew does here, and it is chilling specifically because both men hear almost the same words.

Yissa Pharaoh et rosh'cha, Pharaoh will lift up your head, is used of the butler's restoration to office at 40:13. The identical core phrase returns at 40:19 for the baker, with one addition, me'aleicha, from off you, turning restore your position into remove your head, the same idiom completing itself in two opposite directions depending on a single added phrase.

English restoration language, promoted, and execution language, beheaded, share no vocabulary at all, so the Hebrew's grim wordplay, one shared idiom branching into life and death, is completely invisible once each fate gets its own separate English phrase.

When a narrator delivers parallel news to two characters using visibly similar phrasing, check how closely the underlying words actually match. Shared vocabulary delivering opposite outcomes is a real literary technique, not a translation coincidence, and it is often lost the moment each outcome gets its own natural-sounding English sentence.

Both outcomes are stated plainly by the narrative regardless of phrasing, so no version gets this wrong. What's worth noticing is the wordplay connecting them: the same lift up your head idiom branching into opposite fates, a genuine literary effect that separate, natural-sounding English sentences for each man cannot reproduce.
יִשָּׂא פַרְעֹה אֶת־רֹאשֶׁךָ yissa Pharaoh et rosh'cha · H5375 + H7218

src: The butler's restoration: Genesis 40:13, 20-21
The baker's execution using the same core idiom plus me'aleicha: Genesis 40:19, 22

versions.s: Manasseh, for God hath made me forget; Ephraim, for God hath caused me to be fruitful. Two more names built from the naming sentence itself.

b.t: Every version reads Manasseh and Ephraim as bare transliterated names, with Joseph's explanatory statements translated separately and accurately, but without connecting either name back to its own root the way the Hebrew explicitly does.

By now the pattern should look familiar: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and now Manasseh and Ephraim, thirteen names in a row each built as a pun on the parent's own explanatory sentence. English transliteration keeps none of the wordplay, in Canaan or, as here, in Egypt.

Menashsheh echoes nashah, to forget, from Joseph's own words, God hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house. Ephraim echoes parah, to be fruitful, from for God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. Both names complete the pattern established across every one of Jacob's own sons' births, now applied one generation later, to children born not in Canaan but in Egypt, under Joseph's Egyptian name and Egyptian wife.

English Manasseh and Ephraim are bare proper nouns; the sentences explaining them read as separate commentary rather than as the linguistic source the names were extracted from, so the pattern completing itself one generation later, in a foreign land, is invisible without the Hebrew roots.

Continue tracking the birth-naming-pun device established across Genesis 29-30 all the way through the Joseph narrative. The device does not stop with Jacob's own sons; it continues into the next generation, even after the family relocates to Egypt.

Neither name nor its accompanying explanation is in dispute in any version. This entry rounds out the pattern already established for the rest of the twelve tribes' names, showing it persists one generation further, into Joseph's own Egyptian-born sons.
מְנַשֶּׁה Menashsheh (נָשָׁה nashah, forget) / אֶפְרַיִם Ephraim (פָּרָה parah, fruitful) · H4519 / H5382 / H669 / H6509

src: The same naming-pun pattern across all twelve tribal names: Genesis 29:32-30:24; 35:18
Joseph's own explanatory statements: Genesis 41:51-52

versions.s: A mighty prince among us. Literally, a prince of God, using elohim as a superlative.

b.t: Every version reads mighty prince or great chieftain, correctly conveying the superlative sense without the literal words prince of God ever appearing in translation.

English intensifies with words like **super** or **mega**, or with an adverb, **incredibly great**. Hebrew has another option: attach the word for God to a noun to mean very or utterly. Elohim here is not claiming Abraham is divine; it is doing the job English mega does.

Nesi elohim, literally prince of God, uses elohim the way Hebrew occasionally uses divine vocabulary to intensify an ordinary noun or adjective to its greatest possible degree, a pattern also seen in phrases like an exceedingly great city, literally a city great to God, at Jonah 3:3. The construction is a superlative device, not a theological claim about Abraham's status.

English has no equivalent habit of using God's name as a grammatical intensifier, so a literal translation, prince of God, would mislead an English reader into hearing a theological claim the Hebrew idiom was never making.

When elohim or a divine name appears attached to an ordinary noun in a way that does not fit a normal statement about deity, check whether Hebrew is using it as a superlative intensifier rather than making a religious claim. The construction is rare but attested and easy to over-read.

Translators are not divided here; mighty prince correctly captures the sense and rightly avoids the misleading literal rendering. Worth noting is a genuine grammatical curiosity: Hebrew can reach for God's own name simply to say very, in a way English idiom has no parallel for.
נְשִׂיא אֱלֹהִים nesi elohim · H5387 + H430

src: The same superlative pattern at Jonah 3:3, 'an exceedingly great city,' literally 'great to God'
D. Winton Thomas, 'A Consideration of Some Unusual Ways of Expressing the Superlative in Hebrew,' Vetus Testamentum 3 (1953), on this construction as a Hebrew superlative device

versions.s: He had wrought folly in Israel. A fixed idiom for a grave sexual offense, not an improvised phrase.

b.t: Every version reads some form of folly or outrage in Israel, correctly conveying moral severity, but without necessarily flagging that this is a recurring, semi-technical phrase rather than an ad hoc description invented for this one scene.

English has set phrases for serious wrongdoing, **crossed a line**, **broken faith**, immediately recognizable as formal condemnation rather than casual complaint. Wrought folly in Israel is exactly that kind of fixed idiom in Hebrew, recurring with the same weight in other serious violation narratives.

Nevalah, folly, with the verb asah, to do or work, forms a set idiom, la'asot nevalah, that recurs for grave sexual violations and covenant betrayals at Deuteronomy 22:21, Judges 19:23-24 and 20:6, 10, and 2 Samuel 13:12, describing Tamar's assault in nearly identical language to what is used here for Dinah. The phrase functions as recognized, almost legal, vocabulary for a category of serious offense, not a one-off expression of anger.

English readers meeting wrought folly hear an old-fashioned, almost mild phrase, since modern folly suggests foolishness rather than grave wrongdoing, so the weight the fixed Hebrew idiom carries by recurring in other serious assault and covenant-violation narratives is easy to miss entirely.

When a phrase describing wrongdoing recurs verbatim or nearly verbatim across several separate narratives, treat it as a recognized category or fixed idiom, not as spontaneous language invented fresh each time. Its recurrence is itself evidence of how seriously the culture classified the offense.

Every version gets the basic sense right, a grave wrong. What's worth flagging is that this specific phrase is a recurring formula across several assault and covenant-violation narratives, evidence of how the offense was categorized, not merely how one narrator happened to phrase his outrage.

versions.s: Help meet. Two English words that were never one word, and a Hebrew phrase that says something else again.

b.t: Modern versions read a helper suitable for him, or a helper corresponding to him, or a helper as his complement.

**That is a meet reward.** Meet used to mean fitting. It died, and people who still heard it in the phrase started running the two words together into helpmeet, then helpmate. A word that never existed got invented by ears rather than pens.

The Hebrew is ezer kenegdo. Ezer is a helper, and the word is used most often in the Hebrew Bible of God himself helping Israel, which is not the sense of assistant. Kenegdo is built on neged, meaning in front of or opposite, so the phrase is a helper corresponding to him, one who stands facing him.

Two separate problems stack here. English lost the word meet, meaning fitting, so help meet was misheard as helpmeet and then as helpmate, a word that never existed in the text. And English helper carries a junior connotation that the Hebrew ezer does not.

When a King James phrase has become a single familiar word, check whether it was ever one word. English drift produces some of the most confident misreadings in the Bible, and they are invisible to a reader who only has the English.

There is no real translation dispute here. There is an English-language accident, and then a genuine question about the force of ezer, which every modern version handles slightly differently while none of them says assistant.
עֵזֶר ezer · H5828 / נֶגֶד neged · H5048

versions.s: Man became a living soul. The same phrase is used of the animals.

b.t: The King James reads a living soul here and a living creature at Genesis 1:24 for the same two words. Modern versions read living being or living creature in both places, which is the correction.

**She is a living creature.** That is a statement about being alive, not about having an invisible part. Now imagine your translation used a more spiritual-sounding word in one place and a plainer one somewhere else, for the same original phrase.

Nephesh chayyah. The phrase appears at Genesis 1:20, 21, 24 and 30 of sea creatures, birds and land animals. Nephesh is closer to a life, a self, an appetite, even a throat, than to an immaterial soul. The verse says the man became alive, not that he received a soul the animals lack.
English soul carries centuries of Greek and Christian anthropology that Hebrew nephesh does not. There is no neutral English word, and creature sounds dismissive where soul sounds elevated.

When one Hebrew phrase is rendered two different ways in the same book, look up the other occurrences. Translators sometimes signal a theology by their choice of English word, and the King James does it here.
No Hebrew dispute. Modern versions have standardised on living being, and the King James rendering is the one that produced the popular reading.

src: The identical phrase at Genesis 1:20, 21, 24, 30

versions.s: Flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat. Life and blood are named with the same word, nephesh.

b.t: Every version reads some form of flesh with the life, which is the blood, correctly, though the repetition of nephesh for both life and, by implication, the animal's very self is not obviously visible in English's two separate words, life and blood.

English keeps **blood** and **life** as separate ideas connected only by biology class. This verse states outright, in one Hebrew word doing both jobs, that the blood simply is the life, not a symbol of it or a carrier of it, but the thing itself.

Nephesh, the same word behind a living soul at Genesis 2:7 and the living creatures of chapter 1, is used here to identify the blood directly: basar benaphsho damo, flesh with its life, its blood. The equation, blood is nephesh, becomes the basis for Israel's later dietary law and sacrificial system, restated explicitly at Leviticus 17:11, the life of the flesh is in the blood.

English requires two separate words, life and blood, connected by a verb, to say what Hebrew says by using one word, nephesh, for both. The tight equation Hebrew makes directly, blood is nephesh, becomes in English a looser statement about one thing being associated with another.

When a text says X is Y using the same underlying word for both sides of the sentence, treat the equation as stronger than an English translation using two different vocabulary words will suggest. Nephesh here is not merely near blood; the text names them with one word.

Every version agrees on the basic sense, that blood represents or carries life. The stronger reading, that nephesh here identifies rather than merely associates blood with life, is a matter of how tightly the single Hebrew word is allowed to bind the two ideas together.
נֶפֶשׁ nephesh · H5315

src: The same equation restated: Leviticus 17:11, 'the life of the flesh is in the blood'

versions.s: His life is bound up in the lad's life. Nephesh, the same word as living soul, used twice, bound together.

b.t: Every version reads his life is bound up in the lad's life, correctly, but the repetition of the same underlying Hebrew word, nephesh, for both father and son is smoothed into a single English word, life, used generically rather than as the loaded term it is throughout the rest of Genesis.

English keeps **life** fairly abstract, a general condition rather than a tangible thing you could tie to something. Hebrew nephesh is closer to a person's whole self or throat, concrete enough that describing two nephashot as bound, keshurah, together pictures an actual physical or emotional cord, not merely a sentiment.

Nafsho keshurah b'nafsho, his nephesh is bound in his nephesh, repeats the word already met as the breath of life at 2:7 and living soul throughout chapter 1, now applied twice in one clause to describe Jacob's and Benjamin's selves as tied together, not merely emotionally attached in the abstract sense English life suggests, but bound, a term elsewhere used of physical tying and knotting.

English life is a broad, somewhat abstract noun; nephesh carries a more concrete, almost tangible sense of self or living being throughout Genesis, so describing two nephashot as tied or bound together lands with more physical force in Hebrew than his life is bound up in his life does in ordinary English.

When nephesh recurs at an emotionally weighted moment late in a book, read it against its earlier, more concrete uses, breath, living soul, throat, appetite, rather than assuming it has quietly become the abstract English word life. The word's physical undertone rarely disappears.

Every version lands on the same basic sense, deep attachment. What's easy to lose is nephesh's more concrete, physical undertone, given how loaded the word has already become across chapters 1, 2, and 9 of the same book.
נֶפֶשׁ קְשׁוּרָה nephesh keshurah · H5315 + H7194

src: keshurah, bound or tied, used of physical binding elsewhere: e.g. Job 38:31
nephesh's earlier concrete range: Genesis 1:20-30; 2:7; 9:4

versions.s: The iron entered into his soul. The Hebrew more literally reads his soul came into iron, a difficult phrase ancient translators handled differently.

b.t: Most versions read some form of describing Joseph's affliction in prison, his feet hurt with fetters, his neck or person constrained by iron, with varying degrees of literalness about the famous his soul entered iron phrase.

English the iron entered into his soul is now a familiar idiom for deep inner anguish, but it is also a slightly unusual translation choice: the Hebrew word order more literally has his soul entering iron, not the other way around, a small but real difference ancient translators noticed and handled in at least three different ways.

The Hebrew reads nephesh, soul, life, or person, as entering into iron, backward from the more intuitive image of iron entering a person. The Syriac keeps this direction, his soul went into iron; the Aramaic Targum reverses it, the chain of iron went into his soul; the widely beloved English phrase, the iron entered into his soul, popularized through the Book of Common Prayer, follows the Targum's reversed direction rather than the more literal Hebrew word order.

English readers who know the phrase the iron entered into his soul as a beautiful, familiar idiom for suffering may not realize the phrase's exact grammatical direction was already being debated and reversed by ancient translators, since the literal Hebrew has the person entering the iron, not the iron entering the person.

When a beloved, idiomatic English Bible phrase sounds too poetically perfect to be a plain translation, check its actual grammatical direction against the Hebrew. Some of the most famous English biblical phrases, like this one, already represent an ancient interpretive choice rather than a purely literal rendering.

His soul entered into iron, closer to the literal Hebrew word order, pictures Joseph's whole self being absorbed into confinement. The iron entered into his soul, the beloved reversed idiom following the Targum, pictures suffering piercing inward instead, the version that became proverbial in English despite reversing the Hebrew's own direction.
בַּרְזֶל בָּאָה נַפְשׁוֹ barzel ba'ah naphsho (his soul came into iron) · H1270 + H935 + H5315

versions.s: There were giants in the earth. The Hebrew word, Nephilim, does not itself mean giant.

b.t: The King James, following the Septuagint's gigantes, reads giants, and that rendering has shaped virtually all popular imagination about this verse. Modern versions increasingly leave Nephilim untranslated, since the Hebrew word's own root does not mean large in stature.

Imagine a translator centuries ago rendering a foreign name as though it were the English word it merely resembles. Readers ever since picture something the original text never specified, size, when the word may instead be naming a group by what happened to them, not by how tall they stood.

Nephilim is usually connected to the root naphal, to fall, giving fallen ones, though the derivation is debated and the word is rare, recurring only here and at Numbers 13:33, where the spies again call inhabitants of Canaan Nephilim and compare themselves to grasshoppers beside them, a comparison about being overwhelmed rather than a precise measurement. The Septuagint's gigantes, giants, is itself an interpretive choice, not a translation of a Hebrew word that means large, and the King James inherited that Greek interpretation rather than translating the Hebrew directly.

English giants specifies enormous physical size; Nephilim, whatever its root, does not obviously specify that on its own. The chain from Hebrew Nephilim to Greek gigantes to English giants adds a claim about height that the Hebrew word itself does not make explicit, though the size language later applied to their descendants, the Anakim, at Numbers 13:33 keeps the association alive.

When a familiar English word traces back through a second ancient language rather than directly to the Hebrew, check what that intermediate translation was doing. Giants is a translation of a translation, and each step can add a claim the earlier text did not make.

Giants keeps the King James's inherited Septuagint reading and the popular tradition built on it. Leaving Nephilim untransliterated, as many modern versions now do, admits that the Hebrew word's own meaning, fallen ones or something similar, is not primarily a statement about height, even though later texts associate the same families with great size.

versions.s: Breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. A different word from the one in chapter one.

b.t: All versions read breath. The distinction from the other Hebrew word is invisible in every English Bible.
English has **breath**, **wind**, **air** and **gasp**, and you would not use them interchangeably. Other languages divide the same territory along different lines, and the lines never match.

Neshamah, not ruach. Ruach covers wind, breath and spirit and is the word at Genesis 1:2. Neshamah is narrower, the breath of a living creature, and is used of God and of humans and occasionally of animals. The verse is not saying God put His Spirit in Adam; it uses a different noun for that.
English has one word, breath, standing in for both, so the vocabulary change between chapter one and chapter two cannot be seen.
When two Hebrew words are both rendered by one English word, the change from one to the other is a signal you will never see. Look for it wherever a doctrine is being built on a single verse.
No dispute. This is worth flagging because the ruach and neshamah distinction is routinely collapsed in popular teaching about the human constitution.

versions.s: The LORD smelled a sweet savour. The word for sweet, soothing, shares Noah's own root.

b.t: Every version reads sweet savour, soothing aroma, or pleasing aroma, all correct and all silent about the wordplay, since English sweet, soothing, or pleasing share no sound with Noah at all.

Imagine a story where a character named Rest finally brings the household peace, and the text uses the word **restful** to describe the moment it happens. English would catch that instantly. Hebrew does exactly this with Noah and the soothing smell of his offering, and translation erases the connection completely.

Reyach nichoach, a soothing or restful aroma, uses nichoach, built on the same root as nuach, to rest, the root behind Noah's own name at 5:29. The offering that follows the flood is described, in Hebrew sound, as restful, echoing back to the man whose name promised rest in the first place, a connection reinforced by his father's naming explanation four chapters earlier, even though that earlier explanation had actually reached for comfort, nacham, a related but distinct root.

English sweet, soothing, and pleasing all describe the smell accurately but none of them echoes the sound of Noah, so nothing tips an English reader off that the sentence quietly circles back to the promise made at his naming.

When a name given earlier in a book carries a live root, watch for that root resurfacing later at a significant turn in the story. Hebrew narrative often plants a name's meaning early and lets it echo, sometimes faintly, sometimes precisely, at a later climax.

Sweet savour and its equivalents are uncontested renderings across every version. What's worth noting is a sound-echo of Noah's name that no English rendering of nichoach could preserve, since the connection lives entirely in the shared Hebrew root nuach.

versions.s: He called his name Noah, saying, this shall comfort us. Comfort is nacham; the name Noah is built on the different word nuach, rest.

b.t: Every version reads Noah and comfort without comment, since English has no built-in way to notice that the name and its stated reason come from two different Hebrew roots that merely sound alike.

Imagine naming a baby **Grace** and explaining, **because she will bring us gratitude**. Close, related ideas, but not the same word, and a sharp-eared listener would notice the explanation doesn't quite land on the name. Genesis 5:29 does exactly that in Hebrew.

Noach, the name, is generally traced to the root nuach, to rest or settle. Lamech's explanation uses yenachamenu, from nacham, to comfort or console, a related-sounding but distinct root, the same one behind chapter 6's statement that God was grieved, nacham, that He had made man. The name-explanation is a paronomasia, a sound-play, not a strict derivation, the same kind of move Genesis 2:23 makes with ish and ishah.

English comfort and rest share no sound at all, so an English reader has no way to hear that Lamech's explanation is a near-miss pun rather than a precise etymology. The Hebrew wordplay, closely related consonants doing double duty, is simply gone once translated.

When a biblical name's stated explanation does not use the exact same root as the name, check whether the text is punning on sound rather than reporting derivation. Hebrew narrators do this regularly, and it is not an error to be corrected but a literary device to be noticed.

Both comfort and Noah are rendered correctly in every version; neither word is contested. The point is that the verse's own logic, why this name, works by resemblance rather than by strict etymology, which is exactly the kind of connection English translation cannot preserve.

versions.s: Mind. Understanding and the faculty that does it, in one noun.

b.t: Every version reads mind or understanding.
**Use your head.** **He has a good head on him.** English does this with a body part; Greek does it with an abstract noun.
Nous is the reasoning faculty and also the outlook it produces. It is the root of metanoia, and dianoia at Mark 12:30 is from the same family.
English mind covers the faculty but not the settled outlook, so renewal of the nous sounds like a mental exercise rather than a reorientation.
Words sharing a root across a writer's vocabulary usually belong in the same study. Follow the root rather than the single word.
Mind is the majority rendering throughout.

versions.s: A fugitive and a vagabond. Cain then dwells in the land of Nod, wandering, the same word as his curse.

b.t: Every version reads fugitive and vagabond for the curse and Nod as a place name later, treating them as unrelated: one a description, the other a proper noun that needs no translation.

Imagine a court sentencing someone to **a life of drifting**, and the judgment records afterward that he settled in the town of **Driftwood**. English readers would catch that instantly. Hebrew does the same thing here, and English naming conventions hide it completely.

Na vanad, restless wanderer, uses forms of the roots nua and nud, both meaning to shake, stagger, or wander. Four verses later Cain settles in the land of Nod, built on the same root nud. The place name is not incidental geography; it is the curse turned into an address, Cain settling, ironically, in the land called Wandering.

English transliterates Nod as a bare place name with no built-in meaning, exactly as it does with Eve, so nothing in an English Bible tips a reader off that it repeats the very word used to curse Cain four verses earlier. The pun that closes the episode is invisible without the Hebrew.

When a narrative names a place immediately after using an unusual word, check whether the name is built on that word. Hebrew narrators regularly turn a scene's vocabulary into its geography, and translation strips the connection out by default.

Every version agrees on fugitive and vagabond, and on transliterating Nod as a bare name; nothing there is in dispute. The pun connecting them is simply lost to transliteration, which is how English necessarily treats a proper noun, whatever meaning that noun is carrying in the original.

entries.title: nun
entries.def: to resprout, i.e. propagate by shoots; figuratively, to be perpetual

versions.s: His name shall be continued as long as the sun. Yinnon, a word used only here, read by Jewish tradition as one of the Messiah's own names.

b.t: Every version reads shall be continued, endure, or flourish, treating yinnon as an ordinary Hebrew verb, correctly by the plain grammar, though without capturing the tradition that reads it as a proper name.

Imagine a phrase, his name shall endure, where one Hebrew word for endure occurs nowhere else in the whole Bible, rare enough that later readers began treating it not as an ordinary verb but as a proper name in its own right, Yinnon, a title for a future king to come. English continued keeps the ordinary verb sense and loses the name entirely.

Yinnon, related to a root meaning to sprout, flourish, or continue, is a hapax, its only appearance anywhere in the Hebrew Bible. The Babylonian Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin 98b, records the tradition that Yinnon is one of the Messiah's names, reading the phrase not as his name shall endure but as before the sun, his name is Yinnon, treating the rare word as a title rather than a verb, and connecting it to the wider cluster of sprouting and branch vocabulary associated with messianic expectation.

English continued or endure smooths yinnon into an ordinary predicate, erasing the possibility, taken seriously in the Talmud, that the word functions as an actual name being assigned to a future king, a reading no single-word English translation of a verb can preserve.

When a word is a hapax legomenon and later interpretive tradition treats it as a proper name rather than an ordinary word, take that tradition seriously as evidence of how ancient readers themselves heard the rare word, not merely as a curiosity.

Reading yinnon as an ordinary verb, shall be continued or shall endure, matches standard grammatical analysis and is what every translation prints. Reading it as the proper name Yinnon, following the Talmudic tradition, treats this hapax legomenon as a genuine messianic title embedded in an otherwise royal psalm.
יִנּוֹן Yinnon (נוּן nun/נִין nin, sprout/continue) · H5125

src: Only occurrence in the Hebrew Bible: Psalm 72:17

versions.s: From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God. Olam is built on a root meaning hidden, naming indefinite time rather than philosophical eternity.

b.t: Every version reads everlasting or eternity, correctly conveying the sense of vast duration, though importing centuries of philosophical precision the Hebrew word's own root, hiddenness, does not specifically supply.

English everlasting and eternity name an abstract philosophical category, time without beginning or end, argued about by theologians and philosophers. Hebrew olam is more concrete: time so far back, or so far forward, that it disappears from view, hidden beyond what anyone can trace, a spatial metaphor for duration rather than a formal metaphysical claim.

Olam derives from a root associated with concealment or the vanishing point, the place where something passes out of sight, and by extension names time so extended it cannot be traced to its origin or end, whether looking backward or forward. Me'olam ad olam, from olam to olam, expresses the same idea by doubling the word in both directions rather than by asserting a formal doctrine of timelessness.

English everlasting and eternity carry the weight of later philosophical and theological precision about timelessness; Hebrew olam's own etymology points instead toward duration too vast or too hidden to trace, a related but not identical idea, closer to beyond memory or beyond sight than to a formal metaphysical claim about existing outside time altogether.

When translating time-vocabulary from Hebrew, check whether the English word imports later philosophical categories, timelessness, eternity as a formal metaphysical state, that the Hebrew root itself, often built on very concrete physical images, does not specifically require.

Everlasting or eternity are the natural, traditional English renderings and are not wrong, since the psalm is certainly making a claim about God's duration exceeding any human measure. What is worth keeping in view is that olam's own root sense, hidden or vanishing from sight, pictures indefinite, untraceable duration rather than formally asserting timelessness as a philosophical category.
עוֹלָם olam (מֵעוֹלָם עַד־עוֹלָם me'olam ad olam) · H5769

src: olam's root sense of hidden/concealed: standard Hebrew lexicons
olam also meaning world/age, reflecting the same indefinite-duration sense: Ecclesiastes 3:11

versions.s: A long duration, an age, the far horizon. Usually flattened to forever.

b.t: Versions read forever, everlasting, ancient, or of old.
**That will take forever.** You do not mean infinity. English already uses its eternity word for a long unspecified stretch.
Olam covers the distant past and the distant future, whatever lies beyond the horizon of view. It is used of a slave serving his master olam, which is plainly a lifetime, and of God's covenant.
English forever means unending, so a word about an unseen horizon becomes a claim about infinity.
When a word is rendered both ancient and everlasting in the same Bible, it is about distance in either direction rather than about duration without end.
Forever and everlasting are the majority renderings; ancient and of old appear where the past is in view.
עוֹלָם olam · H5769

src: olam of a lifetime: Exodus 21:6; 1 Samuel 1:22
olam of the distant past: Genesis 6:4; Isaiah 63:9
olam of God's covenant: Genesis 17:7

versions.s: Light. The first thing spoken into existence, and a standing image for life and favour.

b.t: Every version reads light.
**He saw the light.** **Her face lit up.** English uses light for understanding and for favour without any effort.
Or is physical light and also a standing image for life, guidance and divine favour. The face shining on someone in the Aaronic blessing is the same field.
English carries the same metaphors, so almost nothing is lost here.
Not every word is a problem. Some cross into English cleanly, and knowing which ones lets you spend attention on the ones that do not.
Light is universal.

versions.s: A coat of many colours. Modern scholarship increasingly favors a long-sleeved robe, not a rainbow garment.

b.t: The King James reads coat of many colours, following the Septuagint and Vulgate's variegated. Modern versions increasingly read a long robe with sleeves or an ornamented robe, following medieval and modern Hebraists who connect passim to pas, the palm of the hand or sole of the foot, suggesting a garment reaching to the hands and feet rather than one displaying colors.

Picture a phrase translators have guessed at for two thousand years without ever finding a second example to confirm the guess. That is ketonet passim. The colorful coat is a famous, beloved image; it may also simply be wrong.

Passim occurs in this exact phrase only twice in the Hebrew Bible, here and at 2 Samuel 13:18-19 describing the royal garment worn by unmarried princesses, including Tamar, before her own assault. Neither occurrence confirms colors; the connection to pas, palm or sole, suggests a garment with long sleeves and a long hem, marking its wearer as someone who does not do manual labor, a mark of privileged status rather than a rainbow of dyed cloth.

English many colours is vivid, specific, and has anchored centuries of art and storytelling, but the Hebrew phrase behind it is genuinely uncertain, and the strongest linguistic evidence, its only other biblical occurrence describing royal children's clothing, points toward a long, sleeved, privileged garment rather than a colorful one.

A translation tradition this old and this beloved can still rest on a guess. Before trusting a famous image, check whether the Hebrew phrase behind it has a confirmed meaning or only an inherited one, especially when the word recurs elsewhere in a context that points a different direction.

Coat of many colours preserves the image nearly every reader already carries and is not disprovable outright. A long robe with sleeves better fits the word's only other biblical occurrence and its likely connection to pas, and shifts the story's point from bright dye to Joseph being marked as exempt from a laborer's life, a distinction his brothers, who did that labor, would have resented just as sharply.
כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים ketonet passim · H3801 + H6446

src: The only other occurrence, describing royal children's clothing: 2 Samuel 13:18-19
Proposed connection to pas, palm/sole, suggesting long sleeves and hem: Rabbi David Kimhi and modern lexicons
Septuagint poikilos, variegated, behind the Vulgate and King James rendering

versions.s: A mighty hunter before the LORD. Renowned in God's sight, or in open defiance of Him.

b.t: Most English versions read before the LORD without further comment, letting the ambiguity stand. The Septuagint's Greek, enantion, is the same neutral before-God's-presence wording used elsewhere for this construction; the harsher, defiant sense comes later, from rabbinic tradition rather than from the earliest translators.

English **before** can mean **in front of, watched by**, as in a performance before an audience, or it can mean **in defiance of**, as in standing before a judge and refusing to yield. Hebrew's lifney carries the same double life, and this verse never tells you which one is meant.

Lifney, literally to the face of, ordinarily means in the presence of or in the sight of, but can also carry a confrontational sense, standing in defiance to someone's face. Jewish tradition going back to early rabbinic sources reads Nimrod negatively, a tyrant hunting men rather than game and provoking God openly, while the plain sense of the Hebrew by itself supports the more neutral reading, a renowned figure whose fame was plain for all, including God, to see.

English before does carry both senses too, in front of an audience or in defiance of an authority, but English readers default to the neutral sense here because the surrounding phrase, mighty hunter, sounds like an honorific rather than an accusation, a bias the bare Hebrew preposition does not itself supply.

A small preposition can carry a genuinely double range, and later interpretive tradition, here the negative reading of Nimrod, can fill a gap the grammar itself leaves open rather than resolving it. Check whether a confident interpretation is coming from the Hebrew word or from a tradition built around it.

Before the LORD, read neutrally, portrays a legendary figure whose renown God Himself would notice. The negative rabbinic tradition instead reads Nimrod as an early type of the tyrant who founded Babel two verses later, a reading the immediate context, his kingdom beginning at Babel, genuinely supports even though the preposition alone does not force it.
לִפְנֵי lifney (פָּנִים panim, face) · H6440

src: Standard Septuagint text and translations (e.g. Brenton) render the phrase 'before the Lord,' the same neutral wording as the Hebrew, not 'against'
Rabbinic tradition (e.g. reflected in later midrash) reading Nimrod as a tyrant and rebel
Nimrod's kingdom beginning at Babel: Genesis 10:10

versions.s: Face, presence. Plural in form, and used of God constantly.

b.t: Versions read face, presence, or before according to the preposition it sits in.
**Scissors.** **Trousers.** English has plural nouns for single objects and nobody notices. Hebrew does it with face.
Panim is plural in form throughout. It means face, and by extension presence, and it forms a large family of prepositions: before, in front of, because of. My presence shall go with thee is my face.
English separates face and presence, so a request to see God's face reads differently from a request for his presence, when they are one noun.
Hebrew builds many of its prepositions out of body parts. Knowing the noun underneath explains the preposition.
Face and presence are both majority renderings in their own contexts.
פָּנִים panim · H6440

src: panim as presence: Exodus 33:14-15
the bread of the presence, literally bread of the face: Exodus 25:30

versions.s: The glory which I had with thee before the world was. Glory again, and para with the dative.

b.t: Every version reads with thee or in your presence.
**He had it with him.** Alongside, in company. Not sent from a distance.
Para with the dative means beside, in the presence of. The same relational placement as pros ton theon at John 1:1, and the pairing of that verse with this one is the frame of the whole Gospel.
English with is flat enough to carry it, but the deliberate echo of the prologue is not visible.
When a Gospel's last discourse uses the vocabulary of its opening, the echo is structural. Look for the prologue in the prayer.
With you is the majority rendering.
παρά para · G3844

versions.s: Manasseh, for God hath made me forget; Ephraim, for God hath caused me to be fruitful. Two more names built from the naming sentence itself.

b.t: Every version reads Manasseh and Ephraim as bare transliterated names, with Joseph's explanatory statements translated separately and accurately, but without connecting either name back to its own root the way the Hebrew explicitly does.

By now the pattern should look familiar: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and now Manasseh and Ephraim, thirteen names in a row each built as a pun on the parent's own explanatory sentence. English transliteration keeps none of the wordplay, in Canaan or, as here, in Egypt.

Menashsheh echoes nashah, to forget, from Joseph's own words, God hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house. Ephraim echoes parah, to be fruitful, from for God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. Both names complete the pattern established across every one of Jacob's own sons' births, now applied one generation later, to children born not in Canaan but in Egypt, under Joseph's Egyptian name and Egyptian wife.

English Manasseh and Ephraim are bare proper nouns; the sentences explaining them read as separate commentary rather than as the linguistic source the names were extracted from, so the pattern completing itself one generation later, in a foreign land, is invisible without the Hebrew roots.

Continue tracking the birth-naming-pun device established across Genesis 29-30 all the way through the Joseph narrative. The device does not stop with Jacob's own sons; it continues into the next generation, even after the family relocates to Egypt.

Neither name nor its accompanying explanation is in dispute in any version. This entry rounds out the pattern already established for the rest of the twelve tribes' names, showing it persists one generation further, into Joseph's own Egyptian-born sons.
מְנַשֶּׁה Menashsheh (נָשָׁה nashah, forget) / אֶפְרַיִם Ephraim (פָּרָה parah, fruitful) · H4519 / H5382 / H669 / H6509

src: The same naming-pun pattern across all twelve tribal names: Genesis 29:32-30:24; 35:18

versions.s: Comforter, Helper, Advocate, Counselor, Paraclete. Six versions, six words, one Greek noun nobody can carry.

b.t: King James reads Comforter. The ESV and NASB read Helper. The NIV reads Advocate. The NRSV reads Advocate. Older Catholic versions keep Paraclete untranslated, which is the honest surrender.

**Bring me another chair.** Do you mean one more of these chairs, or a different sort of chair entirely? English uses one word for both and lets you work it out. Greek has two, and the speaker has to pick before the sentence leaves his mouth.

Two things at once. Parakletos is built from para, alongside, and kaleo, to call: one called alongside. In ordinary Greek it was close to a legal supporter, someone who stands with you in a proceeding, which is why Advocate keeps turning up. And the adjective is allos, another of the same kind, rather than heteros, another of a different kind. Jesus is not promising a substitute of a different sort. He is promising another like himself.

English has no noun that covers legal advocate, personal encourager and one who is summoned to stand beside you. Every version picks the shade it thinks matters most and loses the other two. And English lost the distinction between the two kinds of another somewhere in its history, so the adjective disappears entirely.
When translations scatter this widely on one noun, stop looking for the right English word. There is not one. Learn what the Greek noun covers and read all the renderings as partial views of it.

Comforter was accurate when comfort meant to strengthen, from the same root as fortify, and it has since drifted to consolation. Helper is broad enough to be safe and vague enough to be weak. Advocate captures the legal sense and drops the personal one. Paraclete admits defeat and makes the reader look it up, which is arguably the most honest of the four.
παράκλητος parakletos · G3875

src: allos against heteros: compare Galatians 1:6-7, where Paul uses both in two verses to make exactly this distinction
The same noun at John 14:26; 15:26; 16:7; and of Christ himself at 1 John 2:1, where most versions read Advocate

versions.s: He hath made me a father to Pharaoh. An Egyptian administrative title, not a family claim.

b.t: Every version reads father to Pharaoh, accurately translating the Hebrew, but without noting that the phrase names a known ancient Egyptian court title rather than describing an actual family relationship.

English father names a family role. A modern equivalent to this ancient title might be something like chief advisor, or elder statesman, an honorific for a senior official's wisdom and standing, not a literal parental claim, the way a company might informally call a longtime advisor its godfather without meaning it genealogically.

Egyptian inscriptions independently attest father of the god, it-netjer, as a title held by senior advisors and officials serving a pharaoh, unrelated to blood kinship and instead marking someone as a trusted source of wisdom and counsel, paired here with lord of all his household and ruler over all the land of Egypt, both concrete administrative claims matching the historically attested role of a vizier.

English father, standing alone, suggests literal parentage or, at best, a vague honorific; it does not carry the specific, documented administrative weight the Egyptian title held, so a reader unfamiliar with Egyptian court titulature can miss that Joseph is describing a specific, historically real office rather than a sentimental relationship.

When a biblical figure describes a foreign court position using a kinship word, father, brother, son, check whether the surrounding culture used that vocabulary as an administrative title before reading it as a literal family claim.

Father to Pharaoh is an accurate rendering of the Hebrew, and no version disputes that. What it needs is the extrabiblical Egyptian background confirming this was a real administrative title, which strengthens rather than merely illustrates the account's claim that Joseph held genuine high office.

versions.s: God shall enlarge Japheth. The verb for enlarge sounds like the name Japheth itself.

b.t: Every version reads may God enlarge Japheth, or a similar rendering, correctly translating the sense but unable to show that enlarge is chosen partly because of how it sounds next to the name it is blessing.

Imagine blessing a son named **Wade** by saying, **may he wade into wide waters**. The blessing works because it echoes the name, not because it is a technical description of what will literally happen. Hebrew does exactly this with Japheth and the verb for enlarge.

Yapht, may he enlarge, and Yephet, Japheth, share the same consonants differently arranged and pointed, a close enough match that most readers take it as deliberate wordplay rather than coincidence, though the connection is not a strict linguistic derivation and a minority of scholars propose other etymologies for the name itself. The verb's root, pathah, to make wide or open, gives the blessing its content, spreading out, territory, breadth, while its sound ties the blessing directly back to the son's own name.

English enlarge and the name Japheth share no sound at all, so an English reader hears a blessing with content but no wordplay, missing the same naming technique Genesis has already used for Cain at 4:1, Noah at 5:29, and the ish/ishah pun at 2:23.

When a blessing or judgment is pronounced over a named character, check whether the key verb echoes the name itself. Genesis returns to this device repeatedly, and each occurrence rewards the same kind of listening for sound, not just sense.

Enlarge is the uncontested sense of the verb in every version. The wordplay connecting it to Japheth's name is widely recognized but, like the Noah/nacham pun three chapters earlier, not a strict etymology, just a close and probably deliberate resemblance the story is using.
יַפְתְּ yapht (פָּתָה pathah, to make wide) / יֶפֶת Yephet · H6601 / H3315

src: The yapht/Yephet wordplay: standard treatment in Genesis commentaries on the Table of Nations blessing
The same naming-wordplay pattern at Genesis 4:1, 5:29, and 2:23

versions.s: In his days was the earth divided. His name, Peleg, means division.

b.t: Every version reads Peleg as a name and divided as a separate statement, correctly, but with no way to show an English reader that the name itself is the Hebrew word for divided.

Imagine a chronicle naming a child **Splitter** the same year a kingdom splits in two, and stating outright that the timing is the point. Genesis does this routinely, and English transliteration, Peleg as a bare name, hides the built-in explanation every time.

Peleg is built directly on the verb palag, to divide or split, the same root behind the noun for a water channel or stream at Psalm 1:3 and Job 38:25, and behind the request confuse, divide their tongues at Psalm 55:9, itself a probable echo of the Babel story two verses later in Genesis. What exactly divided in Peleg's days, the population by language at Babel, or a more literal geological or geographic division, is debated, but the naming device itself is the same one Genesis has already used three times before this chapter.

English Peleg is a bare proper name carrying no built-in meaning, so the sentence in his days was the earth divided reads as a coincidence of timing rather than as the name itself supplying the explanation, which is how the Hebrew presents it.

When Genesis names a person immediately before or after describing a major event, assume the name is doing explanatory work until proven otherwise; this book uses that device more often than any other in the Hebrew Bible.

Every version simply transliterates Peleg as a name, with no dispute about that. What exactly was divided, languages at Babel or something more literal and geographic, is a separate and genuinely open question the naming pun itself does not settle.
פֶּלֶג Peleg (פָּלַג palag, to divide) · H6389

src: palag as divide, used of water channels: Psalm 1:3; Job 38:25
The same root requested of God at Psalm 55:9, 'confuse, divide their tongues,' likely echoing Babel

versions.s: Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: for I have seen God face to face.

b.t: Every version reads Peniel or Penuel as a bare place name, with the explanation translated separately, correctly conveying both halves without showing that the name is built directly from the words explaining it.

Imagine naming the exact spot of a life-changing encounter **Eye-to-Eye**, using the literal words for what just happened as the place's permanent name. That is exactly what Peniel, face of God, does, and English transliteration keeps the name while dropping the sentence it was built from.

Peniel, panim, face, plus el, God, is coined on the spot from Jacob's own statement, ra'iti elohim panim el panim, I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved, the same construction, name built from the explaining sentence's own words, already used repeatedly for people's names across Genesis and now applied to a place.

English Peniel is a bare transliterated place name; the explanatory sentence beside it reads as ordinary narration rather than as the source material the name was extracted from, so the tight, immediate link between event and place name is not visible without the Hebrew.

Genesis names both people and places by exactly this method, extracting the place or person's name directly from the sentence used to explain them. Once you notice the pattern for people's names, watch for the identical device applied to geography.

Peniel and its explanation are both translated accurately by every version. What none of them can show is that the place name itself is built from the explaining sentence, a structural feature of the Hebrew that transliteration and separate translation both obscure.
פְּנִיאֵל Peniel (פָּנִים panim, face + אֵל el, God) · H6439

src: The same naming-from-explanation device used for people: Genesis 4:1, 5:29, 25:26, 29:32-30:24

versions.s: He will be a wild man. The Hebrew literally reads a wild-donkey of a man, animal first.

b.t: Every version reads wild man, wild donkey of a man, or similar, generally preserving the sense but not always flagging the unusual word order that puts the animal image first.

English **a wild man** puts man first and wild as a description. Hebrew here reverses that: pere adam is closer to **a wild-donkey, a human one**, animal noun first, human noun second, the reverse of the ordinary Hebrew word order where the describing word comes after the noun it describes.

Pere, wild donkey, stands before adam, man, reversing the normal Hebrew pattern where a modifying word follows its noun; the expected order would put man first and wild donkey as the descriptor. Instead the wild donkey, an animal proverbial in the ancient Near East for fierce independence, untamed freedom, and life beyond settled territory, is named first, making it the dominant image and man almost an afterthought clarifying which kind of creature is meant.

English word order cannot easily reproduce this reversal without sounding broken; a wild-donkey man puts the animal first the way the Hebrew does but reads as odd English, so translators default to the more natural wild man, losing the emphasis the unusual Hebrew order creates.

When a Hebrew phrase's word order runs backward from what the grammar normally expects, that reversal is itself doing rhetorical work, foregrounding whichever word was moved to the front. Do not read past unusual word order as a translator's stylistic accident.

Wild man keeps a natural English sentence but loses the foregrounded animal image. Wild donkey of a man, closer to the Hebrew word order, keeps the emphasis but reads awkwardly in English, the standard tradeoff between literal word order and natural target-language phrasing.
פֶּרֶא אָדָם pere adam · H6501 + H120

src: pere as the untamed wild donkey, proverbial for wildness elsewhere: Job 39:5-8

versions.s: Transgression. A relational breach, closer to rebellion than to a slip.

b.t: Versions read transgression or rebellion.
**He broke with them.** That is not a mistake. It is a decision about a relationship.
Pesha is used of political revolt as well as of sin against God, which is what fixes its flavour. Where chatta't is failure and avon is crookedness, pesha is deliberate breach.
English transgression sounds like crossing a line in a rulebook rather than breaking with a person.
Where a language has three words for one English idea, the three are a set. Learn them together or you will flatten all three.
Transgression is the majority rendering; rebellion appears where the political sense is clear.

versions.s: She sat in an open place. The Hebrew could be a place name, Enaim, or literally the opening of the eyes.

b.t: The King James reads in an open place, treating the phrase as a description. Other versions, ancient and modern, read it as the place name Enaim, following Joshua 15:34's mention of a town by that name in the same region.

English **open place** reads as a simple description of visibility. The underlying Hebrear could instead be naming an actual town, or could be building a scene where a woman positions herself to be seen at exactly the place named eyes, a difference between plain geography and deliberate staging.

Petach eynayim, most literally opening of the eyes, or the entrance to Eynayim, sits at a genuine crossroads of interpretation: eynayim, eyes, is also plausibly the name of a real town (Joshua 15:34 names Eynayim in the same district), so the phrase could simply mean at the entrance to Eynayim, a geographic marker, or it could be functioning idiomatically, describing a conspicuous, visible spot where Tamar deliberately positions herself to be noticed, playing on the literal sense of eyes even if the place also had that name.

English open place picks the idiomatic, staging-focused reading and loses any sense that a real place name might be doing double duty; a straightforward place-name translation, Enaim, loses the wordplay on eyes and visibility that a scene built around deception and seeing so pointedly seems to want.

When a place name in Hebrew is also a meaningful common word, consider that the narrator may be using it for both functions at once, real geography and pointed wordplay, rather than choosing between them.

Reading it as a real place name, Enaim, keeps the scene concretely located. Reading it idiomatically, the opening of the eyes, or a visible crossroads, keeps the wordplay alive in a story centrally about who sees and who is deceived. Both readings may be simultaneously true, which no single English rendering can hold at once.
פֶּתַח עֵינַיִם Petach Eynayim · H6607 + H5879

versions.s: Both love-words, one chapter, the same relationship. Whatever they are doing, they are not ranking it.

b.t: No English version distinguishes them, and almost no study Bible notes that both appear here.

If someone calls the same person **my mate** in one sentence and **my friend** two sentences later, you do not conclude the friendship got upgraded. Same thing here, except a lot of sermons draw exactly that conclusion.

Verse 3 uses phileo, on the sisters' lips. Verse 5 uses agapao, in the narrator's voice, about the same three people. Verse 36 uses phileo again, on the crowd's lips. One relationship, one chapter, both verbs.
English merges the two, so an English reader cannot see the alternation at all, and therefore cannot see that it does not line up with any hierarchy.
Before accepting that two words rank each other, find a passage where both are used of the same thing. If the ranking survives that, it is real. Here it does not.

There is no dispute in the text. The dispute is in the pulpit, and this chapter is the cleanest evidence against the claim that agapao is the higher love and phileo the lesser one. It is the same evidence that John 21 supplies, in a different book of the same Gospel.
φιλέω phileo · G5368 / ἀγαπάω agapao · G25

src: John 11:3 phileis; 11:5 egapa; 11:36 ephilei
D. A. Carson, Exegetical Fallacies, on the agapao/phileo distinction

versions.s: Two different Greek words for love, and the sermon you have heard about them is probably overselling it.

b.t: No English version distinguishes the two verbs, because English has one word. Study Bibles and pulpits supply the distinction instead.

**He sipped his coffee, then he drank his tea.** Did the writer mean something by sip against drink, or was he just avoiding saying drink twice? Good writers vary words for the sound of it. Before you build anything on a word change, check whether the writer changed other words in the same breath.

Jesus asks twice using agapao and once using phileo. Peter answers all three times with phileo. The standard sermon builds a hierarchy out of this, with agapao as the higher divine love and phileo as mere friendship.
English has one verb where Greek has several, so the variation vanishes. That is a real loss. The question is whether anything was in it.
Before building a doctrine on a word change, check whether the writer varies other words in the same passage. John does, four times over in these three verses, and nobody preaches on those.

John also swaps two words for sheep, two for know, and two for feed and tend in the same exchange. None of those carry theological weight, which makes it hard to argue that one of the five variations is loaded and the other four are style. The honest verdict is that the distinction is probably stylistic, that the Septuagint and Koine use the two verbs largely interchangeably, and that this entry exists to show you what a divergence looks like when it turns out not to matter.
ἀγαπάω agapao · G25 / φιλέω phileo · G5368

src: D. A. Carson, Exegetical Fallacies, on the agapao/phileo distinction as a standard word-study fallacy
Carson, The Gospel According to John (PNTC), at 21:15-17
The parallel variations in the same passage: arnia/probata, oida/ginosko, bosko/poimaino

versions.s: Four Greek words for love, and two of them never appear in the New Testament.

b.t: No English version can show any of this. English has one word, and it is doing the work of four.

English has one word for uncle. Your mother's brother and your father's brother get the same label. Plenty of languages split those, and speakers of those languages find it strange that you do not. Greek splits love the way those languages split uncle. English does not, and the split is invisible to you until someone points at it.

The four-loves scheme is real Greek vocabulary, but it is not a New Testament vocabulary set. It is C. S. Lewis's framework from The Four Loves, published in 1960, built out of classical Greek. Eros does not occur in the New Testament at all. Storge never occurs as a standalone noun or verb; it survives only inside two compounds, astorgos in Romans 1:31 and 2 Timothy 3:3, and philostorgos in Romans 12:10. That leaves philia and agape doing nearly all the work.

English has one noun and one verb for all of it. A language with four words can distinguish the love you did not choose from the love you did, and the love that wants from the love that stays, without ever explaining itself. English has to explain itself every time, or leave it ambiguous.

Learn the four as four verbs, not four nouns. Born into, picked, reaches, stays. Then hold them loosely, because two of them are not in your New Testament and the other two overlap more than the sermons admit.

Nothing to choose, because no translator has the option. The thing worth noticing is what the absences say. A body of literature that never once uses the word for desire, and only ever names family affection by its absence, is not a body of literature indifferent to either. It has simply put its weight somewhere else. The word it reaches for when it commands a husband to love his wife is not eros. It is agape.

versions.s: Two Greek words for love welded into one, and English has to pick a phrase.

b.t: Modern versions read be devoted to one another in brotherly love, or love one another with brotherly affection.
English glues words together too. **Homesick** is not a home and a sickness, it is one idea that needed two words to build. When you meet a glued word, take it apart and ask why those two.

Kindly affectioned is philostorgos, a compound of philos and storge. Brotherly love is philadelphia. The verse stacks the love you pick on top of the love you are born into and tells a congregation to treat each other as both.

English has no compound for this and no word for storge at all, so every version has to build a phrase. Kindly affectioned, devoted, affection: all of them are attempts to say family-feeling-toward-people-you-chose in words English does not have.
Compound words are where a language shows you what it thinks goes together. When your translation reaches for a two-word phrase and a footnote, check whether the Greek was one word.
Nothing textual is in question. The renderings differ in how much of the family sense they try to carry, and devoted carries the least of it.

entries.title: phragellion
entries.def: a whip, i.e. Roman lash as a public punishment

versions.s: A scourge of small cords. The noun occurs once in the New Testament and is a Latin word in Greek dress.

b.t: Versions read whip or scourge of cords.
English is full of borrowed words you never notice. **Restaurant**, **algebra**, **ketchup**. A borrowed word is a fingerprint of contact between two cultures.
Phragellion is the Greek spelling of Latin flagellum. It occurs only here in the New Testament. The related verb appears at Matthew 27:26 and Mark 15:15 of the scourging.
English doesn't lose anything here. The point is what the loan word shows about a Greek text written inside a Roman world.
Loan words in a text date and place it. They are evidence about the writer's setting rather than about his meaning.
Whip is what most modern versions print; the King James reads scourge.

versions.s: The head stone of the corner. Either the foundation stone set first, or the capstone set last at the very top.

b.t: Most versions read cornerstone, assuming the foundational sense. Some scholars argue for capstone or keystone instead, the crowning stone rather than the base, and note that the Greek phrase quoted in the New Testament, kephale gonias, head of the corner, preserves the same ambiguity rather than resolving it.

English cornerstone today usually suggests a foundation, the first stone laid, everything built outward from it. But rosh, head, can just as naturally suggest the topmost position, a capstone or keystone placed last to complete an arch or wall. The Hebrew phrase does not clearly specify which end of the building process is meant.

Rosh pinnah, head of the corner, could describe either the first stone set at a building's foundation, establishing the entire structure's alignment, or the final stone set at the top of an arch or wall, completing rather than beginning the construction. Both are attested architectural uses of similar terminology, and scholars including R.T. France and Ulrich Luz have argued that Matthew's own quotation of this verse deliberately keeps both images alive rather than committing to one.

English cornerstone has settled almost entirely into the foundational sense in modern usage, a building's first and most important stone; readers rarely consider that the Hebrew, and the Greek that quotes it in the New Testament, may instead or additionally be picturing a capstone crowning a structure already built, a different and arguably more dramatic image of exaltation after rejection.

When an architectural metaphor is quoted repeatedly across Scripture, check whether the underlying term specifies which part of the building process is meant before assuming the modern default sense. Ancient building vocabulary did not always map onto modern architectural categories the way translation can imply.

Cornerstone, the foundational reading, pictures the rejected stone becoming the very basis the whole structure depends on from the ground up. Capstone or keystone, the completion reading, pictures the rejected stone becoming the final, crowning piece that finishes and holds together a structure already otherwise built, arguably a more dramatic reversal from rejection to climactic honor.
רֹאשׁ פִּנָּה rosh pinnah · H7218 + H6438

src: Septuagint's kephale gonias preserving the same ambiguity
Matthew 21:42, Acts 4:11, and 1 Peter 2:7 all quoting this verse
R.T. France and Ulrich Luz on the deliberate double reading in Matthew's use

versions.s: Many believed. And Jesus did not believe them. The same verb, twice, deliberately.

b.t: Versions read believed in the first clause and entrust or commit himself in the second.
**They trusted him, and he did not trust them.** Say it with one verb and it lands. Say it with trust and entrust and it reads as two unrelated facts.
Pisteuo appears in verse 23 of the crowd believing and in verse 24 of Jesus not entrusting himself to them. It is the same verb in both, and John is playing one against the other.
There's no single English verb that works both for believing in someone and for entrusting yourself to them, so every version breaks the pair.
When a paragraph reads as two disconnected statements, check whether one verb is doing both. John does this constantly.
Entrust is the majority rendering for the second occurrence; the King James reads commit himself.

versions.s: To believe. In Greek that is closer to entrusting yourself than to agreeing with a claim.

b.t: Every English version reads believe. A few render trust in places where believe would sound too thin.
**I believe the bridge will hold.** **I believe the bridge will hold, so I drove across it.** Only the second sentence is what the Greek verb ordinarily describes.

Pisteuo is the verb from pistis, faith or faithfulness, and it regularly takes a preposition meaning into or upon rather than a plain object. Believing into someone is not an English construction and it is the one John uses constantly.
English believe has narrowed toward accepting a proposition. There is no English verb meaning to commit yourself to something you have judged reliable.
When a Greek verb takes an odd preposition, the preposition is carrying meaning English usually has to supply with extra words.
Believe is the majority rendering everywhere and no major version departs from it. Trust appears in some paraphrases and in footnotes.

versions.s: Ointment of spikenard, very costly. The adjective is a word nobody has settled.

b.t: Versions read pure nard, genuine nard, or expensive perfume made of pure nard.
A recipe with one ingredient nobody can identify. You can still cook it. You just cannot say what it was.
Pistikes qualifies the nard. Proposals include faithful hence genuine, from pistis; liquid, from a different root; a place of origin; and a trade term. All are guesses and the lexicons say so.
English has to print something, and pure is the usual guess with no marker that it is one.
When a lexicon entry lists four unrelated possibilities, the word is undetermined and your translation has quietly chosen one.
Pure nard is the majority modern rendering.

versions.s: Faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ. Greek does not say which.

b.t: Most versions read faith in Christ. The NET, CSB and NRSV all footnote or adopt the faithfulness of Christ. Notice that the King James reads faith of, which leaves the question open exactly the way the Greek does.

**The love of a mother.** Is that the love she gives, or the love you give her? Same four words, opposite directions, and English has no way to mark which. Now try **the fear of God** and notice you have been reading past this problem your whole life.

Pistis Christou is a noun followed by a noun in the genitive. Greek genitives can be objective, where Christ is the object of the faith, or subjective, where Christ is the one doing the believing or being faithful. The form is identical either way.

English prepositions force a choice. In and of point in opposite directions and there is no English preposition that leaves it hanging. The King James of is the closest English gets, which is why a four hundred year old translation preserves an ambiguity that modern versions resolve.

Whenever you see of in an older translation where a modern one says in or for, suspect a genitive. The Greek was joining two nouns and letting the reader work out the relationship. Modern English translations usually decide for you, and the decision is rarely flagged.

Faith in Christ makes the verse about the believer's trust. Faithfulness of Christ makes it about Christ's own obedience, with the believer's faith named separately in the next clause, which otherwise repeats itself. The redundancy argument is the strongest point for the subjective reading. The weight of tradition and of Paul's usage elsewhere is the strongest point for the objective one.
πίστις pistis · G4102

src: Richard B. Hays, The Faith of Jesus Christ (1983, 2nd ed. 2002), the case for the subjective genitive

versions.s: Be filled with the Spirit. The Greek is a command to keep being filled, continuously, and by someone else.

b.t: English versions all read be filled. Some study Bibles add a note about the present tense. No version can carry it in the text.

**Shut the door.** **Keep shutting the door.** English needs a helper word for the second one. Greek does it inside the verb, so a command can carry keep on in its own form. Every English rendering of this verse has to drop that or add words.

Plerousthe is present tense, passive voice, imperative mood, second person plural. Present tense in Greek is aspect rather than time: it presents the action as ongoing. Passive means the filling is done to you. Plural means it is addressed to a congregation, not to an individual.

English imperatives have no aspect. Be filled sounds like a single event you perform once. The Greek is nearer to keep on being filled, and English has no way to say that without adding words the original did not have.

Greek tense is mostly about aspect, not time. When a command feels like a one-time transaction in English, check whether the Greek is present, which frames it as a continuing state, or aorist, which frames it as a whole.

There is no disagreement about the parsing. The disagreement is whether to smuggle the aspect into the English, which makes the sentence heavier, or to leave it and lose it. Every version has chosen to lose it.

versions.s: The wind blows where it wills. Wind and Spirit are the same Greek word, and the sentence needs both at once.

b.t: Every version reads wind in the first half and Spirit in the second, because there is no alternative. A few footnote that the Greek is one word.

Suppose your language had one word for **a breeze** and **a person's inner life**. A sentence could slide from one to the other and land as a single thought. Translate it into English and you get two nouns and a jump.

Pneuma covers wind, breath and spirit. So does Hebrew ruach. Jesus is saying one thing about one word: it goes where it wants, you hear it, you cannot track it, and that is what being born of it is like. In Greek the comparison is a single image. In English it is a simile between two unrelated things.
English split what Greek and Hebrew both kept together, so a pun becomes an analogy and loses most of its force.
When a verse compares two things that share a word in the original, it is usually not a comparison at all. It is one word doing two jobs, and the translation has manufactured the gap.
No translator has an option. The only decision is whether to footnote it, and most do not.

versions.s: God is spirit. Same construction as the last clause of John 1:1, and here nobody reads it as a god.

b.t: The King James reads a Spirit. Every modern version reads God is spirit, with no article at all, which is the qualitative rendering.

**Sam is the doctor.** **Sam is a doctor.** **Sam is doctor.** The third one is not English, and it is what Greek does here. It says what God is by nature, not which spirit God is or that God is one of several.

Pneuma stands before the verb with no article, the same shape as theos in John 1:1c. Nobody proposes rendering it a god there and a spirit here, yet the King James did exactly that. Modern versions corrected it, which is the strongest available evidence for how the construction works.
English forces an article or a bare noun and the bare noun sounds ungrammatical in most sentences. Here it does not, which is why the fix was possible.

When you want to test a grammatical claim, find the same construction in a verse where nothing theological is at stake. If translators handle it one way there and another way in the contested verse, the difference is not grammar.
No modern version defends a Spirit. The King James rendering is the outlier, and correcting it is the same move that produces God was the Word rather than a god in chapter one.

versions.s: Spirit. The same noun means wind and breath, exactly like Hebrew ruach.

b.t: Versions read spirit, Spirit, wind or breath according to context. One Greek word behind all of them.
Imagine one word for **a breeze**, **a sigh** and **a person's inner life**. To a speaker of that language those are obviously the same thing. To you they are three drawers.

Pneuma covers wind, breath and spirit, human and divine. The Septuagint uses it for Hebrew ruach, and the ranges match closely enough that New Testament writers can build arguments across both languages.
English split the three and capitalises one of them, which is a decision no Greek manuscript ever made.
Capitalisation of Spirit in an English New Testament is an interpretive choice. The manuscripts have no capitals at all.
Spirit is the majority rendering; wind and breath appear where the context forces them.

versions.s: Feed my lambs, tend my sheep. Four words vary, not two.

b.t: No version distinguishes any of the pairs, because English has one word for each.
A writer who swaps four pairs of words in three sentences is avoiding repetition. A writer who swaps one is making a point.
Three pairs beyond the love verbs: bosko and poimaino for feed and tend, arnia and probata for lambs and sheep, oida and ginosko for know. All four variations run through the same exchange.
English has one word for each pair, so all four variations vanish and only the first is ever preached.
Before building on one word change, count the others in the same passage. Four is a style. One is an argument.
Feed and take care of are the majority renderings; no version marks any of the pairs.

versions.s: One fold, and one shepherd. The Greek uses two different nouns and the King James uses one.

b.t: The King James reads one fold. Every modern version reads one flock.
**One pen** and **one herd** are not the same claim. One is about the enclosure. The other is about the animals.

The first noun in the verse is aule, a fold or enclosure. The second is poimne, a flock. The Greek says other sheep not of this aule, and they shall become one poimne, one shepherd. The King James printed fold for both, following the Vulgate's ovile.
English has both words. The error is not in the language but in the 1611 rendering, which follows the Latin rather than the Greek.
Where the King James follows the Vulgate against the Greek, a real correction is available and the modern versions have made it.
One flock is what modern versions overwhelmingly print, and outside the King James tradition the correction is universal.

versions.s: The Word was with God. The preposition is not the one you would expect for with.

b.t: Every English version reads with. Some commentaries offer toward, or face to face with, and none of that reaches the text.

**I sat with my wife.** **I turned to my wife.** Both put two people together. Only the second one tells you which way anyone was facing. English with is a flat word. Greek had a choice here and picked the turned-toward one.

The preposition is pros with the accusative. Its ordinary sense is motion toward or orientation facing. Greek had meta and syn available for plain accompaniment, and John used neither. Pros with a person in the accusative carries a sense of being turned toward, in relationship with.
English with is flat. It covers standing next to someone and being in a relationship with them, and no English preposition carries orientation the way pros does.
When a writer picks an unusual preposition where a plain one was available, the preposition is part of the argument. Check which one was the obvious choice and ask why it was passed over.

With is not wrong and there is no better English. The question is only how much weight the preposition will carry, and commentators divide on whether pros here is genuinely relational or simply Koine usage drifting toward the accusative.
πρός pros · G4314

src: Pros with the accusative of person in relational sense: Mark 6:3; 1 Corinthians 16:6-7; Galatians 1:18
The alternatives John did not use: meta, syn, para
