versions.s: Soul. The same word is rendered life a few verses away, and it translates Hebrew nephesh.

b.t: Versions read soul or life depending on the verse, from one Greek word.
**Not a soul in sight.** You mean not a person. English still has the wider sense and only uses it in fixed phrases.

Psuche covers the animating life, the self, and the person. It is the Septuagint's word for Hebrew nephesh, which carries the same range and is used of animals. It is not a technical term for an immaterial part.
English soul carries a Greek philosophical and later Christian freight the biblical usage does not require, and life sounds too plain where soul sounds weighty.
When one word is rendered two ways in adjoining verses, read the passage with a single rendering throughout and see what changes.
Soul and life are both majority renderings in their own contexts, and every version switches between them.
ψυχή psuche · G5590

src: Matthew 16:25-26 uses psuche four times, rendered life then soul
psuche for nephesh throughout the Septuagint
Genesis 1:20-30 uses nephesh of animals

versions.s: Jacob's heart fainted. A rare verb some read as his heart simply stopped, not merely swooned.

b.t: Most versions read fainted, was stunned, or did not believe them, softer options for a word whose exact force is genuinely unclear given how rarely it occurs.

English fainted suggests a brief swoon, someone who recovers in a moment. If the stronger reading of the rare Hebrew verb is right, the sentence is closer to his heart stopped, a far more severe, almost fatal reaction to shocking news, before Jacob's spirit revives in the very next verse.

Vayafag, from the rare root pug, appears seldom enough in the Hebrew Bible that its precise force is debated; at Lamentations 2:18 the same root clearly means cease or stop, which has led some readers, including the medieval commentator Ibn Ezra, to render this verse in stronger terms than a simple faint, and Robert Alter's translation renders it 'his heart went numb' rather than the milder, more traditional fainted.

English fainted names a brief, recoverable swoon; if pug's stronger sense of ceasing or stopping is correct here, the verse is describing something closer to a genuine, momentary cardiac event, a considerably more severe reaction that softer English translations do not convey.

When a rare verb's few other occurrences point toward a stronger sense than the traditional English gloss suggests, weigh the stronger reading seriously rather than defaulting to whichever translation sounds most familiar. Familiarity is not evidence.

Fainted or was stunned keeps the traditional, milder reading and fits smoothly with Jacob's quick recovery the following verse. His heart stopped, following the word's clearer sense at Lamentations 2:18, reads the shock as considerably more severe, a nearly fatal jolt rather than a brief swoon.
וַיָּפָג vayafag (פּוּג pug) · H6313

src: pug clearly meaning cease/stop at Lamentations 2:18
Ibn Ezra's reading of this verse in light of that parallel
Robert Alter's translation, 'his heart went numb'

versions.s: Holy. Set apart for a purpose, before it is anything about moral purity.

b.t: Every version reads holy.
**The good china.** Not morally better china. Set aside for something.

Qadosh carries separation and otherness. The seventh day, the tabernacle furniture and the ground at the burning bush are all qadosh. The command to be holy is a command about belonging before it is about behaviour.
English holy implies attained goodness, which reverses the direction of the idea.
Status words become merit words very easily in English. Check whether the original describes a designation or an achievement.
Holy is universal.
קָדוֹשׁ qadosh · H6918

versions.s: I have gotten a man from the LORD. Or: a man, the LORD. The little word between them decides which.

b.t: Every English version reads from the LORD, with the LORD's help, or a similar rendering that treats et as the preposition with. None reads the more literal, and far stranger, a man, namely the LORD.

**I baked a cake, the winner.** Read that as an appositive and you just said the cake is the winner. Read the comma as separating two items and you said something else. Hebrew's et normally marks exactly the appositive-style reading, and that is the problem here.

Et is overwhelmingly the marker introducing a definite direct object, not a preposition meaning with. Read that way, qaniti ish et YHWH would mean I have gotten a man, the LORD, an equation most readers find unthinkable in Eve's mouth. Grammarians have proposed et functioning here as with the help of, but no clearly parallel case elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible confirms that use, which is why the question stays open rather than settled by grammar alone.

English with and English the marker of a direct object are different words doing different jobs, so a translator has to choose one before the sentence reaches an English reader. The ambiguity that makes Hebrew scholars argue about this verse cannot survive into English at all; the English sentence necessarily picks a side.

When a small grammatical word carries the whole weight of a verse's meaning, check whether its unusual reading here is attested anywhere else in the same corpus. An unparalleled use should be held more loosely than a common one, however theologically attractive it looks.

With the LORD's help is the reading every version prints, and it fits ordinary Hebrew usage of et poorly but fits the context comfortably. A man, the LORD, keeps the ordinary grammar but produces a claim nothing else in the passage supports. Both options have a real cost.
אֶת et (with קָנִיתִי qaniti, I have gotten) · H853 / H7069

src: Et as the standard direct-object marker: any standard Hebrew grammar (e.g. GKC, Joüon-Muraoka)
Dillmann's commentary on Genesis, noting no clearly parallel instrumental use of et elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible
Targum Onkelos and most premodern Jewish and Christian readings take the 'with the LORD's help' sense

versions.s: His life is bound up in the lad's life. Nephesh, the same word as living soul, used twice, bound together.

b.t: Every version reads his life is bound up in the lad's life, correctly, but the repetition of the same underlying Hebrew word, nephesh, for both father and son is smoothed into a single English word, life, used generically rather than as the loaded term it is throughout the rest of Genesis.

English keeps **life** fairly abstract, a general condition rather than a tangible thing you could tie to something. Hebrew nephesh is closer to a person's whole self or throat, concrete enough that describing two nephashot as bound, keshurah, together pictures an actual physical or emotional cord, not merely a sentiment.

Nafsho keshurah b'nafsho, his nephesh is bound in his nephesh, repeats the word already met as the breath of life at 2:7 and living soul throughout chapter 1, now applied twice in one clause to describe Jacob's and Benjamin's selves as tied together, not merely emotionally attached in the abstract sense English life suggests, but bound, a term elsewhere used of physical tying and knotting.

English life is a broad, somewhat abstract noun; nephesh carries a more concrete, almost tangible sense of self or living being throughout Genesis, so describing two nephashot as tied or bound together lands with more physical force in Hebrew than his life is bound up in his life does in ordinary English.

When nephesh recurs at an emotionally weighted moment late in a book, read it against its earlier, more concrete uses, breath, living soul, throat, appetite, rather than assuming it has quietly become the abstract English word life. The word's physical undertone rarely disappears.

Every version lands on the same basic sense, deep attachment. What's easy to lose is nephesh's more concrete, physical undertone, given how loaded the word has already become across chapters 1, 2, and 9 of the same book.
נֶפֶשׁ קְשׁוּרָה nephesh keshurah · H5315 + H7194

src: keshurah, bound or tied, used of physical binding elsewhere: e.g. Job 38:31
nephesh's earlier concrete range: Genesis 1:20-30; 2:7; 9:4

versions.s: Their line is gone out through all the earth. Paul quotes it in Romans 10:18 as their voice, or sound.

b.t: The Hebrew Masoretic Text reads their line, kav, has gone out. The Septuagint, and Paul quoting it at Romans 10:18, reads their voice or sound has gone out, following Greek phthongos.

English line and voice are entirely different words describing entirely different things, a measuring cord versus a sound. The Hebrew word here, qav, line, and the Greek word Paul quotes, phthongos, sound, look close enough in Hebrew consonants, qavam versus qolam, that the difference could be an old textual variant rather than a loose paraphrase.

Qav, line or measuring cord, and qol, voice or sound, are close enough in Hebrew spelling, qavam versus qolam, that some scholars propose the Septuagint's translators worked from a manuscript that actually read qolam, voice, rather than qavam, line, a genuine textual variant rather than a free translation choice. Others read it as an interpretive extension, since a cord can also mean a musical string, and a string produces a sound.

English readers of Romans 10:18 meet voice or sound with no indication that the Old Testament passage being quoted, in most English Bibles' Old Testament translation, actually says line, a visibly different word, leaving the connection between the two texts looking looser than it may actually be.

A New Testament quotation that uses a noticeably different word than your English Old Testament translation is worth checking against the Septuagint. It may reflect a genuine textual variant in the underlying Hebrew consonants rather than loose paraphrase.

Line, following the Masoretic Text, pictures a measuring cord stretched across creation, marking out its extent. Voice or sound, following the Septuagint and Paul's quotation, pictures creation's silent testimony as itself a kind of speech, the reading Paul's argument in Romans 10 needs to make its point about creation preaching to all nations.
קַו qav (line) / קוֹל qol (voice) · H6957 / H6963

src: Septuagint phthongos, sound, at Psalm 19:4 (18:5 LXX)
Paul's quotation at Romans 10:18
qav/qol's close consonantal similarity as the likely source of the variant

versions.s: The destruction that wasteth at noonday. Some ancient versions personify qeteb as a demon; the Hebrew itself, and the King James, keep it impersonal.

b.t: The King James reads destruction, following the Hebrew closely and leaving qeteb impersonal. The Latin Vulgate reads daemonium meridianum, the noonday demon, a personification carried into later Catholic translation tradition and still remembered in the modern idiom the noonday demon for creeping despair.

English destruction names an impersonal force, something that happens rather than someone who acts. Ancient translators working from the same Hebrew word sometimes heard something more personal in it, a noonday demon, an actual malevolent figure, rather than a mere abstract calamity.

Qeteb, from a root associated with cutting off, names ruin or destruction, appearing also at Deuteronomy 32:24 among a list of divine judgments. The Hebrew word itself does not require a personal, demonic reading, but the Greek Septuagint and especially Jerome's Latin Vulgate render it as an actual noonday demon, a personification that later Jewish and early Christian tradition developed further into full-blown spiritual warfare imagery, including a Hebrew exorcism version of this psalm among the Dead Sea Scrolls (11Q11, the Apocryphal Psalms scroll) used against demons, and, separately, an Aramaic Targum tradition that also personifies the danger.

English destruction reads as a plain, impersonal abstraction; the Latin daemonium meridianum, noonday demon, which shaped a long devotional and artistic tradition, personifies the same word into an actual malevolent being, a real difference in how frightening and how agentive the danger described is.

When an ancient translation, especially the Vulgate, personifies an abstract Hebrew noun into a named demon or spirit, treat that as a documented interpretive tradition worth knowing, even where it goes beyond what the Hebrew word itself strictly requires.

Destruction, following the Hebrew and the King James, keeps the danger impersonal, an abstract calamity rather than an agent. The noonday demon, following the Vulgate's personification, casts the same danger as an actual malevolent spiritual being, the reading behind the phrase's continuing life in the idiom noonday demon for creeping spiritual despair.

versions.s: Their line is gone out through all the earth. Paul quotes it in Romans 10:18 as their voice, or sound.

b.t: The Hebrew Masoretic Text reads their line, kav, has gone out. The Septuagint, and Paul quoting it at Romans 10:18, reads their voice or sound has gone out, following Greek phthongos.

English line and voice are entirely different words describing entirely different things, a measuring cord versus a sound. The Hebrew word here, qav, line, and the Greek word Paul quotes, phthongos, sound, look close enough in Hebrew consonants, qavam versus qolam, that the difference could be an old textual variant rather than a loose paraphrase.

Qav, line or measuring cord, and qol, voice or sound, are close enough in Hebrew spelling, qavam versus qolam, that some scholars propose the Septuagint's translators worked from a manuscript that actually read qolam, voice, rather than qavam, line, a genuine textual variant rather than a free translation choice. Others read it as an interpretive extension, since a cord can also mean a musical string, and a string produces a sound.

English readers of Romans 10:18 meet voice or sound with no indication that the Old Testament passage being quoted, in most English Bibles' Old Testament translation, actually says line, a visibly different word, leaving the connection between the two texts looking looser than it may actually be.

A New Testament quotation that uses a noticeably different word than your English Old Testament translation is worth checking against the Septuagint. It may reflect a genuine textual variant in the underlying Hebrew consonants rather than loose paraphrase.

Line, following the Masoretic Text, pictures a measuring cord stretched across creation, marking out its extent. Voice or sound, following the Septuagint and Paul's quotation, pictures creation's silent testimony as itself a kind of speech, the reading Paul's argument in Romans 10 needs to make its point about creation preaching to all nations.

versions.s: The voice of the LORD, seven times. A storm-theophany pattern closely paralleling Ugaritic hymns to the storm-god Baal.

b.t: Every version translates the storm imagery accurately, but nothing in translation signals that scholars widely read this psalm's form and content as adapted from, or directly answering, Canaanite storm-god hymnody rather than composed from scratch.

Imagine a national anthem that turns out to be a rewritten version of a rival nation's anthem, with only the name changed. Scholars argue Psalm 29 may be doing something similar: taking an existing hymn celebrating the Canaanite storm-god's thunder and applying its praise to the LORD instead, asserting that the real storm-god is Israel's God, not Baal.

The voice of the LORD, qol YHWH, recurs seven times through the psalm's central section, describing a storm moving from the sea across Lebanon and Sirion, breaking cedars, shaking the wilderness, a pattern closely resembling the seven thunders associated with Baal in Ugaritic poetry. Some scholars, following Harold Ginsberg's influential proposal, read Psalm 29 as an older Canaanite hymn to Baal repurposed for the LORD by simply replacing the divine name, a deliberate theological claim that the LORD, not Baal, truly commands the storm.

English readers experience the psalm as vivid nature poetry describing a thunderstorm; without the Ugaritic comparative background, the psalm's likely polemical purpose, directly answering and displacing Canaanite Baal worship by claiming his own signature imagery for the LORD, is invisible.

When a psalm's imagery closely parallels attested material from a neighboring ancient culture, read the parallel as potentially polemical, a claim about whose god really controls the phenomenon in question, rather than as coincidental shared nature imagery.

Reading Psalm 29 as an original Israelite composition treats its storm imagery as independently inspired praise poetry. Reading it as an adapted Canaanite hymn, following the comparative Ugaritic evidence, treats the whole psalm as a pointed theological claim, this storm belongs to the LORD, not Baal, embedded in Israel's own hymnbook.
קוֹל יְהוָה qol YHWH (voice of the LORD, sevenfold) · H6963

src: Harold Ginsberg's identification of Psalm 29 with Ugaritic Baal-hymn material

versions.s: The LORD appeared unto him. He lifted up his eyes, and lo, three men stood by him.

b.t: Every version reads the LORD appeared and then three men, correctly, but English readers often smooth the transition into an assumption, three angels, or three men who turn out to represent God, without registering how directly the Hebrew text itself equates the first sentence's subject, the LORD, with one of the figures who then eats a meal.

Imagine a story that opens **the president visited the office**, and the next sentence says **three people walked in and sat down**, with no further comment distinguishing which one was the president. English narrative would flag that explicitly. This chapter does not, and the ambiguity is the point.

The chapter's subject through the meal and the questions about Sarah's laughter remains the LORD in the singular, even while two of the three figures leave for Sodom and are called angels there, while the LORD continues speaking with Abraham alone. The text does not explain the mechanics; it simply narrates a scene in which God, in some form Abraham can host at his table, is present alongside two other beings later identified as angels.

English readers, trained by later theology to expect God's appearances to be marked as visibly supernatural, glide past how ordinary and physical this scene is in the Hebrew: sitting, eating, conversing, with no special visual marker distinguishing the LORD from the other two until the narrative itself tells you two of them go on to Sodom.

When a Hebrew narrative names God as the subject and then describes ordinary human action, do not assume later theological categories, angel, theophany, appearance, were doing organizing work for the original audience the way they do for later readers. Let the plain narrative sequence stand before importing the categories used to explain it.

The wording itself draws no disagreement among translators. The theological question, whether this scene depicts God directly in human form, an angel acting with full divine authority and identified as the LORD by convention, or some combination, is a live one this text raises but does not itself resolve any more than Genesis 16 or Genesis 32 do.

versions.s: The LORD will provide. The Hebrew verb is see, and the chapter has been using it all along.

b.t: All versions read provide in verse 8 and in the name, and most read seen or provided at the end of verse 14. The King James keeps seen at the end, which preserves half the pun.

A story where a character keeps saying **we'll see** and then names the place **Seen** is a story with a spine. Translate half the occurrences as **we'll sort it out** and the spine disappears while every sentence stays accurate.

Ra'ah means to see. In certain forms it extends to see to something, and from there to provide, the same way English see to it works. Verse 8 has God will see to it for himself a lamb, verse 13 has Abraham lifting his eyes and seeing a ram, and verse 14 names the place on that verb twice.
English see and provide are different words. The chapter's repetition of one verb across seeing, being seen and providing cannot survive into English without a footnote.
Hebrew narrative builds by repeating a single root across a passage. When a chapter feels like it is circling something, look for the root rather than the theme.
Provide is clearer and breaks the pattern. See is opaque in English and keeps it. Every version compromises somewhere in the chapter, and none keeps all four occurrences visible.

versions.s: The elder shall serve the younger. Or: the elder, shall the younger serve. The Hebrew word order does not decide it.

b.t: Every English version reads the elder shall serve the younger, settling the ambiguity one way, the reading that fits how the rest of Jacob and Esau's story actually plays out.

English word order tells you who does what: **the dog bit the man** and **the man bit the dog** are opposites, and the order alone carries the meaning. Biblical Hebrew poetry can drop the marker that would normally clarify this, and this oracle is exactly that kind of sentence: both readings are grammatically live.

Verav ya'avod tsa'ir lacks the object marker et that would normally clarify which noun is doing the serving and which is being served, and Hebrew word order alone does not settle it here, since Job 14:19 shows the same pattern can run either direction, subject-object or object-subject. The medieval commentators Radak and Ibn Kaspi already noted the sentence could mean either the elder shall serve the younger or the elder, the younger shall serve, and the cantillation marks in the Masoretic tradition arguably lean toward the second, less common reading.

English syntax fixes word order to meaning in a way Hebrew poetry does not always require, so a translation must pick one direction, and once picked, an English reader is left with no clue that the original oracle was genuinely, grammatically ambiguous rather than plainly stated.

When a Hebrew clause lacks the object marker et and involves two nouns that could each plausibly be subject or object, do not assume word order alone settles the sentence the way it would in English. Check whether ancient commentators already flagged the same ambiguity.

The elder shall serve the younger fits the narrative's outcome, Esau's household eventually subordinate to Jacob's line, and is the reading every translation adopts. The reverse reading, argued from the missing object marker and supported by some cantillation evidence, would make the oracle a genuinely opaque riddle rather than a plain prediction, which some rabbinic tradition takes to be the point.

versions.s: Esau said, I have enough. Jacob said, I have all things. Two different Hebrew words, rav and kol, for two different postures toward wealth.

b.t: Most versions read Esau saying I have enough and Jacob saying I have enough or I have all, sometimes flattening both brothers' statements to the same English phrase and losing the distinction the Hebrew text itself draws between them.

English **I have plenty** and **I have everything** sound similar but are not identical claims. Hebrew marks this same distinction precisely: Esau's rav, much or sufficient, is a claim of comfortable abundance; Jacob's kol, all, is a stronger, almost complete claim, and the two brothers each choose their own word.

Esau's yesh li rav, I have much, uses the ordinary word for abundance or sufficiency, a comfortable, unremarkable claim. Jacob's yesh li kol, I have all, or everything, reaches further, a stronger and more complete claim of provision, spoken by the brother who has spent the chapter making amends and securing goodwill. The difference in word choice, not merely tone, marks a real contrast in how each brother frames his own situation at this reunion.

English translations that render both statements identically, I have enough, erase a distinction the Hebrew vocabulary itself preserves between comfortable sufficiency, rav, and total fullness, kol, a difference some readers connect to Jacob's changed character after Peniel.

When two characters make parallel statements using different vocabulary for what looks like the same idea, check whether the words are actually synonyms or whether one is deliberately stronger than the other. A flattened translation can erase a contrast the original author built on purpose.

Rendering both as I have enough treats the exchange as merely polite and symmetrical. Preserving the distinction, Esau's enough versus Jacob's everything, or all, reads Jacob's word choice as reflecting the transformed outlook of a man who has just wrestled with God and lived.

versions.s: Sin lieth at the door. Its desire is to thee, and thou shalt rule over it. The same crouching-word, and the same two words as 3:16.

b.t: Every English version reads lieth, croucheth, or is crouching, all correctly neutral. Almost none of the popular translations use anything that suggests an ambush or a personified threat, though one modern academic version, the New English Bible, does render it demon.

**The dog is lying by the door.** Harmless. Now imagine the word for lying also names a predator waiting in ambush at a doorway in a neighboring language and culture. Lieth sounds passive in English; the word behind it does not.

Rovets is a participle of the common verb for an animal lying down, but this personified use of sin as the subject crouching at a door closely resembles the Akkadian rabisu, a demon that lurks at thresholds to attack. Whether the Hebrew word is a deliberate echo of that image or simply the ordinary verb applied metaphorically is debated, but the doorway setting matches the Akkadian pattern closely. The same verse then reuses teshuqah, desire, and the verb mashal, rule over, the identical pairing used of the woman and the man at Genesis 3:16, this time offered to Cain as a warning rather than a sentence.

English lieth or crouches names a posture; it carries none of the threshold-demon association some scholars hear behind the Hebrew word, and English has no way to signal that the sentence structure repeats 3:16's marriage language word for word, since a reader would need to notice both verses share teshuqah and mashal in Hebrew to catch it at all.

A common word placed in an unusual setting, here an animal-word applied to sin at a doorway, can carry connotations from the culture's wider vocabulary that a plain gloss will not show. And when a rare phrase repeats verbatim a few verses apart, as teshuqah plus mashal does here, treat the second occurrence as commentary on the first.

Lieth or crouches is the safe, literal rendering every version uses. Whether to import the Akkadian demon imagery is a judgment call resting on comparative Semitic philology rather than the Hebrew word by itself, which is exactly why mainstream translations have stayed with the neutral gloss.

versions.s: Thou hast broken Rahab in pieces. A different word entirely from Rahab the woman of Jericho.

b.t: Every version transliterates both as Rahab, correctly reflecting how each name sounds, but with no way to show an English reader that the underlying Hebrew spellings and roots are entirely unrelated.

Imagine two English words, spelled and pronounced identically, that happen to come from completely different roots with completely different meanings, the way bank the riverbank and bank the money-building share nothing but sound. Rahab the mythological sea monster and Rahab the woman of Jericho are exactly this kind of coincidence, invisible once both are simply transliterated the same way.

The mythological Rahab here is spelled with a heh, from a root meaning storm, arrogance, or, poetically, a primeval chaos-monster, used elsewhere as a symbolic name for Egypt at Isaiah 51:9-10. Rahab of Jericho is spelled with a chet, from a root meaning wide or broad, an entirely separate word. English transliteration erases the difference, producing one identical-looking name for two unconnected Hebrew words.

English readers meeting Rahab in this psalm and Rahab in Joshua have every reason to assume the same figure or at least a related word is meant in both places, when in fact the Hebrew spellings share no root at all, only an accident of how both happen to sound once flattened into English letters.

Never assume two identically transliterated biblical names are linguistically related. Hebrew has more consonant distinctions than English transliteration preserves, and coincidental sound-alikes across unrelated roots are common enough to always check rather than assume.

Rahab as the name is not disputed in either passage. What needs correcting is the natural but mistaken assumption that this psalm's chaos-monster Rahab and Joshua's Rahab of Jericho are in any way the same word or share any linguistic history.

versions.s: Moved, hovered, or swept. One rare verb and a bird.

b.t: Modern versions read hovering, or was moving, or sweeping over. The NET reads moving.

Suppose you found a word that appears three times in every book ever written in English, and only once does the sentence around it make sense. Every dictionary entry for that word is a guess built on that one sentence. You would want to see the guess. That is exactly the situation here.

The verb is rachaph, and it turns up in just three verses of the Hebrew Bible: Genesis 1:2, Deuteronomy 32:11 where an eagle flutters over its young, and Jeremiah 23:9 where a prophet's bones shake. The third one is a different verb stem and BDB lists it as a separate entry, which means the hovering sense may have only two occurrences, and one of those is the verse being explained. Every lexicon entry for this word is reasoning from a single clear context.
With three occurrences there is no statistical base. Translators are reasoning from one clear context to two unclear ones, and reasonable people weight that differently.

Look up how many times a word occurs before you trust a definition, and then check whether all those occurrences are even the same word. Under about five, a lexicon is making an argument rather than reporting a fact, and you should want to see the argument.

Hovering imports the eagle from Deuteronomy 32:11 and reads the opening of Genesis as protective and parental. Moving treats it as motion over water with no bird attached, which is what the King James, Tyndale, the Geneva and the Revised Version all chose. Hovering is a twentieth-century preference, entering the major English versions with the NIV. Neither is unreasonable and the evidence base is two verses.

versions.s: Subdue it, and have dominion. Forceful, even military and royal vocabulary, standing beside Genesis 2's gentler verbs for the same job.

b.t: Every version reads subdue and have dominion, correctly conveying real force, though without necessarily flagging how sharply that force contrasts with the gentler abad and shamar, work and keep, used for the same basic human task at Genesis 2:15.

English subdue and have dominion already sound fairly strong, but the underlying Hebrew is stronger still: kabash is the verb for military conquest, putting a defeated enemy under your foot; radah is royal rule language, a king governing subjects. Two chapters later, the same task is described with work and keep, priestly, custodial language entirely different in tone.

Kabash elsewhere describes military subjugation, putting a conquered population under your feet; radah names the kind of rule a king exercises over subjects. Applied to humanity's relationship with the earth and its creatures, both verbs are considerably more forceful than the abad, serve, and shamar, guard, used of Adam's task in the garden at 2:15, creating a real tension between two pictures of the same human vocation, conquest and custodianship, that the text does not explicitly resolve.

English subdue and dominion already register as fairly strong, but readers moving between chapters 1 and 2 in translation do not necessarily notice that the vocabulary shifts from military and royal force to priestly service and guarding, a genuine change in tone between two accounts of humanity's purpose that disappears once both are smoothed into ordinary English.

When two passages describe what looks like the same task using visibly different registers of vocabulary, forceful versus gentle, royal versus priestly, read the contrast as a real feature of the text's fuller picture rather than assuming the two must simply restate one identical idea.

Reading kabash and radah at full force keeps humanity's mandate as active, even aggressive, shaping of a wild and unfinished world. Reading Genesis 2:15's abad and shamar as the fuller, correcting picture treats dominion as answerable to a prior, gentler custodial calling. The text offers both pictures without explicitly ranking one over the other.

versions.s: Thou hast broken Rahab in pieces. A different word entirely from Rahab the woman of Jericho.

b.t: Every version transliterates both as Rahab, correctly reflecting how each name sounds, but with no way to show an English reader that the underlying Hebrew spellings and roots are entirely unrelated.

Imagine two English words, spelled and pronounced identically, that happen to come from completely different roots with completely different meanings, the way bank the riverbank and bank the money-building share nothing but sound. Rahab the mythological sea monster and Rahab the woman of Jericho are exactly this kind of coincidence, invisible once both are simply transliterated the same way.

The mythological Rahab here is spelled with a heh, from a root meaning storm, arrogance, or, poetically, a primeval chaos-monster, used elsewhere as a symbolic name for Egypt at Isaiah 51:9-10. Rahab of Jericho is spelled with a chet, from a root meaning wide or broad, an entirely separate word. English transliteration erases the difference, producing one identical-looking name for two unconnected Hebrew words.

English readers meeting Rahab in this psalm and Rahab in Joshua have every reason to assume the same figure or at least a related word is meant in both places, when in fact the Hebrew spellings share no root at all, only an accident of how both happen to sound once flattened into English letters.

Never assume two identically transliterated biblical names are linguistically related. Hebrew has more consonant distinctions than English transliteration preserves, and coincidental sound-alikes across unrelated roots are common enough to always check rather than assume.

Rahab as the name is not disputed in either passage. What needs correcting is the natural but mistaken assumption that this psalm's chaos-monster Rahab and Joshua's Rahab of Jericho are in any way the same word or share any linguistic history.

versions.s: Leah was tender eyed. The word could mean weak, or it could mean soft and lovely.

b.t: Translations split roughly down the middle: several read weak or ordinary, reading the description as unflattering, while others read tender or delicate, allowing a gentler, even positive sense.

English **soft-spoken** can be a compliment or, said a certain way, faint praise bordering on an insult. Hebrew rakkot sits in exactly that kind of gap: soft or delicate could mean gentle and attractive, or it could mean weak, pale, lacking the sparkle Rachel's beauty is about to be praised for in the very next clause.

Rakkot, soft or tender, most often describes something delicate or fine elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, but applied to eyes without further qualification, its force is genuinely unclear: does it mean lovely and soft-eyed, or pale and lacking luster, weak by comparison to what follows? The verse immediately contrasts Leah's description with Rachel, who was beautiful and well favoured, a contrast that reads very differently depending on which sense of rakkot is meant.

A single word is what English is forced to pick, weak, tender, or delicate, each committing the translation to a specific emotional tone, complimentary, neutral, or unflattering, that the bare Hebrew word does not clearly settle on its own.

When a physical description sits between two characters being compared, check whether the description word's range includes both a flattering and an unflattering sense before assuming the comparison is entirely one-sided.

Weak or ordinary reads the verse as setting up a stark contrast, Leah unremarkable, Rachel stunning. Tender or delicate allows Leah a real, if quieter, virtue of her own before Rachel's more obvious beauty is introduced. The Hebrew word does not clearly force either reading.

versions.s: Extol him that rideth upon the heavens. A title, rider of the clouds, borrowed directly from Baal's own standing epithet.

b.t: Every version reads rideth upon the heavens or rides through the deserts, both reasonable translations of an ambiguous Hebrew word, but neither flags that the underlying phrase closely matches a specific, attested divine title from the surrounding culture.

Imagine a hymn calling your God by the exact title a rival religion uses for its own storm-god, on purpose, to claim that title belongs to the true God instead. That is what this verse very likely does, taking rider of the clouds straight from Canaanite mythology and redirecting it.

Rokev ba'aravot, rider on the clouds or plains, closely parallels rkb 'rpt, rider of the clouds, a fixed epithet for Baal repeated throughout Ugaritic mythological texts. Applying the identical image directly to the LORD is very likely a deliberate theological claim, that Israel's God, not Baal, is the true rider of the storm clouds, joining Psalm 29's storm-theophany language and Psalm 48's likely claim on Mount Zaphon as a third instance of this same polemical pattern in the Psalter.

English readers meeting rideth upon the heavens hear generic, majestic imagery with no signal that the phrase is likely quoting, and redirecting, a specific rival deity's own standing title, a claim that only registers once the Ugaritic parallel is known.

When the Psalter applies storm or sky imagery to the LORD using phrasing that closely parallels an attested Canaanite divine epithet, read it as part of a consistent, deliberate pattern of theological reclamation running through multiple psalms, not as an isolated poetic coincidence.

Reading the phrase as generic praise imagery misses the likely polemical point. Reading it as a direct appropriation of Baal's own title, alongside Psalm 29 and Psalm 48's similar moves, casts this verse as part of a sustained pattern across the Psalter, actively contesting Canaanite religious claims rather than merely borrowing poetic flourish.

versions.s: Be still, and know that I am God. Harpu is a military command: cease fire, stand down, not sit quietly.

b.t: Every version reads be still, correctly capturing the verb's basic sense of ceasing an activity, but English still now carries almost entirely calm, contemplative connotations the Hebrew military command did not originally have.

English be still now overwhelmingly suggests quiet, calm, meditative stillness, the kind of stillness you seek in a busy day. The Hebrew verb behind it is a battlefield command, closer to stand down or drop your weapons, addressed to warring nations being told the fighting is over because this King has already won.

Harpu, from raphah, to slacken, let drop, or cease, functions elsewhere as a command to lower one's hands or stand down from conflict. In its context here, surrounded by verses about nations raging, kingdoms being moved, and wars being made to cease to the end of the earth, the command reads as a ceasefire order to combatants who have lost, not an invitation to a quiet devotional moment, recognize that this God has already won and stop fighting Him.

English be still has drifted almost entirely toward contemplative, meditative stillness in contemporary popular usage, precisely the association a phrase like this needs today, while the Hebrew military command it translates is addressed to defeated combatants being ordered to stand down, a considerably more confrontational and specific scene.

When a devotional phrase has become detached from its original context through repeated popular quotation, go back and read the surrounding verses. Be still and know that I am God sits inside a psalm about warfare and national upheaval, not a quiet room.

Be still preserves the beloved, contemplative popular reading many readers already carry. Stand down, or cease fighting, closer to the Hebrew military command and its surrounding context of nations raging and wars ceasing, recovers the verse's original, more confrontational scene: a ceasefire ordered by the victor, not a suggestion to relax.

versions.s: Let there be a firmament. A word built on the sense of beating something out flat, likely naming a solid dome, not empty space.

b.t: Older versions read firmament, itself a transliteration of the Latin firmamentum, translating the Greek stereoma, solid structure. Some modern versions read expanse or sky, softening the solidity the underlying words and root more strongly suggest.

English firmament sounds vaguely solid but vague enough that most readers picture open sky. The Hebrew word's root is tied to beating out metal into a flat sheet, the same kind of work a smith does hammering a bowl from a lump of metal, which points toward a solid structure holding back water, not simply open air.

Raqia comes from a root meaning to spread out or beat out, the same action used of hammering metal into a thin sheet, and functions in Genesis 1 to separate waters above from waters below, holding the upper waters back the way a solid barrier would. Comparative ancient Near Eastern cosmology regularly pictures the sky as a solid, dome-like structure, and the linguistic, comparative, and contextual evidence together lead most specialists to conclude the original audience understood raqia as solid, not merely as empty, open space.

English firmament and expanse both allow a reader to imagine open air, while the Hebrew word's root and its ancient cosmological context point more strongly toward an actual solid structure, a real difference in what ancient readers likely pictured when they heard the word.

When translating a cosmological term, check both its root meaning and how the surrounding ancient culture pictured the same concept before assuming a modern, scientifically informed picture of the sky was ever in view. Ancient cosmology and modern cosmology are not obligated to agree, and the text was written within the ancient one.

Firmament preserves some sense of solidity but reads as archaic and vague to most modern ears. Expanse or sky, now common in modern versions, more comfortably fits a modern cosmological picture but likely understates how solid the original Hebrew word and its ancient context actually suggest.

versions.s: The children struggled together within her. A rare, violent verb: crushing, not merely kicking.

b.t: Every version reads struggled or jostled, both reasonable but generic English verbs that undersell how forceful and unusual the underlying Hebrew word actually is.

English **struggled** covers everything from mild wriggling to a real fight. Hebrew's word here sits at the violent end of that range, closer to **they were crushing each other** than to ordinary prenatal movement, and Rebekah's alarmed response in the very same verse matches that intensity.

Vayitrotzetzu is a rare hitpael form of ratsats, to crush or break in pieces, used here in a mutual, reciprocal sense: the children were crushing or violently colliding with one another. The verb's intensity is severe enough that Rebekah immediately goes to inquire of the LORD, alarmed by what she is feeling, and the violence in the womb previews the lifelong national conflict the LORD's answer in the next verse explicitly announces.

English struggled is a mild, general-purpose verb; it does not carry the crushing, violent-collision sense of the rare Hebrew root, so an English reader misses how extreme Rebekah's physical experience, and its symbolic weight, actually was.

When ordinary translation smooths a rare, intense verb into a generic English equivalent, check the word's root meaning elsewhere before assuming the action described was mild. The intensity of a rare verb is often exactly the detail a smooth translation loses first.

Struggled is accurate but undersells the Hebrew's violence. Crushed one another or collided violently is closer to ratsats's ordinary sense but reads oddly applied to an unborn child, which is likely why every major translation has settled on the gentler English verb despite the mismatch.
וַיִּתְרֹצֲצוּ vayitrotzetzu (רָצַץ ratsats, hitpael) · H7533

versions.s: In the beginning, or when God began. The first word is shaped like half a phrase.

b.t: The King James, ESV, NIV and NASB read In the beginning. The JPS reads When God began to create. The NRSV footnotes it and the NET discusses it at length.

**In the beginning.** Beginning of what? English lets you leave that open. Hebrew usually does not, because a word like that normally has to be attached to something, the way **the top of** needs a stair.

Bereshit is the noun reshit, beginning, with a prefixed preposition and no definite article. In Hebrew that shape usually signals a construct, a noun leaning on the next word, which would give when God began to create rather than in the beginning. The vowel pointing that makes it absolute was added by scribes over a thousand years later.
English prepositions do not lean. In the beginning is grammatically complete the moment you write it, so the question never arises for an English reader.

Hebrew nouns that lean on the next word are the commonest structural feature English cannot show. When a translation footnote offers you a whole different sentence shape rather than a different word, this is usually why.

Absolute gives a first act of creation and a universe with a start. Construct gives a scene-setting clause with the real main verb in verse 3. The consonants permit both, the ancient versions mostly took it as absolute, and the grammar leans construct. This is a live argument, not a settled one.
בְּרֵאשִׁית bereshit · H7225

src: reshit in construct: Jeremiah 26:1; Hosea 9:10; Proverbs 8:22
Septuagint and Vulgate both read the absolute
Rashi takes the construct reading, which puts a medieval Jewish commentator on the same side as modern grammarians

versions.s: Pharaoh shall lift up thine head. For the butler, restored to office. For the baker, the same phrase, with one word added, means beheaded.

b.t: Every version reads lift up thine head for the butler and either the same phrase or lift up thy head from off thee for the baker, correctly conveying restoration and execution respectively, though not every translation preserves how close the two phrasings actually sit to each other in Hebrew.

Imagine telling two coworkers on the same day, **you're getting a promotion** and **you're getting let go**, using the exact same sentence structure for both, except one has a single extra word that flips the entire meaning. That is precisely what Joseph's Hebrew does here, and it is chilling specifically because both men hear almost the same words.

Yissa Pharaoh et rosh'cha, Pharaoh will lift up your head, is used of the butler's restoration to office at 40:13. The identical core phrase returns at 40:19 for the baker, with one addition, me'aleicha, from off you, turning restore your position into remove your head, the same idiom completing itself in two opposite directions depending on a single added phrase.

English restoration language, promoted, and execution language, beheaded, share no vocabulary at all, so the Hebrew's grim wordplay, one shared idiom branching into life and death, is completely invisible once each fate gets its own separate English phrase.

When a narrator delivers parallel news to two characters using visibly similar phrasing, check how closely the underlying words actually match. Shared vocabulary delivering opposite outcomes is a real literary technique, not a translation coincidence, and it is often lost the moment each outcome gets its own natural-sounding English sentence.

Both outcomes are stated plainly by the narrative regardless of phrasing, so no version gets this wrong. What's worth noticing is the wordplay connecting them: the same lift up your head idiom branching into opposite fates, a genuine literary effect that separate, natural-sounding English sentences for each man cannot reproduce.
יִשָּׂא פַרְעֹה אֶת־רֹאשֶׁךָ yissa Pharaoh et rosh'cha · H5375 + H7218

src: The butler's restoration: Genesis 40:13, 20-21
The baker's execution using the same core idiom plus me'aleicha: Genesis 40:19, 22

versions.s: The head stone of the corner. Either the foundation stone set first, or the capstone set last at the very top.

b.t: Most versions read cornerstone, assuming the foundational sense. Some scholars argue for capstone or keystone instead, the crowning stone rather than the base, and note that the Greek phrase quoted in the New Testament, kephale gonias, head of the corner, preserves the same ambiguity rather than resolving it.

English cornerstone today usually suggests a foundation, the first stone laid, everything built outward from it. But rosh, head, can just as naturally suggest the topmost position, a capstone or keystone placed last to complete an arch or wall. The Hebrew phrase does not clearly specify which end of the building process is meant.

Rosh pinnah, head of the corner, could describe either the first stone set at a building's foundation, establishing the entire structure's alignment, or the final stone set at the top of an arch or wall, completing rather than beginning the construction. Both are attested architectural uses of similar terminology, and scholars including R.T. France and Ulrich Luz have argued that Matthew's own quotation of this verse deliberately keeps both images alive rather than committing to one.

English cornerstone has settled almost entirely into the foundational sense in modern usage, a building's first and most important stone; readers rarely consider that the Hebrew, and the Greek that quotes it in the New Testament, may instead or additionally be picturing a capstone crowning a structure already built, a different and arguably more dramatic image of exaltation after rejection.

When an architectural metaphor is quoted repeatedly across Scripture, check whether the underlying term specifies which part of the building process is meant before assuming the modern default sense. Ancient building vocabulary did not always map onto modern architectural categories the way translation can imply.

Cornerstone, the foundational reading, pictures the rejected stone becoming the very basis the whole structure depends on from the ground up. Capstone or keystone, the completion reading, pictures the rejected stone becoming the final, crowning piece that finishes and holds together a structure already otherwise built, arguably a more dramatic reversal from rejection to climactic honor.
רֹאשׁ פִּנָּה rosh pinnah · H7218 + H6438

src: Septuagint's kephale gonias preserving the same ambiguity
Matthew 21:42, Acts 4:11, and 1 Peter 2:7 all quoting this verse

versions.s: The cool of the day. The Hebrew word is the same one translated Spirit.

b.t: Nearly every version reads cool of the day or evening breeze, following a translation tradition going back through the King James. Some recent scholarship instead reads the phrase as describing an approaching storm.

English keeps **wind**, **breath**, and **spirit** as three separate words. Hebrew has one word for all three, ruach, the same word from Genesis 1:2. This verse uses it, and cool is not one of the things ruach otherwise ever means.

The phrase is leruach hayom, literally in the ruach, wind or spirit, of the day. Ruach is the same noun used of the Spirit of God at Genesis 1:2 and of breath and wind throughout the Hebrew Bible; nowhere else does it mean temperature. Some scholars argue the scene depicts God arriving the way He does elsewhere, in a rushing, forceful wind rather than a mild breeze, making this a small theophany rather than a stroll at sunset.

English cool has no connection to wind, breath, or spirit at all; it names a temperature. Ruach never names a temperature in Hebrew, so the traditional English rendering supplies a sense the word does not otherwise carry, hiding the word's ordinary link to Spirit and storm imagery elsewhere in the Bible.

When a familiar English phrase does not correspond to any of a word's attested senses, be suspicious of the phrase, not the word. Cool of the day is a translation tradition, not a lexical entry for ruach.

Cool of the day preserves the long-settled picture of a garden walk at evening. Wind, or an approaching storm, follows the word's ordinary range and the pattern of divine appearances elsewhere in Scripture. Both are argued in current scholarship; the mild-breeze picture is the inherited default rather than the only reading available.
רוּחַ ruach · H7307

src: Septuagint renders the phrase to deilinon, the afternoon; the Vulgate ad auram post meridiem, the afternoon breeze
ruach in storm-theophany contexts: Exodus 14:21; Psalm 18:10-15; Ezekiel 1:4
ruach never elsewhere denotes temperature; its attested ranges are wind, breath, and spirit

versions.s: Renew a right spirit within me. The same noun runs through the next two verses meaning different things.

b.t: Versions read a right spirit, a steadfast spirit, a loyal spirit. Verse 11 reads thy holy Spirit and verse 12 reads a free or willing spirit. Same noun each time.
A paragraph that uses one word three times is building something. A translation that renders it three different ways leaves you reading three sentences that happen to be next to each other.

Ruach appears at verses 10, 11 and 12: a steadfast ruach in the man, God's holy ruach not taken away, and a willing ruach to uphold him. The psalm is asking for an exchange of inner dispositions and grounding it in God's own. In Hebrew that is one word repeating. In English it is a human attitude, then the third person of the Trinity, then a human attitude again.
English spirit covers the human inner life and the divine person, but readers switch registers between the two and the repetition reads as coincidence rather than structure.
Count the repetitions before you interpret the passage. Hebrew poetry argues by repeating a word, and English translation argues by varying it.
No dispute. Every version renders all three accurately and none of them can show that they are one word.

versions.s: Who maketh his angels spirits. Ruach, the same word for wind, breath, and spirit, used twice in one sentence about natural forces.

b.t: Every version reads angels spirits, following the Septuagint's angelous, angels, and pneumata, spirits or winds, the reading Hebrews 1:7 explicitly builds on. Some modern versions instead read he makes the winds his messengers, treating the verse as being about natural forces, not angelic beings.

English angels and English winds name completely different kinds of things, spiritual beings versus weather. The Hebrew word ruach spans both, and this verse's other use of ruach in the same breath, describing actual wind, tilts the more natural reading toward God making the winds themselves his messengers, not creating angelic beings out of wind.

Ruach occurs twice in this two-verse Hebrew sentence, and the first occurrence, describing God walking on the wings of the ruach, clearly means wind, making it more natural to read the second occurrence the same way rather than switching senses mid-sentence, giving he makes the winds his messengers, natural forces personified as servants, a common ancient Near Eastern image for divine sovereignty over nature. The Septuagint instead reads both occurrences as angels and spirits, the reading Hebrews 1:7 explicitly quotes to argue that angels are servants subordinate to the Son.

English must choose either angels/spirits, following the Septuagint's interpretive translation, or winds/messengers, following the more natural Hebrew reading in context, and Hebrews 1:7's well-known quotation locks many readers into the angelic sense without their ever seeing the more natural, nature-focused alternative reading.

When ruach appears twice in close proximity, check whether both occurrences plausibly share the same sense, wind, breath, or spirit, before assuming a shift in meaning mid-passage. The most natural reading often keeps the sense consistent within one sentence.

Angels spirits, following the Septuagint and Hebrews 1:7, reads the verse as being about heavenly beings and grounds an argument about angelic subordination to Christ. Winds his messengers, following the more natural sense of ruach's first occurrence in the same sentence, reads the verse as praising God's sovereignty over natural forces, a psalm about creation rather than angelology.
רוּחוֹת ruchot (רוּחַ ruach, wind/breath/spirit) · H7307

src: ruach's first occurrence in the same sentence clearly meaning wind: Psalm 104:3
Septuagint's angelous/pneumata rendering, quoted at Hebrews 1:7
Ancient Near Eastern parallels personifying natural forces as divine servants

versions.s: Breath, wind, and Spirit. One Hebrew word, three English words, all in one vision.

b.t: Every English version does the same thing, because every English version has to. The renderings shift between breath, wind and Spirit according to what each verse seems to need.

Imagine a language with one word covering **a sigh**, **a storm** and **a person's inner life**. To a speaker of that language those are obviously the same thing: invisible, moving, and the difference between a live body and a dead one. Now imagine translating a poem that plays on all three at once into English, which files them in three separate drawers.

Ruach covers breath, wind, and spirit, including the Spirit of God. Ezekiel's vision runs all three senses through one image: dry bones with no breath, wind summoned from four directions, and God's Spirit put inside a restored people. In Hebrew that is one word repeating and building. In English it is three unrelated nouns and the repetition vanishes.

English split what Hebrew kept together, and once split it cannot be rejoined. There is no English word that means moving air and inner life at the same time, so a translator has to choose a sense per verse and the pattern across the chapter dissolves.

When one chapter of your Bible keeps circling the same idea with different English nouns, check whether the original was repeating a single word. Hebrew builds by repetition far more than English does, and translations that vary the wording for readability erase the structure.
Every version faces the same impossible choice and makes it verse by verse, breath here, wind there, Spirit there. The only real decision is whether to footnote the connection, and most do not.

versions.s: The whole earth was of one language. Literally, one lip, and one set of words.

b.t: Every version reads one language, correctly capturing the sense, but the substitution of the abstract noun language for the concrete body part lip is invisible once translated.

English keeps **lip service** and **read my lips** as fixed idioms, small leftovers of using a body part to mean speech. Hebrew safah, lip, is the ordinary, everyday word for language itself, not a special poetic flourish, and this verse uses it in its most literal sense: one lip for the whole earth.

Safah, lip, functions as Hebrew's standard word for language or speech throughout the Old Testament, a settled use of the body part for its function, technically called metonymy. This verse pairs it with devarim achadim, one set of words, so the sentence names both the form of speech, one lip, and its content, one shared vocabulary.

English can say language directly without borrowing a body-part word to do it, so the sentence's underlying image, everyone sharing a single lip, disappears the moment lip becomes the abstract noun language in translation.

When a Hebrew abstraction is built on a concrete body-part word, notice the image before it dissolves into an English abstraction. Hebrew regularly builds its vocabulary for inner or abstract realities out of very physical, embodied words.

One language is the only workable English rendering, and no version disputes it. What's worth flagging is the concrete image, a single lip shared by the whole earth, that the abstract translation necessarily leaves behind.
שָׂפָה safah (lip, language) · H8193

src: safah as the standard Hebrew word for language: e.g. Isaiah 19:18; Zephaniah 3:9

versions.s: The flesh profiteth nothing. Said immediately after a discourse about eating flesh.

b.t: Every version reads flesh.
**He is my own flesh and blood.** **The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak.** One English word, two unrelated ideas, and you sort them instantly by context.

Sarx covers meat, the physical body, and a whole orientation of life. Verses 51 to 58 use it in the first sense; verse 63 uses it in the last. The apparent contradiction dissolves once the range is in view and does not dissolve any other way.
English flesh has the same range, so the ambiguity is preserved rather than created. What English cannot do is mark which sense is in play.
When a paragraph seems to contradict itself one verse later, check whether the shared word is being used in two of its senses.
Flesh is universal.
σάρξ sarx · G4561

sarx as orientation: Romans 8:5-8; Galatians 5:19

versions.s: Flesh. Sometimes meat, sometimes the body, sometimes a whole orientation of life.

b.t: Versions read flesh, sinful nature, or human nature. The NIV used sinful nature for years and reverted to flesh in 2011.
**He is my own flesh and blood.** Nothing about meat. English already uses the word for kinship and for weakness, and you never confuse them.
Sarx covers meat, the physical body, human beings generally, kinship, and in Paul a way of living oriented away from God. Which one is meant is decided by context every single time.
English flesh is overwhelmingly physical, so Paul's non-physical use reads as a claim about bodies that he is not making.
A word with a wide range is decided by context, not by its most common meaning. Reading the most common sense into every occurrence is how a word study goes wrong.
Flesh is the majority rendering and the NIV's return to it in 2011 settled the main modern departure.

versions.s: He called the name of the well Sitnah. The same root behind the word Satan.

b.t: Every version transliterates Esek, Sitnah, and Rehoboth as bare place names, correctly, since none of the three carries built-in meaning once rendered in English letters.

Imagine naming a disputed parking spot **Accuser**, using the exact word your language later uses for a courtroom prosecutor or a cosmic adversary. English place names rarely carry that kind of loaded vocabulary. Hebrew does it constantly, and Sitnah is a clean example.

Esek, contention, from a root meaning to dispute; Sitnah, accusation or enmity, sharing its root with satan, the accuser, used of the adversarial figure in Job and Zechariah; and Rehoboth, room or open spaces, mark an escalation and then a resolution across the three well-naming episodes. Sitnah is not simply an unpleasant-sounding name; it is built from the same three consonants that later name the Hebrew Bible's chief adversarial figure.

English readers meet Esek, Sitnah, and Rehoboth as bare, interchangeable-sounding proper nouns, and nothing about the spelling lets them pick up that the second one carries the same loaded root as a major theological term used elsewhere in the same Bible.

When a place name in a dispute narrative sounds unusually pointed, check its root against other, more theologically weighted uses of the same consonants elsewhere in Scripture. Hebrew narrators frequently choose or record names precisely because of this kind of resonance.

Transliterating the three names draws no disagreement among translators. The connection between Sitnah and satan is a matter of shared Hebrew root, not a claim that this well dispute was itself supernatural; this note simply makes that shared vocabulary visible.
שִׂטְנָה Sitnah (cf. שָׂטָן satan) · H7856 / H7854

src: satan as accuser/adversary from the same root: Job 1:6-12; Zechariah 3:1-2
The escalation across all three well names: Genesis 26:20-22

versions.s: The beginning of miracles. John's word is sign, and he never uses the usual word for miracle.

b.t: The King James reads miracles. Modern versions read signs.
**A sign of trouble.** A sign points past itself. A **marvel** stops at itself. Two different jobs and English has both words.

Semeion means a sign, something pointing beyond itself. The other Gospels use dunamis, act of power, and teras, wonder. John uses semeion throughout and structures the first half of his Gospel around seven of them.
English miracle emphasises the breach of ordinary cause. Sign emphasises significance. The Greek word chosen is the second one and the King James printed the first.
When one Gospel consistently uses a different word from the other three for the same events, the difference is the writer's argument.
Signs is what nearly every modern version prints. The King James miracles is the outlier and is the reason the popular phrase is seven miracles rather than seven signs.
σημεῖον semeion · G4592

src: semeion at John 2:11; 4:54; 20:30-31
dunamis in the Synoptics: Matthew 11:20; Mark 6:2
John 20:30-31 states the purpose of the signs

versions.s: God rested. The verb means stopped, not recovered.

b.t: Every English version reads rested here, and later at Exodus 20:11 for the same day, using one English word for two different Hebrew verbs.

**I stopped for lunch.** That says nothing about being tired. **I rested after the race.** That does, because rest in English leans toward recovering strength. The verb behind Sabbath only ever says the first one.

Vayishbot, from shabat, to cease, desist, stop an activity. It is the root behind the noun Sabbath itself, and it says nothing about fatigue or recovery. Exodus 20:11, the fourth commandment, describes the same day with a different verb, vayanach, from nuach, to settle down or rest. Genesis 2 does not use that verb.

English rest almost always implies tiredness relieved. Hebrew shabat is a verb of stopping, applied here to a God the text never says grew tired. One English word covers a distinction the Hebrew draws across two different books of the Torah.

Track a key verb across its first occurrence and its most famous one. Genesis 2 and Exodus 20 describe the same seventh day with two different Hebrew verbs, and no English Bible has ever needed two different words to say it.

No real dispute over the English gloss; rested is the natural word in both places. What matters here is that the vocabulary shift between Genesis 2 and Exodus 20 disappears once both are translated rest, and it is worth knowing before building an argument about divine fatigue on either verse.

versions.s: Neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. Shachat most literally means pit, the grave, with decay only as an extension.

b.t: Most versions read corruption or decay, following the extended, figurative sense the Septuagint's Greek diaphthora already carries and that Peter's speech in Acts 2:27 explicitly builds its resurrection argument on.

English corruption names a process, decaying, rotting. Hebrew shachat more literally names a place, the pit or grave itself. Saying someone will not see the pit is a slightly different claim from saying they will not experience decay, though the two ideas sit close enough together that the shift from one sense to the other carries real theological weight.

Shachat's root sense is pit, the grave as a physical location; its extended, figurative sense as corruption or decay is a natural association, since a body left in a pit decays, but it is genuinely a step beyond the word's most literal meaning. The Septuagint translates it with Greek diaphthora, decay or corruption, and Peter's sermon in Acts 2:27, 31 builds directly on that Greek sense to argue Jesus's body did not decay in the tomb, an argument that depends on reading shachat through its Greek translation's extended sense rather than its bare Hebrew literal one.

English corruption commits to the figurative, decay-focused sense; a more literal English rendering, the pit or the grave, would describe David's hope in terms of place rather than process, a real difference in emphasis that the New Testament's own use of this verse leans into rather than flattens.

A New Testament argument that depends on one specific sense of an Old Testament word is worth checking twice: is that sense the word's most literal one, or an extension the Greek translation makes more explicit than the Hebrew does on its own? Both can be legitimate, but they are not identical claims.

Corruption or decay follows the Septuagint and the New Testament's own argument, reading the verse as a resurrection promise about the body not decaying. The pit or the grave keeps closer to shachat's most literal Hebrew sense, a hope about not remaining in the place of the dead, which decay is naturally associated with but is not, strictly, the same claim.

versions.s: I am the Almighty God. El Shaddai, a title whose root meaning is genuinely uncertain.

b.t: Every version reads Almighty God, a strong, confident English translation supplying a settled sense the Hebrew word's own etymology does not actually have.

Almighty is confident, clear English. Shaddai's own root is not confident or clear at all; serious scholars have proposed it comes from words for a mountain, for a breast, and for violent overpowering, three pictures of God's power that would each shape the sentence differently if any one were certain.

Shaddai's derivation is disputed among three live proposals: from Akkadian shadu, mountain, giving God of the mountain, ancient imagery of strength and permanence; from Hebrew shad, breast, giving a nourishing, sustaining God, an image some scholars connect to Jacob's later blessing at Genesis 49:25, blessings of the breasts and of the womb; or from the root shadad, to overpower or destroy, giving a God of overwhelming might. A later Jewish tradition reads it instead as a compound, sha, who, plus dai, is sufficient, giving the all-sufficient one, but this is a homiletical reading of the sound rather than a linguistic derivation.

English Almighty commits to one general sense, overwhelming power, that happens to fit the shadad proposal reasonably well but flattens the genuinely live possibility that the name instead pictures God as a mountain or as a nurturing, breast-like source of sustenance, pictures Almighty does not evoke at all.

When a divine name's etymology is genuinely disputed among proposals that shape entirely different pictures of God, translating it with one confident English word settles a question scholarship has not settled. Hold the translation more loosely than its confident sound suggests.

Almighty is the traditional and functional English rendering, generically capturing power without committing to any one etymology. Each specific proposal, mountain, breast, or overpowering, produces a genuinely different mental picture of what this particular covenant scene is emphasizing about God's character.
אֵל שַׁדַּי El Shaddai · H410 + H7706

versions.s: Over Edom will I cast out my shoe. A legal gesture claiming ownership, the same custom used to finalize a transaction at Ruth 4:7.

b.t: Every version reads cast out my shoe or throw my sandal, accurately translating the gesture but without necessarily explaining that it names a specific, recognized ancient legal custom rather than a colorful metaphor invented for this poem alone.

Imagine a culture where signing a deed involved physically removing your shoe and handing it to the other party, a small ritual gesture that meant something specific and binding. Casting a shoe over a territory in this psalm performs the same kind of formal claim, not a random insult but a recognized legal act.

Casting or removing a shoe functioned as a formal gesture of transferring or claiming property rights, most explicitly explained at Ruth 4:7-8, where a shoe is removed to finalize a land transaction between kinsmen. Applying the same gesture to Edom in this military psalm claims the territory the way a shoe-casting would finalize any other property claim, a specific legal idiom repurposed for national conquest.

English cast out my shoe reads as an odd, perhaps contemptuous gesture with no built-in explanation, so a reader has no way to connect it to the specific, documented legal custom Ruth 4:7 explains in detail, a connection that turns a strange image into a recognizable formal claim.

When an unusual physical gesture appears in poetry, check whether a narrative passage elsewhere explains the same gesture in a legal or social context. Ruth 4:7's explicit explanation of shoe-removal is exactly the kind of key that unlocks this psalm's otherwise puzzling image.

Cast out my shoe is not seriously disputed as the literal rendering. What the translation leaves out is the legal background, explained directly at Ruth 4:7, that turns what looks like an arbitrary insult into a specific, formal claim of ownership over Edom.
אַשְׁלִיךְ נַעֲלִי ashlich na'ali (cast my shoe) · H7993 / H5275

src: The shoe-removal legal custom explained directly: Ruth 4:7-8
The same custom for renouncing a levirate obligation: Deuteronomy 25:9

versions.s: Melchizedek, king of Salem. His name means king of righteousness; Salem means peace.

b.t: Every version reads Melchizedek and Salem as bare proper names, transliterated, since neither carries any built-in meaning once rendered into English letters.

Imagine a story where a stranger named **Justice** arrives from the city of **Peace**, and later readers treat both names as meaningful rather than coincidental. That is exactly the case Hebrews later makes about Melchizedek, and it only works if you know what his name and city mean in the original language.

Melchizedek is built from melech, king, and tsedek, righteousness, giving king of righteousness, while Salem, shalem, shares its root with shalom, peace, giving king of peace, or king of Salem read doubly. Hebrews 7:2 explicitly draws out both meanings, treating the king-priest's very name and title as prefiguring the righteousness and peace later associated with the Messiah, an argument that depends entirely on the reader knowing what the Hebrew names mean.

English transliterates both Melchizedek and Salem as bare proper nouns, so a reader meeting Hebrews 7's argument about righteousness and peace can't tell where those concepts come from unless someone explains that the names themselves are doing the work.

When a name is significant enough that a later biblical writer stops to explain its meaning, as Hebrews does here, treat that explanation as confirmation that Hebrew names throughout Scripture are regularly meant to be heard, not simply used as labels.

Melchizedek and Salem draw no real disagreement among translators as proper names; there is no live alternative rendering. What matters here is that the meaning behind both names, preserved and explained in Hebrews 7:2, stays otherwise completely inaccessible to a reader working only from the English text of Genesis.

versions.s: Peace. Wholeness and completeness, not merely the absence of conflict.

b.t: Every version reads peace, or well-being and prosperity in some contexts.
**All settled.** **Everything's sorted.** English says wholeness with phrases rather than with a noun.
Shalom is from a root meaning complete or whole. It covers physical safety, health, prosperity, and right relationship. Asking after someone's shalom is asking whether everything is as it should be.
English peace inherited the narrower Greek sense through the Septuagint and Latin, and means mostly the absence of war.
Greeting words carry a culture's idea of what a good state is. They are worth looking up in any language.
Peace is the majority rendering; well-being and prosperity appear where peace would be plainly wrong.

versions.s: Hear, O Israel. In Hebrew, hearing that does not change anything is not hearing.

b.t: Versions divide on the last clause. Some read the LORD our God, the LORD is one. Others read the LORD is our God, the LORD alone. The JPS reads the LORD alone. The difference is whether the verse is about God's oneness or about Israel's exclusive loyalty.

**Are you listening to me?** A parent saying that to a child is not asking about the child's ears. English already has a sense of hear that includes doing what you were told, and you use it without noticing. Hebrew has only that sense.

Shema means to hear, to listen, to obey, with no boundary between them. Hebrew has no separate verb for obey; it uses this one. So the command is not asking for attention, it is asking for compliance, and the name the whole prayer is known by is that verb. The closing clause has four Hebrew words and no verb, which is why translators have to supply one and why the two readings both work.

English split hearing from obeying. Once you have two verbs, the first one becomes optional and the second becomes the demand. In Hebrew you cannot obey without hearing or hear without obeying, because there is nothing else to be.
When a Hebrew command uses a verb of perception, check whether the language has a separate verb for the response. Where it does not, the perception verb is already the command.

One LORD makes the verse a statement about God's nature and has fifteen hundred years of Christian reading behind it. The LORD alone makes it a demand for exclusive allegiance, fits the covenant context of Deuteronomy, and is the reading Jewish tradition largely carries. Both are grammatically available because the Hebrew has no verb in the clause.
