versions.s: To work it and keep it. The same two verbs describe the Levites guarding the tabernacle.

b.t: Every version reads some pair like work and keep, till and keep, or cultivate and guard. None can show that the identical pair recurs elsewhere as a fixed phrase for priestly duty.

**He tends the garden.** **He guards the temple.** English keeps those as two different jobs done by two different kinds of people. This verse uses the same two verbs for Adam that a later book uses for priests on duty.

Abad, to work or serve, and shamar, to keep or guard, appear together describing Adam's task in the garden. The same two verbs appear together describing the Levites' duty toward the tabernacle at Numbers 3:7-8 and 18:5-6, and shamar alone covers guarding it from intruders at Numbers 1:53. The garden is being described in the vocabulary later used for sanctuary service.

English work and keep are ordinary household words. They carry none of the specialized, cultic resonance the same two verbs carry when the same corpus later uses them for tabernacle duty, so the priestly overtone of Adam's job is simply not visible in translation.

A common-sounding word pair can be a technical phrase elsewhere in the same body of literature. Before assuming ordinary vocabulary, check whether the same combination recurs in a specialized context.

There is no dispute about the plain gloss, work and keep. The disagreement is how much weight to put on the Numbers parallel, whether the echo is a deliberate signal that Eden is being described as sanctuary space, or a coincidence of two common verbs appearing together twice.

versions.s: The heaven and the earth. Not two items. One idea named by its opposite ends.

b.t: All versions read the heavens and the earth. None flags the construction, and none needs to, because English has the same figure.

**They searched high and low.** Nobody thinks two altitudes were searched. **She read it cover to cover.** Naming the two ends is how English says everything in between, and you have never once stopped to notice.

This is a merism: two opposite terms standing for the whole. Hebrew uses it constantly. The phrase does not mean sky plus ground. It means the entire ordered cosmos, and Hebrew had no single word for that.
English does have this figure, which is why nothing is lost. The problem is that English readers treat biblical phrases as technical and stop hearing the figure they use themselves every day.
A pair of opposites joined by and is usually one idea, not two. Test it by asking whether the writer meant to exclude the middle. If not, you have a merism.
Nothing to choose. This entry is here because readers argue about what heaven means as though it were a separate item being inventoried, rather than half of a single figure of speech.

versions.s: A tower whose top may reach unto heaven. Standard ancient building-inscription language, not a literal engineering claim.

b.t: Every version reads reach unto heaven, or reach into the heavens, as a literal-sounding architectural boast, since English has no equivalent stock phrase from ancient building inscriptions to signal that this was a known formula rather than a fresh claim.

When a modern city calls its tallest building a **skyscraper**, nobody thinks it literally scrapes the sky. Ancient Mesopotamian temple towers, ziggurats, were routinely described in royal inscriptions with the same kind of formulaic exaggeration, reaching to heaven, and Genesis is using their own language against them.

Ziggurats, the stepped temple towers of Mesopotamia, were regularly described in their own dedicatory inscriptions with towers whose head reaches to heaven, standard temple-building language expressing the tower's function as a bridge between the human and divine realms, not a literal claim about altitude. Genesis 11:4 borrows this exact convention, and the builders' accompanying goal, let us make us a name, plays against the divine naming and blessing language of the chapters just before it, humanity securing its own reputation rather than receiving one.

English readers, unfamiliar with Mesopotamian building-inscription conventions, hear reach unto heaven as unique hyperbole invented for this story, when it is in fact the text quoting a genre its original audience would have recognized immediately, the exact vocabulary of the civilization Babel is criticizing.

Before reading a phrase as this story's own invention, check whether it was stock language in the surrounding ancient culture. Genesis frequently borrows the vocabulary of the civilizations it is critiquing and turns that vocabulary against them.

Reach unto heaven is the uncontested sense of the Hebrew in every version. What English cannot supply on its own is the recognition that this is a quoted convention from Mesopotamian temple-building inscriptions, which changes the verse from an isolated boast into a pointed piece of cultural mimicry.

versions.s: Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed. The Hebrew word order is a mirror around the center.

b.t: Every version reads whoever sheds man's blood, by man his blood shall be shed, correctly following the sense, but English sentence order, subject before verb, cannot reproduce a mirror shape the way Hebrew's more flexible word order can.

English can say **the punishment fits the crime**, but that is commentary, a sentence about the sentence. Hebrew builds the fit directly into word order: sheds, blood, man, man, blood, shed, the same words running forward and then backward around a hinge in the middle.

The Hebrew runs shofekh dam ha'adam, ba'adam damo yishafekh: sheds blood-of-man, by-man his-blood shall-be-shed. The verb for shedding opens the first half and closes the second, the noun for blood and the noun for man swap positions around the center, a structure grammarians call a chiasm, an A-B-C-C'-B'-A' pattern that visually and aurally enacts the very reciprocity, blood for blood, that the sentence is announcing.

English word order is comparatively fixed, subject-verb-object, so it cannot rearrange itself into a mirror shape the way Hebrew's freer word order allows here. A translation can state the principle of equal retribution but cannot make the sentence's shape perform it the way the Hebrew does.

Look for chiastic word order whenever a verse states a principle of exact correspondence, reciprocity, or reversal. Hebrew narrative and law use mirrored word order as a rhetorical device in its own right, not merely as a stylistic accident, and it rarely survives translation intact.

The legal content itself isn't contested; every version agrees on the sense. What is lost is entirely formal: the chiastic shape itself, which is not a matter of word choice but of an arrangement English syntax is not free enough to reproduce.

versions.s: By sevens, seven and seven. The Hebrew just repeats the numeral; English has to add a preposition to get the same sense.

b.t: Every version reads by sevens or seven pairs, correctly, for clean animals, against two, two of a kind, three verses earlier at 6:19-20 for animals generally. Read carelessly in translation, the two instructions look like a straightforward contradiction; read together, sevens for the animals fit for sacrifice, twos as the baseline for every kind, they resolve as one instruction refining the other rather than clashing with it.

Hebrew can say a distributive the way a coach says **two, two, two**, walking down a line splitting people into pairs. Just repeat the number. English cannot do this without inserting a word like **by** or **each**, so shivah shivah becomes by sevens, a translation that adds a word the Hebrew never needed.

Shivah shivah, literally seven seven, is simple reduplication of the numeral used to express a distributive sense, seven of each. Hebrew forms distributives this way elsewhere, repeating a number or a noun rather than adding a preposition, a pattern with no direct grammatical equivalent in English syntax.

English has no bare-repetition distributive; two two on its own does not read as a grammatical construction the way shivah shivah does in Hebrew, so translators must supply by or each, adding a word that has no counterpart in the Hebrew text itself.

When you meet a doubled Hebrew word functioning as one grammatical unit, check whether it is marking a distributive sense before assuming it is simple emphasis, and read instructions that seem to conflict across nearby verses as a single set of directions before assuming a contradiction.

By sevens is the correct and unavoidable English rendering, and no version disputes it. The apparent tension with the two-of-a-kind instruction at 6:19-20 is a matter of reading both verses as one coherent set of instructions, sevens for clean animals headed for sacrifice, twos as the general rule, rather than a genuine grammatical problem.

versions.s: I have given to thee one portion above thy brethren. Literally, one shechem, the same word as the city Shechem.

b.t: Every version reads one portion, or a similar generic English phrase, correctly conveying the sense of an extra share but with no way to preserve the pun on the place name Shechem.

Imagine an inheritance clause that says **I leave you one extra Boston**, using a place name as a unit of measurement. That is roughly what Jacob's Hebrew does here, naming an amount of land with the same word as a specific city his sons had once conquered by the sword.

Shechem ordinarily means shoulder or a ridge of high ground, and functions here as a play on words with the city of Shechem, the site of Simeon and Levi's violent reprisal after Dinah's assault at Genesis 34. Jacob's phrase, one shechem, can be read as simply one portion or, more pointedly, as a wry reference to the very city his sons had taken by force, now formally assigned to Joseph's line.

English portion is a generic word with no double meaning at all, so the pun connecting Joseph's extra inheritance to the specific, bloody history of Shechem in chapter 34 disappears completely once shechem is translated as a plain, place-name-free noun.

When an inheritance or blessing names a quantity using a word that also happens to be a place name from earlier in the same book, consider that the connection may be deliberate rather than coincidental, especially where the place carries real narrative weight, as Shechem does here.

Portion is the agreed general sense in every version. The pun connecting it to the city of Shechem is, by the Anchor Bible's own description, an obscure allusion, acknowledged but not fully explained by any major commentary, which is itself part of why it is worth flagging rather than resolving.

versions.s: Name, and with it reputation, character and authority.

b.t: Every version reads name.
**He has a name in this town.** English still has the reputation sense and uses it constantly.

Shem covers the label, the reputation attached to it, and the authority it carries. Making a name at Babel, a good name in Proverbs, and calling on the name of the LORD are all the same noun doing different work.
English name kept the reputation sense in idiom but lost it in ordinary use, so the biblical phrases sound formal rather than natural.
When a common noun appears in several fixed biblical phrases, the phrases are usually exploiting a range the English word has lost.
Name is universal.
שֵׁם shem · H8034

versions.s: The greater light and the lesser light. Not shemesh, sun, and yareach, moon, the same words as the sun-god and moon-god.

b.t: Every version reads the greater light and the lesser light, correctly, but nothing in the English signals that Hebrew had two perfectly ordinary, available words, shemesh and yareach, for sun and moon that the verse conspicuously does not use.

Imagine a creation account that carefully avoids saying **the sun** and **the moon** by name, calling them only **the big glowing thing** and **the smaller glowing thing**, specifically because those proper names doubled as the names of rival gods everyone around you worshipped. That is exactly what this verse does.

Shemesh, sun, was also the name of Shamash, the Mesopotamian sun-god; yareach, moon, shares its root with Yarikh, the Canaanite moon-god. Genesis 1 calls them simply hama'or hagadol and hama'or hakaton, the greater light and the lesser light, functional, almost deliberately unglamorous descriptions, stripping them of any name that could double as a divine title and reducing them to created objects doing a job, marking appointed times, rather than deities to be worshipped.

English greater light and lesser light already sound intentionally plain, but without knowing that Hebrew had perfectly good, ordinary proper names available and pointedly did not use them, an English reader cannot see that this is a deliberate polemic against the sun and moon worship of Israel's neighbors, not merely a poetic or repetitive style choice.

When a text conspicuously avoids an obvious, available word, ask what that word would have implied if used. Genesis 1's avoidance of shemesh and yareach here is a calculated theological move, not an accident of vocabulary or a coincidence of style.

No translation dispute over greater light and lesser light as accurate renderings. What is worth flagging is that the deliberate avoidance of the ordinary, available words for sun and moon, precisely because those words were also divine names, is a polemical statement entirely dependent on knowing what words were not used.

versions.s: So he giveth his beloved sleep. Or: he gives to his beloved even in their sleep, provision without anxious toil.

b.t: The King James and many traditional versions read he giveth his beloved sleep, treating rest as the gift itself. Other versions and commentators read he provides for his beloved even in their sleep, or a similar phrase, treating sleep as the circumstance during which provision happens rather than the provision itself.

English he gives his beloved sleep sounds like a straightforward gift, rest itself as the present. A different, equally defensible reading treats sleep as describing when the gift happens rather than what the gift is: God provides everything his beloved need even while, effortlessly, they are asleep, a claim about provision without striving rather than a claim about the gift of rest specifically.

The Hebrew construction genuinely supports both readings, and the ambiguity is old enough that the Septuagint and Latin Vulgate already handle it with some interpretive looseness rather than settling it definitively. The verse's larger point, contrasted with rising early and staying up late in anxious toil, works either way: whether the gift is sleep itself or effortless provision that continues even during sleep, both readings emphasize God's care operating apart from human striving.

English he giveth his beloved sleep commits to one specific gift, rest; the alternative reading commits instead to a broader claim about provision happening automatically, without effort, even during sleep, a difference in emphasis between what is given and how effortlessly it arrives.

When a beloved, quotable English phrase turns out to rest on a genuinely ambiguous Hebrew construction, hold the familiar wording a little more loosely. Sometimes the memorable translation has settled one of two equally live readings simply by being first, or by being more quotable.

He giveth his beloved sleep is the more famous, more quotable English rendering, treating rest as the specific gift described. He provides for his beloved even while they sleep broadens the claim to effortless provision generally, a reading some scholars find better fits the psalm's contrast with anxious toil in the surrounding verses.

versions.s: I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Sheol, whose precise nature the Old Testament never fully defines.

b.t: The King James mostly reads grave or hell depending on context, inconsistently by modern standards. Modern versions frequently leave sheol untranslated or render it grave, avoiding hell's loaded connotations.

English hell carries centuries of specific theological content, fire, judgment, eternal punishment, that the Old Testament word sheol simply does not carry the same way. Grave is closer but sounds like a single burial plot rather than a shared realm every dead person, righteous or wicked, is described as going to.

Sheol describes a shadowy, shared destination for the dead throughout most of the Old Testament, with both righteous and wicked figures described as going there, and without the later, more developed distinctions between a place of comfort and a place of punishment that appear only in later Second Temple Jewish and New Testament writings. Its exact nature, literal grave, collective underworld, or something more like death personified, is genuinely debated and may not have been fully fixed even within the Old Testament's own usage.

English hell imports theological content, eternal conscious punishment, that developed later than most Old Testament usage of sheol actually supports; English grave undersells the word's broader, communal, underworld-like associations elsewhere. Neither English word maps cleanly onto the Hebrew term's own, somewhat fluid range.

Resist reading later, more developed afterlife theology back into an Old Testament word like sheol. Track how the word is actually used across its many Old Testament occurrences before assuming it means what a much later doctrine of hell means.

Grave keeps the reference concrete and avoids importing later theology, but undersells sheol's broader, shared-underworld sense. Hell imports specific, later doctrinal content the Hebrew word does not clearly carry on its own. Leaving sheol untranslated, increasingly common in modern versions, is the most honest option, though it asks more of the reader.

versions.s: The realm of the dead. Not hell, and not nothing.

b.t: The King James reads hell, grave or pit. Modern versions usually transliterate Sheol or read the realm of the dead.
One word rendered three ways in one Bible produces three different ideas, and nothing on the page tells you they were ever one word.
Sheol is where the dead go, righteous and wicked alike. Jacob expects to go there mourning. It is not a place of punishment in the Old Testament and it is not annihilation either.
English hell carries a fully developed later doctrine, and grave carries none of the realm sense. Neither fits.
When modern versions transliterate a word the King James translated, the transliteration is usually an admission that no English word works.

versions.s: A Shiggaion of David. A label used only twice in the whole Bible, with no confirmed meaning.

b.t: Every version simply transliterates Shiggaion, since there is no settled English equivalent, treating it the way Selah is treated, as a technical term left in its original form rather than translated.

Imagine a musical score marked with a term you find in only one other piece of sheet music ever written, no dictionary, no manual, nothing to compare it against except that one other piece. That is Shiggaion's situation: two data points, and centuries of guessing between them.

Shiggaion appears in the heading of this psalm and, in its plural form shigionoth, in the heading of Habakkuk 3, a prayer explicitly set to music. Proposed derivations connect it to a root meaning to wander or reel, suggesting a wild, emotionally intense, perhaps irregular musical or poetic form, a dithyramb or rhapsody in the loose sense of impassioned, less formally structured song, though no occurrence outside these two headings exists to confirm the guess.

English readers meet Shiggaion as an untranslated label at the top of a psalm, easy to skip past as mere technical scaffolding, with no way to sense how genuinely uncertain its meaning is, resting on only two attestations in the whole Bible.

A technical heading transliterated rather than translated, especially one this rare, is worth pausing on rather than skimming past. The translator's silence is itself information about how much, or how little, is actually known.

No translation is offered by any major version. The proposed sense, an intense, perhaps musically irregular or emotionally wild composition, is a reasonable guess from the proposed root and from the psalm's own agitated content, but remains unconfirmed by any third occurrence.

entries.title: shiloh
entries.summary: Shiloh, an epithet of the Messiah
entries.def: Shiloh, an epithet of the Messiah

versions.s: Until Shiloh come. A word read as a place, a title, or a messianic figure, and translators still disagree.

b.t: Some versions transliterate Shiloh as a place name. Others read until he comes to whom it belongs or until tribute comes to him, treating the Hebrew as a title or a corrupted phrase rather than a proper noun. The Septuagint avoids the term Shiloh altogether, translating around it.

Picture a single word in a will that could mean **until the town**, **until it is rightfully his**, or **until the promised heir**, three entirely different legal outcomes hanging on one ambiguous term. Shiloh in this verse creates exactly that kind of interpretive fork.

The Masoretic vowel pointing supports reading Shiloh as a proper name, but an alternative reading divides the same or very similar consonants into shelloh, that which belongs to him, or ad ki yavo shiloh could reflect a slightly different original phrase now obscured by scribal transmission. Jewish and Christian interpreters alike have long read the verse messianically, a ruler to whom ultimate authority belongs, while others read Shiloh as the town in Ephraim later associated with the tabernacle, an intelligible but contextually awkward reading given the verse is about Judah's own line.

English translations must commit to treating Shiloh as either a proper name or a spelled-out title, decisions that produce visibly different English sentences, so a reader of any single translation has no way to see how contested the underlying Hebrew word actually is.

When a single word anchors a famous prophetic verse and ancient translations, the Septuagint included, visibly struggle with or avoid it, treat that struggle as evidence of real difficulty in the source text, not merely as translators failing to agree on an otherwise clear word.

Shiloh as a place name is grammatically straightforward but sits awkwardly in a blessing focused on Judah's own future rule. He to whom it belongs, reading the same consonants as a title, fits the immediate context of ongoing rule and has driven the dominant messianic reading in both Jewish and Christian tradition, though it requires reparsing the consonants against the Masoretic vowel points.

versions.s: They digged down a wall. Or: they hamstrung oxen. The consonants are the same; only the vowels, added centuries later, decide.

b.t: The King James reads wall, following the Vulgate's murum and the Targums. Most modern versions read oxen, following the Masoretic Text's own vowel pointing and the Septuagint's tauron, bull.

Imagine a sentence in a language written without vowels, where the same three letters could spell either **wall** or **ox** depending on how you say it aloud. That is exactly the situation here: shr can be read shor, ox, or shur, wall, and the Hebrew text as originally written does not settle which.

The consonantal text שור can be vocalized shor, ox, matching the Masoretic tradition's own pointing and the Septuagint's Greek, or shur, wall, matching the Vulgate and the Aramaic Targums. Since vowel points were added to the Hebrew text centuries after the consonants were fixed, this is a case where two ancient, respected translation traditions genuinely disagree on which vowels the unpointed consonants originally carried.

English wall and English ox are entirely different images, one a act of vandalism against property, the other a crippling act of violence against animals, so the translation a reader receives depends entirely on a vowel-pointing decision made centuries after the consonants themselves were fixed, a decision no English reader can see happening.

Remember that the earliest Hebrew text was consonants only; vowel points were a later addition, authoritative but not infallible. Where ancient versions split over the same consonants, as they do here, the ambiguity is genuine and older than any existing manuscript with vowels.

Wall follows the Vulgate and Targums and reads Simeon and Levi's violence as including property destruction. Oxen follows the Masoretic Text's own pointing and the Septuagint, reading the violence as extending to hamstringing livestock, itself a serious act of economic sabotage in the ancient world. Both are defensible from the same unpointed consonants.

versions.s: I will dwell in the house of the LORD. The consonants also allow I will return.

b.t: Every English version reads dwell. The footnotes in the NET and a handful of academic translations note the alternative.
Write **RD** and let a reader supply the vowels. Read, red, ride, rode, rude. Hebrew was written without vowels for centuries, and the marks that fix them were added long after the words were.

The Masoretic pointing, weshavti, actually parses most straightforwardly as a form of shuv, to return, giving I will return to the house of the LORD. The traditional dwell reading instead takes the word as built from yashav, to dwell or sit, the reading nearly every version and most of Jewish and Christian interpretive tradition has long assumed, even though the pointed form's more natural derivation is from shuv; Hebrew grammarians continue to debate how to explain the mismatch. The vowel points were added by the Masoretes between roughly the seventh and tenth centuries.
English has to print one word. There is no way to render a sentence that is undecided between dwelling and returning without a footnote.
Hebrew vowel points are a later layer. When a translation footnote offers a completely different verb rather than a different shade, the consonants are usually the reason.

Dwell has the ancient versions, the Septuagint included, and nearly universal traditional usage behind it, even though the pointed Hebrew form more naturally parses as shuv, return. Return follows the pointed consonants' more straightforward grammatical derivation and fits a psalm about being led back, but stays the minority reading precisely because dwell is so deeply established. Dwell remains the better-supported reading on tradition and versional evidence; the grammar of the pointing itself is the part that actually favors return.
שׁוּב shuv · H7725 / יָשַׁב yashav · H3427

Septuagint reads dwelling, supporting the Masoretic pointing

versions.s: It shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel. Same verb, four occurrences total, and bruise may be too gentle for either half.

b.t: The King James and many traditional versions read bruise for both halves. A growing number of modern versions read crush for the head-strike and strike or bite for the heel-strike, no longer using one English verb for both.

**She bruised her knee.** **He crushed the can.** English has to pick one verb and commit to a severity. The Hebrew verse uses one rare verb for both the fatal blow and the survivable one, and no single English word covers that whole range.

Shuph occurs only here, twice, and at Job 9:17 and Psalm 139:11, four occurrences in total, possibly spanning two distinct roots tangled together across them. The attested sense ranges from crush or bruise to a more violent strike or snap at. Because the same rare verb covers a lethal head-wound and a non-lethal heel-wound in one verse, translators have increasingly split it into two different English verbs to fit the two different outcomes, something the Hebrew itself does not do.

No single English verb plausibly covers both a fatal blow to the head and a survivable bite to the heel, the way one Hebrew verb apparently does. Any English rendering has to either flatten the difference with one soft word, as the King James does, or introduce an asymmetry between the two lines that the Hebrew's own choice of vocabulary does not make.

When one rare verb covers actions of very different severity in the same verse, resist the urge to supply two different English verbs to match the outcomes. That interpretive step may be reasonable, but it is commentary, not translation.

Bruise keeps a single, symmetrical verb for both halves, closer to what the Hebrew grammar actually presents. Crush and strike, or crush and bite, read theological weight into each half separately, which fits the traditional reading of the verse as the first promise of the serpent's defeat but goes beyond what shuph alone specifies.
שׁוּף shuph · H7779

src: Four occurrences: Genesis 3:15 (twice); Job 9:17; Psalm 139:11
The Septuagint renders both halves with the same Greek verb, tereo, to watch for or lie in wait against, a third image distinct from either bruise or crush
HALOT lists the attested range as crush, bruise, strike at

versions.s: Siloam, which is by interpretation, Sent. John stops to translate again.

b.t: Every version keeps the gloss, since it is in the text.
A writer who stops to translate a place name is telling you two things: what it means, and that he expects you not to know.

Siloam is from Hebrew shiloach, from the root to send. John glosses it apestalmenos, sent, which is the perfect participle of the verb he uses of Jesus being sent by the Father over forty times in this Gospel.
Nothing is lost. The connection between the gloss and John's vocabulary elsewhere is the part that has to be noticed rather than translated.
When a writer glosses a name, check whether the gloss uses vocabulary he uses elsewhere. The translation may be doing double duty.
The gloss is printed in every version.

entries.title: sitnah
entries.summary: Sitnah, the name of a well in Pal
entries.def: Sitnah, the name of a well in Pal

versions.s: He called the name of the well Sitnah. The same root behind the word Satan.

b.t: Every version transliterates Esek, Sitnah, and Rehoboth as bare place names, correctly, since none of the three carries built-in meaning once rendered in English letters.

Imagine naming a disputed parking spot **Accuser**, using the exact word your language later uses for a courtroom prosecutor or a cosmic adversary. English place names rarely carry that kind of loaded vocabulary. Hebrew does it constantly, and Sitnah is a clean example.

Esek, contention, from a root meaning to dispute; Sitnah, accusation or enmity, sharing its root with satan, the accuser, used of the adversarial figure in Job and Zechariah; and Rehoboth, room or open spaces, mark an escalation and then a resolution across the three well-naming episodes. Sitnah is not simply an unpleasant-sounding name; it is built from the same three consonants that later name the Hebrew Bible's chief adversarial figure.

English readers meet Esek, Sitnah, and Rehoboth as bare, interchangeable-sounding proper nouns, and nothing about the spelling lets them pick up that the second one carries the same loaded root as a major theological term used elsewhere in the same Bible.

When a place name in a dispute narrative sounds unusually pointed, check its root against other, more theologically weighted uses of the same consonants elsewhere in Scripture. Hebrew narrators frequently choose or record names precisely because of this kind of resonance.

Transliterating the three names draws no disagreement among translators. The connection between Sitnah and satan is a matter of shared Hebrew root, not a claim that this well dispute was itself supernatural; this note simply makes that shared vocabulary visible.
שִׂטְנָה Sitnah (cf. שָׂטָן satan) · H7856 / H7854

src: satan as accuser/adversary from the same root: Job 1:6-12; Zechariah 3:1-2
The escalation across all three well names: Genesis 26:20-22

versions.s: Dwelt among us. The verb is built on the word for tent, and the whole Old Testament is inside it.

b.t: Modern versions read dwelt, or lived, or made his dwelling. Some add a footnote reading tabernacled.

**He stayed with us** against **he pitched his tent with us.** The second one is a picture, not just a fact. If your family has camped in the same spot for forty years, the second sentence means something to you that the first does not. That is the difference here.

Eskenosen is from skene, tent. The related noun is what the Septuagint uses for the tabernacle, the tent where God's presence settled among Israel. The verse is not saying the Word moved into the neighbourhood. It is saying the tabernacle happened again, in a body.

English dwelt is a plain word with no architecture in it. There is no English verb meaning to pitch a tent and take up residence as the presence of God, so the allusion has to be carried by a footnote or lost.

Greek words built on concrete nouns often carry the noun with them. When a verb looks abstract in English, check what object it was built from, because the Septuagint may have been using that object for four hundred years already.
No dispute about meaning. The dispute is whether to write tabernacled, which is precise and archaic, or dwelt, which is readable and flat. Every major version has chosen readable.
σκηνόω skenoo · G4637

src: Skene in the Septuagint for the tabernacle: Exodus 25-40 throughout
Revelation 21:3 uses the same verb of the final dwelling of God with humanity

versions.s: Body. The word Paul chooses for the church, and deliberately not the other one.

b.t: Every version reads body. No dispute.
**The body of the report.** **A body of water.** English uses the word for an organised whole without anyone thinking of anatomy.
Soma is the physical body and also an organised whole. Paul uses it positively throughout, including of the church and of the resurrection body, where sarx carries the negative weight.
English uses the word the same double way, so nothing is lost there. What is lost is the contrast with the other Greek word, which English flattens.
When two near-synonyms are used with opposite valence by the same writer, the pair is the argument. Read them together rather than separately.
Every English version reads body.
σῶμα soma · G4983

src: soma of the church: Romans 12:5; 1 Corinthians 12:12-27
soma of the resurrection body: 1 Corinthians 15:44

versions.s: To save. One Greek verb covers rescue from danger, healing from disease, and eternal salvation.

b.t: Versions read save, heal, or make well according to context. The same Greek verb is behind all of them.

**The lifeboat saved them.** **The surgeon saved her.** **He was saved.** English still uses one word for all three and only the last one sounds churchy, which tells you the drift is in the ear rather than the dictionary.
Sozo is used of rescue from drowning, of physical healing, and of salvation. Thy faith hath made thee whole and thy faith hath saved thee are the same Greek sentence.
English has the word but has narrowed its religious use so far that the overlap is invisible.
When one Greek word is rendered by several English words inside one Gospel, list the places. The range is usually the point the writer was making.
Save, heal and make well are all majority renderings in their own contexts and no version distinguishes them by a different Greek word, because there is not one.
σῴζω sozo · G4982

src: sozo of healing: Mark 5:34; 10:52; Luke 17:19
sozo of rescue: Matthew 8:25; 14:30
sozo of salvation: Romans 10:9; Ephesians 2:8

versions.s: Him hath God the Father sealed. A commercial and legal word for marking ownership.

b.t: Versions read sealed, set his seal on, or placed his seal of approval on.
**Stamped and signed.** A stamp says who stands behind this. It does not say the thing is shut.
Sphragizo is to affix a seal: to authenticate a document, to mark goods as owned, to certify. Paul uses it of believers being sealed with the Spirit. The sense is certification, not closure.
English seal kept the closure sense and largely lost the authentication one outside legal language.
When an English word has narrowed to one of two senses, check which sense the ancient world used more. Commercial vocabulary usually survives in papyri.
Most modern versions print set his seal on; the King James reads sealed.
σφραγίζω sphragizo · G4972

src: sphragizo of believers: 2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13; 4:30
Commercial use on goods and documents in the papyri
Revelation 7:3-8 uses it of marking

versions.s: Have no dealings with. A rare verb, and it may mean do not share vessels.

b.t: Versions read have no dealings with, do not associate with, or do not share things in common with.
A single-occurrence word is a word with no witnesses. You guess from the sentence and from whatever else the culture has left behind.

Sugchraomai occurs only here in the New Testament. The narrower reading is that Jews would not use vessels in common with Samaritans, which fits the scene exactly, since the dispute is about a drinking vessel.
There's no English verb for ritual non-sharing of utensils, so every rendering generalises to social avoidance, and the point about the cup is lost.
When a rare word sits in a clause explaining a scene, read it against the scene. The narrative is usually the best evidence available.
Do not associate with is the majority modern rendering; the narrower vessel reading appears in footnotes and commentaries.
συγχράομαι sugchraomai · G4798

versions.s: God created great whales. The Hebrew word, tannin, elsewhere names the mythological sea-monster Leviathan.

b.t: Most versions read great whales, great sea creatures, or great sea monsters. The Septuagint translates tannin as dragon everywhere else it appears, but shifts to a more generic sea-monster word here, following the calmer context.

Imagine a creation story that lists **the dragon** among the ordinary animals made that day, with no more drama than the fish and birds around it, specifically to say that the terrifying sea-monster other nations feared and worshipped is, in this account, just another creature. That is what tannin is doing here.

Tannin, used here of ordinary sea creatures God creates on day five, is the same word applied to Leviathan and Rahab at Isaiah 27:1 and 51:9, mythological chaos-monsters associated in the wider ancient Near East, especially in Ugaritic literature, with primeval cosmic rebellion against a creator god. By calling these creatures tanninim and placing them calmly among the fish and birds God creates by simple speech, Genesis 1 strips any cosmic rivalry from the picture: the sea monster is not a threat God must defeat in combat, as in neighboring creation myths, but an animal God straightforwardly makes.

English great whales or sea creatures sounds entirely zoological, with no hint that the underlying word is the same one used elsewhere for a mythological chaos-monster; the polemical point, that even the most feared cosmic symbol of chaos is just another creature here, depends entirely on recognizing the shared Hebrew word.

When Genesis 1 names something with vocabulary that elsewhere carries mythological weight, tehom the deep, tannin the sea monster, read the calm, list-like context as doing real theological work: taking a term charged with meaning in the surrounding culture and deliberately defusing it.

Great whales domesticates the word for a modern audience unfamiliar with its mythological associations. Great sea monsters or sea dragons keeps the connection to Leviathan and Rahab visible, letting the verse's quiet polemic against neighboring creation myths register the way it likely did for its original audience.

versions.s: The fountains of the great deep, and the windows of heaven. The word for deep is a cousin of the name of a Babylonian sea-goddess.

b.t: Every version reads the deep or the great deep, an ordinary common noun with no personal or mythological overtone in English at all.

Imagine two neighboring languages both having a word that traces back to the same ancient root for the sea, and one of those languages later personifies that word as a goddess while the other keeps it as an ordinary noun for deep water. That is roughly the relationship between Hebrew tehom and Babylonian Tiamat.

Tehom, the deep, at Genesis 1:2 and again here at 7:11, is a recognized linguistic cognate of Akkadian tiamtu, the ocean, personified in Babylonian myth as the goddess Tiamat, whom Marduk defeats in the creation epic Enuma Elish. Older scholarship argued Genesis preserves a demythologized version of that combat story; more recent comparative Semitic work argues both words simply descend independently from a common Proto-Semitic word for the deep, without one being a suppressed retelling of the other. The windows of heaven, arubbot, opening alongside the deep pictures the flood as creation's waters, once held back at Genesis 1, breaking loose again.

English deep is a plain descriptive noun carrying no mythological freight; a reader has no way to hear a cognate relationship to a Babylonian goddess's name sitting behind the ordinary English word, nor to notice that the flood is described as creation's original waters returning.

A linguistic cognate between a biblical term and a name from a neighboring mythology is real evidence of shared ancient vocabulary, but it is not by itself proof of borrowing a myth. Keep those two claims, shared word history and shared story, separate, and check which one a given scholar is actually arguing.

Every version renders it deep without argument. The live scholarly question is how much weight to put on the tehom/Tiamat connection: strong echo of a suppressed combat myth, or simply two related Semitic languages independently using an inherited word for the sea.

versions.s: It is finished. One word, in a tense that means done and still in force.

b.t: Every version reads it is finished or it is completed. None can carry the tense, and none tries.
**I locked the door.** That tells you about a moment. **The door is locked.** That tells you about now. Imagine one verb form that says both at once, and imagine it being the last thing someone says.

Tetelestai is perfect tense, passive voice, third person singular. The Greek perfect describes a completed action whose result stands in the present. A popular preaching tradition also holds that tetelestai was written across settled commercial accounts of the period, meaning paid in full; that specific claim traces to a misreading of ancient tax receipts, whose actual abbreviation is a different word, tetelonetai, toll or tax paid, and current papyrological work treats paid in full as a popular legend rather than established usage.

There's no single English word for a completed act with a standing result. It is finished is a present statement about a past act, which is nearer than most languages get, and still two ideas stapled together.
Greek perfect tense is the one aspect English genuinely cannot carry. When a verse feels like it is saying more than the words do, check whether the verb is perfect.

The grammar itself is not in question; every version makes the same perfect-tense compromise. The popular commercial paid in full gloss, often used to make that compromise vivid, is itself disputed and probably should not be leaned on.
τελέω teleo · G5055

src: The Greek perfect described in Fanning, Verbal Aspect in New Testament Greek
teleo and telos share a root; compare eis telos at John 13:1
The 'paid in full' commercial-receipt claim reassessed against the actual papyri, which read tetelonetai (toll/tax paid), not tetelestai

versions.s: He loved them unto the end. To the finish, or to the utmost.

b.t: The King James and ESV read to the end. The NIV reads the full extent of his love. The NASB reads to the end and footnotes perfectly.
**She went to the end.** Until it was over, or as far as anyone could go? English has the same double meaning and usually leaves you to work it out from context. Here the context does not settle it.
Eis telos can be temporal, to the last, or intensive, completely, utterly. Telos itself means both a finish and a goal, which is the same range that makes Romans 10:4 an argument.
English end carries both, but the phrase to the end has hardened into the temporal sense, so a reader gets one of the two for free and never sees the other.
When you meet a word twice in a tool, the second meeting is the test. You already know telos splits between finish and goal. Watch it split again here.

Temporal fits the narrative, which is moving toward the cross. Intensive fits the foot-washing that immediately follows, which is an act of love taken to its limit. Both are defensible and the Greek allows either.
εἰς τέλος eis telos · G5056

src: eis telos temporal: Matthew 10:22; Mark 13:13
eis telos intensive: Luke 18:5; 1 Thessalonians 2:16
The foot-washing in John 13:2-17 is the immediate context

versions.s: Christ is the end of the law. Stopped, or arrived at? The Greek noun means both.

b.t: The King James, ESV and NASB read end. The NIV reads culmination. The CSB reads end of the law with a footnote. The NET reads end with a substantial note.

**The end of the road.** Is that where the road stops existing, or the place it was taking you all along? Same three words, and only the rest of the sentence tells you. English has this ambiguity and rarely notices it.

Telos means a finish, and it also means a goal, a purpose, the point at which something arrives at what it was for. English end has both senses too, which is why the rendering survives, but modern English weights it heavily toward termination.
English end still technically carries both, so no translator is forced to choose. But the reader chooses without knowing there was a choice, and most readers now hear termination.
Some English words still carry the full range of the Greek and have quietly narrowed in usage. Those are the dangerous ones, because nothing in the text looks odd enough to make you check.

End as termination makes the verse a statement that the law's era is over. End as goal makes it a statement that the law was pointing here all along and has arrived. The word carries both, the context in Romans 9 and 10 is argued both ways, and this is one of the genuine open questions in Pauline scholarship rather than a case where one side is careless.
τέλος telos · G5056

src: Telos as goal or outcome: 1 Timothy 1:5; James 5:11; 1 Peter 1:9
Telos as termination: Matthew 24:6; Mark 3:26
The literature on Romans 10:4 divides along exactly this line; NET translators' note at the verse summarises both

versions.s: Rachel had stolen the images. Household gods whose possession, per comparable ancient legal custom, could carry inheritance rights.

b.t: Every version reads household gods, idols, or images, correctly identifying the objects religiously but giving no indication of the possible legal weight their possession carried in the surrounding culture.

Imagine stealing not a family heirloom but the actual deed to an estate, an object whose possession functions as legal proof of who inherits. That is closer to what Rachel may have been doing than simply taking a religious keepsake, based on comparable legal documents from a nearby ancient culture.

Teraphim, household idols or figurines, appear in a family property dispute here, and a once-influential reading of tablets from Nuzi, describing family and inheritance law in roughly the same broad region and era, argued that possessing a father-in-law's household gods could under certain circumstances support a claim to his estate. Read against that background, Rachel's theft and Laban's urgent, week-long pursuit look less like anger over stolen trinkets and more like a dispute over inheritance and family headship. That specific inheritance-via-possession argument, associated with Cyrus Gordon, has since been challenged: Moshe Greenberg argued the Nuzi evidence points to family headship rather than a title to inheritance, and Karel van der Toorn has rejected the household-deity identification of teraphim more broadly, calling the standard Nuzi-based reading one-sided.

English household gods or idols names the religious category accurately but carries no hint of any possible legal function, so a reader is left unable to gauge why Laban's reaction is so disproportionately urgent unless told about the Nuzi background, itself now a debated reading, separately.

When an object's theft provokes a reaction that seems disproportionate to its apparent value, check whether comparable ancient Near Eastern legal or social custom assigned it a function beyond the obvious one, and check how settled that comparison still is. Teraphim here is a case where background documents change the stakes of an otherwise puzzling scene, but the specific legal argument built on them is itself contested.

Household gods as the basic sense of teraphim is not contested. The larger legal-custom reading, informed by Nuzi parallels rather than by the Hebrew text alone, adds a dimension to the scene that translation by itself cannot supply, but it is a dated proposal some specialists now reject rather than a settled background fact.
תְּרָפִים teraphim · H8655

src: Nuzi tablets on household gods and inheritance/family-headship rights: Cyrus Gordon's classic proposal
Laban's urgent pursuit: Genesis 31:22-23
Challenges to the inheritance reading: Moshe Greenberg, JBL 81 (1962); Karel van der Toorn on teraphim and household deities

entries.title: teshuqah
entries.where: teshuqah is tagged 3 times, across 2 books: genesis 2 · songofsolomon 1.

versions.s: Thy desire shall be to thy husband. Three occurrences in the whole Bible, and they do not agree.

b.t: Nearly all versions read desire. A minority tradition reads desire to control or contrary to, following an argument from the Genesis 4:7 parallel. The ESV moved to contrary to in 2016 and drew heavy criticism.

A word that turns up three times in an entire library is not defined, it is guessed at. If two of those three appearances point one way and the third points another, every dictionary entry for it is an argument wearing a definition's clothes.

Teshuqah occurs at Genesis 3:16, Genesis 4:7 and Song of Songs 7:10. At 4:7 sin's teshuqah is toward Cain and he must rule over it, using the same two words as here, which is what drives the control reading. At Song 7:10 it is plainly longing.
English desire covers longing, appetite and craving but not a bid for mastery. Whichever sense a translator picks, the other two occurrences start pulling against it.
Three occurrences is below the floor where a lexicon can report rather than argue. When a contested doctrine rests on a word this rare, that rarity is the first thing to say out loud.

Longing fits Song of Songs and the plain sense. Contrary to or a bid to control fits the Genesis 4:7 parallel and the ruling clause that follows. The parallel is genuinely close and the sample is genuinely tiny, which is why this is filed contested rather than decided.
תְּשׁוּקָה teshuqah · H8669

versions.s: Sin lieth at the door. Its desire is to thee, and thou shalt rule over it. The same crouching-word, and the same two words as 3:16.

b.t: Every English version reads lieth, croucheth, or is crouching, all correctly neutral. Almost none of the popular translations use anything that suggests an ambush or a personified threat, though one modern academic version, the New English Bible, does render it demon.

**The dog is lying by the door.** Harmless. Now imagine the word for lying also names a predator waiting in ambush at a doorway in a neighboring language and culture. Lieth sounds passive in English; the word behind it does not.

Rovets is a participle of the common verb for an animal lying down, but this personified use of sin as the subject crouching at a door closely resembles the Akkadian rabisu, a demon that lurks at thresholds to attack. Whether the Hebrew word is a deliberate echo of that image or simply the ordinary verb applied metaphorically is debated, but the doorway setting matches the Akkadian pattern closely. The same verse then reuses teshuqah, desire, and the verb mashal, rule over, the identical pairing used of the woman and the man at Genesis 3:16, this time offered to Cain as a warning rather than a sentence.

English lieth or crouches names a posture; it carries none of the threshold-demon association some scholars hear behind the Hebrew word, and English has no way to signal that the sentence structure repeats 3:16's marriage language word for word, since a reader would need to notice both verses share teshuqah and mashal in Hebrew to catch it at all.

A common word placed in an unusual setting, here an animal-word applied to sin at a doorway, can carry connotations from the culture's wider vocabulary that a plain gloss will not show. And when a rare phrase repeats verbatim a few verses apart, as teshuqah plus mashal does here, treat the second occurrence as commentary on the first.

Lieth or crouches is the safe, literal rendering every version uses. Whether to import the Akkadian demon imagery is a judgment call resting on comparative Semitic philology rather than the Hebrew word by itself, which is exactly why mainstream translations have stayed with the neutral gloss.

versions.s: The Word was God, or the Word was a god. The difference is one missing article.

b.t: Every mainstream English version reads the Word was God. The New World Translation reads a god, and the entire argument turns on the article.

Say it three ways. **Sam is the doctor.** That picks out one doctor, the one we were talking about. **Sam is a doctor.** That makes Sam one of many. **Sam is doctor.** That is not English, and your ear rejects it. But it is perfectly good Greek, and it means neither of the first two. It means Sam has the nature of a doctor. English gives you the and a and nothing else. Greek has a third option, and it is the one John used.

Greek has a definite article and no indefinite one. In the last clause the first God has the article, ton theon, and the second does not, theos. Word order also matters: theos stands before the verb. A Greek noun in that position without an article is normally qualitative. It is telling you what the Word is, not which individual the Word is.

English has to insert something. You must write the God, a god, or God, and each of those says more than the Greek did. The Greek had a way to say what something is by nature without identifying it as a particular individual, and English does not.

When your versions split between God and a god, or between the truth and truth, look for whether the Greek noun has the article. Absence of the article in Greek is not the same as a in English. It usually means the writer is talking about character rather than identity.

Rendering it a god takes the missing article as indefinite. Rendering it God takes it as qualitative. The qualitative reading is the standard grammatical one and it also makes sense of the middle clause: the Word was with God, so the Word is not simply identical to the one he was with, and yet is what that one is.
θεός theos · G2316

versions.s: The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended. Yet David's name appears on psalms well after this point.

b.t: Every version reads the prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended, accurately translating a straightforward Hebrew sentence, but without necessarily flagging how strange the claim is once a reader notices David's name reattached to psalms later in the book, including 86, 101, 103, and many more.

Imagine a book with a note halfway through saying the author's contributions end here, and then the same author's chapters keep appearing for the rest of the book. That contradiction is a visible seam, evidence the book was assembled out of smaller pieces at different times, exactly what this verse shows about how the Psalter itself was put together.

This colophon almost certainly closes an earlier, smaller collection of Davidic psalms compiled before the Psalter reached its final, five-book form, a collection later scribes and editors incorporated into the larger work without removing this now-outdated closing note. Scholars debate whether it originally marked the end of a scroll or a specific anthology, but either way it is a visible fossil of the book's own layered compilation history, left standing even after later editors kept adding more Davidic psalms beyond it.

English readers meeting the prayers of David are ended at Psalm 72 have no reason to notice the claim is factually overtaken by dozens of later psalms in the same book still attributed to David, so the verse's real function, as a preserved trace of an earlier editorial stage, is invisible without checking the rest of the Psalter's attributions.

When an editorial statement inside a biblical book is contradicted by material appearing later in the same book, read the contradiction as evidence of the book's compilation history rather than assuming either the statement or the later material must be in error. Both can be original to their own stage of the text's growth.

Reading the colophon as simply describing Book II, Psalms 42-72, as a self-contained Davidic collection treats it as accurate for its original, smaller context. Reading it as a claim about David's total contribution to the finished Psalter runs immediately into the dozens of Davidic psalms that follow, showing the verse was never updated to match the book's later growth.

versions.s: These are the generations. A recurring formula, not a genealogy header.

b.t: Every version reads generations, or account, or history. None can mark that the identical Hebrew phrase recurs ten more times through Genesis as a structural heading.

**Chapter two.** A modern book uses headings to mark a new section. Hebrew narrative uses a repeated phrase instead, the same words every time, like a heading a reader learns to recognize on sight, then watches recur through the whole book.

Toledot, from yalad, to bear or beget, most literally means begettings, what was brought forth. The formula 'these are the toledot of X' opens eleven sections of Genesis, each one introducing what came from the person or thing just named. At 2:4 it stands over the heavens and the earth themselves, extending a genealogical formula to cosmology.

No single English word is both a genealogical term and a verbatim structural heading repeated across a book. Generations captures the family-tree sense and loses the marker function, so an English reader has no way to notice the repetition without being told.

When an unusual phrase recurs word for word, treat it as a heading, not ordinary prose. Genesis is built out of ten more of these toledot headings, and the book's own structure is invisible without seeing the word.

No translation dispute over the gloss. The issue is that any single English rendering, whether generations, account, or history, cannot also function as a recognizable repeated heading the way the one Hebrew word does across all eleven uses.

versions.s: The Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.

b.t: Every version reads our place, and some footnote temple.
**The House voted.** **Downing Street responded.** English uses places for institutions constantly, and only insiders catch every one.

Topos, place, is used in Jewish Greek as a way of referring to the temple without naming it, as at Acts 6:13-14 and 21:28. The Sanhedrin is worrying about the sanctuary and the nation, which is exactly what happened in AD 70.
English place is too general, so the specific reference is lost unless a footnote supplies it.
Common nouns used as institutional euphemisms are invisible to outsiders. When a sentence seems oddly vague, ask what it was polite not to name.
Our place is the majority rendering; our temple appears in some modern versions and in footnotes.

versions.s: Thy law. The Hebrew word is instruction, and the psalm has eight words for it.

b.t: Every version reads law for torah. Some footnote instruction or teaching. None changes the main rendering, because law is entrenched.

**Rules** and **guidance** describe the same advice from a parent, and produce two completely different feelings about the parent. One word, and you decide in advance what kind of relationship you are reading about.

Torah is from a root meaning to throw or point, and means instruction or direction. The psalm cycles eight terms through 176 verses: torah, edut, piqqudim, choq, mitzvah, mishpat, davar and imrah, roughly instruction, testimony, precepts, statute, commandment, judgment, word and saying. The variety is the point, and so is the affection.
English law means legislation and courts. Hebrew torah includes narrative, poetry and genealogy, none of which is legislation. The Septuagint chose nomos and English inherited the narrowing.
When a psalm expresses delight in something that sounds like paperwork, suspect the English noun before you suspect the psalmist.
Instruction is accurate and loses two thousand years of usage. Law is entrenched and misdirects. No major version has been willing to move, and the footnote is the compromise everyone has settled on.

entries.where: trogo is tagged 6 times, across 2 books: john 5 · matthew 1.

versions.s: Whoso eateth my flesh. The verb changes at verse 54 to a word for chewing.

b.t: Every version reads eat throughout.
**Eat** and **chew**. If a speaker switched from the first to the second halfway through an argument, you would hear it, and you would know he was pressing.

Verses 50 to 53 use phago, the ordinary verb for eating. From verse 54 onward John switches to trogo, a verb that can carry a more physical, audible sense of eating but that Matthew 24:38 uses for entirely ordinary eating and drinking, so the switch by itself is not proof of a deliberate shift to gnawing. The switch coinciding with the offence in verse 60 is the stronger argument that it is doing rhetorical work.
English has chew, but it is too physical to print in a solemn discourse, so every version smooths it to eat and the escalation vanishes.
When an audience reacts badly at a specific verse, look at what changed in the verses just before it.

Eat is universal in English versions. The verb change is noted in commentaries, and the NET Bible's own translator's notes flag it too, while cautioning that the switch may simply reflect a stylistic preference for one verb over the other rather than a deliberate escalation to gnawing.
τρώγω trogo · G5176

versions.s: Army, host. The plural in the title LORD of Hosts.

b.t: Versions read hosts, or Almighty, or heavenly armies.
**Host** now means someone who has you round for dinner. It used to mean an army, and the Bible is the last place most people meet the old sense.

Tsava is an army or an organised body. YHWH tsevaot is Yahweh of armies, which may mean Israel's armies, the heavenly host, or both. The Septuagint sometimes transliterates and sometimes renders it Almighty.
English hosts has drifted so far that the title reads as archaic decoration rather than as a military claim.
When a title is rendered by an English word that no longer carries its meaning, look up the noun. Titles are the last place language gets updated.
Hosts is the majority rendering; the NIV reads LORD Almighty.

versions.s: Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed. The verb tsachak becomes his son's name, Yitzchak, Isaac, he laughs.

b.t: Every version reads laughed here, correctly, and later reads Isaac as a bare proper name at his birth, with no way for an English reader to hear that the name is the same word as the laughter that preceded it, twice.

Imagine naming a baby **Chuckles** because both parents laughed, separately, at the news he was coming, and the joke gets repeated every time someone says his name for the rest of the story. Genesis does exactly this, in Hebrew sound, and English Isaac carries none of the joke.

Tsachak, laughed, here at Abraham's reaction, becomes the root of Yitzchak, Isaac, he laughs or he will laugh, the name eventually given to the promised son. The same pun recurs when Sarah laughs at the promise in Genesis 18:12, and again when Sarah declares after his birth, at 21:6, God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me, using the same root a third time. The child's very name is the family's skepticism, turned by the end of the story into shared joy, permanently recorded in one repeated Hebrew sound.

English Isaac is a bare transliterated name carrying no meaning at all to an English ear, so the running pun, laughter at disbelief becoming laughter at fulfillment, three separate times across three chapters, is entirely invisible unless a reader is told the name means laughs.

When a child's name is given following a strong emotional reaction, check whether the name and the reaction share a root. Genesis does this repeatedly, and the pun is often built to recur more than once, turning a single naming moment into a thread running through several later chapters.

Laughed and the transliterated name Isaac are both settled; nothing here divides translators. What's worth flagging is that the pun tying them together, and its later repetitions at 18:12 and 21:6, depends entirely on hearing tsachak inside Yitzchak, something no English rendering of either word can supply on its own.
צָחַק tsachak (יִצְחָק Yitzchak, Isaac) · H6711 / H3327

versions.s: Sarah saw the son of Hagar mocking. The verb, metzachek, is built from the same root as Isaac's name.

b.t: Every version reads mocking, playing, or laughing, correctly, but no English word can carry both the ordinary sense of the verb and its pointed echo of Isaac's own name in the same breath.

Imagine a story where a rival taunts a boy named Joy by literally performing the verb **joying** at him in a hostile way, and the sentence relies on you catching that the taunt and the name are the same word. English mocking and the name Isaac share no sound at all; Hebrew's metzachek and Yitzchak do.

Metzachek is the piel, intensive form of tsachak, the same root behind Yitzchak, Isaac, and behind Sarah's laughter at 18:12 and 21:6. What exactly the verb describes here, playing, mocking, or something harsher, is debated, but the wordplay itself is not: Ishmael is doing something to, or with, Isaac's own name-word, at the very feast celebrating that name.

One sense is what English is forced to pick, mocking or playing, and once chosen it reads as an ordinary verb with no connection at all to the name Isaac. The central pun, that the boy causing trouble is verbally performing his half-brother's name at him, disappears from view entirely.

When a verb describing an action toward a named character shares that character's own root, treat the wordplay as deliberate regardless of how the verb's precise sense is otherwise resolved. The pun itself is not in dispute even where the action it describes is.

Mocking reads the scene as open hostility, justifying Sarah's demand that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away. Playing or laughing reads it more mildly, perhaps still provoking Sarah's jealousy without describing genuine cruelty. Both readings share the same underlying wordplay on Isaac's name; they differ only in how harshly the piel stem should be taken here.
מְצַחֵק metzachek (צָחַק tsachak, piel) · H6711

src: The same root at Sarah's laughter: Genesis 18:12; 21:6

versions.s: Isaac was sporting with Rebekah his wife. The same root as laughed and mocked, now meaning caressed or fondled.

b.t: Every version reads sporting, caressing, or fondling, correctly conveying that the couple's behavior reveals they are not merely brother and sister, but none can show this is the same root already used twice before for laughing and mocking.

One English root rarely stretches to cover laughing, mocking, and marital affection all at once; English would use three unrelated words. Hebrew tsachak covers all three here, the same consonants doing joyful laughter at 17:17, hostile mockery at 21:9, and, in this intensive form, spousal intimacy.

Metzachek here, the same piel form seen at 21:9 for Ishmael's mocking, describes physical affection intimate enough that Abimelech, watching from a window, immediately concludes Rebekah must be Isaac's wife rather than his sister. The verb's range, from joyful laughter to hostile mockery to marital intimacy, is unified only by its root sense of vigorous, animated activity, which context alone sorts into very different English words.

No English verb flexes enough to mean laugh, mock, and caress depending on context; each sense needs an entirely different English word, so the recurring thread tying Isaac's whole family story together through one Hebrew root goes invisible across translation.

Track a rare or repeated root across a family's story rather than treating each occurrence as an isolated translation choice. Tsachak's spread across Genesis 17 through 26 is a single thread an English reader can only see by being told to look for it.

Sporting or caressing as the sense here is not contested among translators. This note rounds out the picture of tsachak's range across the whole Isaac narrative, laughter, mockery, and marital affection, three English words for one Hebrew root.

versions.s: The elder shall serve the younger. Or: the elder, shall the younger serve. The Hebrew word order does not decide it.

b.t: Every English version reads the elder shall serve the younger, settling the ambiguity one way, the reading that fits how the rest of Jacob and Esau's story actually plays out.

English word order tells you who does what: **the dog bit the man** and **the man bit the dog** are opposites, and the order alone carries the meaning. Biblical Hebrew poetry can drop the marker that would normally clarify this, and this oracle is exactly that kind of sentence: both readings are grammatically live.

Verav ya'avod tsa'ir lacks the object marker et that would normally clarify which noun is doing the serving and which is being served, and Hebrew word order alone does not settle it here, since Job 14:19 shows the same pattern can run either direction, subject-object or object-subject. The medieval commentators Radak and Ibn Kaspi already noted the sentence could mean either the elder shall serve the younger or the elder, the younger shall serve, and the cantillation marks in the Masoretic tradition arguably lean toward the second, less common reading.

English syntax fixes word order to meaning in a way Hebrew poetry does not always require, so a translation must pick one direction, and once picked, an English reader is left with no clue that the original oracle was genuinely, grammatically ambiguous rather than plainly stated.

When a Hebrew clause lacks the object marker et and involves two nouns that could each plausibly be subject or object, do not assume word order alone settles the sentence the way it would in English. Check whether ancient commentators already flagged the same ambiguity.

The elder shall serve the younger fits the narrative's outcome, Esau's household eventually subordinate to Jacob's line, and is the reading every translation adopts. The reverse reading, argued from the missing object marker and supported by some cantillation evidence, would make the oracle a genuinely opaque riddle rather than a plain prediction, which some rabbinic tradition takes to be the point.

versions.s: The valley of the shadow of death. Possibly not shadow plus death at all, but one word meaning deepest darkness.

b.t: Every version reads shadow of death or, in some more recent translations, deep darkness or deepest darkness, reflecting this exact disagreement about the word's actual construction.

English shadow of death is a vivid compound, two ideas fused into one image. Some scholars argue the underlying Hebrew was never really shadow plus death at all, but a single intensive word built the way English forms darkness from dark, later reread by tradition as though it contained the separate word for death.

Tsalmavet looks like a compound of tsel, shadow, and mavet, death, but some scholars argue it derives instead from a root meaning simply intense darkness, with the ending later re-pointed by the Masoretic vocalizers to resemble mavet, death, once that reading had become traditional. An Akkadian cognate meaning darkness supports the intensive-darkness reading, while the traditional compound reading, shadow of death, has by far the longer devotional history and remains linguistically defensible either way.

English shadow of death carries centuries of funeral and mortality associations built on the compound reading; deep darkness or deepest darkness conveys a more general, if still ominous, sense of danger and gloom without necessarily invoking death specifically, a real difference in what the verse is picturing.

When a compound-looking Hebrew word could also be analyzed as a single intensive form, check whether the compound reading might be a later, traditional reinterpretation of an originally simpler word. Both readings can be linguistically defensible at once, as they are here.

Shadow of death keeps the traditional, deeply loved reading and its long devotional history, the one nearly every reader already carries. Deepest darkness follows the intensive-noun analysis and a plausible Akkadian cognate, and either way the psalm is naming the darkest, most dangerous place a shepherd would need to walk a flock through.

versions.s: Mount Zion, on the sides of the north. Yarkete tsaphon, likely naming Mount Zaphon, the Canaanite storm-god Baal's own mythological mountain.

b.t: Every version reads sides of the north, the far north, or recesses of the north, a geographically vague-sounding English phrase that gives no indication the underlying words are very likely naming a specific, religiously loaded mountain in Canaanite mythology.

Imagine a hymn claiming your own local hill is really Mount Olympus, the true home of the gods, aimed directly at a rival religion's most sacred site. That is roughly the claim this verse may be making, borrowing the name of Baal's own mountain and applying it to Zion instead.

Tsaphon, north, is also the proper name of Mount Zaphon, modern Jebel Aqraa on the Syrian coast, the Canaanite storm-god Baal's mythological dwelling and the meeting place of the gods in Ugaritic texts. Applying yarkete tsaphon, the recesses of Zaphon, to Mount Zion is very likely a deliberate polemical claim, asserting that Zion, not Baal's mountain, is the true cosmic mountain and true seat of divine assembly, the same move already seen in Psalm 29's likely adaptation of Baal-hymn material.

English sides of the north reads as a plain, if slightly odd, compass direction; it gives no hint that the underlying Hebrew is very likely naming a specific rival deity's mythological mountain, turning an apparently geographic description into a pointed theological claim.

When Genesis or the Psalms use vocabulary that doubles as a proper name from neighboring mythology, tsaphon here, tehom at Genesis 1:2, tannin at Genesis 1:21, read the passage as likely making a deliberate comparative or polemical claim rather than simply describing geography or nature.

Sides of the north, read as plain geography, misses the likely mythological reference entirely. Reading tsaphon as naming Mount Zaphon directly casts the verse as a pointed claim that Zion has displaced Baal's own mountain as the true dwelling place of God, a reading well supported by the wider comparative evidence and by Psalm 29's similar move.

versions.s: Righteousness, and just as often justice. English splits them.

b.t: Versions read righteousness in narrative and justice in the Prophets, from one word.
**That was not right.** **That was not just.** Two complaints in English, one in Hebrew.
Tsedaqah is rightness inside relationship, including obligations to people with no legal claim on you. In the Prophets it is regularly paired with mishpat and concerns the treatment of the poor.
English divided the word along a line Hebrew never drew, and the two halves now sound like different subjects.
Read a passage substituting the other English word. It is the quickest way to hear what the division costs.
Righteousness is the majority rendering in the Torah and justice in the Prophets.

versions.s: One of his ribs. The same word names the side chambers of the tabernacle everywhere else.

b.t: Every major English version reads rib. A minority of scholars and some newer study notes argue for side, but no widely used translation has switched, so rib remains the reading every reader meets.

**He built a shelf from one board.** **He built an addition onto the side of the house.** One is a single piece; the other is a whole section. The word behind rib usually means the second kind of thing: a side, a flank, a chamber.

Tsela occurs forty-one times in thirty-two verses. Only these two, Genesis 2:21-22, are ever rendered rib. Everywhere else, the tabernacle's side chambers and boards at Exodus 25:12 and 26:26-27, the temple's side chambers at 1 Kings 6:5, 34, even a hillside at 2 Samuel 16:13, it is side, side chamber, board, or slope. The single-bone reading rests on these two verses alone.

English rib names one specific bone; English side is broad enough to mean a flank, a section, or a chamber. The Hebrew word defaults to the broad sense everywhere except here, and only the traditional reading of this one story keeps the narrow sense attached to it in English.

When a word is translated one way in exactly two verses and a completely different way everywhere else, check what is driving the outlier. Sometimes it is genuine context; sometimes it is a translation tradition nobody has revisited.

Rib keeps four hundred years of English reading and the picture most people carry of the story. Side follows the word's overwhelming usage elsewhere and reads the operation as taking a whole section, not extracting a single bone. The Hebrew consonants support either; the tradition has settled on the rarer sense.

versions.s: In our image, after our likeness. Two nouns, and probably one idea.

b.t: Every version reads image and likeness. Some older theological systems treat them as separate endowments, one lost at the fall and one retained.

**Safe and sound.** **Null and void.** English pairs words that mean nearly the same thing all the time, and nobody hunts for the difference between null and void. Hebrew does the same, and readers hunt anyway.

Tselem is a physical representation, including a carved idol. Demut is a resemblance. In Genesis 5:3 the two are swapped around with the prepositions reversed, which is what makes a technical distinction hard to sustain. Read together they say one thing: humanity is God's representative image on the ground, the way a king's statue in a province represented the king.
English can print both nouns but cannot signal that the pair is a single idea, so readers naturally assume two.
When two near-synonyms appear together, check whether the writer ever swaps or reverses them. If he does, the distinction you are looking for is probably not there.
There is no translation dispute. There is a long tradition of distinguishing the two, and the internal evidence at Genesis 5:3 is the argument against it.
